doi:10.1002/cam4.72302.abstract: Active surveillance is recommended as the first-line management for desmoid-type fibromatosis (DF); however, data on DF of the head and neck (H&N) and shoulder regions are limited. We examined patients with DF located in the H&N and shoulder regions, comparing baseline characteristics and event-free survival (EFS). A subgroup analysis was performed among patients initially managed with active surveillance. H&N accounted for 4% of all DF cases, and shoulder accounted for 5%. Pain (62% vs. 53% and 33%, respectively; p = 0.01) and functional impairment (29% vs. 0% and 6%, respectively; p = 0.002) were significantly more frequent in shoulder DF compared with H&N DF and DF at other sites. Regardless of initial management, the 3-year EFS rates for H&N and shoulder were similar to those for other locations (p = 0.74). Among patients initially managed with active surveillance, the 3-year EFS rates for H&N and shoulder were similar to that for DF at other locations (p = 0.63). Pain and functional impairment differed significantly by location; however, the outcomes of both H&N and shoulder DF did not differ significantly from those of DF at other locations. This investigation was registered under the clinical trial registration number NCT02867033.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72309.abstract: Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) frequently disseminates within the lipid-rich peritoneal cavity, where tumor progression is accompanied by metabolic adaptations involving lipid utilization and mitochondrial function. Although these metabolic alterations are increasingly recognized as important features of EOC progression and peritoneal metastasis, the molecular factors linking mitochondrial-lipid metabolic remodeling with aggressive tumor behavior remain incompletely characterized. We therefore integrated mitochondrial- and lipid metabolism-related transcriptomic analyses to identify candidate regulators and further investigated the clinical and biological features associated with CDS2. Seven key genes associated with mitochondrial and lipid metabolism were identified in EOC through comprehensive bioinformatic analyses and were used to construct the MALRS prognostic model. Further integration of FIGO stage, histologic grade, and MALRS scores yielded a nomogram whose calibration plots showed good agreement between predicted and observed 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival probabilities. Subsequent screening of these candidate genes in chemotherapy-resistant datasets identified CDP-diacylglycerol synthase 2 (CDS2) as the most consistently upregulated candidate gene. Clinical validation confirmed that CDS2 was significantly overexpressed in tumor tissues and was associated with advanced disease stage, and survival analysis showed that higher CDS2 expression was associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) in stage III/IV patients. Functional characterization demonstrated that CDS2 overexpression promoted both lipid droplet accumulation and migratory capacity in ovarian cancer cells. Pathway analysis identified significant enrichment of PI3K/AKT signaling, and experimental validation confirmed CDS2-mediated hyperactivation of PI3K/AKT phosphorylation. Computational immune-deconvolution analyses further identified exploratory associations between CDS2 expression, estimated T-cell abundance, and immune-checkpoint transcripts. CDS2 is a lipid metabolism-associated candidate biomarker linked to aggressive clinicopathological features in EOC. Our findings associate CDS2 with disease progression, PI3K/AKT-related signaling, and immune-related transcriptomic features, supporting its further evaluation as a candidate prognostic marker.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72312.abstract: ABSTRACT Background This cross‐sectional study aimed to identify symptom profiles and their associated factors in Chinese patients with multiple myeloma, thereby providing an evidence‐based foundation for developing targeted symptom management strategies. Methods Patients with multiple myeloma were recruited via convenience sampling from the hematology departments of three tertiary general hospitals in Zhejiang Province, China, between January and March 2024. Data collection utilized a sociodemographic and clinical characteristics questionnaire and the Chinese version of the M.D. Anderson Symptom Inventory‐Multiple Myeloma Module (MDASI‐MM) scale. The research conducted a latent profile analysis of symptom characteristics, followed by univariate analysis and multivariable multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with profile membership. Results The study included 265 Chinese patients with multiple myeloma. Latent profile analysis identified three distinct symptom profiles: “Low Symptom Burden with Walking Distress” (46.7%), “Moderate Physical Symptoms with Daily Life Interference” (37.9%), and “High Global Symptom Burden” (15.4%). Multinomial logistic regression analysis demonstrated that age, marital status, combination chemotherapy status, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status were significantly associated with symptom profile membership ( p < 0.05). Specifically, patients of advanced age and those with higher ECOG scores were more likely to belong to the higher burden profiles, while patients receiving combination chemotherapy and those who were unmarried/divorced/widowed were more likely to belong to the low‐burden profile. Conclusions Patients with multiple myeloma exhibit heterogeneous symptom experiences, classifiable into three latent profiles. Our findings suggest that age, marital status, combination chemotherapy, and ECOG performance status may help identify patients at risk for higher symptom burden. Future longitudinal research is needed to evaluate whether profile‐based interventions reduce symptom burden and improve quality of life.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72313.abstract: Skin cancer is the most common type of cancer worldwide, categorized into melanoma and non-melanoma types. While genetics play a crucial role in the development of skin cancer, recent developments in metabolomics have revealed that circulating metabolites influence genetic risk profiles. In this study, we utilized a bidirectional two-sample Mendelian Randomization (MR) approach, analyzing metabolite datasets from the Canadian Longitudinal Study of Aging (CLSA) and skin cancer datasets from the UK Biobank. Replication analyses were performed with the 10th round of the FinnGen project. Instrumental variables (IVs) were chosen according to established MR criteria and assessed through the Wald ratio, IVW, MR-Egger, and weighted median methods. Various sensitivity analyses were conducted utilizing Cochrane's Q, Egger's intercept, MR-PRESSO, and leave-one-out (LOO) techniques. After meticulous analysis, we identified causal relationships between circulating metabolites and skin cancer risks. Specifically, levels of 1,2-dilinoleoyl-GPE (18:2/18:2), 1-palmitoyl-2-linoleoyl-gpc (16:0/18:2), 1-stearoyl-2-arachidonoyl-gpc (18:0/20:4), 1-stearoyl-2-linoleoyl-gpc (18:0/18:2), and Docosapentaenoate n3 DPA, the ratio of Arachidonate (20:4n6) to oleate to vaccenate (18:1), and Oleoyl-linoleoyl-glycerol (18:1 to 18:2) to linoleoyl-arachidonoyl-glycerol (18:2 to 20:4) were linked to non-melanoma skin cancer, whereas levels of trans-urocanate were causally linked to melanoma of skin, and S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) showed a putative association. It should be noted that docosapentaenoate n3 DPA and SAH were each supported by a single SNP and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive causal evidence. Reverse MR analysis highlighted robust causal relationships with 18 and 10 metabolites and non-melanoma skin cancer and melanoma of skin, respectively. These findings enhance our understanding of skin cancer etiology and risk factors, providing genetic evidence for hypothesis-generating associations that support the development of targeted therapies and aid in the identification of potential biomarkers.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72320.abstract: Observational studies report an overall-survival advantage for postoperative radioactive iodine (RAI) in lymph node-positive papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), but such estimates are vulnerable to confounding by indication and to bias from immortal time and the healthy-user effect. We assessed the credibility of this apparent benefit rather than RAI efficacy itself. Using SEER (2010-2015), we assembled a cohort of N1b, M0, totally thyroidectomized PTC patients and applied a 3-month landmark analysis (sensitivity analyses at 1 and 6 months) with stabilized inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting. We estimated RAI effects on overall survival, cancer-specific survival, and relative survival, and on a negative-control outcome-non-thyroid-cancer death-that RAI cannot plausibly affect. Residual confounding was quantified with E-values. Among 4275 patients, RAI showed an apparent survival benefit in direction across all three endpoints. However, the negative-control outcome likewise showed an apparent benefit (IPTW hazard ratio 0.713, 95% CI 0.562-0.906), indicating residual confounding not removed by weighting. The apparent survival benefits therefore could not be distinguished from unmeasured confounding. In registry data lacking key confounders, a negative control identifies the apparent RAI survival benefit as a candidate artifact of unmeasured confounding. The findings neither support nor refute RAI efficacy.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72322.abstract: Cancer cells within a single pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are most often heterogeneous in their expression of the basal or classical transcriptional program. Predominance of the basal subtype has been associated with poorer patient outcomes and increased resistance to chemotherapy. Based on this, we predicted that basal subtype would be enriched in tumors previously treated with chemotherapy, and in metastases derived from primary PDAC tumors with a mixed basal/classical population. To create matched classical and basal cell lines, we stably transduced two classical PDAC cell lines (AsPC1 and HPAFII) with the basal program transcriptional driver ∆Np63α or an mCherry control and assessed their growth, metastasis, and response to chemotherapy both in vitro and in vivo. Forced expression of ∆Np63α successfully converted both cell lines to basal transcriptomic subtype, yet the basal program failed to drive increased cell growth or chemoresistance in culture and did not affect tumor growth of AsPC1 in the murine pancreas. In mice orthotopically engrafted with ∆Np63α-expressing cells, no statistically significant increase in spontaneous pulmonary metastases was observed for AsPC1 or HPAFII, however, pulmonary metastases were enriched for ∆Np63 expression as compared to established primary tumors, including expression of endogenous ∆Np63 in the mCherry control. Increased resistance to irinotecan chemotherapy was observed in ∆Np63α + HPAFII, yet treatment selected for ∆Np63-negative cells in both HPAFII and ASPC1. In summary, our data show that PDAC metastases are enriched for basal subtype, but chemotherapy treatment does not preferentially select for basal-type cells.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72334.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is among the leading causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Previous treatment regimens often have limited efficacy due to drug resistance and recurrence. Metabolic reprogramming participates in the initiation and progression of NSCLC, with prominent changes in lipid metabolism. Mutations in specific driver genes directly remodel lipid metabolic reprogramming in NSCLC by rewiring lipid synthesis, uptake, and catabolism, which confers cancer cells with enhanced proliferative and metastatic capacity. On this basis, targeted lipid metabolism reprogramming has become a promising new direction for the treatment of NSCLC. In this review, we examined the alterations in lipid metabolism in NSCLC, explored the mechanisms by which driver gene mutations change lipid metabolism in NSCLC, and provided possible therapeutic strategies targeting key lipid metabolism pathways at the current stage, aiming to offer a theoretical basis and prospects for the development of novel therapies targeting specific gene mutation subtypes of NSCLC.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72335.abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed the treatment landscape for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet resistance mediated by the tumor microenvironment (TME) limits its efficacy in most patients. This review aims to synthesize the current understanding of the TME as an integrated network driving immunotherapy resistance and to evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at overcoming it. We conducted a comprehensive narrative review of key literature in the field, sourced from PubMed and major conference proceedings. The focus was on mechanistic studies elucidating immunosuppressive cell circuits, metabolic reprogramming, epigenetic regulation, spatial heterogeneity, and microbiome interactions within the lung cancer TME. Preclinical and clinical evidence for TME-targeted combination therapies and biomarker development was also critically analyzed. The TME orchestrates resistance through highly interconnected axes: (1) cellular circuits including myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), regulatory T cells (Tregs), and M2-polarized tumor-associated macrophages (M2-TAMs), (2) metabolic barriers (lactate acidosis, nutrient depletion), (3) epigenetic reprogramming, and (4) systemic communication via exosomes and the microbiome. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that driver mutations (e.g., EGFR, KRAS) shape distinct immune-excluded architectures. To disrupt this network, rational combination strategies-such as immune checkpoint inhibitors with metabolic modulators (LDHAi), epigenetic drugs, targeted agents (METi), or microbiome interventions-show synergistic potential in early-phase trials. Furthermore, a tiered biomarker system integrating spatial, metabolic, and microbial features is proposed to guide patient stratification. Overcoming immunotherapy resistance requires a paradigm shift from single-target to network-targeted therapy. This review provides an integrated framework for understanding TME-mediated resistance and translates these insights into a roadmap for clinical translation. Future efforts must prioritize biomarker-validated, rationally designed combination therapies to improve outcomes for patients with resistant NSCLC.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72335.title: Targeting the Tumor Microenvironment Network to Overcome Immunotherapy Resistance in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: Mechanisms to Clinical Translation.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72342.abstract: Existing deep learning models for predicting biochemical recurrence (BCR) after radical prostatectomy often ignore the biological context beyond the tumor. This study aims to develop and validate a transformer-based model combining multi-regional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features and clinical data to improve BCR prediction after radical prostatectomy in prostate cancer (PCa). We enrolled 232 Pca patients from three medical centers between 2013 and 2020. Multi-parametric MRI sequences, including T2-weighted fat-suppressed and diffusion-weighted imaging, were collected before surgery. Patients from centers 1 and 2 were assigned to a discovery cohort (training: n = 146; internal validation: n = 36), and patients from center 3 (n = 50) formed an external test cohort. A transformer-based deep learning (DL) model was developed using imaging features from intratumoral, peritumoral, and periprostatic regions, combined with clinical variables. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and prognostic value was assessed via Kaplan-Meier (K-M) survival analysis. The combined three-region MRI-based model demonstrated superior predictive performance for BCR risk across all sets, with an AUC of 0.801 (0.663-0.920) on the external test set and an AUC of 0.799 (0.715-0.872) on the validation set. Notably, the integrated DL model, which combined MRI data with clinical characteristics, outperformed the MRI-based and clinical models. The three-region with clinical combined model improved AUCs from 0.801 (95% CI: 0.663-0.920) to 0.863 (95% CI: 0.697-0.975) on the external test set and from 0.799 (95% CI: 0.715-0.872) to 0.832 (95% CI: 0.746-0.904) on the validation set. K-M curve analysis revealed that the integrated model provided significantly better predictions than the MRI-based and clinical models (p < 0.0001). By combining intratumoral, peritumoral, and periprostatic regions from multi-parametric MRI with clinical data, the transformer-based DL model provides a multimodal approach for predicting BCR in PCa patients.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72348.abstract: Colorectal cancer remains a major global health burden, and although population-based screening is beneficial, current programs have notable limitations. Risk-stratified screening has been proposed, yet existing prediction models vary in performance and in the inclusion of predictors. Data-adaptive modeling (machine learning) may strengthen risk prediction but depends on high-quality input data. Expert consensus methods offer a structured way to identify clinically meaningful variables for future tools. To establish expert consensus on the selection of relevant variables and refinement of self-reported questionnaire items for next-generation colorectal cancer risk-prediction tools. A modified Delphi study was conducted with seventeen internationally recognized experts. The process consisted of anonymized, email-based rounds aimed at refining a questionnaire for colorectal cancer risk prediction. Across three iterative rounds, experts rated item relevance, proposed revisions, and identified missing domains while reviewing group-level summaries of ratings and comments. Items not meeting predefined thresholds were removed, and validated lifestyle-related items were incorporated. Consensus was defined as 15 of 17 experts rating an item within a similar three-point range. All seventeen experts completed all rounds. The final I-CRC-RISK Questionnaire comprises 23 items across seven categories: Demography, Health Status, Family Health History, Dietary Patterns, Physical Activity, Smoking, and Alcohol Consumption. Expert consensus was reached for 19 items. The I-CRC-RISK Questionnaire provides an expert-informed set of self-reported variables to support future risk prediction efforts. It offers a structured basis for further validation and psychometric testing before prospective data collection may be undertaken. This foundational work could enhance the predictive performance of both traditional and machine-learning approaches by improving the consistency and relevance of input data.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72352.abstract: Cysteine-rich angiogenic inducer 61 (CYR61), a matricellular protein, has been implicated in gastric cancer aggressiveness through activation of integrin-mediated NF-κB signaling; however, effective pharmacological strategies targeting this axis remain limited. Cyclopiane, a bioactive small-molecule compound, has shown potential anti-tumor activity, but its role and underlying mechanisms in gastric cancer have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to investigate whether Cyclopiane suppresses gastric cancer invasion and angiogenesis via modulation of the CYR61/αvβ3 integrin/NF-κB signaling pathway. Human gastric cancer cell lines AGS and MKN45 were treated with increasing concentrations of Cyclopiane. Cell viability was assessed using MTT assays, while invasive capacity was evaluated using Matrigel-coated Transwell assays. TUNEL staining was used to assess changes in apoptosis in tumor cells. The expression of invasion-, angiogenesis-, and inflammation-related proteins was analyzed by Western blot (WB) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Transcriptomic profiling of AGS cells treated with Cyclopiane versus vehicle control was performed to identify differentially expressed genes and enriched signaling pathways. CYR61 overexpression was achieved via adeno-associated virus (AAV-CYR61), with its pathway involvement further validated using integrin αvβ3 antagonists. The conventional anticancer drug 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) was employed to compare Cyclopiane's therapeutic effects. In vivo experiments utilized a nude mouse xenograft model to evaluate changes in tumor growth, angiogenesis, and inflammatory responses following Cyclopiane treatment. We found that Cyclopiane significantly reduced cell viability, invasive capacity of AGS and MKN45 cells and promoted apoptosis in a dose-dependent manner, with its high-dose effects comparable to those of 5-FU. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that Cyclopiane downregulated CCN1/CYR61, ITGAV and ITGB3 expression, with pathway enrichment identifying integrin signaling, ECM-receptor interaction, focal adhesion and NF-κB pathways as the top modulated terms. In vivo experiments demonstrated that Cyclopiane significantly inhibited tumor growth and progression. Both in vivo and in vitro studies showed Cyclopiane significantly downregulated vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2), and MMP-9 expression while inhibiting integrin αvβ3 expression and NF-κB activation, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation levels of p65 and IκBα. Overexpression of CYR61 partially reversed the inhibition of invasion, angiogenic factor production, and NF-κB signaling mediated by Cyclopiane. The αvβ3/αvβ5 integrin antagonist Cilengitide also exhibited tumor-suppressive effects, and the co-treatment of Cyclopiane with Cilengitide achieved the strongest tumor-suppressive effect. These findings suggest that modulation of the CYR61/integrin/NF-κB signaling axis contributes, at least in part, to the anti-invasive and anti-angiogenic effects of Cyclopiane in preclinical gastric cancer models. Further studies are required to establish its molecular target specificity, safety, selectivity, and translational potential.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72356.abstract: Patients with chemotherapy- and androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI)-naïve metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) have generally shown worse overall survival (OS) with abiraterone versus enzalutamide in claims database studies. Given limitations of claims data, analysis using detailed electronic health records (EHRs) is needed to confirm this finding. This EHR-based analysis (2014-2023) of the Flatiron Health database included patients with chemotherapy- and ARPI-naïve mCRPC who initiated first-line ARPI (abiraterone or enzalutamide). OS, treatment duration, and time to subsequent therapy were assessed. A subgroup analysis evaluated patients who received first-line ARPI only with no subsequent treatments. Kaplan-Meier method and Cox proportional hazards models evaluated time-to-event outcomes. Stabilized inverse probability treatment weighting (sIPTW) adjusted for baseline differences. Among 2731 patients, 1316 received first-line abiraterone and 1415 enzalutamide (median follow-up: 21.8 and 23.2 months, respectively). sIPTW-adjusted median OS (24.6 vs. 25.8 months; hazard ratio [HR] 1.13; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.03-1.23), treatment duration (7.9 vs. 9.5 months; HR 1.21; 95% CI, 1.11-1.31), and time to subsequent therapy (14.7 vs. 17.9 months; HR 1.20; 95% CI, 1.08-1.32) were shorter with abiraterone versus enzalutamide. Among the 40% with no subsequent treatment (n = 1102), sIPTW-adjusted median OS (14.0 vs. 17.7 months; HR 1.32; 95% CI, 1.14-1.53), and treatment duration (7.5 vs. 10.6 months; HR 1.30; 95% CI, 1.12-1.50) were also shorter with abiraterone versus enzalutamide. Using more detailed data abstraction, these results confirm prior claims-based analyses showing that despite early use of subsequent therapy, first-line abiraterone is associated with shorter OS versus enzalutamide in ARPI- and chemotherapy-naïve mCRPC. Clinical Trial ID: NCT05968599.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72357.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are increasingly used in patients with gastrointestinal cancer (GIC). However, ICI-associated adverse event (AE) profiles in GIC remain poorly characterized, and whether AE incidence is associated with clinical outcomes is unclear. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through February 2025. Primary outcomes included treatment-related AEs (TRAEs) and immune-related AEs (irAEs) (any grade/Grade 3+). Single-arm random-effects meta-analysis pooled AE incidences; risk ratios (RRs) compared toxicity across ICI regimens. Digitized Kaplan-Meier curves reconstructed survival data for pooled analysis and Cox models. Weighted Spearman's tests assessed correlations between AE incidences and median overall survival (OS)/progression-free survival (PFS). Forty RCTs enrolling 10,233 patients investigated ICI monotherapy, dual-ICI therapy, and ICI combination regimens. Pooled any-grade TRAE incidences were 68.0% (monotherapy, 95% CI: 60%-76%, I2 = 97.4%, p < 0.001), 87.0% (dual therapy, 95% CI: 73%-100%, I2 = 98.0%, p < 0.001), and 90.0% (combination therapy, 95% CI: 83%-96%, I2 = 94.6%, p < 0.001). IrAE incidences reached 24.0% (monotherapy, 95% CI: 18%-29%, I2 = 67.2%, p < 0.05) and 37.0% (combination therapy, 95% CI: 25%-49%, I2 = 98.8%, p < 0.001). Relative to monotherapy, dual-ICI therapy elevated any-grade (RR = 1.28, 95% CI: 1.05-1.55) and grade ≥ 3 TRAEs (RR = 2.71, 95% CI: 1.84-3.99); ICI combination therapy increased any-grade (RR = 1.32, 95% CI: 1.15-1.51) and grade ≥ 3 TRAEs (RR = 2.98, 95% CI: 2.30-3.87). Any-grade TRAEs moderately correlated with median OS (R = 0.46, p < 0.001) and PFS (R = 0.50, p < 0.001). Any-grade irAEs strongly correlated with median OS (R = 0.90, p < 0.001) and moderately with PFS (R = 0.57, p < 0.001). While AE incidence is high among GIC patients receiving ICIs, most events are low-grade. Dual-ICI and ICI-based combination therapies carry higher TRAE and irAE risks than monotherapy. At the trial level, higher non-severe irAE incidence correlated with favorable survival outcomes; this exploratory ecological association does not apply to individual patients. This study was registered on International Platform of Registered Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Protocols (INPLASY202230144).

doi:10.1002/cam4.72360.abstract: The objective of this study was to verify that a strategy involving prophylactic exposure of the inferior parathyroid glands and preservation of their venous blood flow-achieved through early identification and protection of their venous drainage-can enhance the success rate of maintaining glandular perfusion and effectively reduce the incidence of postoperative hypoparathyroidism. This study included 600 patients who underwent total thyroidectomy with concomitant bilateral central neck dissection between November 2019 and December 2025. Patients were divided into two groups based on the surgical technique: Group A (n = 244), in which a prophylactic approach was used to protect the venous drainage of the inferior parathyroid glands, and Group B (n = 356), which underwent conventional in situ preservation of the inferior parathyroid glands. A comparison was made between the two groups regarding both the percentage of inferior parathyroid glands successfully preserved in situ and the incidence of postoperative hypoparathyroidism. The rate of visualization of inferior parathyroid glands with optimal blood supply was significantly higher in Group A than in Group B (p < 0.001). Postoperation parathyroid hormone level in Group A was significantly higher than that in Group B (25.15 [19.39, 33.58] pg/mL vs. 19.12 [9.82, 28.85] pg/mL, p < 0.001). In Group A, the rates of postoperative hypoparathyroidism-encompassing both transient and permanent forms-were significantly lower than those in Group B (p < 0.001). The method of prophylactically exposing the inferior parathyroid glands and preserving their venous system-termed prophylactic preservation of inferior parathyroid venous blood flow-is achieved through early identification and protection of their venous drainage. This approach enhances the success rate of maintaining glandular blood supply and effectively reduces the incidence of postoperative hypoparathyroidism.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72365.abstract: Systemic metastasis remains the leading cause of mortality in patients with advanced prostate cancer, particularly in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), for which effective systemic therapeutic options are limited. Gene therapy is a potential strategy for achieving selective tumor targeting and systemic disease control in metastatic settings. This study aimed to establish a systemic metastasis animal model for CRPC and evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of JC polyomavirus (JCPyV) virus-like particle (VLPs)-based gene therapy against metastatic disease. A near-infrared fluorescent protein (iRFP)-expressing CRPC cell line was used to establish a systemic metastasis model by tail-vein injection in mice. The therapeutic efficacy of JCPyV VLPs carrying a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) promoter-driven suicide gene (PSAtk-VLPs), administered in combination with ganciclovir (GCV), was evaluated longitudinally by fluorescence molecular tomography (FMT), with enzalutamide/leuprorelin acetate (ENZ/LEU) included as a clinical treatment comparator. CRPC metastases in the lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, and bones were detected by FMT in real time. Control mice exhibited exponential CRPC growth, whereas ENZ/LEU treatment delayed CRPC progression. PSAtk-VLPs/GCV significantly inhibited the growth of metastatic CRPC. However, no significant differences in survival were observed among the MOCK, ENZ/LEU, and PSAtk-VLP/GCV groups (log-rank test, p = 0.7351). These findings support that JCPyV-derived virus-like particles constitute a promising therapeutic approach for metastatic CRPC, enabling systemic delivery of suicide gene therapy with selective inhibition of tumor growth and translational relevance.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72366.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Platinum‐doublet concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) for locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC) is frequently complicated by severe neutropenia. This Phase II trial investigated whether combining active bone marrow‐sparing (ABMS) radiotherapy with prophylactic pegylated recombinant human granulocyte colony‐stimulating factor (PEG‐rhG‐CSF) could reduce the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia below a prespecified historical benchmark of 30%. Methods Patients with FIGO 2018 stage IIA2–IVA LACC received SPECT‐guided ABMS radiotherapy (45 Gy external beam plus 30 Gy brachytherapy) concurrent with paclitaxel/carboplatin every 21 days for 4 cycles followed by prophylactic PEG‐rhG‐CSF. Using Simon's two‐stage design ( α = 0.05, β = 0.20), we tested whether grade ≥ 3 neutropenia could be reduced from a historical benchmark of 30% to ≤ 15%. The primary endpoint was grade ≥ 3 neutropenia incidence; secondary endpoints included other cytopenias, treatment completion, and survival outcomes. Results Fifty‐four patients were enrolled. Grade ≥ 3 neutropenia occurred in 13.0% (7/54; 95% CI: 5.4%–24.9%), meeting the prespecified success criterion (one‐sided exact binomial test, p = 0.003 versus the 30% benchmark). Other grade ≥ 3 toxicities included leukopenia (18.5%), anemia (3.7%), thrombocytopenia (5.6%), and febrile neutropenia (1.9%). Overall, 85.2% of patients completed all 4 planned chemotherapy cycles, and all completed radiotherapy within 8 weeks (median overall treatment time: 50 days). At a median follow‐up of 40 months, the 3‐year progression‐free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) rates were 88.8% and 88.9%, respectively (6 events each); the study was not powered for survival efficacy. Conclusions The combination of ABMS radiotherapy and prophylactic PEG‐rhG‐CSF was associated with a grade ≥ 3 neutropenia rate of 13.0% and a chemotherapy completion rate of 85.2% during platinum‐doublet CCRT for LACC. Because the single‐arm design and reliance on historical controls preclude causal inference, these findings are hypothesis‐generating and primarily establish the operational feasibility of this dual hematoprotection approach. Formal evaluation of safety and efficacy requires the ongoing randomized trial (ChiCTR2400087321). Trial Registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2100046911. Registered May 30, 2021

doi:10.1002/cam4.72367.abstract: Young breast cancer (YBC), defined as diagnosis at or before the age of 40 years, is characterized by an aggressive phenotype and poor prognosis. The tumor microenvironment (TME), comprising immune and stromal cells, plays a critical role in tumor initiation and progression and is closely associated with clinical outcomes. However, alterations in cell states and the organization of multicellular ecosystems within the YBC microenvironment remain poorly understood. We analyzed 7379 bulk transcriptome samples and spatial transcriptomic data from eight samples using EcoTyper and complementary spatial analyses. The abundance of CD4+ T cells (S07), fibroblasts (S05), monocytes/macrophages (S09), and epithelial cells (S05) was significantly lower in young than in older patients with breast cancer. CD4+ T cells (S07), fibroblasts (S05), and monocytes/macrophages (S09) formed a spatially organized multicellular ecosystem with putative interactions involving CDH1-PTPRF/ERBB3. Lower ecosystem abundance was associated with poorer prognosis, including among patients who did not achieve a pathological complete response after neoadjuvant therapy. These findings identify a distinct multicellular ecosystem within the YBC microenvironment, providing insights into the microenvironmental features associated with disease progression.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72368.abstract: We previously developed multiple machine-learning and regression-based risk prediction models using retrospective electronic health records (EHR) to estimate near-term risk of pancreatic cancer (PC). This pilot study aimed to assess the feasibility of an early detection strategy combining initial EHR-based risk prediction with downstream imaging and blood-based testing. This prospective study included adults aged 50-84 years with an estimated ≥ 1% 18-month risk of PC, identified between January 2021 and March 2023 using four previously validated models. Patients with a history or active suspicion of PC were excluded. Participants completed cross-sectional imaging and CA19-9 Labs at baseline and again at 18 months. Outcomes included enrollment rates, test completion rate, and burden of incidental findings. Of 1251 eligible patients, 102 (8.2%) enrolled (median age 69 years [IQR 62-75]; 58% women; 48% Hispanic, 34% White, 11% Black, and 7% Asian). At baseline, 89 (87%) completed imaging and 98 (96%) completed CA19-9. At 18 months, 79% completed both imaging and CA19-9. Ten (10%) participants underwent additional clinical evaluations triggered by imaging findings. Evaluations included an endoscopic ultrasound, renal imaging, and FibroScan. CA19-9 results were normal in most participants, though 18% had elevated levels at baseline. Real-time EHR-based ML algorithms can be combined with blood- and imaging-based surveillance for early detection of PC with acceptable burden of incidental findings. However, improved patient engagement is a key aspect that will need to be addressed in order to successfully scale an AI-guided strategy for early detection.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72369.abstract: Spatial heterogeneity in the colorectal cancer (CRC) tumor microenvironment (TME) is closely related to stromal organization and may influence treatment-related features. In this study, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic data from CRC tissues to examine cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF)-dominant spatial domains. GPC1 and CHPF were enriched in stromal regions and showed higher expression in CRC tissues than in normal tissues. In the analyzed cohorts, higher GPC1 and CHPF expression was associated with advanced clinicopathological features and poorer survival outcomes in univariate analyses. Single-cell analyses showed that GPC1 and CHPF were mainly expressed in fibroblasts and were enriched in an ADAM12-associated fibroblast subset with myofibroblast-like features, extracellular matrix-related genes, and hypoxia/glycolysis-related signatures. Cell-cell communication analysis suggested that this fibroblast subset was linked to higher inferred WNT signaling. Drug-response and immunotherapy-related analyses further showed that GPC1 and CHPF expression was associated with transcriptomic patterns related to treatment response. In mucinous adenocarcinoma (MA), the ADAM12-associated fibroblast program showed stronger inferred MIF-related signaling and was associated with macrophage M2-like features. Spatial mapping and multiplex immunofluorescence supported partial colocalization of GPC1, CHPF, and ADAM12 in CAF-rich stromal regions. In CAFs, GPC1 or CHPF knockdown reduced ADAM12, CAF activation markers, and WNT/MIF-related proteins, while ADAM12 knockdown weakened macrophage M2-like marker expression in a co-culture model. These findings suggest that GPC1 and CHPF mark an ADAM12-associated CAF program linked to stromal remodeling and immune-related features in CRC, especially in MA, but further studies are needed to define its functional role.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72371.abstract: Healthcare services and data ecosystems remain fragmented, inequitable and misaligned with patient, clinician and public health needs. Three pathways to patient-centred Artificial Intelligence (AI) have emerged to address this: data collaboration, Whole System Approaches and digital inclusion. Each has advanced the field. However, none delivers the continuous, participatory and outcome-grounded learning that equitable AI demands. The populations whose data drives AI learning must also be the populations who benefit from it. This principle has not been structurally embedded in any existing pathway. This narrative review defines a framework for operationalising Adaptive Machine Learning (AML) as a fourth, integrative pathway to patient-centred AI. AML is defined as continuous learning from real-world individual-level data to generate personalised, population-level insights returning direct benefit to the communities who produce them. A narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar (2018-2025) was conducted across five thematic domains: AI and machine learning in healthcare; real-world data and evidence; patient-centred care and digital health; data governance and AI regulation; and adaptive clinical trial design. Search terms covered healthcare AI applications and adaptive, continuously learning systems, emphasising prediction-oriented rather than static diagnostic approaches. Eligibility was determined through iterative thematic analysis. Eight systemic barriers to patient-centred AI are identified and the three existing pathways critically examined for limitations in addressing bias, validation and equitable implementation. AML is proposed as the mechanism that closes this gap, connecting systems medicine, personalised medicine and precision medicine through continuous, outcome-based learning, identifying three original conceptual contributions as enablers: Integrative Data Governance (IDG), Adaptive Clinical Trial (ACT) designs and Evidence Sandbox Facilities (ESFs). Progress requires globally standardised Healthcare Data Recycling frameworks, adaptive evaluation methodologies and ESFs enabling multi-stakeholder validation. Future research should address federated AML validation, collective consent mechanisms and alignment of regulatory frameworks with international AI governance standards.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72376.abstract: Prostate cancer (PCa) mortality disparities are partly driven by unequal access to care. Transportation barriers may limit access to definitive treatment. We studied how driving travel time affects receipt of definitive PCa treatment. We conducted a cohort study of men with non-metastatic PCa (2000-2015; follow-up through 2018) across the metropolitan area cancer registries of seven US states. Travel time was estimated using Google Maps isochrones representing driving time thresholds to reach the hospital appended to geomasked residential addresses. Outcomes were "no treatment," "radical surgery," or "radiotherapy". Covariate-adjusted multinomial logistic regression with interaction terms assessed modification by sociodemographic factors. The study included 132,939 men, of whom 37.0% received no treatment, 41.0% underwent surgery, and 22.0% received radiotherapy. Longer driving time (≥ 90 min vs. < 30 min) was associated with higher radical prostatectomy (aOR: 1.08, 95% CI: 1.03, 1.12), but lower radiotherapy (0.72, 95% CI: 0.69-0.76). Subgroup analyses revealed higher surgery associated with longer driving times among those in nSES Q1 (aOR: 1.33, 95% CI: 1.21-1.45) vs. Q5 (aOR: 0.94, 95% CI: 0.86-1.04), those in low (aOR: 1.16, 95% CI: 1.09-1.24) vs. high (aOR: 1.03, 95% CI: 0.98-1.09) population density areas, and those with regional (aOR: 1.30, 95% CI: 1.14-1.48) vs. localized (aOR: 1.05, 95% CI: 1.00-1.09) disease. Longer driving time was mostly associated with lower odds of radiotherapy across sociodemographic subgroups. Higher travel time was associated with lower radiotherapy receipt, but higher surgery use in deprived and rural patients, warranting further investigation.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72377.abstract: Electronic patient-reported outcome (ePRO) systems support symptom monitoring after chemotherapy; however, their integration into structured nurse-led oncology workflows remains limited. In this study, we aimed to develop and evaluate the short-term feasibility and usability of a nurse-led ePRO system for home-based postchemotherapy symptom monitoring and structured nursing triage for cancer patients. This single-arm feasibility study was conducted at a cancer center in Taiwan between April and September 2024 among adult patients requiring home-based symptom monitoring after hospital-based chemotherapy care. The nurse-led digital system was designed to support weekly self-reporting of 12 chemotherapy-related symptoms using the Chemotherapy Toxicity Self-Assessment Questionnaire. The system incorporated rule-based triage categorization using green, orange, and red risk levels and predefined nurse response protocols. Feasibility outcomes included report adherence, triage alert management, and system performance. Usability was evaluated using the System Usability Scale. Forty-two patients submitted 306 symptom reports during the 8-week monitoring period, corresponding to an overall adherence rate of 91.1%. Among all reports, 16.3% generated orange alerts requiring nurse follow-up and 6.5% generated red alerts requiring urgent review. Fatigue, pain, and hand-foot syndrome were the most frequently reported abnormal symptoms. All orange and red alerts had documented nursing review. The system met the predefined technical performance indicators during simulated load testing, and achieved a mean System Usability Scale score of 92.6 ± 6.46. This nurse-led ePRO system demonstrated favorable short-term feasibility and usability for home-based postchemotherapy symptom monitoring and structured nursing triage. These findings support the practicality of integrating structured ePRO monitoring into postchemotherapy nursing care. Further multicenter and comparative studies are warranted to evaluate long-term engagement, scalability, and clinical outcomes.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72378.abstract: This study investigated relationships between the skeletal muscle index (SMI) and the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), peripheral immune phenotypes, and serum biomarkers in advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and evaluated the prognostic significance of these parameters. A retrospective analysis of 119 advanced PDAC patients was performed. Sarcopenia was diagnosed using sex-specific SMI cut-offs from baseline L3-level computed tomography (CT) images. The TIME was characterized by multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF; n = 31), peripheral immunity by flow cytometry, and serum biomarkers by routine testing. Associations with SMI were examined using Spearman correlation; prognostic relevance was assessed using Cox proportional hazards models. Sarcopenia (56/119, 47.1%) was associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) (8.83 vs. 12.03 months, p = 0.016) and overall survival (OS) (10.20 vs. 17.33 months, p = 0.014). SMI correlated most strongly with stromal CD8+ T cells (ρ = 0.52), stromal total T cells (ρ = 0.52), and stromal M2 macrophages (ρ = 0.50) in the TIME; with circulating Th2-like cells (ρ = -0.58) and CD4+ memory T cells (ρ = 0.45) peripherally; and with hemoglobin (ρ = 0.32) among serum markers. In multivariable Cox regression, stromal CD4+ Treg percentage independently predicted OS (hazard ratio [HR] = 7.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.60-36.22, p = 0.011), stromal CD56dim natural killer (NK)-cell density predicted PFS (HR = 1.015, 95% CI 1.001-1.028, p = 0.031), and the lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR) predicted both PFS (HR = 0.86, p = 0.023) and OS (HR = 0.83, p = 0.009). No peripheral lymphocyte subset reached prognostic significance. SMI is broadly associated with local and systemic immune phenotypes in advanced PDAC. Stromal CD4+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), CD56dim NK cells, and LMR carry independent prognostic information and may complement body-composition assessment.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72380.abstract: New-onset diabetes (NOD) potentially associated with pancreatic cancer (PC) requires further investigation to assess its potential as a tool for PC screening. In this longitudinal nationwide register study, which includes 14,712 PC patients and 18 years of follow-up time (2000-2018), we aimed to assess the prevalence of diabetes by using a large national registry. Survival was analyzed according to diabetes status and duration (long-term diabetes, i.e., DM diagnosed > 3 years prior to PC, NOD, i.e., DM diagnosed 0-3 years prior to PC, or DM diagnosed after PC diagnosis) and treatment status (curative intent vs. palliative) using multivariable Cox regression analysis. Overall, 18% of PC patients had diabetes. The median time interval between DM and PC diagnoses was 4.8 months. In the multivariable Cox regression analysis, only DM diagnosed after PC was associated with worse survival, both in the palliative intent treatment group (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.03-1.23, p = 0.011) and in the curative intent treatment group (HR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14-1.81, p = 0.002). Among patients diagnosed with diabetes prior to PC, neither long-term nor NOD significantly affected survival. Most of the diabetic PC-patients have been diagnosed with DM within a close proximity of cancer diagnosis. The progression from diabetes to clinically detectable cancer seems to be rapid-less than 6 months. Given the aggressive nature of PC and the fact that NOD can be an early sign, screening may need to begin at the time of diabetes diagnosis. The fact that a DM diagnosis made after a PC diagnosis is associated with worse survival may suggest that pancreatic tumors that cause hyperglycemia are particularly aggressive.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72385.abstract: Household size and composition may be associated with health-related quality of life (HRQoL), yet these associations remain poorly characterized among cancer survivors. We examined how household adult composition and presence of children were associated with HRQoL among U.S. cancer survivors. Adult (aged ≥ 18 years) cancer survivors were included from the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) 2017-2024. Household composition was defined by number of adults (1, 2, or ≥ 3) and presence of children (none vs. ≥ 1). Outcomes included poor physical health (PPH), poor mental health (PMH; each defined as ≥ 14 days/month), and fair/poor general health. Multivariable Poisson regression was used to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) with 95% confidence intervals. Among 138,360 cancer survivors, 45.2% (n = 62,605) resided in single-adult households, 47.1% (n = 65,132) in two-adult households, and 7.7% (n = 10,623) in households with ≥ 3 adults; children were present in 5.1% (n = 7063) of households. After adjustment, two-adult household residence was associated with lower prevalence of poor physical health (adjusted prevalence ratio [aPR] 0.93, 95% CI 0.87-0.99), poor mental health (aPR 0.90, 95% CI 0.82-0.98), and fair/poor general health (aPR 0.92, 95% CI 0.88-0.97; all p ≤ 0.019) compared with single-adult households. Residence with ≥ 3 adults and child presence was not associated with any examined HRQoL outcome after adjustment. Exploratory stratified analyses identified associations within several sociodemographic subgroups. Two-adult household residence was consistently associated with better HRQoL. Single-adult household status may represent a simple social risk marker to inform survivorship assessment.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72386.abstract: TP53 mutations are linked to poor prognoses in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL), indicating that specific p53 target genes may contribute to drug resistance. Although the impact of specific genetic alterations on drug sensitivity has been reported in BCP-ALL, the effects of TP53 mutations on sensitivity to individual agents remain poorly defined in the clinical setting because of the use of combination chemotherapy regimens. In the present study, we addressed this issue through two complementary analyses using a large panel of BCP-ALL cell lines. Initially, 30 cell lines harboring TP53 mutations demonstrated significantly greater resistance to daunorubicin (DNR), mafosfamide (MAF; an active analog of cyclophosphamide), 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), and prednisolone compared to 46 cell lines without mutations. Second, 11 CRISPR/Cas9-mediated TP53-knockout sublines derived from cell lines with wild-type TP53 recapitulated resistance to DNR, MAF, and 6-MP, as well as to vincristine (VCR) and cytarabine (Ara-C). Consistent with these findings, re-evaluation of genome-wide CRISPR screening datasets revealed significant enrichment of TP53 gRNAs in cells treated with DNR, MAF, 6-MP, Ara-C, and VCR. Furthermore, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of p53 target genes in the two cell line models, along with re-evaluation of genome-wide CRISPR screening datasets, identified BAX, BBC3, and FDXR as key p53 target genes associated with multidrug resistance. These results highlight the potential value of targeting these p53 downstream pathways to improve outcomes in TP53-mutated BCP-ALL cases.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72388.abstract: Radiotherapy efficacy is constrained by tumor radioresistance, which arises in part from the interplay between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and epigenetic regulation. This review systematically synthesizes the bidirectional "epigenetics-ROS interactive network" that governs tumor radiosensitivity. We propose that this network operates through three core principles: stress adaptation (acute ROS triggers transient epigenetic adjustments for redox recovery), malignant reinforcement (chronic ROS drives stable epigenetic reprogramming toward therapy resistance), and contextual determinacy (cellular outcomes depend on integrated ROS-epigenetic patterns rather than individual signals). Mechanistically, we delineate four regulatory layers including DNA methylation, histone modifications, non-coding RNAs, and chromatin remodeling, through which the epigenetic machinery controls ROS homeostasis, and conversely, how radiation-induced ROS reshape the epigenetic landscape via oxidative modification of epigenetic enzymes and signaling pathways. These bidirectional interactions form feedback circuits that ultimately dictate whether cells undergo repair, senescence, apoptosis, or ferroptosis. Based on this mechanism, we propose a context-dependent decision framework that matches four distinct combination strategies (ROS amplification, epigenetic priming, hypoxia relief, and multi-pathway cell death induction) with four tumor subtypes defined by their oxidative and epigenetic profiles. We also identify five translational roadblocks including toxicity, delivery inefficiency, manufacturing scalability, regulatory uncertainty, and preclinical-clinical discordance. Resolving these barriers is essential for unlocking the therapeutic potential of this regulatory axis. Strategically targeting the epigenetics-ROS network offers a transformative paradigm for overcoming radioresistance and personalizing cancer radiotherapy.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72393.abstract: The global burden of liver cancer has been increasing over recent decades, whereas the incidence in Switzerland has remained relatively stable. This study assessed long-term trends in incidence, mortality, and 1- and 5-year relative survival of primary liver cancer in the Swiss canton of Zurich from 1980 to 2022, stratified by sex and age. This population-based retrospective analysis included all primary liver cancer cases diagnosed in the canton of Zurich and registered in the Cancer Registry of the cantons of Zurich, Zug, Schaffhausen and Schwyz between 1980 and 2022. Mortality data were obtained from the Federal Statistical Office. Cases were classified according to ICD-O-3 topography and morphology and, from 2003 onward, TNM stage. Age-standardised incidence and mortality rates were calculated using the 1976 European standard population. Temporal trends were analysed using Joinpoint regression and reported as Average Annual Percentage Changes (AAPCs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Relative survival was estimated using the Ederer II method and standardised according to international standards. Among 3866 incident cases, 71.3% were hepatocellular carcinomas and 70.7% occurred in men. Overall age-standardised incidence remained stable in both men (AAPC -0.1%, 95% CI -0.6 to 0.3%) and women (-0.2%, -0.9% to 0.4%). However, incidence increased significantly among individuals younger than 65 years, particularly in women (AAPC 2.3%, 1.3%-3.3%) and men (1.2%, 0.6%-1.9%). Mortality remained broadly stable in men and increased modestly in women. One- and five-year relative survival improved substantially, from 13.8% and 3.5% in 1980-1999 to 53.9% and 25.8% in 2016-2022, respectively. Improvements were greater in men than women. These findings reflect major advances in liver cancer diagnosis and treatment over the past four decades. Continued prevention, targeted screening of high-risk groups, and epidemiological monitoring remain important.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72395.abstract: Relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (R/R B-ALL) patients exhibit heterogeneous responses to CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. However, current studies primarily focus on the CAR-T cells or the leukemia blasts, and the patient's intrinsic molecular characteristics before treatment remain poorly understood. Fifteen R/R B-ALL patients enrolled in a phase II, single-arm clinical trial (NCT04684147) were stratified at a three-month landmark into 8 good responders and 7 poor responders. Clinical characteristics, genetic alterations and pre-treatment bone marrow transcriptomics were compared between groups, and an exploratory gene-expression score was derived. Differential expression and enrichment analyses identified a myeloid-like signature and upregulation of myeloid-related genes in poor responders. Seven myeloid-related genes were examined in independent patient cohorts, in B-ALL cell lines and at single-cell resolution in one patient; three were expressed by the leukemic cells themselves and four predominantly by monocytes and macrophages. A separate, variance-derived seven-gene least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) score separated response groups in the discovery cohort (apparent area under the curve, AUC 1.00), with bias-corrected and external estimates of approximately 0.57-0.59 (external cohort AUC 0.592, 95% confidence interval 0.356-0.828). Pre-treatment transcriptomic profiling revealed a myeloid-like signature in R/R B-ALL patients with poor CD19 CAR-T response, warranting further investigation as a candidate correlate of treatment outcome.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72400.abstract: Most patients with hypopharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (HPSCC) achieve partial response (PR) after induction chemotherapy. However, optimal post-induction management remains controversial. We compared survival outcomes of post-induction strategies for PR-HPSCC, with emphasis on advanced post-induction tumor stage (ycT) using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW-ATO) to mitigate confounding by indication. This retrospective study included 149 patients with PR-HPSCC after induction chemotherapy who subsequently received surgery-based therapy (SBT; n = 71) or definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT; n = 78). IPTW-ATO was used to address covariate imbalances between groups. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were evaluated using weighted Kaplan-Meier analyses and IPTW-ATO-adjusted Cox proportional hazards models. Sensitivity analyses compared findings across unadjusted, multivariable, and propensity score-weighted models. In unadjusted analyses, OS and PFS did not differ significantly between groups. After IPTW-ATO adjustment, SBT was associated with improved OS and PFS versus CRT. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested a potential differential treatment effect across ycT strata; however, interaction tests were not statistically significant, and no significant survival difference was observed in patients with early ycT disease. In multivariable analyses, thyroid invasion was independently associated with worse OS, whereas anti-PD-1 therapy was associated with improved OS. Outcomes among patients with PR-HPSCC are heterogeneous. After adjustment for covariate imbalances, SBT was associated with favorable survival. These findings suggest that PR should not be treated as a uniform entity and that post-induction ycT classification may help stratify patients for future prospective evaluation.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72402.abstract: Tissue biomarkers may improve risk stratification in locally advanced cervical cancer before definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT). We evaluated pretreatment expression of chromobox 4 (CBX4), NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4), specificity protein 1 (SP1), and copper transporter 1 (CTR1) in relation to CCRT response and overall survival. In this retrospective 1:1 matched case-control study, pretreatment biopsies from 40 patients with locally advanced cervical squamous cell carcinoma (20 CCRT-resistant, 20 CCRT-sensitive) were quantified by AI-assisted digital pathology using H-scores. A parsimonious CBX4 + NOX4 logistic model was evaluated by apparent ROC, leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation, and bootstrap optimism correction. Overall survival analyses were exploratory. CBX4 and NOX4 expression was lower in CCRT-resistant tumors (median H-score: CBX4, 40.47 vs. 79.62; NOX4, 7.00 vs. 53.93; both p < 0.001), whereas SP1 and CTR1 did not differ. Apparent AUCs were 0.840 for CBX4 and 0.843 for NOX4. The two-marker model had an apparent AUC of 0.903, LOOCV AUC 0.845, repeated 5-fold CV AUC 0.854 ± 0.022, and bootstrap-corrected AUC 0.883. High CBX4 and NOX4 expression was associated with better 5-year overall survival; in joint Cox models, hazard ratios per 1-SD increase were 0.31 (95% CI 0.13-0.74) for CBX4 and 0.48 (0.26-0.90) for NOX4. No histochemically detectable copper deposits were observed. Lower pretreatment CBX4 and NOX4 expression was associated with a CCRT-resistant phenotype and poorer overall survival in this small, response-enriched cohort. Internal resampling suggested discrimination, but same-dataset marker selection may introduce residual optimism and does not establish generalizability. Independent validation in a consecutively recruited cohort is required before clinical application. No mechanisms involving DNA repair, ROS, or chemoradiotherapy sensitivity were established.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72408.abstract: Chemoimmunotherapy (CIT) had long been used to treat chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) until 2014 when the first novel agent, ibrutinib, was approved in the United States. Numerous novel therapies have since become available. Nevertheless, as novel therapies have largely replaced CIT in CLL/SLL, its impact on survival has yet to be examined on the population level. In this study, we used the SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results) database to compare survival in patients with CLL/SLL before and after the approval of the first novel therapy. We included 9913 patients who started treatment within 2 years of CLL/SLL diagnosis. In the multivariable analyses, the overall survival improved significantly (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.86, 95% confidence interval: 0.81, 0.92), and death from CLL/SLL and other cancer (subdistribution-HR: 0.69 and 0.77) also decreased significantly. Nevertheless, CLL/SLL remains the main cause of death during the novel agent era.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72410.abstract: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) frequently occur during combination immune checkpoint inhibition. However, their prognostic impact may vary according to organ involvement and severity. In this study, we exploratorily evaluated whether severe non-endocrine irAEs represent a temporally distinct and prognostically unfavorable clinical phenotype in patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) treated with ipilimumab plus nivolumab. We analyzed 63 patients with mRCC treated with ipilimumab plus nivolumab who were followed for at least 5 years. Patients were categorized into non-irAE, non-severe + severe endocrine irAE, and severe non-endocrine irAE groups. Overall survival (OS) was assessed. Multistate modeling was used to evaluate the transitions between treatment, irAE occurrence, and death. Landmark analyses were performed at 8 and 12 weeks to address immortal time bias. The severe non-endocrine irAE group was associated with inferior OS. The multistate analysis revealed a potentially increased risk of direct transition from ipilimumab plus nivolumab to death in the severe non-endocrine irAE group. A significantly higher proportion of patients in the severe non-endocrine irAE group experienced irAEs within 30 days. No significant association was observed in the 8- and 12-week landmark analyses. In this exploratory retrospective study, severe non-endocrine irAEs showed an association with early onset and potentially unfavorable clinical outcomes in patients with mRCC receiving ipilimumab plus nivolumab. Given the limited sample size, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and require confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70852.abstract: Thoracic radiotherapy can cause delayed cardiac fibrosis, but the immune mechanisms linking radiation injury to fibroblast activation remain unclear. We investigated whether CCR2+ monocytes contribute to radiation-induced cardiac fibrosis and whether AXL regulates their fibroblast-activating activity. C57BL/6 mice received 20 Gy whole-thorax irradiation, and remodelling was assessed from IR_D0 to IR_D60. Bulk RNA sequencing was integrated with single-cell datasets and CIBERSORTx deconvolution, lineage tracing, and tissue staining. CCR2+ monocyte function was examined by CCR2 neutralisation, and circulating CCR2+Ly6Cʰi monocytes were quantified by flow cytometry. AXL was investigated using inducible myeloid Axl deletion and bemcentinib (R428). MAPK signalling was assessed by transcriptomic analysis and immunoblotting of sorted CCR2+Ly6Cʰi monocytes. Conditioned medium from sorted monocytes after Axl deletion, AXL inhibition with R428, or MEK1/2 inhibition with U0126 was applied to cardiac fibroblasts. Cardiac fibrosis was established by IR_D30, while leukocyte infiltration and apoptotic signals remained above baseline. Transcriptomic analyses and lineage tracing showed increased cardiac accumulation of CCR2+ monocytes. CCR2 neutralisation reduced circulating CCR2+Ly6Cʰi monocytes and attenuated interstitial collagen deposition and fibrotic marker expression. Axl was enriched in the CCR2+ monocyte compartment. Myeloid Axl deletion and R428 reduced cardiac fibrosis. Axl deletion suppressed MAPK-related transcriptional programs, whereas genetic or pharmacological AXL targeting reduced MEK and ERK phosphorylation in sorted monocytes. Conditioned medium from IR_D30 monocytes induced COL1A1 and α-SMA expression in fibroblasts, and this effect was reduced by Axl deletion, R428, or U0126 treatment of donor monocytes. AXL signalling contributes to the fibroblast-activating paracrine activity of cardiac CCR2+ monocytes after irradiation, at least in part through MEK/ERK signalling. Radiation exposure induces cardiac fibrosis through immunestromal interactions. CCR2+ monocytes promote fibroblast activation during radiation-induced cardiac fibrosis. AXL regulates monocyte-mediated fibroblast activation through MEK/ERK signaling. Targeting the AXL-MEK/ERK pathway may provide a potential strategy for preventing radiation-induced cardiac fibrosis.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70854.abstract: Allergic rhinitis (AR) remains a global health challenge. However, the transcriptional and epigenetic features associated with seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR) and perennial allergic rhinitis (PAR) relative to non-allergic rhinitis (NAR) remain poorly characterised at single-cell resolution. We performed integrated single-cell transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of nasal mucosal tissues from 22 patients, including NAR (n = 8), SAR (n = 6), and PAR (n = 8), to characterise transcriptional and epigenetic patterns associated with immune cell heterogeneity. We identified eight major immune cell types and 29 immune cell subsets across the nasal mucosa. Comparisons with NAR revealed distinct transcriptional and epigenetic features in SAR and PAR across both myeloid and T-cell compartments. In Macro_CCL3 cells, SAR showed enrichment of inflammation-associated programs, whereas PAR showed greater enrichment of antigen-presentation-related features. CD4_Tcm cells exhibited subtype-associated epigenetic differences, with IL-1β/IL-17-related features enriched in SAR and eosinophil- and Th2-associated programs enriched in PAR. CD8_Trm cells in both AR groups showed cytotoxicity-related features, including increased accessibility near GZMB and PRF1, while distinct inferred regulatory patterns were observed across the two AR groups. In addition, T-cell co-expression modules identified by hdWGCNA showed distinct associations with NAR, SAR, and PAR. sLDSC analysis revealed significant enrichment of pollinosis-associated heritability in CD8 T-cell open chromatin regions. Our study characterises distinct immune regulatory features associated with SAR and PAR relative to NAR across innate and adaptive immune compartments, providing a multi-omic framework for characterising AR heterogeneity and identifying subtype-associated molecular features for further investigation.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70856.abstract: Early identification of vulnerable carotid plaques is crucial for stroke prevention, but the upstream metabolic processes linked to endothelial transition and immune recruitment remain poorly defined. We characterised lactate metabolism in ACKR1+ endothelial cells (ECs) in human carotid plaques and derived a machine-learning signature for discriminating plaque vulnerability. Internal and external (GSE253903) single-cell datasets were integrated to identify endothelial subpopulations, and bulk transcriptomic (GSE163154) and in-house proteomic data were used to assess metabolism-immune correlations. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression selected core features for a logistic model, which was locked and applied to three independent cohorts: GSE43292 (Stary stage ≥ IV vs. I-II), GSE28829 (early vs. advanced lesions) and GSE100927 (normal vs. atherosclerotic arteries). Key molecules were validated in situ by immunohistochemistry (IHC) and spatial transcriptomics in independent plaques (five stable, five unstable). An ACKR1+ EC subpopulation linked to neovascularisation showed hyperactive glycolysis and enhanced lactate metabolism. Computational inference linked lactate accumulation to HIF-1α stability, CXCL12 release and CD8+ T-cell infiltration via the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis, and the monocarboxylate transporters SLC16A3 and SLC16A4 emerged as quantitative readouts of this 'lactate-immune' state. In unstable plaques, IHC confirmed higher atypical chemokine receptor 1 (ACKR1; geometric mean ratio [GMR] = 6.82), CD8+ T-cell density (GMR = 4.63), SLC16A3 (GMR = 4.74) and HIF-1α (GMR = 4.02; all q < .05), with lactylation elevated in the lipid core. A four-feature model (ACKR1, SLC16A3, SLC16A4, CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity score) performed well in training and retained discrimination in the progression-stratified cohorts, while in GSE100927 it showed high disease-identification performance across three arterial beds. Lactate metabolic reprogramming under hypoxia is associated with ACKR1+ EC-related CD8+ T-cell recruitment and plaque instability. This chain is an association-based hypothesis requiring functional confirmation. The signature discriminates robustly at both the vulnerability-stratification and disease-identification levels, providing a quantifiable framework for molecular classification of atherosclerotic plaques.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70857.abstract: Mitochondrial transplantation is built on a simple idea: failing cells might be rescued by healthy mitochondria. The approach has entered early clinical testing, and encapsulation and cell-type targeting have improved uptake in selected systems. Better delivery, however, does not explain the therapy. Internalised donor mitochondria encounter an established network, quality-control machinery and sensors for mitochondrial material. Donor material may remain in the endolysosomal system or reach the cytosol. Cytosolic fates include network integration, clearance and a candidate functional contribution without fusion. Intracellular processing may also generate bioactive cargo. These fates imply different mechanisms and evidence requirements. This Review examines how recipient cells shape the contribution of internalised mitochondria, while recognising extracellular routes to benefit. We distinguish direct transplantation evidence from mechanistic support drawn from endogenous mitochondrial biology and natural intercellular transfer. The required donor fate and duration depend on the therapeutic task. Transient rescue may rely on short-term donor function or productive processing in specific models; sustained support may depend on continued donor function, recipient adaptation or redosing. Durable mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) correction requires donor-mtDNA retention and replication. Linking these tasks to product design, safety assessment and clinical endpoints shifts the question from how many mitochondria enter cells to what they accomplish after arrival. Recipient-cell handling shapes what transplanted mitochondria do after uptake. Uptake, structural integration and donor mitochondrial DNA retention require distinct evidence. Transient rescue, sustained support and durable mitochondrial DNA correction impose different requirements. Therapeutic goals should guide donor selection, product testing and clinical endpoints.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70858.abstract: Spatiotemporal transcriptomics (STT) integrates spatially resolved gene expression with temporal information derived from staged samples, paired treatment specimens, or computational inference, providing a framework for reconstructing tissue-level dynamics. In the tumour microenvironment (TME), STT extends static molecular and cellular maps by revealing how cellular neighbourhoods and functional niches are reorganised during tumour evolution. This review examines how STT characterises TME remodelling during malignant transformation, invasion, metastasis, ageing, and treatment response. We discuss strategies for resolving temporal dynamics, including stage-stratified sampling, paired or serial specimens, pseudotime and trajectory inference, and complementary intravital imaging. We further consider how spatiotemporal analyses can connect changes in cellular states, spatial organisation, and intercellular interactions with clinically relevant tumour phenotypes. By linking the spatial organisation of the TME with stage- and treatment-associated molecular changes, STT may improve the prioritisation of candidate targets, treatment stratification, and the development of precision oncology strategies.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70861.abstract: Recent studies have established that the nervous system is not merely a bystander in tumour progression but can actively remodel the tumour microenvironment through the neuro-tumour axis, thereby promoting tumour invasion, metastasis and survival. Semaphorin 3C (SEMA3C) has been reported to regulate tumour migration, angiogenesis and immune suppression, highlighting its potential role in tumour progression. Although the neuro-tumour axis has been identified in multiple cancer types, its role and underlying mechanisms in gastric cancer peritoneal metastasis (GCPM) remain unclear. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) of GCPM tissues to profile tumour cell heterogeneity and identify tumour cell populations associated with neural-related signalling. Candidate tumour-microenvironmental interactions were further investigated using patient-derived organoids and co-culture models, and the identified signalling axis was validated using corresponding in vivo models. SnRNA-seq identified a distinct subpopulation of poorly differentiated tumour cells with pronounced stem-like properties and high SEMA3C expression. This subpopulation was associated with neural-related features and interacted with tumour-associated endothelial cells, thereby contributing to remodelling of the metastatic microenvironment. Furthermore, these cells enhanced tumour-endothelial communication by activating the fibroblast growth factor receptor-associated signalling pathway. The transcription factor early B-cell factor 2 (EBF2) regulates the expression of FGF7 within this subpopulation, thereby strengthening FGF7-FGFR2 signalling and promoting tumour progression. Functional validation further demonstrated that SEMA3C depletion impaired organoid growth and tumour-endothelial interactions, whereas disruption of the SEMA3C-EBF2-FGF7-FGFR2 signalling axis attenuated tumour growth and peritoneal tumour burden in vivo. Additional experimental validation supported the potential involvement of neural-related signalling in the SEMA3C-associated tumour cell state. Our findings identify a SEMA3C+ tumour cell subpopulation associated with neural-related signalling and suggest that SEMA3C promotes tumour-endothelial interactions through the EBF2-FGF7-FGFR2 signalling axis, providing a potential mechanistic link between neural regulation and microenvironmental remodelling in peritoneal metastasis of gastric cancer.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70863.abstract: Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a pivotal lipid-sensing receptor that governs the functional plasticity and metabolic fitness of mononuclear phagocytes, including microglia, osteoclasts, dendritic cells and tissue-resident macrophages. While originally identified as a genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), TREM2 functions as a context-dependent immunometabolic checkpoint rather than a uniform phenotypic driver, exerting divergent biological outputs dictated by distinct tissue microenvironments and ligand repertoires. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of TREM2 immunobiology, detailing how ligand engagement-including cell-surface phospholipids and apolipoprotein E (ApoE)-activates the DAP12/DAP10-SYK-PI3K-mTOR signalling axis. This coordinated intracellular cascade instructively drives myeloid adaptation towards metabolically competent disease-associated microglia (DAM) and lipid-associated macrophage (LAM) states, sustaining bioenergetics and debris clearance under pathological stress. Across neurodegenerative proteinopathies and acute cerebral ischemia, TREM2 signalling is predominantly neuroprotective by promoting aggregate compaction and mitigating secondary excitotoxicity, although chronic dysregulated activation may drive stage-dependent neuroinflammation. In peripheral inflammatory pathologies such as rheumatoid arthritis and sepsis, TREM2 fine-tunes macrophage efferocytosis and systemic metabolic thresholds. In oncology, TREM2 displays a complex, microenvironment-dependent divergence: in central nervous system malignancies such as glioblastoma (GBM), TREM2 exerts controversial, stage-dependent effects, spanning microglial tumour containment in early stages versus pro-tumoural myelin recycling and immunosuppression by monocyte-derived macrophages in post-treatment recurrence; conversely, in peripheral solid tumours, monocyte-derived TREM2+ tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) predominantly orchestrate an immunosuppressive, nutrient-deprived niche that impairs cytotoxic T-cell function. Furthermore, we synthesise emerging paradigms along the bidirectional microbiome-gut-brain-tumour axis, elucidating how commensal and intra-tumoural microbial cues dynamically calibrate myeloid signalling tone and therapeutic susceptibility. We address translation bottlenecks-including blood-brain barrier (BBB) shuttles, human trial scarcity and soluble TREM2 (sTREM2) biomarker harmonisation-outlining a biomarker-guided, context-tailored precision therapeutic framework for targeting the TREM2 axis.
