doi:10.1002/jso.70415.abstract: Hepatic adenomas (HAs) are rare benign liver tumors traditionally associated with young women, yet contemporary epidemiologic trends reveal increasing recognition among men. Historically, universal resection in males has been recommended because of a nearly tenfold increased risk of malignant transformation as reported by Farges et al. in a single-institution surgical series; however, advances in molecular profiling and imaging have challenged this paradigm. β-catenin-activated and inflammatory subtypes account for most cases in men, often associated with anabolic steroid exposure, obesity, or metabolic syndrome. β-catenin-activated adenomas-particularly those harboring CTNNB1 exon 3 mutations-demonstrate the strongest correlation with malignant potential. Magnetic resonance imaging with hepatobiliary contrast agents can suggest subtype but lacks perfect accuracy; biopsy offers improved diagnostic precision and enables molecular confirmation. Current ACG and EASL guidelines still endorse routine resection for all hepatic adenomas in males; however, available retrospective data suggest that malignant transformation appears to be uncommon in small (5 cm) lesions lacking exon 3 CTNNB1 mutations; however, this observation is derived from limited, predominantly retrospective data and does not exclude the possibility of malignant transformation in this subgroup. These data support selective, biopsy-guided surveillance for small, indeterminate tumors within experienced multidisciplinary centers where longitudinal follow-up is reliable. Resection remains the standard recommendation for large or β-catenin-mutated adenomas, with minimally invasive surgery demonstrating excellent outcomes. Modern management of hepatic adenomas in men should be individualized, integrating molecular subtype, size, risk factors, and patient context. A multidisciplinary and molecularly informed strategy is essential to optimize outcomes while avoiding unnecessary intervention.

doi:10.1002/jso.70415.title: Hepatic Adenomas in Men: Diagnostic Considerations and Management in the Modern Era.

doi:10.1002/jso.70419.abstract: Among patient with early-stage breast cancer, breast conservation surgery (BCS) is the most performed surgery, utilized in approximately two-thirds of patients. While 5-year overall-survival rates are strong-typically above 90%-additional re-excisions can occur in up to 25% of patients who undergo index BCS and some patients will require subsequent surgery for new breast cancer or recurrences. As such, these additional procedures can complicate patients' pathway to survivorship, negatively impact quality of life, and lead to excess healthcare costs. This retrospective cohort study used linked claims and an electronic healthcare record database to (1) characterize patients at higher risk for additional breast oncologic surgery (aBOS) following BCS, and (2) quantify the long-term financial impact of aBOS after BCS. In total, 87,190 patients with breast cancer, who had an index BCS between January 1, 2012, to March 31, 2023, were followed for up to 5-years post-operatively. Patients with and without aBOS were analyzed, comparing demographics, tumor characteristics, healthcare utilization, and per-person-per-month (PPPM) costs. Twenty-three percent (n = 20,212) of patients underwent aBOS. These patients were younger, had higher tumor grades and larger tumor sizes, and incurred greater healthcare costs compared to patients who did not undergo a secondary surgery. This study highlights significant factors influencing BCS outcomes and healthcare utilization, underscoring the need for tailored therapeutic strategies for patients with breast cancer.

doi:10.1002/jso.70419.title: Repeat Breast Cancer Surgeries After Segmental Mastectomy Meaningfully Increase Long Term Healthcare Costs.

doi:10.1002/jso.70420.abstract: Goldilocks-based breast reconstruction (GBR) offers an autologous, implant-free option for patients seeking breast mound restoration after mastectomy. It is particularly suited for patients with macromastia, ptosis, or significant comorbidities. Despite its growing adoption, limited studies have examined patient understanding and expectations. We interviewed patients who underwent GBR after mastectomy within our institution. Demographic, oncologic, and perioperative data were collected. Semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore patient understanding, decision making process and post-operative experience based on Ottawa Decision Support Framework. Nine participants were included. Mean age was 58.1 years (range: 41-71), and mean body mass index was 34.9 kg/m2 (range: 24.3-46.1). Most participants demonstrated a good understanding of the procedure and why it was offered. Common reasons for selecting this approach were a desire to avoid implants and additional surgeries. Misunderstandings regarding the amount of residual breast tissue, expected postoperative volume, and the need for post-mastectomy surveillance contributed to dissatisfaction. However, decisional regrets were rare. Motivations for choosing GBR consistently revolve around avoidance of implant placement and desire for single-stage surgery. Common misconceptions regarding the extent of oncological resection and expectations for achievable volume from GBR should be addressed pre-operatively.

doi:10.1002/jso.70422.abstract: Upper extremity soft tissue sarcomas (UE STS) present unique management challenges; existing prognostic nomograms were developed from mixed anatomic cohorts. This study develops anatomically specific machine learning (ML) models to predict UE-STS outcomes and benchmarks them against established tools. Time-to-event models for local recurrence (LR), distant metastasis (DM), and overall survival (OS) were developed in 188 patients treated at a single sarcoma center, treating death as a competing risk. Five survival algorithms were compared within a nested cross-validation framework. Discrimination was benchmarked against the Sarculator, PERSARC, and MSKCC nomograms. Five-year event rates were 24% (LR), 20% (DM), and 13% (death) over a median follow-up of 3.9 years. Best-performing models achieved competing-risks concordance indices of 0.79 (LR), 0.67 (DM), and 0.75 (OS). Parsimonious models performed comparably. Discrimination was similar to Sarculator and PERSARC and higher than the MSKCC nomogram for LR (C-index 0.90 vs. 0.68). Predicted-risk groups separated clearly on cumulative-incidence and survival curves (p < 0.001). These results demonstrate the feasibility and potential value of anatomy-specific, time-to-event risk modeling in UE STS, achieving discrimination comparable to established nomograms despite a smaller cohort. Multicenter cohorts and multidimensional data may strengthen future efforts. External validation is warranted.

doi:10.1002/jso.70423.abstract: Timely medical intervention is critical to achieve optimal outcomes in gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, yet numerous patients experience delayed or forgone (D/F) medical care. This study aimed to evaluate the national impact of D/F care on emergency surgical interventions and associated healthcare expenditures among patients with GI cancers. Adults with a self-reported history of GI cancer were identified from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, 2007-2017. Multivariable regression analyzes was performed to assess associations between D/F medical care, ED-associated GI surgery, inpatient utilization, and related healthcare expenditures after adjusting for demographic and socioeconomic variables. Among a weighted sample of 6 517 883 patients with GI cancers, 8.5% (n = 552 751) reported D/F medical care. Patients with D/F care were older (76 years [IQR: 69-82] vs. 68 years [IQR: 58-76]), more frequently male (57.3% vs. 50.6%) and frequently had family income below the poverty line (40.2% vs. 11.3%) (all p < 0.001). Furthermore, individuals reporting D/F care were more likely to have emergency department visits (44.2% vs. 27.4%), hospitalizations (64.6% vs. 34.5%) (both p < 0.05), or undergo ED-associated GI surgery (41.0% vs. 19.1%; p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, after adjusting for relevant factors, D/F care was associated with markedly greater odds of ED-associated GI surgery (OR 2.70, 95%CI 1.47-4.95) and higher annual inpatient healthcare costs (β +$31,410, 95% CI $23,592-$39,227) compared with individuals who did not report D/F care. Self-reported D/F medical care was associated with greater acute healthcare utilization, higher odds of ED-associated GI surgery, and greater healthcare expenditures. These findings highlight the importance of understanding barriers to healthcare access among adults with a history of GI cancer.

doi:10.1002/jso.70424.abstract: Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) remain underutilized in musculoskeletal oncology, with only 4.9% of tumor-focused articles incorporating them. This review synthesizes current PROM instruments-including Toronto Extremity Salvage Score, PROMIS, and emerging tools such as the Sarcoma Assessment Measure-and identifies barriers unique to this population, including psychological distress, workflow complexity, and disease heterogeneity. Future directions include flexible baseline collection, EHR-integrated dashboards, national registry linkage, wearable technology, and AI-driven processing to increase PROMs utilization.

doi:10.1002/jso.70425.abstract: Adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) following breast-conserving surgery reduces local recurrence but can introduce reconstructive morbidity. Although recent trials support the safe omission of RT in selected patients, its impact on surgical and patient-reported outcomes following oncoplastic breast-conserving surgery (OPBCS) remains poorly defined. We evaluated surgical and long-term patient-reported outcomes in patients undergoing OPBCS, stratified by receipt of RT. We retrospectively studied consecutive patients who underwent OPBCS between 2017 and 2024 for stage 0-3 breast cancer. Patients were stratified based on receipt of RT. Postoperative complications, unplanned reoperation, and revision procedures were compared between cohorts. Long-term patient-reported outcomes were assessed using the validated BREAST-Q Reconstruction Module. Multivariable regression was used to evaluate the independent association between RT status and outcomes. We identified 257 patients; 210 patients received RT (81.7%) and 47 underwent RT de-escalation (18.3%). Surgical site infection (p = 0.100), delayed wound healing (p = 0.300), and skin flap necrosis rates (p = 0.0300) were similar between cohorts. Seroma (30% vs. 13%; p = 0.006) and unplanned reoperation (21% vs. 7.1%; p = 0.006) were more frequent with RT omission. Patients who did not receive RT demonstrated significantly higher mean Satisfaction with Breasts scores compared with those who received RT (57 ± 25 vs. 23 ± 24; p = 0.001). In adjusted models, RT de-escalation was associated with a 36-point increase in Satisfaction with Breasts scores (β = 36.0; 95% CI, 18.0-54.0; p < 0.001). RT omission was independently associated with higher patient-reported satisfaction with breasts, though patients had higher seroma and reoperation rates. These data support balanced shared decision-making for RT de-escalation in appropriately selected patients.

doi:10.1002/jso.70428.abstract: Recurrence risk after hepatectomy for colorectal liver metastases (CRLMs) changes during follow-up, but whether baseline tumor burden remains prognostically relevant with increasing recurrence-free time is unclear. We evaluated the time-dependent prognostic relevance of liver metastasis number. We retrospectively analyzed 226 patients who underwent initial curative-intent hepatectomy for CRLMs between 2007 and 2022. Three-year conditional recurrence-free survival (RFS) was estimated at surgery and after 6, 12, and 24 months without recurrence. Landmark Cox models evaluated liver metastasis number (< 4 vs. ≥ 4), adjusting for RAS status, with supplementary expanded models. Three-year conditional RFS improved from 27.1% at surgery to 33.3%, 49.3%, and 76.6% after 6, 12, and 24 months without recurrence, respectively. However, subsequent RFS remained worse in patients with ≥ 4 liver metastases at the 6-month (adjusted hazard ratio [HR]: 1.83, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.14-2.94; p = 0.012) and 12-month (HR: 2.14, 95% CI: 1.08-4.27; p = 0.030) landmarks. In supplementary expanded models, the associations remained directionally similar but were attenuated. Recurrence risk improved with increasing recurrence-free time, but survivors remained heterogeneous according to baseline tumor burden. Liver metastasis number retained prognostic relevance at early postoperative landmarks.

doi:10.1002/jso.70430.abstract: Incisional hernia is a prevalent long-term complication after open abdominal surgery, with reported rates exceeding 20%-30%. Despite extensive research on abdominal wall failure, evidence regarding incisional hernia after retroperitoneal sarcoma resections is scarce. Retroperitoneal sarcoma frequently requires wide exposure, and combined incisions are often used, yet their effect on incisional hernia risk is unknown. Our aim was to determine the incisional hernia rate in these surgeries and to determine its association with incision type. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 134 patients who underwent primary RPS resection between 2004 and 2025 at a tertiary referral center. Patients were grouped according to incision type: single midline or combined incisions. Clinicopathologic variables were collected from a prospectively maintained institutional database. Incisional hernia was identified by cross-sectional imaging. Incisional hernia occurred in 33.5% of patients, with no significant difference between simple and combined incision groups (32.7% vs. 37.0%, p = 0.883). Time to hernia development was similar (log-rank p = 0.829). Tumor size was the only independent predictor of incisional hernia in a logistic regression model: larger tumors were associated with reduced hernia risk (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.47-0.98, p = 0.042). Incision type and other known risk factors were not associated with incisional hernia. Combined incisions were not associated with a higher risk of incisional hernia, indicating that the additional exposure required for complex retroperitoneal sarcoma resections does not compromise long-term abdominal wall integrity. These findings support prioritizing optimal oncologic exposure when selecting incision type, without concern for increased hernia risk.

doi:10.1002/jso.70431.abstract: Oncoplastic breast surgery integrates oncologic resection with reconstructive techniques to optimize both tumor control and aesthetic outcomes. The Modified Oncoplastic Lift and Lymphatic Excision and Reconstruction (MOLLER) technique is a reconstructive approach incorporating lymphatic preservation principles while aiming to preserve breast contour. However, perioperative outcomes remain incompletely characterized. A single-center retrospective cohort study included adult women undergoing partial mastectomy or lumpectomy for malignant or benign breast conditions with the MOLLER technique (2011-2021). Primary outcomes were immediate and delayed postoperative complications; secondary outcomes were re-excision and radiation-related complications. A total of 136 patients were included. Median follow-up was 3 years. Immediate complications were infrequent: hematoma and wound dehiscence each occurred in 3 patients (2.2%); seroma, infection, and paresthesia each in 2 (1.5%). Delayed complications were uncommon: arm lymphedema in 5 patients (3.7%); fat necrosis and breast lymphedema each in 4 (2.9%). The re-excision rate was 4.4%. Radiation-related complications were uncommon, most commonly skin discoloration (7.4%) and skin thickening (5.1%); no delayed wound healing occurred. The MOLLER technique is a safe reconstructive approach associated with low rates of postoperative complications, re-excision, and lymphedema. Its lymphatic preservation principles may be associated with reduced lymphatic morbidity. Prospective studies are warranted to validate these findings.

doi:10.1002/pan.70328.abstract: Induction of anesthesia is one of the most distressing moments for pediatric patients during their perioperative experience. They may consequently refuse induction at the last minute. Anesthesia providers are then placed in a challenging ethical dilemma: they must seek to gain the child's cooperation, force the child to undergo induction using restraint, or delay the case. In the moment, it can be difficult to parse the relevant clinical and ethical factors to determine the most appropriate course of action. The purpose of this perspective paper is to provide a clinical ethics framework to support anesthesia provider decision making during instances of last-minute pediatric refusal of anesthesia induction. Three prominent pediatric ethics concepts support this framework, including the harm principle, best interests, and emerging autonomy. This framework uses the criteria of (1) urgency of intervention, (2) decision-making ability of the patient, and (3) harms to the patient from a forced induction. Each of these criteria is discussed in depth as it relates to last-minute pediatric refusal. Case illustrations are provided to demonstrate the clinical utility of this framework in everyday practice.

doi:10.1002/pan.70329.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring during pediatric anesthesia may improve perioperative safety by optimizing anesthetic titration and reducing adverse outcomes. However, little is known about patient and caregiver perceptions regarding this technology and its implementation into routine anesthesia care. This study evaluates perceived importance, utility, and extent of reassurance provided by intra-operative EEG monitoring among pediatric patients and their parents. Secondary aims include identifying concerns surrounding general anesthesia (GA), concerns surrounding EEG monitoring, cost and willingness to pay, and sociodemographic and medical factors shaping these attitudes. We conducted an exploratory cross-sectional survey at a tertiary pediatric hospital in Singapore between July 2022 and September 2025. Respondents were parents of children aged 1-18 years and children aged 12-18 scheduled for elective procedures under general anesthesia. A 16-item anonymized questionnaire assessed perceptions of intra-operative EEG monitoring, concerns about anesthesia, and attitudes regarding the cost of EEG monitoring. Of 400 respondents (100 children, 300 parents), 83.5% rated intra-operative brain monitoring as "very" or "quite" important and 93% reported feeling more reassured by its use. Children were most concerned about intraoperative awareness and failure to awaken, whereas parents were most concerned about anesthetic side effects and dosage. Parents with higher education and whose children had prior anesthetic exposure reported greater reassurance from EEG monitoring. Cost was the leading concern regarding EEG monitoring, particularly among parents from families residing in public housing. Despite this, most parents (75%) and children (59%) expressed willingness to pay for EEG monitoring. Pediatric patients and parents viewed intra-operative EEG monitoring as important and reassuring, and expressed willingness to support its implementation despite cost concerns. These findings suggest that families are unlikely to be a major barrier to EEG adoption and highlight the need for clinician- and system-level strategies to integrate EEG monitoring into family-centered pediatric anesthesia care.

doi:10.1002/pan.70329.title: Perceptions of Intra-Operative EEG Brain Monitoring During Pediatric Anesthesia Among Children and Parents: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Survey.

doi:10.1002/pan.70330.abstract: Women anesthesiologists face unique challenges that threaten their well-being and retention. This includes high rates of imposter phenomenon, higher rates of attrition compared to male colleagues, and high rates of suicide. While group coaching is increasingly recognized as a developmental modality to foster growth in complex work environments, gaps remain in understanding how group coaching supports women who face imposter syndrome or how effective this modality is for women anesthesiologists. This study examines the impact of a pilot group coaching intervention that focused on addressing imposter syndrome in women anesthesiologists participating in the Women's Empowerment and Leadership Initiative (WELI). Fifteen women pediatric anesthesiologists, split across two groups, took part in seven monthly group coaching sessions. A post-coaching survey was then conducted in which participants were asked about their experiences before and after group coaching. Eight of the participants volunteered to participate in semi-structured interviews about their experiences. Qualitative data were coded using an inductive thematic analysis approach. The survey showed that following group coaching, participants demonstrated an increase in self-reported compassion and acceptance of others. They also reported learning more about themselves and how to amend their own behavior in helpful ways compared to pre-intervention. Two overarching themes emerged: a sense of community (fueled by psychological safety, validation, shared experience, and addressing imposter syndrome through the group coaching) and tools gained (including clearer priorities, work/life integration, and proactive social support). Results of this pilot intervention suggest group coaching programs for anesthesiologists have the potential to build resilience in the current work environment, thereby benefiting not only individuals but the anesthesiology workforce as a whole.

doi:10.1002/pan.70331.abstract: This educational review describes the historical development of pediatric congenital cardiac anesthesia and its expanding role in the care of patients with congenital heart disease (CHD). Over the past eight decades, the specialty has evolved from an era in which few congenital heart defects were surgically treatable and perioperative mortality was high to one in which survival into adulthood is expected for most children with CHD. This transformation has been driven by parallel advances in surgical techniques, cardiopulmonary bypass technology, myocardial protection, monitoring, intensive care, and anesthetic management. From the first successful patent ductus arteriosus ligation in 1938 to the development of fetal cardiac interventions and the many major technological and scientific advances of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, anesthesiologists have played a pivotal role in improving the care of patients with CHD. As survival has improved, the population of adults and elderly patients living with repaired or palliated CHD has grown, and the specialty's focus has expanded beyond reducing perioperative mortality to improving lifelong outcomes. Today, congenital cardiac anesthesiologists are integral members of multidisciplinary teams responsible for perioperative risk assessment, hemodynamic optimization, neuroprotection, coagulation management, mechanical circulatory support, and enhanced recovery. The history of the specialty highlights the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration and continued scientific progress in improving patient safety, recovery, and long-term outcomes.

doi:10.1002/pan.70332.abstract: The systemic inflammatory response syndrome to cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) affects all organ systems including the brain. Perioperative brain injury in children with congenital heart disease is often clinically silent in the acute perioperative period and may not be detected until patients are older. The plasma biomarkers neuron-specific enolase (NSE) and S100ß protein show potential for detecting neurological injury in the perioperative period. The three objectives of this study were to examine the correlation of NSE and S100ß protein levels with inflammatory cytokines, parameters of CPB, and the development of neurological injury in the intensive care unit following cardiac surgery in children. 50 children undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB had blood samples drawn at three time points: after induction of anesthesia, 30 min post-CPB, and 24 h post-CPB. Blood samples were analyzed for NSE, S100ß, and the inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-8, and IL-10. Data were collected on CPB durations and neurological injury diagnosed in the postoperative period. NSE and S100ß increased significantly following bypass and correlated with increases of IL-6, IL-8, and IL-10. There was a significant positive correlation of NSE and S100ß with duration of CPB, and of S100ß with duration of aortic cross clamp. Three patients suffered neurological insult. These patients had greater levels of NSE during the post-CPB period (p = 0.02) and S100ß at 24 h post-CPB (p = 0.02) than patients without neurological deficits. The positive correlation between NSE, S100ß, inflammatory cytokines, and neurological deficits suggests that the systemic inflammatory response to CPB may contribute to neurological injury and that NSE and S100ß may be useful tools to detect neurological injury following CPB.

doi:10.1002/path.70127.abstract: Pretreatment prediction of neoadjuvant response remains an unresolved challenge in locally advanced rectal cancer, where management is moving towards risk-adapted and response-oriented treatment strategies. Prediction remains difficult because response reflects interacting tumour-intrinsic, immune, stromal, and spatial processes that are incompletely captured by standard clinical and radiological assessment. From a technology-centred perspective, in this Review we assess how molecular, spatial, image-based, and artificial intelligence-enabled approaches are being used to study and predict response to neoadjuvant treatment from pretreatment biopsies and how readily they may be translated into clinical workflows. Genomic profiling has its clearest current clinical role in identifying hypermutated immune-responsive subgroups, whereas broader genomic, epigenomic, and immune-repertoire markers remain largely investigational. Bulk transcriptomics has generated multiple response signatures with variable reproducibility but has consistently highlighted immune activation, interferon signalling, stromal remodelling, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition as recurrent response-associated programmes; its most feasible clinical route is likely through targeted expression panels rather than open-ended transcriptome profiling. Higher-resolution approaches such as spatial transcriptomic and proteomic platforms refine these observations by localising signals to tumour, immune, and stromal compartments and capturing therapy-induced tissue reorganisation, but they are currently best positioned for deepening biological understanding and nominating rational treatment combinations for future testing. Established platforms such as digital pathology are closer to routine deployment as they build on clinically embedded workflows, although response-prediction algorithms still require robust external validation, calibration, and regulatory-grade implementation. Patient-derived models provide functional systems for testing candidate biomarkers and resistance mechanisms. Multimodal artificial intelligence may support response prediction by identifying complementary signals across data types and distilling complex signatures into parsimonious models suitable for clinical translation. Progress will depend on harmonised, longitudinal, multi-centre studies that couple biological depth with assay standardisation, model reduction, and prospective evidence that response predictors improve patient management. © 2026 The Author(s). doi:10.1002/path.70136.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) with anaplastic features is a rare and highly aggressive subtype with an extremely poor prognosis. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying anaplastic transformation remain poorly understood. To characterize the anaplastic transformation molecular landscape, we analyzed genomic alterations in 5,997 conventional PDAC and 41 anaplastic carcinoma cases from the Memorial Sloan Kettering-Integrated Mutation Profiling of Actionable Cancer Targets (MSK-IMPACT) cohort. Additionally, four PDAC samples from the Kyorin cohort with both tubular and anaplastic components were subjected to spatial transcriptomics using the Visium platform. Differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses were performed to identify key molecular drivers. Genomic analysis revealed higher KRAS (90 versus 75%), TP53 (85 versus 60%), and CDKN2A (50 versus 30%) mutation frequencies, but notably fewer SMAD4 mutations (5 versus 20%; p = 0.022), in anaplastic carcinoma than in conventional PDAC. Spatial transcriptomics identified distinct molecular signatures, with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathways significantly enriched in anaplastic regions. Levels of ELF3, an epithelial transcription factor, were consistently downregulated in all anaplastic components. Importantly, we detected a strong inverse correlation between SMAD4 and ELF3 expression in both the bulk RNA sequencing cohort and spatial transcriptomic data. Functional validation using the KC-shSmad4 mouse model demonstrated that increased Smad4 suppressed Elf3 expression and promoted mesenchymal reprogramming. Our findings suggest a novel SMAD4-ELF3 regulatory axis that may contribute to anaplastic transformation in PDAC. The retention of SMAD4 functions coupled with ELF3 downregulation may promote EMT and contribute to tumor dedifferentiation. This SMAD4-ELF3 regulatory axis may provide a framework for identifying therapeutic vulnerabilities in this aggressive PDAC variant and further highlight the utility of spatial transcriptomics for understanding tumor heterogeneity. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

doi:10.1002/path.70137.abstract: Forkhead box protein C2 (FOXC2) is frequently overexpressed in osteosarcoma (OS) and has been implicated in tumor proliferation and metastasis; however, its role in regulating the tumor immune microenvironment remains poorly understood. In this study, integrative bioinformatics analyses of the TCGA-SARC (The Cancer Genome Atlas sarcoma cohort) dataset were performed to evaluate the clinical significance of FOXC2 in OS. High FOXC2 expression was significantly associated with poorer overall survival in patients with OS (p < 0.001). Functional experiments demonstrated that FOXC2 knockdown significantly reduced the overall viable cell/metabolic signal, migration, and invasion in U-2 OS and SaOS-2 cells (p < 0.05). Mechanistically, FOXC2 was found to regulate the CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling axis. ELISA, RT-qPCR, and western blotting analyses showed that FOXC2 knockdown decreased CXCL12 expression, whereas FOXC2 overexpression significantly increased CXCL12 levels. ChIP-qPCR analysis demonstrated significant enrichment of FOXC2 at the CXCL12 promoter and detectable enrichment at the CXCR4 promoter in SaOS-2 cells, and dual-luciferase reporter assays further showed that FOXC2 overexpression significantly increased CXCL12 promoter activity whereas FOXC2 knockdown reduced it, supporting direct transcriptional regulation of the CXCL12/CXCR4 axis by FOXC2. In macrophage co-culture experiments, FOXC2 knockdown promoted M1-like macrophage polarization and reduced M2-like macrophage markers, whereas activation of CXCR4 partially reversed these effects. Flow cytometric analysis further confirmed that FOXC2 knockdown significantly increased the M1/M2 macrophage ratio. In vivo, FOXC2 knockdown markedly reduced tumor growth and lung metastases in a xenograft mouse model, with tumor volume and lung metastatic burden reduced by approximately 50% and 43%, respectively. Tumor tissues from FOXC2-knockdown mice exhibited increased M1-like macrophage infiltration and reduced M2-like macrophage markers. Together, these findings demonstrate that FOXC2 regulates macrophage polarization and OS progression through transcriptional modulation of the CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling axis, highlighting FOXC2 as a potential regulator of the tumor immune microenvironment in OS. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

doi:10.1002/path.70144.abstract: Endometrial stromal sarcomas (ESSs) comprise a heterogeneous group of uterine mesenchymal tumors characterized by diverse morphological features and recurrent molecular alterations. Although molecular classification has substantially improved ESS diagnosis, the relationship between specific genetic alterations and morphological phenotypes remains incompletely understood. We performed an integrated molecular and histopathological analysis of ESS to investigate genotype-phenotype correlations and refine tumor classification. A total of 61 patients with histologically suspected ESSs were initially enrolled, and 51 successfully underwent targeted RNA sequencing, followed by comprehensive morphological reassessment, immunohistochemical evaluation, molecular validation, and clinicopathological correlation. Molecularly confirmed ESSs demonstrated distinct genotype-associated morphological patterns. PHF1-rearranged low-grade ESSs showed a strong association with hypocellular growth and prominent collagenized stroma. Quantitative cellularity analysis further demonstrated significantly lower tumor cellularity in PHF1-rearranged low-grade ESSs compared with JAZF1::SUZ12-rearranged tumors (p < 0.001). High-grade ESSs with YWHAE::NUTM2 and BCOR::ZC3H7B alterations showed higher mitotic activity than low-grade ESSs and demonstrated tongue-like infiltration patterns in both primary and metastatic lesions, indicating that this growth pattern, traditionally emphasized in low-grade ESSs, may represent a broader morphological feature of ESSs. Molecular reassessment led to the reclassification of 10 cases (19.6%, 10/51), identifying tumors with alternative molecular alterations that were initially diagnosed as ESSs based on morphology alone. Among these cases, a uterine sarcoma harboring a novel GATA6::SRF fusion exhibited a low-grade ESS-like morphological phenotype but lacked the characteristic molecular alterations of conventional ESSs, suggesting a potential molecularly defined uterine sarcoma subtype requiring further investigation. Our findings demonstrate that integrated molecular and histopathological analysis extends beyond diagnostic refinement by revealing genotype-phenotype relationships, expanding the molecular spectrum of ESSs and ESS-like uterine sarcomas, and providing new insights into the biological heterogeneity of these rare tumors. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

doi:10.1007/s00262-026-04585-8.abstract: Abstract Background Relapsed B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) after allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), particularly with extramedullary disease (EMD), has a dismal prognosis. The efficacy and durability of allogeneic chimeric antigen receptor T cell (allo-CAR-T) therapy in this setting remain unclear. Methods Fourteen patients with post-transplant relapsed B-ALL received allogeneic anti-CD19 CAR-T cells, including eight with EMD. Clinical responses, survival, CAR-T kinetics, and toxicities were evaluated. Results With a median follow-up of 13.8 months (range, 4.4–52.9 months), the overall complete remission (CR) rate was 92.9% (13/14), with a median duration of remission (DOR) of 12.7 months (range, 3.5–50.3 months). Among patients with EMD, 87.5% (7/8) achieved CR, with a median DOR of 14.7 months (range, 3.5–50.3 months). Of the eight patients with EMD, four were Philadelphia chromosome-positive and received maintenance therapy with tyrosine kinase inhibitors after allo-CAR-T, including dasatinib ( n =1), ponatinib ( n =2), and olverembatinib ( n =1). Median overall survival and event-free survival were not reached in either the overall cohort or EMD subgroup. CAR-T cells persisted in vivo for a median of 5.9 months (range, 1.2–51.6 months). One patient experienced grade 3 cytokine release syndrome and grade 4 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome. One patient developed acute gastrointestinal graft-versus-host disease, followed by chronic graft-versus-host disease involving the skin and lungs. Conclusion Allo-CAR-T therapy induces sustained remissions in patients with post-transplant relapsed B-ALL, including patients with EMD, and may serve as an effective backbone for tailored combination strategies. Trial registration ChiCTR2000036350, registered on August 22, 2020; retrospectively registered.

doi:10.1007/s00262-026-04592-9.abstract: Abstract High-dose vitamin C (HDVC) exhibits antitumor and immunomodulatory properties and may enhance the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs); however, its ability to reprogram the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) in pancreatic cancer, particularly through modulating tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) polarization, remains unclear. In this study, the antitumor activity of HDVC was evaluated in a subcutaneous KPC mouse model, while in vitro models utilizing lipopolysaccharide (LPS) + IFN-γ-stimulated mouse and human macrophages were employed to investigate polarization. Mechanisms were probed by RNA sequencing, western blotting, flow cytometry, pharmacological inhibition, and siRNA-mediated JAK2 knockdown. Macrophage involvement was confirmed in vivo via clodronate liposome-mediated depletion, and the combinatory effect of HDVC with anti-PD-1 therapy was assessed. The results showed that HDVC significantly inhibited pancreatic tumor growth and prolonged survival in vivo. Mechanistically, HDVC enhanced LPS + IFN-γ-induced M1 macrophage polarization, at least in part through activation of the JAK2-STAT1 signaling pathway, without markedly increasing M2-associated features. The antitumor efficacy of HDVC was markedly attenuated upon macrophage depletion, supporting the involvement of macrophage-dependent immune modulation. Furthermore, HDVC enhanced the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy, accompanied by increased M1-like macrophages and CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration in the TME. These findings identify HDVC as a potential immunomodulator that remodels the immunosuppressive TME of pancreatic cancer through macrophage-centered immune remodeling, providing a rationale for further investigating HDVC-based combination strategies with ICIs in pancreatic cancer.

doi:10.1007/s00262-026-04594-7.abstract: Abstract Despite growing enthusiasm for immunotherapy in cancer treatment, only a few colorectal cancer (CRC) patients experience lasting therapeutic effect. This limited efficacy is likely driven by different tumor-intrinsic resistance mechanisms, including loss or downregulation of HLA-I molecules, which may impair antigen presentation and cytotoxic T cell recognition. Interestingly, the downregulation of HLA-I can augment tumor susceptibility to natural killer (NK) cell attack. However, NK cell activity may be inhibited by immunosuppressive signals within the tumor microenvironment. This study describes two patients with metastatic CRC and microsatellite instability who showed durable responses to pembrolizumab despite unfavorable prognostic factors (tumor recurrence, BRAF V600E mutation and markedly reduced HLA-I on tumor cells). Tumor samples obtained at surgical resection also revealed PD-L1 expression on tumor cells and a substantial fraction of tumor-infiltrating PD-1 + NK cells. These findings raise the hypothesis that PD-1/PD-L1 blockade may have contributed to NK-cell-mediated antitumor activity in the context of markedly reduced HLA-I expression. Furthermore, assessing PD-L1 and HLA-I expression on tumor cells at diagnosis could help identify patients who could benefit most from pembrolizumab treatment, alone or combined with inhibitors of HLA-I-specific inhibitory NK receptors. These observations provide a rationale for further investigation in larger and multicenter patient cohorts.

doi:10.1007/s00262-026-04595-6.abstract: Abstract Effective therapies remain limited for neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)- and schwannomatosis (SWN)-related nerve sheath tumors, particularly for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs). Although tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy induces durable responses in multiple solid tumors, its feasibility and optimized manufacturing workflows have not been established for these hereditary neoplasms. Herein, we evaluated T cell infiltration in 109 clinical specimens and detected moderate-to-high CD3⁺ T cell infiltration in most neurofibromas (84.0%), schwannomas (98.3%), and MPNSTs (75.0%), supporting the biological prerequisite for TIL intervention in this disease. We established OM-400, a pre-rapid expansion (pre-REP) protocol utilizing CD3/CD28-bead co-stimulation plus low-dose IL-2 (400 IU/mL) for NF1/SWN-related nerve sheath tumor-derived TILs. Compared with the traditional high-dose-IL-2 method, OM-400 achieved 100% expansion success, shortened culture duration, enriched CD8⁺ effector T cells, showed preliminary evidence of better preservation of original TCR repertoires based on analysis of one representative specimen, and enhanced autologous tumor-reactive cytotoxicity and IFN-γ secretion. Exploratory subgroup analysis across 15 independent patient samples covering NF1, SWN, and NF1-related MPNST revealed no statistically significant differences in TIL performance among subtypes. However, the study was not powered to establish equivalence, and larger cohorts are needed to definitively assess the impact of tumor subtype. Using autologous MPNST patient-derived xenograft models, we confirmed that OM-400-expanded TILs infiltrated tumor tissue and significantly suppressed in vivo tumor growth. In summary, this work provides first preclinical proof of concept for TIL-based immunotherapy against NF1/SWN-related nerve sheath tumors and establishes a reproducible manufacturing platform to facilitate future clinical translation.

doi:10.1007/s00432-026-06563-0.abstract: Nucleotide excision repair (NER) is a critical DNA repair pathway responsible for removing bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions, including ultraviolet radiation-induced photoproducts and platinum drug-DNA adducts. This review provides a comprehensive overview of current understanding of NER in cancer, with particular emphasis on its role in therapeutic response. We discuss the molecular mechanisms of DNA repair in cancer, the significance of NER in platinum-based therapies, results from in vitro studies across various cancer types, findings from patient-based studies, and outcomes from clinical trials. Special attention is given to ERCC1, ERCC2/XPD, XPA, and XPC molecules as potential biomarkers of treatment response and therapeutic targets, and incorporating the most recent discoveries regarding NER inhibitors, mutational signatures, and synthetic lethality-based approaches.

doi:10.1007/s00432-026-06566-x.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are among the most abundant cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME), with M1 and M2 polarization exhibiting anti-tumorigenic and tumorigenic functions, respectively. Originating from both embryonic precursors and circulating monocytes derived from hematopoietic stem cells, TAMs acquire distinct transcriptional, metabolic, and functional identities shaped by the TME. The interactions in the TME among various cells, including cancerous and non-cancerous cells, can determine the polarization and function of TAMs within the tumor. More recently, TAMs have garnered significant interest as a promising therapeutic target in oncology. The TAMs have been shown to enhance proliferation, metastasis, and angiogenesis in human cancers. Notably, cytokines and chemokines, among others, can regulate the infiltration of TAMs in TME. Given the crucial role of macrophages in regulating inflammation and immune responses, targeting these cells has become a significant focus in cancer immunotherapy. Currently, macrophages have been targeted through three strategies, including suppressing macrophage/monocyte recruitment, depletion of TAMs, and re-education of TAMs. Each of these approaches is being investigated in preclinical models and clinical trials, either as monotherapy or in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors. TAMs can also be engineered to act as drug delivery tools, carrying nanoparticles directly into tumors. In the clinic, some types of TAMs, marked by proteins like CD163 and CD204, can help predict patient outcomes in several cancers. This review investigates the origins of TAMs and the mechanisms underlying their polarization and metabolism. Furthermore, we study macrophage-driven tumor progression and devising effective targeting strategies, as well as challenges that remain and where the field may go next in macrophage-based cancer treatment. Going forward, combining single-cell profiling with multi-target therapies may offer the best path toward more effective, TAM-based cancer treatments.

doi:10.1007/s00432-026-06639-x.abstract: Abstract Background Evidence of treatment strategies in frail patients (i.e. not fit for combination therapies) with unresectable metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) is limited to dose-reduced doublet regimens or oral fluoropyrimidines (FP) with bevacizumab. We conducted a systematic review analyzing evidence for oral FPs with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-directed monoclonal antibodies for patients with RAS wild-type (WT) mCRC across treatment lines. Methods We searched PubMed and Cochrane Library for phase II and phase III studies evaluating oral FPs (capecitabine, S-1 or trifluridine/tipiracil (FTD/TPI)) plus EGFR-directed monoclonal antibody (panitumumab or cetuximab) in mCRC. Outcomes included efficacy and safety. Results Seven publications met inclusion criteria (n = 262 patients). First-line data was limited to elderly cohorts receiving capecitabine plus cetuximab or panitumumab with a median progression-free survival (PFS)/median overall survival (OS) of 7.2/17.1 months (cetuximab) and 7.5/23.7 months (panitumumab), respectively. In third-line and beyond, median PFS for the combination of FTD/TPI plus cetuximab or panitumumab ranged from 2.4 (cetuximab) to 5.8 months (panitumumab), and OS from 9.8 (cetuximab) to 14.2 months (panitumumab). S-1 plus cetuximab was associated with a median PFS of 5.5 months and OS of 13.6 months. Conclusion While capecitabine should not be used together with anti-EGFR antibodies, FTD/TPI in combination with an EGFR-directed antibody appears feasible, shows promising activity and manageable toxicity profile in RAS WT mCRC potentially offering an alternative for frail patients; prospective trials are needed.

doi:10.1007/s00432-026-06642-2.abstract: CT-based staging of the clinically node-negative (cN0) neck in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) has limited sensitivity, and occult nodal metastasis remains common. Whether the CT-to-surgery interval influences pathological nodal outcome is unclear. This retrospective study included 329 patients with primary cN0 OSCC undergoing CT staging and neck dissection (2011-2024). Associations with lymph node positivity, lymph node count, and extranodal extension (ENE) were assessed using logistic and negative binomial regression, with sensitivity analyses (quartiles, exclusion of extreme intervals, lymph node yield adjustment). Median CT-to-surgery interval was 9.0 days (IQR 5.0-15.0), and 53 patients (16.1%) had lymph node metastasis. The interval was associated with lymph node positivity in univariable analysis (OR 1.031, p = 0.035), but not after adjustment for age and smoking (OR 1.027, p = 0.065); lymph node count showed a similar non-significant association (IRR 1.027, p = 0.068). The association with nodal positivity was not robust across interval quartiles (p = 0.969), after excluding intervals >30 days (OR 0.995, p = 0.824), or after adjustment for lymph node yield (OR 1.015, p = 0.334). However, patients with intervals >30 days (n = 13) had higher nodal positivity than those with shorter intervals (53.8% vs. 14.6%). The interval was not associated with ENE (p = 0.740), and tumor localization was not associated with nodal positivity (p = 0.175). An initially significant, unadjusted association was not robust to sensitivity testing and was confined to a small subgroup with substantially prolonged intervals. This offers some reassurance that the CT-to-surgery interval is not strongly associated with occult nodal metastasis in cN0 OSCC, while substantially delayed surgery warrants further investigation.

doi:10.1007/s00432-026-06646-y.abstract: Following the EV-302/KEYNOTE-A39 study, the combination therapy of enfortumab vedotin and pembrolizumab (EV-P) has been established as a new first-line treatment for metastatic urothelial carcinoma. With increasing use, the documentation and publication of unexpected side effects and complications are essential to systematize procedures. We report on a 56-year-old patient who experienced an extravasation of EV-P during the first cycle due to dislocation of the port catheter from the cephalic vein. Extensive subcutaneous necrosis of the infraclavicular region required surgical debridement and application of a vacuum-assisted closure system, followed by secondary wound healing. The wound healed with a residual scar but no functional impairment or persistent pain. The therapy was resumed via a peripheral venous catheter, and the patient achieved a deep partial response. To our knowledge, this represents the first reported case of central venous EV-P extravasation (CTCAE grade 3) requiring surgical therapy. Because of its cytotoxic payload, EV in particular may pose a high risk of local complications in the context of extravasations.

doi:10.1007/s00432-026-06651-1.abstract: Advanced sarcomas remain therapeutically challenging. We evaluated treatment implementation and clinical outcomes after molecular tumor board recommendations. We retrospectively analyzed 125 sarcoma patients discussed in our multidisciplinary Molecular and Familial Tumor Board between 2017 and 2023. Clinical benefit was assessed by treatment implementation and by the ratio of progression-free survival on molecularly guided therapy versus the preceding treatment line (PFS2/PFS1). Overall survival (OS) was measured from first board discussion. A total of 252 pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant records across 133 genes were identified. Molecular profiling enabled therapy recommendations in 71 of 125 patients (56.8%), with treatment implementation in 41 (32.8%). PFS2/PFS1 evaluation was feasible in 29 patients, and nine (31.0%) had a documented ratio > 1.3. Median PFS2 was 102 days (95% CI 63-233). Two of seven patients (28.6%) receiving poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitor-containing regimens had ratios > 1.3. Median OS in 124 patients was 14.6 months (95% CI 11.7-18.5; global log-rank p = 0.220). Molecular tumor board-guided therapy identified treatment options for selected sarcoma patients. Prolonged disease control in individual PARP-treated cases provides a positive signal that warrants prospective evaluation.

doi:10.1007/s00540-026-03916-4.abstract: To develop and validate a risk prediction model for postpartum urinary retention (PUR) among parturients receiving epidural analgesia (EA) during vaginal delivery, to support individualized bladder management. This dual-center retrospective cohort study analyzed electronic medical records from two hospitals (2022-2024). Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used to select independent predictors from demographic, labor, and analgesia-related variables. A clinical nomogram was developed. The model underwent internal and external validation; performance was assessed using calibration, discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]), and decision curve analysis (DCA). Among 1019 parturients receiving EA (PUR incidence 16.09%), prolonged analgesia duration and prolonged second-stage labor were independently associated with PUR, whereas higher intermittent catheterization frequency (ICF) was associated with a lower rate of recorded PUR. The model demonstrated excellent discrimination, satisfactory calibration, and clinical net benefit across validation cohorts. The validated nomogram provides real-time, individualized estimates of PUR risk during late labor. By identifying parturients at elevated risk, it offers an evidence-based basis for risk-adaptive bladder monitoring and individualized care; however, whether such model-guided management ultimately reduces PUR incidence remains to be established in prospective interventional studies.

doi:10.1007/s00540-026-03921-7.abstract: This study examined whether the stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) at intensive care unit (ICU) admission is associated with major postoperative complications after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass and whether this association differs from that of absolute ICU admission glucose. This single-center retrospective study included 731 surgical episodes from 709 adults who underwent cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. SHR was calculated as the first ICU glucose divided by HbA1c-derived estimated average glucose. The primary outcome was an unweighted composite of 30-day mortality, stroke, Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes stage 3 acute kidney injury, reoperation for bleeding, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and deep sternal wound infection. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for clinically relevant covariates. The composite outcome occurred in 90 surgical episodes (12.3%). SHR was associated with the composite outcome after adjustment (odds ratio [OR], 1.103 per 0.1 increase; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.008-1.208; P = 0.033), whereas ICU admission glucose was not significantly associated (OR, 1.019 per 10 mg/dL increase; 95% CI 0.946-1.096; P = 0.626). SHR at ICU admission was associated with major postoperative complications in the primary analysis, whereas absolute ICU admission glucose was not significantly associated after multivariable adjustment. Confidence intervals for SHR included 1.0 in several sensitivity analyses. SHR warrants prospective evaluation as an early postoperative risk marker after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass.

doi:10.1007/s00540-026-03923-5.abstract: The primary objective was to evaluate the influence of needle tip positioning during suprazygomatic maxillary nerve block on bupivacaine concentration within the pterygopalatine fossa (PPF). The secondary objective was to correlate early injectate spread on computed tomography (CT) with PPF bupivacaine concentrations. Suprazygomatic maxillary nerve block attempts (n=34) were performed on 17 human cadaveric heads with different needle tip positions. Each attempt involved injection of 5 mL containing 0.4% bupivacaine, iohexol, and methylene blue. Computed tomography was used to determine needle tip location and early injectate spread. PPF samples were harvested via a transmaxillary approach for bupivacaine quantification by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. The highest median [Q1-Q3] bupivacaine concentrations were observed when needle tip was positioned within pterygomaxillary fissure or PPF, with 829.3 [728.1-1015.7] µg/g, and when positioned directly against maxillary tuberosity, with 535.3 [355.7-820.7] µg/g. Concentrations were highly variable with off-bone infratemporal placements (range, 0.1-335.8 µg/g). Lateral needle displacement was associated with lower bupivacaine concentrations (β=-0.193, 95% CI -0.301 to -0.086; P<0.001), whereas anterior (β=0.107, 95% CI 0.018-0.196; P=0.020) and cranial displacement (β=0.079, 95% CI 0.017-0.141; P=0.014) were associated with higher concentrations. CT contrast spread between temporalis and lateral pterygoid muscles was not associated with higher PPF bupivacaine concentrations (P=0.117). Needle tip position influenced bupivacaine concentration within PPF, with concentrations generally increasing as the needle approached PPF and with more anterior positioning, including placement at the maxillary tuberosity. More superficial or posterior infratemporal placements yielded lower and more variable concentrations. Moreover, infratemporal contrast spread on early CT imaging was not associated with higher PPF bupivacaine concentrations.

doi:10.1007/s00540-026-03926-2.abstract: Pain during propofol injection is common, yet little is known about how often patients remember this experience after anesthesia or which perioperative factors influence memory formation during induction. In this prospective single-center observational cohort study, English-speaking adults (≥ 18 years) receiving propofol under general anesthesia (GA) or monitored anesthesia care (MAC) were enrolled. Perioperative characteristics, intravenous access details, anesthetic medications and clinician-observed injection pain were recorded. On postoperative day 1, patients were interviewed using a standardized questionnaire assessing recall of discomfort during induction. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses calculated adjusted odds ratios (aOR) and identified factors associated with recall. Of the 1,699 enrolled patients, 1,319 completed the postoperative day 1 assessment; 8.1% reported recall of injection discomfort. Multivariate analysis indicated that younger age (aOR = 1.03; 95% CI = 1.01-1.04; p < 0.001), female gender (aOR = 1.69; 95% CI = 1.02-2.82; p = 0.044), hand IV placement (aOR = 2.164; CI 95% = 1.287-3.636; p = 0.004), and absence of midazolam premedication (aOR = 2.62; 95% CI = 1.44-4.78; p = 0.002) were associated with increased recall. Approximately one in twelve patients recalled discomfort during propofol injection. Patient characteristics and modifiable anesthetic practices, particularly premedication and intravenous access site, were associated with memory of propofol injection discomfort. These findings highlight that memory formation during induction represents a distinct and clinically relevant patient-centered outcome.

doi:10.1007/s00540-026-03927-1.abstract: Anesthetic management in general surgery poses substantial risks in elderly patients because age-related physiologic decline and preexisting comorbidities increase vulnerability to peri-operative complications. Older adults have reduced physiological reserve, impaired organ function, and slower recovery from surgical and anesthetic stress, placing them at increased risk for postoperative delirium and early postoperative cognitive impairment. Dexmedetomidine, a selective α2-adrenergic receptor agonist, has sedative, anti-inflammatory, and opioid-sparing properties that may influence early postoperative cognitive outcomes without significant respiratory depression. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the association between dexmedetomidine and 24-h postoperative delirium/early postoperative cognitive impairment in elderly patients undergoing general surgery. Four studies involving 479 patients met the inclusion criteria. Across the included studies, dexmedetomidine was generally administered as a 1 µg/kg loading dose followed by continuous intraoperative maintenance infusion of 0.2-0.7 µg/kg/h. Pooled analysis showed that dexmedetomidine was associated with significantly lower odds of 24-h postoperative delirium/early postoperative cognitive impairment compared with control treatment (pooled OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.24-0.61; p < 0.001). These findings suggest that dexmedetomidine is associated with lower odds of early postoperative cognitive outcomes in elderly surgical patients compared with control treatment. Larger, long-term studies are needed to confirm these findings and establish standardized dosing protocols.

doi:10.1007/s00540-026-03935-1.abstract: Some parturients experience discomfort, pain, and nausea/vomiting during cesarean delivery under neuraxial anesthesia. We evaluated whether intravenous dexmedetomidine administered after fetal delivery and cord clamping improved maternal intraoperative experience. In this prospective, triple-blind, placebo-controlled trial, women aged 20-45 years undergoing elective cesarean delivery under combined spinal-epidural anesthesia were randomized 1:1 to dexmedetomidine or saline. Dexmedetomidine was administered after cord clamping as a loading dose of 1 μg/kg over 10 min, followed by 0.4 μg/kg/hr until peritoneal closure; controls received equivalent-volume saline. The primary outcome was satisfaction with intraoperative sedation/analgesia, assessed on postoperative day 1 using a 7-point verbal rating scale. Secondary outcomes were Quality of Recovery-40 score, maximum intraoperative pain score, intraoperative nausea/vomiting, and motor recovery time. Eighty-three participants were randomized; 81 contributed to the available-case analysis. Satisfaction scores were higher with dexmedetomidine than saline (Hodges-Lehmann location shift, 1.0 point; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.0 to 2.0; P < 0.001). In ordinal logistic regression, dexmedetomidine was associated with higher satisfaction scores (common odds ratio, 13.4; 95% CI 4.6 to 39.0). Dexmedetomidine reduced intraoperative pain and intraoperative nausea/vomiting, but did not improve 24-h Quality of Recovery-40 scores and modestly prolonged motor recovery. Post-delivery intravenous dexmedetomidine improved patient-reported satisfaction with intraoperative sedation and analgesia. Exploratory findings suggested reduced pain and nausea/vomiting without improved 24-h recovery. These findings support further evaluation of dexmedetomidine as a selective adjunct rather than for routine sedation. doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08094-1.abstract: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the potential impact of a Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared artificial intelligence (AI)-based decision support tool for breast ultrasound in reducing benign biopsies. This study was conducted at two academic medical centers from March to May 2025 following the clinical implementation of an FDA-cleared AI-based decision support tool for breast ultrasound interpretation (Koios DS; New York, NY). Fourteen breast imaging radiologists documented BI-RADS 4 (suspicious) cases, along with the corresponding AI output. AI assessments were compared with biopsy pathology results to characterize AI classification within this selected cohort. Overall, 271 lesions in 253 women (mean age, 54 years; range, 24-92 years) were categorized as BI-RADS 4 and were biopsied, aspirated, and/or surgically excised. Of these, 23.2% (63/271) yielded malignant pathology, while 76.8% (208/271) were benign. The AI tool classified 90.5% (57/63) of malignant lesions as BI-RADS 4 and 9.5% (6/63) as BI-RADS 2 or 3. Among benign cases, the AI tool assigned 41.8% (87/208) as BI-RADS 2 (benign), 18.8% (39/208) as BI-RADS 3 (probably benign), and 39.4% (82/208) as BI-RADS 4 (suspicious). Retrospective application of the AI output to biopsy triage decisions suggests the potential for reduction in benign biopsy recommendations, with 60.6% (126/208) of benign lesions classified by the AI tool as BI-RADS 2 or 3. AI may help reduce benign biopsy recommendations among lesions assessed as BI-RADS 4 by radiologists; however, careful integration with radiologist judgment and clinical history is essential to ensure timely cancer diagnosis.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08095-0.abstract: Various social determinants of health (SDOH) have been shown to negatively impact breast cancer outcomes. Though there are recommendations for comprehensive SDOH assessment, little is known about the optimal frequency of reassessments and change in health-related social needs (HRSN) over time for specific patient populations. We sought to characterize SDOH screening and HRSN patterns among patients with breast cancer in a safety-net system. A retrospective study was conducted to evaluate SDOH survey responses in the electronic medical records and screening frequency from patients diagnosed with breast cancer between January 2021 to January 2024 at Parkland Health. There were 566 patients diagnosed with breast cancer with a mean age at diagnosis of 55.0 (standard deviation, SD: 11.4) years. There were 54 (9.5%) with Stage IV breast cancer. Patients were initially at risk for 1.36 (SD: 1.39) out of the 11 HRSN domains. Patients completed an average 17.3 (SD: 8.9) out of 28 questions on initial survey. The most common risk domains identified were Alcohol Use and Food Insecurity. No patients were screened for Interpersonal Violence. The median time from initial survey to first change in risk level for any domain was 8.7 months. Patients with Stage IV disease underwent fewer SDOH re-screenings compared to patients with Stage I, II, and III disease (p < 0.001). Within our system, greater attention should be placed towards fully assessing patients' HRSN and screening for interpersonal violence. SDOH screening at 6-month intervals may help to capture changes in HSRNs and assess the impact of resource interventions.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08097-y.abstract: Breast conservation for invasive breast cancer is associated with better survival and fewer complications than mastectomy, which is especially relevant for older patients. It is unclear whether this can be extrapolated to ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). This population-based cohort study used data from the Breast Cancer Database Sweden (BCBaSe 3.0) to compare overall survival (OS), breast cancer-specific survival (BCSS) and local recurrence (LR) probabilities in three different age groups (< 60, 60-69, 70 + years) of women with primary DCIS undergoing breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy (BCS + RT), mastectomy without radiotherapy (Mx-RT), or breast-conserving surgery without radiotherapy (BCS-RT) during 2008-2019. Complete cases (CC) and multiple imputation (MI) analyses were applied. In 7165 women, treatment was BCS + RT (53.3%), BCS-RT (13.4%), or Mx-RT (33.2%). Estimated 10-year OS was 90.4% (95% CI 89.3-91.5) and BCSS 98.8% (98.3-99.2). After adjustments for patient and tumour factors, including socioeconomic status and comorbidity, Mx-RT was associated with a higher overall mortality than BCS + RT in CC (HR 2.10; 95% CI 1.20-3.67) but not in MI analyses (HR 1.29; 0.95-1.76). In age 70 + years, however, the overall mortality was consistently increased (CC: HR 2.48; 1.09-5.62, MI: HR 1.89; 1.23-2.90). Also BCS-RT was associated with a higher overall mortality than BCS + RT (CC: HR 2.68; 1.34-5.34, and MI: HR 1.72; 1.23-2.39). The 10-year LR probability was low (7.2%, 95% CI 6.3-8.0). Compared to BCS + RT, Mx-RT was associated with a lower (HR 0.18, 95% CI 0.11-0.28) and BCS-RT with a higher LR risk (HR 1.79; 1.31-2.46), especially among ages 70+. BCS + RT in DCIS appears safe. Acknowledging potential selection bias, BCS + RT may be associated with favourable overall survival outcomes in older women despite a higher risk of local recurrence.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08098-x.abstract: To compare late toxicities, cosmetic outcomes, and reconstruction failure in patients undergoing immediate autologous reconstruction (AR) versus implant-based reconstruction (IBR) followed by postmastectomy radiotherapy (PMRT). A multi-institutional retrospective cohort study (2013-2024) assessed patients undergoing mastectomy with immediate reconstruction and PMRT. Primary endpoints were reconstruction failure (loss or replacement of the index implant reconstruction, or total flap loss) and late toxicities, including contracture, fat necrosis, and cosmesis (Kroll scale). 113 patients were included (68 AR, 45 IBR). AR utilised deep inferior epigastric perforator flaps; IBR cohort consisted of 41 direct-to-implant procedures and four latissimus dorsi flaps combined with implants. Among available baseline variables, cohorts were broadly similar except that AR patients were slightly older. Reconstruction failure was analysed in all IBR patients; four IBR patients were not evaluable for subsequent capsular contracture and cosmetic assessment because of implant removal before late assessment. Reconstruction failure occurred exclusively in IBR (28.9% [13 of 45] vs. 0% [0/68] in AR; P < 0.001). Clinically significant firmness was observed in 46.3% (19/41) of IBR versus 14.7% (10/68) of AR patients (P < 0.001). Fat necrosis occurred in 16.2% of AR patients without flap loss. Good/Excellent physician-assessed cosmesis was more frequent after AR (83.8% vs. 36.6%; P < 0.001). Recurrence rates were comparable between cohorts. AR was associated with higher reconstruction survival and more favourable physician-assessed cosmetic outcomes compared with predominantly direct-to-implant, subpectoral IBR after PMRT. For patients with a high probability of requiring PMRT, AR should be discussed early and strongly considered when clinically feasible.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08100-6.abstract: Podany et al. examined associations between Area Deprivation Index (ADI) and tumor genomics, PI3K inhibitor use, and survival in 1,127 patients with metastatic breast cancer. While their multi-institutional, genomically annotated dataset is a valuable contribution, several methodological issues warrant scrutiny. We critically reviewed the study's statistical approach, focusing on multiple-comparison handling, potential confounding from ctDNA shedding variability, and the reliability of subgroup survival estimates. Key findings (TP53, AKT1, overall survival, PI3Ki-use disparity, and Black patient survival disadvantage) relied on borderline p-values from uncorrected multiple comparisons across 19 supplementary tables. Lower visceral, nodal, and soft-tissue metastasis rates in high-deprivation patients suggest reduced ctDNA shedding, which could confound reported mutation-frequency differences, particularly for AKT1. The AKT1 subgroup hazard ratio (6.27) derived from roughly five events, far below recommended events-per-variable thresholds, raising concerns about estimate stability. Addressing multiplicity correction, ctDNA shedding assessment, and transparent event-count reporting would strengthen confidence in the study's conclusions and better inform future prospective research.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08101-5.abstract: Drug resistance is a major cause of treatment failure in breast cancer patients. Numerous genetic and epigenetic markers have been proposed to influence Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy (NACT) response, and genes that regulate the effectiveness of chemotherapeutic agents undergo expression regulation via methylation. In this study, we aimed to investigate the methylation levels of KDM5A, KDM5B, and KDM5C, as well as their associated genes, EZH2, TFAP2C, ZMYND8, and SIN3B (Exon 1-2 and 19-20), in blood samples collected from patients before and after NACT treatment. Besides, we also examined potential variations in the KDM5A, KDM5B, and KDM5C gene regions. Twenty patients were diagnosed with breast cancer, and 30 healthy control individuals were included in the study. Blood samples were taken from the patients twice, before and after NACT. Methylation levels of KDM5 family genes and related genes were analyzed using Methylation-specific PCR (MSP). Additionally, potential variants in the KDM5A, KDM5B, and KDM5C gene regions were identified using Sanger sequencing. According to the methylation analysis results, the SIN3B (Exon 19-20), KDM5C, EZH2, and TFAP2C genes were prominent in patients with pathological partial response, while the KDM5A, KDM5B, KDM5C, EZH2, TFAP2C, and SIN3B (Exon 19-20) genes were prominent in patients with pathological complete response. According to genotyping results, rs41308616 and rs971896841 variants were detected as heterozygous in the KDM5C gene region in two patients, respectively. The methylation percentages and genetic variations in the KDM5 family and related gene regions identified in this study may serve as potential biomarkers for developing treatment strategies for breast cancer patients.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08102-4.abstract: Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis (IGM) is a benign inflammatory breast condition that can resemble mastitis or malignancy clinically and radiographically. We aimed to develop a quantitative scoring system, based off the Komen Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC) scoring system [1], evaluating clinical and radiologic features to distinguish IGM from benign and malignant breast conditions. We conducted a retrospective chart review of biopsy-proven IGM patients diagnosed from 2014 to 2025 via institutional electronic medical records. Clinical symptom onset, features, and diagnostic imaging were analyzed. A continuous scoring scale (1-50) was created, encompassing three categories: symptom onset, clinical features, and radiographic findings. Scores of IGM patients were compared with those of patients diagnosed with IBC, mastitis (lactational and non-lactational), and locally advanced breast cancer (LABC). Welch's two-sample t-test assessed statistical differences, and Youden index identified the optimal score threshold for predicting IGM. Among 148 IGM patients, predominantly Hispanic (56.8%) and Asian (26.7%), the mean age was 37.2 years, older than mastitis patients and younger than IBC patients. Key clinical features included pain or painful breast mass (100%), fistula or draining wound (77.7%), erythema (94.6%), and phlegmon (87.8%). Imaging revealed mass with collection in 84.6% and multiple masses/collections in 38.9%. The mean IGM score (35.5) was significantly higher than scores for IBC, mastitis, and LABC groups (14.4, 18, and 15.2, respectively; p ≤ 0.05). A score ≥ 24.5 predicted IGM with 93% sensitivity and 95% specificity. This novel scoring system provides an objective framework to differentiate IGM from similar breast conditions, facilitating early diagnosis and guiding appropriate management. not applicable.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08104-2.abstract: Germline genetic testing is increasing. While testing barriers are well characterized, less is known about post-testing needs and utilization of screening and prevention resources by women with pathogenic variants (PVs) in breast cancer susceptibility genes. A 38-question online survey was developed by Facing Our Risk of Cancer Empowered (FORCE), a patient advocacy group, and administered electronically to subscribers from February-May 2024. Study eligibility criteria included female sex and a germline PV conferring elevated lifetime risk of breast cancer (ATM, BARD1, BRCA1, BRCA2, CDH1, CHEK2, PALB2, PTEN, RAD51C, RAD51D, STK11, or TP53). Of 1,025 respondents who initiated the survey, 937 were women. Most were non-Hispanic White (91.7%) and from the United States (81.6%). The most common PVs were BRCA2 (31.4%), BRCA1 (25.5%) and CHEK2 (9.2%). The most frequently used resources were education and information services about medical options (39.3%) and peer support (28.1%). Few respondents used financial navigation (4.0%) or financial support (5.3%), but up to 45% reported needing these services. Among breast screening users (53.8% used mammogram, 42.2% magnetic resonance imaging, 19.4% ultrasound), 37.8% found it hard to prepare emotionally for results and 14% found it hard to pay for screening. One-third (37.1%) of respondents found deciding whether to have risk-reducing mastectomy hard; two-thirds (64.0%) found physical recovery hard, more than half (60.2%) found emotional recovery hard, and one-quarter (24.7%) found paying for risk-reducing mastectomy hard. In this contemporary sample of women at elevated risk of breast cancer, more than one-third had unmet financial needs and up to two-thirds had difficulty with screening or risk-reducing surgery. Closing these gaps will be essential to improve outcomes for women with hereditary breast cancer.

doi:10.1007/s10549-026-08105-1.abstract: High-volume hospitals deliver improved outcomes for patients with breast cancer, supporting referrals for breast cancer surgical care to high-volume regional facilities. This retrospective cohort study investigated how multidisciplinary cancer care trajectories and patient care experiences varied by surgical facility classification (regional vs. community as a proxy for high- vs. low-volume) and whether effects differed by rural-residence. We used Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results-Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems (SEER-CAHPS) data for Medicare beneficiaries who received surgery for non-metastatic breast cancer from 2009 to 2019. We mapped cancer care trajectories using facility classification and oncologist specialty and performed state sequence analysis to identify care trajectory clusters. We used linear mixed-effects models to examine associations of surgical facility classification with patient-reported experience measures and assessed effect modification by rurality. Of the 3,327 patients in our cohort, 15.4% were rural-residing and 68.8% received surgery at a regional facility. Care trajectories indicated that patients tended to receive adjuvant care from the same type of facility as their surgical treatment. Patients who received surgery at community facilities (vs. regional) were significantly more likely to report better experiences with getting needed care (Est. (95%CI) = 3.5 (0.10,6.9), p = 0.043), with no significant differences for getting care quickly, care coordination, or doctor communication. Rural-residence was not a significant effect modifier. Receiving surgery at community facilities is associated with better patient-reported experiences for getting needed care. Moreover, surgical facility classification appears to influence the setting for subsequent cancer care, which may impact patient experiences in getting needed care. Not applicable.
