doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.002.abstract: Patients from more deprived backgrounds experience poorer postoperative outcomes. We analysed preoperative characteristics in UK Perioperative Quality Improvement Programme participants according to socioeconomic position to explore opportunities for targeted interventions. Participants were adults aged ≥18 yr undergoing major elective surgery at UK Perioperative Quality Improvement Programme sites. Socioeconomic position was determined using postcode data and the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) standardised aggregate scale of area-level deprivation. Associations between IMD position and patient characteristics, health behaviours, and comorbidities were analysed using descriptive statistics with appropriate parametric and nonparametric testing. Of 55 938 participants included, quintile 1 (most deprived) represented the smallest subgroup (14.2%), with recruitment varying by region and site. Median age was 66 yr with IMD 1 participants 5 yr younger (62 yr) than IMD 5 (67 yr). Deprivation gradients (IMD 5 to 1) were seen for home ownership, occupation, and educational attainment. Prevalences of smoking, inactivity, and obesity increased from IMD 5 to 1. Higher prevalences of major long-term conditions including diabetes mellitus, heart failure, stroke, and ASA physical status 3-4 were observed in more deprived quintiles. Prevalence rates of dementia and renal impairment were similar across quintiles despite the age gradient. Notably, the proportions of patients living with frailty and disability increased with deprivation. Patients presenting for major surgery from more deprived backgrounds do so in poorer overall health. They can encounter barriers to both research participation and available preoperative support. Addressing this unmet need to prevent widening perioperative health inequalities requires interventions tailored to the patient's socioeconomic context.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.012.abstract: Adverse neurocognitive and functional outcomes are common after cardiac surgery. Cerebral near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) monitors regional cerebral oxygen saturation, allowing clinicians to detect and reverse cerebral desaturation. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs to evaluate whether intraoperative NIRS monitoring improves neurocognitive outcomes after cardiac surgery. We searched CENTRAL, CINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science for RCTs comparing NIRS-guided intraoperative management with usual care in adults undergoing on-pump cardiac surgery, assessing the outcomes of postoperative cognitive decline, delirium, stroke, mortality, and functional recovery. We pooled data using random-effects meta-analysis and assessed certainty of evidence using GRADE methodology. We included 17 RCTs (N=2288). NIRS-guided management probably reduces early postoperative cognitive decline (risk ratio [RR] 0.65, 95% CI 0.42-0.99; I2=65%, moderate certainty), may have little or no effect on stroke (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.42-1.91; low certainty) or mortality (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.47-1.52; low certainty), and may have no effect on delirium (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.56-1.09; I2=32%, low certainty). Findings were primarily derived from small, single-centre trials with heterogenous NIRS thresholds and intervention algorithms. Few studies evaluated outcomes beyond 30 days, and none evaluated validated measures of quality of life or function. Although NIRS-guided intraoperative care shows promise for reducing early postoperative cognitive decline after cardiac surgery, evidence of benefit for other neurocognitive or clinical outcomes remains limited. Large multicentre studies are needed to confirm its utility, refine intervention thresholds, and determine its impact on long-term cognition, function, and quality of life. Systematic review protocol. PROSPERO (CRD42022336468).

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.015.abstract: Acute respiratory acid-base changes induce pH-dependent electrolyte redistribution. Although this response has been characterised in vitro, the in vivo changes depend on multicompartment buffering and remain poorly defined. We conducted a multicentre retrospective study of patients undergoing apnoea testing for organ donation after determination of brain death, a clinical model allowing in vivo study of acute ventilatory changes. The primary outcome was the pH-dependent change in strong ion difference (SID). Secondary analyses examined individual electrolytes, pH-SID effect modification by physiological variables, and how well the derived model agreed with observed SID changes compared with a simple bedside pH-correction method (ΔSID=-15×ΔpH). In 263 participants, pH decreased from 7.40 (0.07) to 7.23 (0.07) and returned to 7.40 (0.08). Per pH unit increase, SID changed by -11.7 meq L-1 (95% CI -13.1 to -10.3; P<0.001), driven primarily by sodium ion (Na) (52% of change -7.2 mM; P<0.001) and chloride ion (Cl) (36% of change +3.7 mM; P<0.001). Higher haemoglobin concentration was associated with a higher pH-dependent SID change, together explaining 53% of within-patient variability. Agreement between predicted and observed SID changes was only modestly improved by using the derived model vs a simplified pH-correction model (sd of differences 1.74 vs 1.92 meq L-1). Acute respiratory acid-base disturbances produce in vivo Na and Cl redistribution associated with pH change that are modulated by haemoglobin concentration. The observed pH-dependent electrolyte redistribution is consistent with physiological buffering and can be reasonably approximated using a simple bedside pH-correction model.

doi:10.1016/j.bja.2026.09.016.abstract: Pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg positioning during laparoscopic colorectal surgery promote atelectasis and increase the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs). Electrical impedance tomography (EIT) enables individualised PEEP titration by visualising regional lung collapse, facilitating lung-protective ventilation. However, evidence of its effect on clinical PPCs remains limited. In this single-centre, parallel-group RCT, adults with intermediate to high risk for PPCs (ARISCAT score ≥26) who underwent laparoscopic colorectal surgery were randomly assigned to receive intraoperative PEEP titration guided by EIT or a conventional fixed PEEP of 5 cm H2O. The primary outcome was PPCs incidence within 30 days, as determined by a multidisciplinary adjudication team using standardised criteria. Among the 117 randomised participants (mean [range] age: 62 [37-80] yr; 37% female), EIT-guided PEEP (n=59) resulted in lower driving pressure (16 [15-18] cm H2O) compared with fixed PEEP (n=58; 19 [17-22] cm H2O; P<0.0001). The incidence of 30 day PPCs was lower among participants randomised to EIT-guided PEEP (29/59 [49.2%]) than those in the fixed-PEEP group (42/58 [72.4%]; hazard ratio: 0.53; 95% CI, 0.33-0.85; P=0.009). PPCs including atelectasis and pneumonia occurred less frequently among participants randomised to EIT-guided PEEP. Compared with conventional fixed PEEP of 5 cm H2O, EIT-guided PEEP was associated with a lower incidence of PPCs among patients at intermediate to high PPCs risk undergoing laparoscopic colorectal surgery, suggesting a role for EIT in intraoperative lung protection. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2300076677.

doi:10.1016/j.bjao.2026.100857.abstract: Scientific satire occupies an unusual place in medical publishing. This editorial discusses the role of medical satire by highlighting an article that poses as a retrospective observational trial using a large database, and compares a clinically relevant outcome between two arbitrary, physiologically meaningless groups. The differences between the groups are statistically significant, but physiologically nonsensical. The editorial explores epistemology as it applies to the practice of medicine. The greatest value of the satire may be medical education and its teaching of clinical reasoning. It reminds clinicians that cognitive heuristics, arbitrary categorisation, and large datasets can combine to produce statistically convincing, yet clinically meaningless, associations.

doi:10.1016/j.bjao.2026.100864.abstract: Patients with obesity are at an increased risk of postoperative pulmonary complications and impaired lung function after general anaesthesia. Although higher levels of PEEP combined with recruitment manoeuvres may improve intraoperative respiratory mechanics, their effect on postoperative lung function remains uncertain. We evaluated whether high PEEP with recruitment manoeuvres improves postoperative spirometry in obese patients undergoing abdominal surgery. This single-centre substudy of the Protective Ventilation in Obese Patients randomised controlled trial was conducted at Ghent University Hospital, Belgium. Adults with a BMI of ≥35 kg·m-2 undergoing abdominal surgery were randomised to high PEEP (12 cm H2O) with recruitment manoeuvres or low PEEP (4 cm H2O) without routine recruitment manoeuvres. Both groups received low tidal volume ventilation (7 mL·kg-1 predicted body weight). The primary outcome was the change in forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) from baseline to postoperative day 1. Secondary outcomes included changes in spirometry variables and oxygen saturation. Postoperative spirometry data were available for 44 patients (23 low PEEP, 21 high PEEP). Postoperative lung function declined in all patients. The change in FEV1 from baseline to postoperative day 1 did not differ between the low- and high-PEEP groups (-0.90 [0.68] L vs -0.93 [0.66] L; between-group effect 0.0 L; 95% confidence interval -0.4 to 0.4 L; P=0.89). No differences were observed in secondary outcomes. In obese patients undergoing abdominal surgery with low tidal volume ventilation, high PEEP with recruitment manoeuvers did not improve postoperative spirometric outcomes or oxygen saturation compared with low PEEP without routine recruitment manoeuvres. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02148692.

doi:10.1016/j.bjao.2026.100865.abstract: Acute pain management is shifting away from traditional paternalistic models towards more collaborative, patient-centred approaches that emphasise shared decision making and the use of digital health technologies. Here, we review recent advances in digital health technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) that support shared decision making, including interactive decision aids, video narratives, and AI-assisted tools. These innovations have the potential to optimise analgesia, reduce the risks associated with opioids and opioid-related harms, and enhance patient autonomy across surgical, emergency, and primary care settings. Although emerging evidence shows promise in improving prescribing efficiency and increasing patient satisfaction, there are still significant barriers to implementation. These include resource limitations, challenges in selecting appropriate tools, and the necessity for robust validation of AI systems. Herein, we critically evaluate the current evidence, discuss practical strategies for implementation, and provide recommendations for integrating these technologies into routine clinical practice.

doi:10.1016/j.bjao.2026.100868.abstract: Prehabilitation optimises patients' physical, nutritional, and psychological readiness before major surgery, but remains largely absent from Austrian clinical practice. We aimed to identify stakeholder-perceived barriers to prehabilitation implementation and assess the readiness of the healthcare system. An exploratory qualitative study using semi-structured interviews was conducted with eight purposively sampled stakeholders representing anaesthesiology (n=2), surgery (n=2), outpatient cardiology (n=1), clinical psychology (n=1), physiotherapy (n=1), and health insurance administration (n=1). Interviews conducted between February and March 2024 were analysed using descriptive thematic content analysis and mapped to the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. Six themes emerged: attitudes towards prehabilitation, work environment, healthcare system structure, economic factors, cultural factors, and politics, evidence, and guidelines. Despite unanimous recognition of clinical value, knowledge of prehabilitation varied widely. Critical barriers included the structural and financial separation between inpatient and outpatient sectors, the absence of reimbursement mechanisms, workforce shortages, organisational inertia, and limited advocacy by professional societies. Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research mapping identified barriers across all five domains, with outer setting barriers-particularly fragmented financing and the absence of national guidelines-being the most prominent. These exploratory findings reveal conceptual, systemic, and cultural barriers to prehabilitation in Austria. The simultaneous absence of integrated financing, professional society advocacy, and coordinated governance may explain Austria's particularly limited uptake compared to that in the UK and the Netherlands. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation through larger-scale qualitative studies, quantitative surveys, and pilot implementation trials that include patient perspectives and economic modelling.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103250.abstract: Cancer incidence is rising among young adults in several high-income countries, yet comprehensive data from Southern Europe, particularly Portugal, remain limited. We characterized temporal trends in cancer incidence among young adults (20-49 years) in Portugal between 2001 and 2022, comparing them with older adults (≥50 years). This nationwide population-based cohort study included 1,102,774 incident cancer cases recorded by the Portuguese National Cancer Registry. Age-standardized incidence rates (ASIR) per 100,000 inhabitants were calculated using the European Standard Population. Temporal trends were analysed using joinpoint regression, estimating annual percentage changes (APC) and average annual percentage changes (AAPC) by sex, age group, and cancer type. Cancer cases increased from 36,604 in 2001 to 60,926 in 2022. Young adults accounted for 13.0% of all cases. Among young women, ASIR increased by 31.6% (from 156.2 to 205.6; AAPC: +1.48%), driven largely by breast cancer (+50.0%), thyroid (+94.1%), melanoma (+84.1%), and lung cancer (+78.7%). In contrast, young men showed stable overall ASIR (AAPC: -0.05%), with a biphasic pattern of increase (2001-2010) followed by decline (2010-2022). However, young men experienced substantial rises in colorectal (+56.6%), thyroid (+185.1%), and melanoma (+70.1%) incidence, alongside declines in stomach (-67.0%), oesophageal (-56.8%), and lung (-45.8%) cancers. Older adults demonstrated significant ASIR increases driven by trends before 2011, with subsequent stabilization or decline. Cancer incidence among young Portuguese adults is increasing, particularly among women, with sex-specific and site-specific patterns. While declines in tobacco-related cancers reflect successful prevention efforts, rising rates of breast, colorectal, thyroid, and melanoma in young adults signal the need for enhanced targeted prevention strategies and continued etiological research.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103251.abstract: The five-year relative survival (RS) for cervical cancer in Puerto Rico and the United States (US) is less than 70%. To assess survival trends in the past decades, we compared the five-year RS of cervical cancer in Puerto Rico and in the US. Data was obtained from the Puerto Rico Central Cancer Registry and the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program. We included microscopically confirmed cases of cervical carcinoma between 2000 and 2021. The five-year RS trends were analyzed with Joinpoint regression models using the JPSurv software, which estimated the Average Absolute Change in Survival (AAC_S). Puerto Rico showed a lower five-year RS than US overall across the study period. In the US, the AAC_S was -0.78 for patients diagnosed between 2000 and 2003 (95%CI: -1.32 to -0.23), -0.22 for 2003-2013 (95%CI: -0.36 to -0.08), and 0.25 for 2013-2021 (95%CI: 0.01-0.49). In Puerto Rico, the AAC_S was -0.03 for 2000-2011 (95%CI: -0.56-0.51), 1.71 for 2011-2016 (95%CI: 0.60-2.83), and -1.10 for 2016-2021 (95%CI: -3.12-0.92). Puerto Rico shows poorer cervical cancer five-year RS than the US. Increased five-year RS was observed in the US overall population after 2013. In Puerto Rico, improvements in five-year RS were observed after 2011, but these were halted after 2016. This finding may suggest that barriers to accessing care during periods of extreme events, such as the convergence of the 2017 hurricanes and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic challenges, likely affected survival trends from 2016 to 2021. Future research should further characterize barriers to improve cervical cancer survival.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103252.abstract: The burden of second primary cancers (SPCs) is rising, partly because patients with a first cancer now survive longer. Two metrics coexist to quantify SPC risk: cumulative incidence, whose dependence on survival is well recognised, and the standardized incidence ratio (SIR), widely treated as survival-robust because it accounts for person-years at risk. Calendar-era SIR trends are increasingly reported and interpreted as real changes in risk, yet whether such trends could instead arise artefactually from concurrent gains in index-cancer survival has never been tested. We combined a calibrated simulation with an empirical analysis of SEER 17 (2000-2023). The simulation generated cohorts with strictly constant, stage-specific SPC risk, allowing only index-cancer 12-month survival to vary according to SEER-measured values, and applied a 12-month latency exclusion reproducing the SEER*Stat multiple-primary SIR procedure. Empirically, across 27 site × stage strata spanning wide survival-gain gradients, we related the observed 12-month survival gain (2004-09 vs 2015-18) to the calendar-year slope of the SPC SIR (Poisson regression), with six sensitivity analyses and a power calculation. At constant stage-specific risk, the simulated SIR drifted with survival, but across 200 Monte-Carlo replications the median bias-attributable slope was more than an order of magnitude smaller than the observed SIR slope (0.28 vs 7.9 × 10⁻³ per year), despite per-stage SIRs differing enough for the mechanism to act. Empirically, survival gain and SIR slope were unrelated (Pearson r = -0.00, p = 0.99), robust across all sensitivity analyses; power was adequate to detect r ≥ 0.50. Survivor-recomposition bias in the SPC SIR exists in principle but was small on average in the sites and calendar period studied. Unlike cumulative incidence, the SIR can generally be interpreted across calendar eras without major survival correction, although weak, site-specific, or longer-term effects cannot be excluded.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103253.abstract: Breast cancer treatment, commonly involving chemo- and/or radiotherapy, is associated with adverse cardiac effects, including cardiac dysfunction. While most research focuses on adverse effects during treatment, breast cancer survivors may also be at risk of developing cardiac dysfunction ≥ 5 years post-treatment. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of cardiac dysfunction in long-term female breast cancer survivors. CINAHL, Embase, and MEDLINE were systematically searched for articles that included breast cancer survivors treated with chemo- and/or radiotherapy and measured left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≥ 5 years post-diagnosis. The pooled prevalence of cardiac dysfunction, defined as LVEF ≤ 54% or a decline in LVEF of > 10% compared to baseline, was calculated and presented in a forest plot. Subgroup analyses based on treatment modality were performed, along with additional explorative forest plots to explore heterogeneity. Twenty-three studies encompassing 7309 patients were included with a median follow-up time since diagnosis of 5-30 years; Four studies included patients all treated with radiotherapy, of which two studies with radiotherapy as monotherapy and twenty studies included patients all treated with chemotherapy in combination with other therapies. Prevalence of cardiac dysfunction varied from 0% to 30%,. The pooled prevalence was estimated to be 10.8%, with significant heterogeneity (I² = 92.4%). Visual exploration of stratified analysis did not indicate explanations for this heterogeneity. Prevalence of cardiac dysfunction appears to be higher among long-term breast cancer survivors compared to the general population. Long-term breast cancer survivors remain at risk of cardiac dysfunction years after treatment, supporting the integration of cardiovascular risk assessment into survivorship care.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103254.abstract: Experimental studies suggest that thyroid hormones may influence tumor development through endocrine and cellular signaling pathways. Although malignant melanoma (MM) is primarily associated with ultraviolet radiation exposure, the potential role of thyroid dysfunction in melanoma development remains unclear. We investigated the association between hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism and the rate of MM in a nationwide cohort of Danish women. Our cohort comprised 1,058,939 women born between January 1, 1960, and December 31, 1997, and was followed from 1996 to 2022. Information on thyroid disease, MM diagnoses, covariates and follow-up was obtained from Danish nationwide registries. Cox proportional hazards models with attained age as the underlying scale were used to estimate Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Analyses were stratified by time since diagnosis, menopausal status and histological subtype. Hyperthyroidism was not associated with the rate of overall MM (HR: 0.94; 95% CI: 0.79-1.12). For hypothyroidism, the HR for overall MM was 0.89 (95% CI: 0.77-1.02). Estimates for superficial spreading MM were similar. Among women diagnosed with hypothyroidism within the past 10 years, the HR for superficial spreading MM was 0.80 (95% CI: 0.66-0.98). Stratification by menopausal status did not materially alter the associations. Our findings do not provide clear evidence of an association between thyroid dysfunction and the rate of MM in women. The observed decreased rate of superficial spreading MM among women with hypothyroidism within 10 years of diagnosis should be interpreted cautiously, as it was the only statistically significant finding among multiple subgroup analyses and may represent a chance finding. Further studies incorporating detailed clinical and biochemical measures of thyroid function are warranted.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103255.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. However, comprehensive population-level data describing etiologic patterns, treatment exposure, healthcare utilisation, and survival remain limited in many countries. This study aimed to characterise the national burden, care patterns, and outcomes of HCC in Turkey. We performed a nationwide, real-world analysis of adult patients diagnosed with HCC between 2016 and 2024 using administrative health data. Cases were identified by an administrative case definition requiring at least three separate records of ICD-10 codes C22, C22.0, or C22.9; at least one C22.0 code was not required, so HCC could not be confirmed at the individual level. Baseline comorbidities were restricted to conditions recorded on or before the date of diagnosis. Demographic characteristics, underlying liver disease, etiologic factors, treatment exposure, and the level and type of diagnosing institution were assessed. Overall survival (OS) was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. To reduce immortal-time bias, treatment exposure was analysed in a three-month landmark cohort; because treatment dates were unavailable, this reduces but does not eliminate the bias. Multivariable Cox regression was performed within the same cohort. A total of 13,674 patients (64.6% male; median age 64 years, IQR 55-73) were included, of whom 61.4% had died at the data cutoff; median follow-up was 53.0 months. The median OS was 13.2 months (95% CI 12.1-14.5), with 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS of 50.9%, 41.1%, and 36.9%; because patients dying before three qualifying records accumulated could not enter the cohort, these estimates apply to patients meeting the case-identification algorithm and are likely to overstate population survival. OS was markedly longer in women than in men (median 50.9 vs 8.2 months), and longer in patients without cirrhosis recorded at diagnosis than in those with cirrhosis (18.5 vs 9.0 months; both P < 0.001). Hepatitis B was the most frequently recorded specific etiology (29.4%); among mutually exclusive categories, NAFLD-associated HCC had the most favourable survival (5-year OS 61.0%) and alcohol-related HCC the least (median 8.8 months), while HBV-HDV co-infection was associated with longer survival than HBV mono-infection (58.2 vs 12.0 months; P < 0.001), a difference that persisted after adjustment for age, sex, and cirrhosis; no specific etiology could be assigned in 56.1% of patients. Sensitivity analyses restricting etiologic ascertainment to codes recorded within 3 months before to 3 months after diagnosis, or incorporating viral serology, attenuated the survival of the specific viral etiologies, indicating survival-dependent ascertainment. In a multivariable Cox model fitted in the three-month landmark cohort (n = 8958), older age, male sex, cirrhosis, and systemic therapy were associated with higher mortality (all P < 0.001), with time-varying associations for age, cirrhosis, and systemic therapy. The association of local therapy with mortality was not constant over follow-up (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.72-0.85 during 0-24 months after the landmark and 1.22, 1.04-1.43 thereafter); the overall association was no longer evident after liver transplantation was excluded from the local-therapy category. Care was highly centralised within secondary and tertiary institutions. In this nationwide analysis, HCC in Turkey was characterised by limited OS and pronounced sex-based disparities, with survival differing by cirrhosis status and recorded etiology; etiologic ascertainment was itself survival-dependent, so these contrasts describe recorded categories. Hepatitis B was the most frequently recorded specific etiology, underscoring the continued importance of HBV prevention, screening, and surveillance, while HCV, HDV, alcohol-related and metabolic liver disease accounted for smaller recorded proportions; temporal trends in etiology were not analysed. Because tumour stage and liver function were unavailable, the treatment-survival associations are descriptive and subject to confounding by indication. Efforts focused on HBV control, earlier detection, risk-based surveillance of patients with cirrhosis, and improved referral pathways may improve population-level outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103256.abstract: We assessed contemporaneous changes in gastric adenocarcinoma incidence, presentation, registry-recorded treatment, and survival. Two complementary analyses used Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) 17 data. Incidence during 2000-2023 was analyzed using Joinpoint regression. A clinical cohort diagnosed during 2004-2023 at prespecified stomach subsites (C16.1-C16.6, C16.8, and C16.9) was compared across four periods. Surgery trends were decomposed into stage-composition and within-stage components. Outcomes included overall survival (OS), cause-specific survival (CSS), and 36-month restricted mean survival time (RMST); adjusted Cox models separately summarized associations over 0-60 months. The clinical cohort comprised 66,391 tumor records from 66,025 patients. Incidence declined during 2000-2019 (annual percent change, -1.32%; 95% CI, -1.61% to -1.08%) and increased during 2019-2023 (4.96%; 95% CI, 2.51-9.91%). Comparing 2004-2008 with 2019-2023, distant-stage disease increased from 36.1% to 43.0%, whereas surgery among records with known surgery status decreased from 51.9% to 36.3%. Stage-composition change represented 25.7% of the surgery decline. Recorded chemotherapy increased from 35.7% to 54.4%. Median potential follow-up was 206.0 versus 27.4 months; latest-period fixed-time estimates were reported at 12 and 36 months. Three-year OS increased from 25.2% to 29.1% and CSS from 31.4% to 35.6%. Unadjusted 36-month RMST differences were 1.80 months (95% CI, 1.47-2.15) for OS and 1.86 months (95% CI, 1.53-2.22) for CSS. Distant-stage presentation became more frequent while recorded surgery declined and short-term survival improved modestly. Within-stage changes represented most of the surgery decline. Additional registry years are needed to assess persistence of the post-2019 incidence increase.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103260.abstract: Mesothelioma mortality continues to reflect asbestos exposure because of its long latency. While previous Spanish studies focused primarily on pleural disease, this study assessed mesothelioma mortality across the ICD-10 C45 category in Spain from 1999 to 2024. A population-based time-trend study was conducted using mortality data (ICD-10 C45) from the Spanish National Statistics Institute. Age-standardised mortality rates (ASMRs) were calculated using the 2013 European Standard Population. Temporal trends and sex-specific parallelism were evaluated using Joinpoint regression. Among 9733 recorded mesothelioma deaths (7311 men, 2422 women), ASMRs were consistently higher in men, although temporal trends were parallel by sex. Overall mortality increased until 2016 (annual percentage change [APC] 2.3%, 95% CI 1.5-3.0) and subsequently declined non-significantly, yielding an average annual percentage change (AAPC) of 1.0% (95% CI 0.2-1.7) for 1999-2024. Pleural mortality increased until 2011 before declining non-significantly, whereas recorded peritoneal mortality increased throughout the study period (AAPC 2.0%, 95% CI 0.7-3.2). Deaths coded as unspecified site (C45.9) showed the largest increase in ASMR (AAPC 2.1%, 95% CI 1.1-3.1) and accounted for 43.5% of male and 31.8% of female mesothelioma deaths in 2024. Absolute mesothelioma deaths increased in Spain while age-standardised rates attenuated after 2016. The continued increase in recorded peritoneal mortality and the substantial contribution of unspecified-site deaths indicate that surveillance should not rely solely on pleural mesothelioma, highlighting the need for comprehensive monitoring of the complete ICD-10 C45 category and improved anatomical classification.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103264.abstract: Head and neck cancer (HNC) imposes a substantial burden in Aotearoa New Zealand (AoNZ), yet contemporary population-level data on incidence and early mortality across sociodemographic groups remain limited. This population-based retrospective cohort study used New Zealand Cancer Registry to identify all primary HNC diagnoses from 2009 to 2020 (n = 6980). The cases were classified according to ICD-10 subsites. Incidence rates (IRs), age-standardised IRs, and age-standardised rate ratios were estimated by age, sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic deprivation, and rurality. Regression models were used to estimate annual percentage change in IRs and to estimate adjusted risk ratios for two-year all-cause mortality. In total 6980 people were diagnosed with HNC; an overall incidence rate of 13.5 per 100,000 person-years (PY). Oropharyngeal cancer (OPC), the most common subsite, increased from 3.4 per 100,000 PY in 2009-2011-4.9 per 100,000 PY in 2018-2020, whereas IRs for oral cavity cancer (OCC), the second most common, were more stable. HNC IRs were higher among males, older adults, Māori, Pacific Peoples and people living in the most socioeconomically deprived areas, with subsite-specific differences: Māori experienced higher OPC incidence rates, while Pacific Peoples experienced higher OCC IRs. Within two years of diagnosis, 25.2% of patients had died. Two-year all-cause mortality was 44.4% for hypopharyngeal cancer, 30.9% for OCC, and 22.7% for OPC. Among people diagnosed with HNC, after adjusting for available sociodemographic factors and treatment timing, two-year all-cause mortality was higher for Māori, Pacific Peoples, and those in the most deprived quintile. Rurality showed no consistent association with incidence or two-year mortality. These findings indicate an OPC-driven shift in HNC epidemiology in AoNZ and a persistent inequitable burden of both disease occurrence and early mortality, supporting stronger surveillance and equity-focused cancer-control responses.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218859.abstract: Metal ions serve as key regulators of the dynamic equilibrium within the tumor microenvironment (TME). In recent years, the TME has emerged as a central regulatory hub for tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis; its complexity has become both a frontier and a major challenge in oncology research. Current therapies are often constrained by immune tolerance, metabolic heterogeneity, and microenvironment-mediated escape mechanisms, necessitating breakthroughs in novel targets and strategies. Metal ions, functioning as enzyme cofactors, signaling molecules, and redox regulators, profoundly affect tumor progression by modulating redox homeostasis, immune responses, and metabolic reprogramming. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in metal ion-mediated regulation of the TME. It focuses on elucidating the multidimensional mechanisms by which metal ions facilitate immunogenic remodeling and metabolic interactions, and prospectively explores innovative metal-ion-based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. It further highlights the potential of personalized metal metabolomics to advance precision oncology and facilitate the clinical translation of metal ion-based theranostic strategies.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218861.abstract: Tumor drug resistance is still the core obstacle limiting the long-term benefit of modern anticancer therapy, especially in the context of treatment tolerance, persistence of minimal residual disease (MRD) and recurrence after treatment. Increasing evidence has shown that therapy-associated myeloid niches can involve cell recruitment, enrichment of pre-existing populations, or state reprogramming, together with local relationships among myeloid cells, tumor cells, stroma, vessels, and other immune cells. These niches can support residual tumor-cell survival, immune escape, local regrowth, and distant dissemination through overlapping mechanisms linking fibrotic exclusion and perivascular organization with hypoxic metabolic suppression and myeloid replenishment. The formation of neutrophil extracellular traps, failure of antigen uptake and presentation, impaired T-cell priming, and phagocytic escape can further sustain treatment tolerance. Focusing on the myeloid cell state and common molecular circuits, this article presents an evidence assessment framework that interprets spatial and clinical associations alongside functional and pharmacologic findings without assigning hierarchical ranks. It summarizes lessons from clinical failure, considering potentially limited target contributions, compensatory pathways, inadequate exposure, and toxicity, while distinguishing drug exposure and local pharmacodynamic changes from clinical benefit. Candidate biomarkers, intervention windows, and selective delivery approaches require validation to guide mechanism-matched combinations. In the future, longitudinal tissue analyses, functional validation, and prospective studies should test whether these combinations provide durable benefit with acceptable safety in defined patient populations and treatment settings.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218879.abstract: Prolonged colonic inflammation and ulcerative colitis lead to colon cancer. The rapid growth and treatment-resistant nature of these tumors are primarily influenced by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which is led by tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). However, factors influencing or regulating the immunosuppressive nature of TAMs have not been sufficiently studied. In this manuscript, we use a mouse model of colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CRC) to demonstrate that WNT expression in TAMs regulates their immunosuppressive function by inhibiting Glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) within the macrophages, possibly through an autofeedback loop. GSK3β is a positive regulator of PD-1 and PD-L1 expression in macrophages and promotes an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Therefore, GSK-3β inhibition alters the immunosuppressive nature of the immune microenvironment and effectively controls tumor growth. In Csf1r.iCre; Porcnfl/fl mice, the absence of macrophage-derived WNT promotes tumor growth in the model of colitis-associated colon cancer. Absence of macrophage-derived WNT stabilizes GSK-3β in macrophages and promotes an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. We also show that pharmacological inhibition of GSK-3β in a macrophage-specific manner, achieved by systemic delivery of a lipo-GSK3β inhibitor, effectively inhibits tumor growth. Therefore, this manuscript demonstrates for the first time that the macrophage-specific modulation of GSK3β can be a potential target to treat colitis-associated colon cancer.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218880.abstract: Sensitive biomarkers for recurrence risk stratification, recurrence surveillance and adjuvant therapy guidance are of unmet need for patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) undergoing liver transplantation (LT). Herein, we explored the potential of profiling circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for prediction and prevention of recurrence in HCC after LT. HCC patients (n=91) who underwent LT were prospectively enrolled. ctDNA was assayed using next-generation sequencing from perioperative plasma (n=408). Associations between ctDNA status with clinicopathological parameters, tumor recurrence, and adjuvant treatment effect were analyzed. Higher preoperative ctDNA burden correlated with microvascular invasion (median: 45.0 vs 5.1 MTM/mL, P=0.003) and recurrence (156.2 vs 7.7 MTM/mL, P<0.001). ctDNA clearance was noted in 87.7% patients after LT and patients who kept positive postoperative ctDNA showed higher recurrence risk (HR=8.86, P<0.001), especially early recurrence (within 1 year; 75.0% vs 10.1%, P<0.001). During follow-up, positive longitudinal ctDNA was similarly predictive of recurrence (HR=36.50, P<0.001). The AUC of longitudinal ctDNA for predicting recurrence was 0.930-significantly higher than alpha-fetoprotein (0.655, P<0.001). Longitudinal ctDNA detected radiologically evidenced recurrence with a median lead time of 5.1 months compared to standard-of-care surveillance. Among patients who received adjuvant therapy, those with positive postoperative ctDNA could benefit (HR=0.11, P=0.003) and those with decreased ctDNA burden following treatment experienced longer interval from ctDNA positivity to recurrence (HR=0.17, P=0.006). Serial ctDNA analysis demonstrates strong prognostic value, capable of heralding tumor recurrence prior to radiological recurrence and measuring treatment efficacy. Its integration into clinical practice of HCC provides unique opportunities for adjuvant therapy decision-making following LT.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218884.abstract: Immunotherapy has improved outcomes for patients with breast cancer, yet therapeutic resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Therefore, we integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data from breast cancer cohorts treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors to identify resistance-associated cellular populations and pathways, with validation across eight independent bulk RNA-seq immunotherapy cohorts. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) were isolated from anti-PD-1-resistant breast tumors for functional studies, including in vitro co-culture and in vivo models. Mitochondrial function and metabolic alterations were assessed by flow cytometry, transmission electron microscopy, ATP and adenosine quantification, and JC-1 staining. Tumor mitochondrial metabolism was markedly upregulated in anti-PD-1 non-responders and consistently associated with poor therapeutic response across validation cohorts. MDK-expressing CAFs were enriched in resistant tumors, exhibited strong interactions with tumor cells, and were negatively associated with intratumoral CD8+ T cell infiltration. Single-cell source contribution and depletion analyses identified CAF-derived MDK as the major paracrine mediator linking stromal signaling to tumor metabolic adaptation and immune suppression. Mechanistically, MDK activated SDC1-dependent PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling in cancer cells, promoting mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming, ATP production, and CD38/CD73-dependent extracellular adenosine accumulation, thereby suppressing CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity. Receptor-depletion experiments further identified SDC1 as the principal functional receptor mediating these effects. Importantly, CAF-specific MDK depletion or pharmacological MDK inhibition enhanced anti-PD-1 efficacy and restored CD8+ T cell effector activity in vivo. Collectively, MDK+ CAFs facilitate anti-PD-1 resistance via mitochondrial rewiring and adenosine-mediated immunosuppression, supporting the MDK-SDC1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for overcoming resistance and improving immunotherapy efficacy in breast cancer.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218886.abstract: The Merlin protein, encoded by the tumor suppressor gene Neurofibromatosis type II (NF2), serves as a linker between the actin cytoskeleton, the plasma membrane receptors, and other intracellular signaling molecules. While there is a basic understanding of how Merlin regulates oncogenic signaling pathways, current targeted therapies have yet to demonstrate consistent clinical efficacy. Using a library of protein kinase inhibitors, we found that NF2-null Schwann cells (SCs) were uniquely sensitive to prexasertib, a drug that targets the DNA damage response pathway kinases CHK1/2 (Checkpoint Kinase 1 and 2). NF2-null SC proliferation was also sensitive to small molecule inhibitors of CHK1/2 downstream effectors. At baseline, NF2-null SCs have increased RAC1 activity, elevated levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and higher levels of DNA damage. Exposing NF2-null SCs to DNA damaging agents such as doxorubicin or carboplatin, alone or in combination with prexasertib, further decreased their proliferation. Consistent with this idea, suppressing RAC1 or NOX2 activity with small molecule inhibitors, decreased ROS production and restored resistance to prexasertib in NF2-null hSCs, suggesting that active RAC1 and high ROS render NF2-null hSC uniquely vulnerable to DNA damage. Furthermore, restoring NF2 expression in NF2-null Schwann cells restored their resistance to prexasertib, reduced RAC1 activity, and lowered levels of ROS and DNA damage. The intrinsic elevation of RAC1, ROS, and DNA damage in NF2-null hSCs suggest that inhibiting DNA damage response pathways might be clinically useful in patients with NF2-null schwannomas.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218888.abstract: Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is a telomerase-independent telomere maintenance mechanism that supports the growth of approximately 5-10% of human tumors and represents an attractive but insufficiently explored therapeutic target. CRISPR-based functional genomics has emerged as a powerful approach to systematically interrogate ALT biology and identify genetic dependencies associated with the ALT state. In this Review, we discuss the CRISPR-based strategies applied to ALT, including hypothesis-driven targeted loss-of-function screens, phenotype-driven optical screens, in silico mining of large-scale dependency datasets, and genome-wide screens in ALT-adjacent states. Across these approaches, recurrent dependencies converge on pathways mediating replication stress buffering, DNA repair, and telomere maintenance, including FANCM, SMARCAL1, and SUB1. Collectively, these findings support a model in which ALT-positive cells rely not on a unique ALT-specific factor, but rather on stress-buffering mechanisms that prevent chronic telomeric dysfunction from triggering replication catastrophe and cell death, highlighting these pathways as promising candidates for further therapeutic investigation.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218889.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is driven by cancer stemness and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which collectively contribute to therapeutic resistance. While the RNA-binding protein HNRNPC has been implicated in tumor progression, it has primarily been characterized as a downstream effector, and its autonomous regulatory functions, particularly in governing cancer stemness, remain entirely unexplored. Through multi-omics analyses of HCC cohorts, we identified HNRNPC as a pivotal driver of a high-risk molecular subtype. Mechanistically, HNRNPC expression was transcriptionally activated via WDR5/KMT2A complex-mediated deposition of H3K4me3 at its promoter. Functionally, HNRNPC was essential for maintaining cancer stemness, promoting tumor growth and metastasis, and conferring oxaliplatin resistance. Notably, depletion of HNRNPC reprogrammed the immunosuppressive microenvironment by enhancing CD8+ T cell infiltration, reducing T cell exhaustion, and polarizing macrophages toward an M1-like anti-tumor phenotype. At the molecular level, HNRNPC bound to the m6A-modified 3'UTR of CD24 mRNA in an RNP2 motif-dependent manner, thereby enhancing its stability and elevating CD24 protein expression. Therapeutically, we developed a novel lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulating siRNA against HNRNPC. Systemically administered AP-EG-si potently suppressed tumor growth, attenuated stemness, and synergized with anti-PD-L1 therapy to enhance anti-tumor immunity. Our findings thus unveil the H3K4me3-HNRNPC-CD24 axis as a central epigenetic and post-transcriptional regulatory pathway that coordinately drives HCC stemness and immune evasion, nominating HNRNPC-targeted nanotherapy as a promising strategy for advanced HCC.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218890.abstract: Rising incidence of colorectal cancer (CRC) and limited therapeutic options highlight the urgent need to define the drivers of its progression. The SPP1+ tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) subset identified by single-cell transcriptomics is a functionally dominant population that extends beyond the classical M1/M2 paradigm. Here, we dissected the molecular mechanisms by which SPP1+ TAMs reprogram tumor progression and determined whether the gut microbiota regulates this process in colorectal cancer. Using a multi-platform strategy integrating clinical specimens, murine models and CRC cell lines, we found that SPP1+ TAMs increase progressively during CRC evolution and exhibit crosstalk with malignant epithelial cells, and their abundance is associated with adverse clinical outcome. Integrative analysis reveals a significant positive correlation between SPP1 and ARG2 expression. Further, TAM-derived SPP1 engages CD44 on CRC cells to induce ARG2 expression. Mechanistically, ARG2 facilitates the interaction between USP10 and c-Myc to deubiquitinate and stabilize c-Myc, which transactivates the glycolytic enzyme HK2, driving Warburg metabolism that fuels CRC cell proliferation. Moreover, ARG2 secreted by CRC cells is internalized by TAMs, which reciprocally upregulates SPP1, creating a feed-forward loop that drives a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment. Notably, Bifidobacterium longum downregulates CD44 expression on tumor cells, thereby disrupting the SPP1-ARG2 axis and attenuating CRC progression. These findings identify the SPP1-ARG2 circuit as a therapeutic target and propose B. longum as a microbiome-derived precision adjuvant therapy for CRC suppression.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218891.abstract: Although neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT) has improved survival in locally advanced gastric cancer (GC) and gastroesophageal junction cancer (GEJC), lymph node metastasis (LNM) patterns following NICT remain undefined. We aimed to characterize topographical LNM patterns after NICT and evaluate the association between lymphadenectomy extent, surgical approach, and survival outcomes. Data were pooled from 4 prospective clinical trials (NEOSUMMIT-01 - 04), comprising 126 patients with GC (n = 61) or GEJC (n = 65) undergoing curative gastrectomy following NICT. ypN0 was achieved in 71 patients (56%). In GEJC, station No. 3, 7 were high risk; No. 1, 2, 9, and 11 were intermediate risk; and No. 4, 5, 6, 8, 12 were low risk. In GC, station No. 12 was low-risk; D1 stations (No. 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) were high-risk, D1+ stations (No. 8, 9) and No. 11 were intermediate-risk. At a median follow-up of 36.2 months, 24-month EFS and OS rates were 76.4% and 90.5%. Nodal yield (≥ 30 vs. < 30) was not significantly associated with EFS (P = .611) or OS (P = .911). In exploratory comparisons within the GEJC cohort, EFS (P = .219) and OS (P = .290) did not differ significantly between proximal and total gastrectomy. In GEJC, distal perigastric lymph node stations (No. 4, 5, 6, and 12) exhibited low metastasis rates, while exploratory survival outcomes support prospective clinical trials of proximal gastrectomy in appropriately selected patients. Conversely, the broader residual nodal involvement in GC reinforces the continued role of standard D2 lymphadenectomy.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218892.abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is characterized by a highly infiltrated yet immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), in which tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) contribute to disease progression. Here, we identify an extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated LMP1-NF-κB-LIF signaling axis that promotes macrophage reprogramming and immune suppression in NPC. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis revealed that EV exposure induces transcriptional remodeling across tumor and immune-cell populations, accompanied by an increased proportion of TAMs within the myeloid compartment. NPC-derived EVs were taken up by macrophages, where EV-associated LMP1 induced NF-κB activation, LIF expression, and polarization toward an immunosuppressive phenotype. Loss- and gain-of-function studies, together with structure-function analyses of the LMP1 CTAR1/CTAR2 domains, further supported the requirement of these CTAR domains for efficient NF-κB activation and LIF induction. Functionally, EV-educated macrophages exhibited impaired phagocytic activity and promoted inhibitory T-cell responses. In zebrafish, 3D spheroid, and mouse xenograft models, EV-educated macrophages promoted NPC growth and vascular dissemination, whereas blockade of LIF signaling with soluble LIFR attenuated these effects. Tumor LIF expression positively correlated with CTLA4 expression. In NPC tissues, LIF expression was preferentially associated with stromal macrophages, and elevated stromal LIF expression was associated with metastasis, advanced nodal disease, and advanced clinical stage. Stromal immune-cell LMP1 expression also correlated with LIF expression and was higher in patients who developed metastasis. Collectively, these findings support an EV-associated LMP1-NF-κB-LIF axis that links EBV-positive NPC cells to macrophage-mediated immune suppression and tumor progression and provide a basis for further investigating this pathway as a potential therapeutic target.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218893.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) drive the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), promoting oncogenic progression, metastasis and treatment resistance. While we previously established that intratumoral administration of poly(I:C) and R848 (TLR3 and TLR7/8 agonists) has strong therapeutic efficacy and triggers STAT1-mediated TAM reprogramming superior to monotherapies, this study evaluates the translational potential, systemic tolerability and immunological impact of their combined systemic (intravenous) delivery. Across diverse syngeneic murine models of solid tumors, including lung adenocarcinoma, triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), fibrosarcoma and glioblastoma, systemic poly(I:C)+R848 administration significantly inhibited primary tumor growth and spontaneous lung metastasis. The treatment exhibited good tolerability under the conditions tested, with no body weight loss or histopathological damage to major organs. Treatment triggered a transient trend toward elevation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IFN-γ, CXCL10, CCL5), while anti-inflammatory markers (IL-10, IL-4) remained unchanged. In primary tumors, treatment-induced TAM reprogramming was evidenced by upregulated M1-like markers (Irf7, Ccl5) and decreased M2-like markers (Arg1), accompanied by enhanced Cd8 and Cd4 T cell markers and cytotoxic effectors (Prf-1 and Gzmb). Multispectral immunophenotyping confirmed this shift toward an antitumor macrophage phenotype, characterized by increased CD86 and decreased ARG1 across all primary tumors. Furthermore, treatment significantly prevented lung metastasis and tumor-induced splenomegaly, shifting splenic macrophages toward an elevated M1/M2 ratio in both fibrosarcoma and TNBC models. These findings demonstrate that intravenous administration of the poly(I:C)+R848 combination effectively reprograms TAMs, suppressing tumor progression and preventing metastasis across a variety of preclinical models of difficult-to-treat solid tumors.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218894.abstract: Atovaquone is an approved antimalarial drug which could sensitise tumours to radiation and may modulate tumour immune microenvironment. Here we evaluated the triple combination of radiation with atovaquone plus anti-PD-L1 in HNSCC syngeneic mouse tumour models. We observed significant tumour growth delay induced by the triple combination treatment with differential responses in three different mouse models. There was complete tumour eradication in 6 of 12 mice in the MOCL1 model but not in the other two murine models. The triple combination was associated with increased populations of CD8+-T Granzyme B+ cells as well as decreased populations of Tregs, CD11b+Gr1+ granulocytic MDSCs and CD11b+ Ly.6G+ neutrophils. Atovaquone inhibited EGFR and its downstream signalling as well as reduced PD-L1 expression. The differential antitumour effects of the triple combination may be due to different basal and post-treatment levels of PD-L1, pERK1/2 and pS6, in particular, their levels were reduced by atovaquone +/- RT in MOCL1 models and not in the other two murine models. Radiotherapy plus atovaquone combination increased cell cycle arrest in G2/M phase, which led to inhibition of DNA damage repair by homologous recombination and increased cell death. We also observed increased activation of CD8+-T cells that led to enhanced killing in our HNSCC patient-derived organoid models treated with the triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. Overall, our results suggest that the triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade has the potential to increase the efficacy of radiotherapy and/or immunotherapy. Thus, this may provide a rationale to further validate this triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in clinical trials to improve treatment outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218895.abstract: Antiapoptotic buffering in solid tumors is generally mediated by both BCLXL and MCL1, so that BH3 mimetic drugs targeting only one have limited efficacy. To identify agents that may sensitize tumors to BH3 mimetics targeting BCLXL, we screened prostate cancer cells against a panel of mitochondria-targeted drugs in combination with navitoclax, a BH3 mimetic targeting BCL2 and BCLXL. Homoharringtonine (HHT) in combination with navitoclax and as a single agent emerged as a potent inducer of apoptosis. HHT has been identified as an inhibitor of protein translation, and proteomic analysis showed broad suppression of translation-related pathways, while immunoblotting demonstrated rapid decreases in short-lived proteins, including MCL1. HHT dose response and time course studies showed marked declines in MCL1 within 2 hours that were associated with apoptosis in response to BCLXL inhibition with navitoclax or A1331852. Further cell viability assays showed synergy between HHT and BCLXL inhibitors in multiple prostate, lung, and colorectal cancer cell lines. HHT monotherapy in vivo caused tumor regression in two prostate cancer xenograft models. Analysis of tumor tissue taken at 4 hours after dosing showed decreases in MCL1 and MYC, indicating that HHT levels obtainable in vivo are adequate to deplete short-lived proteins and potentially sensitize to BH3 mimetics targeting BCLXL. These findings support further exploration of HHT as a single agent in solid tumors and establish a rationale for investigating safer, tumor-selective approaches to combine HHT-mediated translational inhibition with BCLXL targeting.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218896.abstract: Reciprocal interactions between immune and stromal cells are increasingly recognized as major determinants of colorectal cancer (CRC) progression. However, the specific macrophage and fibroblast states cooperating to establish and sustain a tumor-promoting microenvironment remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify a self-reinforcing inflammatory circuit linking monocyte-derived IL-1β+ macrophages with IL1R1+ cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in CRC. Integrated single-cell transcriptomic analyses of human CRC revealed a marked expansion of IL1B-associated inflammatory macrophages and IL1R1+ inflammatory CAFs, with their respective and combined transcriptional signatures associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Pseudotime analysis and Ms4a3 lineage tracing supported a predominantly monocyte-derived origin of IL-1β+ macrophages in the tumor microenvironment. Mechanistically, macrophage-derived IL-1β activated IL1R1 signaling in fibroblasts, promoting the acquisition and expansion of an inflammatory CAF state. Myeloid Il1b deletion or fibroblast-lineage Il1r1 deletion disrupted this interaction and suppressed tumor growth in vivo. In turn, IL1R1+ CAFs produced abundant CCL2, which recruited CCR2+ monocytes and replenished the IL-1β+ macrophage population. Fibroblast-lineage Ccl2 deletion, myeloid Ccr2 deletion, and CCL2 rescue experiments established the functional requirement of the CCL2-CCR2 axis for closure of this reciprocal circuit. Acquisition of the IL-1β+ inflammatory macrophage program was further supported by coordinated NF-κB and AP-1 activity, with RELA and JUN/FOS contributing to IL1B transcriptional regulation. Finally, therapeutic blockade of either IL-1β or CCL2 disrupted the macrophage-CAF circuit, increased intratumoral CD8+ T-cell responses, and enhanced the antitumor efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy. Collectively, our findings establish the IL-1β-IL1R1-CCL2-CCR2 axis as a self-amplifying immune-stromal circuit that sustains a tumor-promoting and immunosuppressive microenvironment in CRC. By demonstrating that disruption of this circuit restores antitumor immune activity and sensitizes tumors to PD-1 blockade, our study provides a mechanistic and preclinical rationale for targeting IL-1β-CCL2-mediated macrophage-CAF crosstalk as a combination strategy to improve immunotherapy responses in CRC.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218900.abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) remains a major cause of cancer mortality, yet the metabolic mechanisms that remodel metastatic RNA-splicing programs are poorly defined. Here, integrated quantitative proteomics and lysine 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation (Khib) proteomics of patient-matched normal mucosa, primary CRCs, and liver metastases revealed a progressive increase in global Khib, with enrichment on RNA-splicing proteins. Serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 9 (SRSF9) emerged as a Khib-modified splicing factor whose expression and K155 Khib levels increased from normal tissue to primary tumors and liver metastases. Gain and loss of function studies in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, subcutaneous xenografts, and splenic injection liver metastasis models showed that SRSF9 promotes proliferation, invasion, tumor growth, and liver colonization. Mechanistically, K155 Khib stabilized SRSF9 protein; the K155R mutation accelerated degradation and abolished SRSF9-driven malignant phenotypes. KAT7 and SIRT6 act as regulators of Khib modification, which positively and negatively modulate the K155 Khib modification of SRSF9, respectively. SRSF9 bound CD44 pre-mRNA through its RRM1 domain and promoted alternative splicing toward the oncogenic CD44V8-10 isoform, which was elevated in patient tumors and metastases and rescued the impaired proliferation and metastatic capacity caused by SRSF9 loss. Finally, a CD44V8-10-targeting antisense oligonucleotide suppressed CRC growth and liver metastasis in preclinical models. These findings define a KAT7/SIRT6-regulated Khib-SRSF9-CD44V8-10 axis that couples metabolic acylation to metastatic splicing and nominate CD44V8-10 as a therapeutic vulnerability in CRC liver metastasis.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218901.abstract: The specific mechanisms of Verbascoside (VB) in ovarian cancer (OC) remain insufficient. This study aimed to explore the anti-tumor mechanisms of VB in OC, focusing on its ability to modulate the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), particularly through targeting neutrophil infiltration and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). The anti-tumor and anti-NETosis efficacy of VB was evaluated in vivo using subcutaneous, orthotopic, and pulmonary metastasis mouse models of OC. Microproteomics and bioinformatics analysis identified the direct molecular target of VB and the key neutrophil chemoattractant. The underlying mechanisms were validated in vitro and in vivo (using SKOV3, ID8, and neutrophils), alongside loss-of-function approaches. The combination of VB with anti-PD-1 immunotherapy was also assessed. VB inhibited OC proliferation/metastasis, promoted anti-tumor immunity, and suppressed neutrophil infiltration and NETosis. Neutrophil depletion attenuated VB's anti-metastatic effect. Microproteomics and bioinformatics screening identified IRAK4 as a direct molecular target of VB and CXCL5 as a key neutrophil chemoattractant. SPR confirmed the direct binding between VB and IRAK4, and molecular docking revealed specific hydrogen bond interactions. Mechanistically, VB treatment or IRAK4 knockdown suppressed CXCL5 expression, and consequently reduced neutrophil infiltration and NETosis. Consistently, CXCL5 overexpression abrogated the inhibitory effects of VB on neutrophil NETosis and recruitment. Furthermore, VB synergized with anti-PD-1 therapy, thereby achieving superior tumor growth inhibition, reduced Ki67 expression, and enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration. In conclusion, VB exerts potent anti-tumor effects in OC by targeting the IRAK4/CXCL5 axis, thereby inhibiting neutrophil infiltration and NETosis, reshaping the immunosuppressive TME, and restoring anti-tumor immunity.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218902.abstract: Advanced-stage cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) frequently develops resistance to chemotherapy, highlighting an urgent unmet need for novel therapeutic strategies. Here, we analyzed 16 pairs of CCA and adjacent non-tumor tissues, and demonstrated that dysregulation of the cell cycle machinery is a hallmark of CCA, closely associated with chemoresistance and poor prognosis. Targeting aberrant cell cycle regulation therefore represents a promising approach to improve current treatment outcomes. We identify the CDC7 inhibitor XL413 as an effective agent capable of re-sensitizing gemcitabine-resistant tumors across multiple preclinical models of CCA. Mechanistic analyses, including transcriptomic profiling, reveal that combination therapy activates senescence-associated pathways, with therapeutic efficacy is mediated via a ROS-DNA damage-senescence cascade. Notably, synergistic induction of cellular senescence is observed in CCA cells upon co-treatment with a CDC7 inhibitor and gemcitabine. Collectively, these findings provide robust preclinical evidence supporting the combination of gemcitabine and CDC7 inhibitors as a viable therapeutic strategy to enhance the clinical management of CCA.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218904.abstract: It remains largely unclear whether oncogenic super-enhancers (SEs) can drive expression of circular RNAs (circRNAs). In this study, we for the first time profiled the comprehensive circRNA landscapes of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) after suppressing genome-wide SE activities. We identified a novel SE-driven circPRRC2B, as the product of back-splicing of exons 2, 3, 4 and 5 of PRRC2B pre-mRNA, which was controlled by RNA binding protein HuR. Indeed, SE drives high levels of PRRC2B transcription, promotes production of PRRC2B pre-mRNAs, boosts back-splicing of PRRC2B pre-mRNAs, and elevates circPRRC2B expression. ETS1 acts as a key transcriptional factor in SE-driven PRRC2B transcription and circPRRC2B biogenesis. Interestingly, circPRRC2B, but not PRRC2B, could promote proliferation, invasion and metastasis of ESCC in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, circPRRC2B binds to TALDO1 and enhances BAP1-mediated TALDO1 de-ubiquitination in ESCC cells. Therefore, circPRRC2B stabilizes and sustains high expression of TALDO1, activates the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), elevates the glutathione levels via supplying more NADPH via the PPP, inhibits production of reactive oxygen species in mitochondrion, maintains cellular redox equilibrium, and, thus, leads to cancer progression. Importantly, we developed antisense oligonucleotides targeting circPRRC2B which exhibited remarkable inhibition of ESCC growth. Our findings highlighted circPRRC2B as a key target preserving the PPP metabolic flux and redox homeostasis of malignant cells, thereby offering insight into developing novel therapeutics for cancers.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218905.abstract: While immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized treatment of the patients with aero-upper digestive squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs), including esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), only a subset of patients benefit from ICIs, therefore entailing exploration of the mechanisms to regulate treatment responsiveness. POLE, as a subunit of DNA polymerase ε, possesses 3'-5' proofreading activity, and its mutations have been associated with favourable response to ICIs in several solid tumors. However, post-translational modification (PTM) of POLE and its impact on the therapeutic efficacy of ICIs are unknown. Here, this study demonstrates that ubiquitin-like protein 3 (Ubl3), whose expression is markedly downregulated in SCCs, covalently binds to Pole, reduces nuclear Pole levels, triggers DNA damage, and activates cGAS-STING signaling pathway. Notably, Ubl3 modification of Pole significantly primes the local immune microenvironment to mitigate the growth of murine aero-upper digestive SCC cells and boost the efficacy of αPD-1 treatment in vivo. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis further revealed that UBL3 expression is positively correlated with better clinical outcomes in a cohort of ESCC patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy combined with αPD-1. Together, our findings unravel UBL3 modification as a novel PTM mechanism governing subcellular location of POLE and its influence on immunotherapy responsiveness, thus making UBL3 modification as a promising immunomodulatory approach to enhance immunotherapy efficacy in patients with aero-upper digestive SCCs.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218906.abstract: Cancer is not biologically confined to the tumor bed. Cachexia, fatigue, metabolic dysfunction, circadian disruption, and immune dysfunction reflect disturbances that local models alone cannot fully explain. The brain is well positioned to participate in these processes because it continuously samples circulating signals and coordinates endocrine and autonomic responses. Yet the afferent side of this communication has received less attention than its downstream consequences. Here, we synthesize evidence showing that cytokines, hormones, metabolites, and cargo carried by extracellular vesicles can engage central sensory interfaces and integrative regions, particularly circumventricular organs and hypothalamic and brainstem circuits. We use the term Endocriception to describe afferent humoral sensing and early central decoding of circulating biochemical signals, and focus here on how tumor- and host-associated changes engage this process in cancer. Central neuroendocrine governance refers to the subsequent integration of this information and the generation of autonomic and endocrine outputs. Persistent inflammation, stress, circadian disruption, and impaired feedback may gradually reconfigure this regulatory system. The resulting changes can affect systemic immunity, metabolism, behavior, and host tolerance of cancer. Evidence is strongest for a limited number of pathways, whereas many proposed links remain incomplete or dependent on tumor type and experimental context. We therefore present central neuroendocrine governance as a working framework for organizing current evidence and guiding mechanistic studies, biomarker development, and interventions aimed at restoring host physiology.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218907.abstract: The prognosis for glioblastoma (GBM) is correlated with the extent of resection. Continuous en bloc resection (CEBR) is a surgical strategy that involves the removal of the gross tumor along with its normal adjacent tissue (NAT) as "one whole block". However, its impact on the survival of patients with GBM in non-eloquent areas is unknown. We found that CEBR significantly prolongs both overall survival and progression-free survival in patients with GBM in non-eloquent areas. We further reported that the molecular drivers, transcriptomic abnormalities, and microenvironmental alterations akin to those found in tumors were detected in the NAT. These tumor-like molecular and microenvironmental alterations were predominantly present in the NAT within 10 mm around the tumor, despite the absence of identifiable tumor cells on rigorous histological examination. Overall, CEBR improved survival in patients with GBM in non-eloquent areas, while tumor-like alterations were present in brain tissue adjacent to the tumor. These findings provide the rationale to incorporate NAT into the extent of resection in the CEBR strategy and support further investigation of the association between its resection and patient prognosis.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218908.abstract: Despite durable clinical responses to immunotherapy in a subset of patients, most solid tumors remain refractory owing to an immune-excluded phenotype characterized by limited trafficking, infiltration, and function of effector immune cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Tumor endothelial cells (TECs) function as vascular immune gatekeepers that orchestrate this process. Driven by persistent pro-angiogenic signaling and metabolic stress, TECs establish a multilayered immune barrier through structurally abnormal, poorly perfused vasculature, endothelial anergy, and active immunosuppressive programs. TECs directly suppress effector T-cell and natural killer (NK)-cell function through checkpoint-like ligands, death-ligand pathways, and immunometabolic mechanisms involving adenosine production and tryptophan catabolism. Simultaneously, they recruit, retain, and reprogram immunosuppressive leukocytes, thereby reinforcing immune exclusion and therapeutic resistance. Here, we propose a TEC-centric vascular immune gatekeeping framework and review strategies to reprogram tumor vessels from immune barriers into conduits for effective immune-cell trafficking and activation. We discuss endothelial-directed monotherapies that transiently normalize or reset TEC states, together with combination strategies integrating vascular modulation with immune checkpoint blockade, adoptive and innate immune-cell therapies, cancer vaccines, oncolytic viruses, STING agonists, and multifunctional antibodies. We also highlight key translational considerations, including biomarker-guided patient stratification, pharmacodynamic monitoring using mechanism-based endpoints, and optimization of treatment dose and scheduling within the vascular normalization window. Overall, this review establishes endothelial reprogramming as a central strategy for overcoming vascular immune gatekeeping and provides a mechanistic framework for biomarker-guided vascular-immune combination therapies in solid tumors.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218909.abstract: Tissue normalisation has emerged as an interesting therapeutic concept in oncology, aiming to correct the structural, metabolic, and immunological tissue abnormalities that enable tumour progression and treatment resistance. Rather than targeting cancer cells directly, this approach aims to re-establish homeostatic tissue architecture, immune surveillance, and metabolic balance. Interventions that target stromal components, such as cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), immune cells, or stiffness of extracellular matrix (ECM), have been shown to shift tumour cells toward a less aggressive state, underscoring the plasticity of cancer cells and the importance of their interactions with the microenvironment. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly recognised as both contributors to tissue dysfunction in tumours and promising tools for restoring tissue homeostasis. EVs circulate across most biofluids and can cross biological barriers to reach distant tissues. They naturally carry nucleic acids, including regulatory miRNAs, along with proteins, lipids, and metabolites that influence cell behaviour, making them attractive tools for tissue normalisation. Moreover, engineered EVs could be designed to deliver targeted "normalisation signals" and hold strong clinical potential as next-generation delivery systems. Here, we explore how EVs, whether native or engineered, can intervene in key tumour-driving processes, including senescence, fibrosis, inflammation, and immune evasion, to shift the microenvironment toward a normalised, less malignant state.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218910.abstract: Plasma cholesterol is correlated with worse outcomes in breast and ovarian cancer. Prior work indicates that myeloid immune cells are highly responsive to cholesterol metabolism. Interestingly, Liver Receptor Homolog-1 (LRH-1, or NR5A2), a key transcriptional regulator of cholesterol homeostasis is highly expressed in neutrophils and is associated with increased survival time. However, the roles of LRH-1 within neutrophils remain unclear. We therefore focused on how LRH-1 influences neutrophil behaviors relevant to cancer. Small molecule ligands for LRH-1 regulated neutrophil migration towards cancer cells. Phagocytosis was also regulated by LRH-1 ligands, the extent being dependent on type of bait (e. coli vs. cancer cells). In T cell co-cultures, neutrophils pretreated with an LRH-1 agonist promoted greater T cell expansion, particularly in CD4+ cells, while LRH-1 inhibition suppressed this response. NETosis is a known trigger of recurrence from dormancy and subsequent tumor growth. Importantly LRH-1 activation reduced NETosis, while treatment with an antagonist or inverse agonist enhanced NETosis, likely through altered reactive oxygen species. Treatment of mice with an inverse agonist of LRH-1 increased the growth of mammary tumors in a NET-dependent manner. Mice harboring dormant D2.0R mammary cancer lesions treated with an LRH-1 inverse agonist exhibited earlier tumor recurrence and enhanced metastatic progression. In contrast, treatment with BL001, a small chemical LRH-1 agonist, delayed recurrence in D2.0R-grafted mice. These findings reveal that LRH-1 is a novel regulator of neutrophil-driven immune responses within the tumor microenvironment. LRH-1 is thus a promising therapeutic target to suppress the progression of breast and ovarian cancer.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218911.abstract: Cancer-associated adipocytes (CAAs) are increasingly recognized as active and heterogeneous components of the tumor microenvironment. Initially defined as tumor-adjacent adipocytes characterized by lipid depletion, reduced expression of mature adipocyte markers, and inflammatory activation, CAAs are now understood to encompass a spectrum of context-dependent states. These states are shaped by anatomical location, preexisting adipocyte properties, tumor-derived signals, and therapeutic exposure. Through metabolic exchange, paracrine signaling, direct cell contact, extracellular-vesicle communication, and matrix remodeling, CAAs influence tumor-cell plasticity, metastatic colonization, immune dysfunction, stromal organization, and treatment response. In turn, signals from tumor, immune, and stromal cells continuously reshape adipocyte identity and function, placing CAAs within reciprocal multicellular networks. This review examines the evolving criteria used to identify CAAs, their lineage origins and plasticity, their spatial organization, and their interactions with tumor, immune, and stromal compartments. The contribution of CAAs to therapeutic adaptation is also discussed, together with potential intervention points involving CAA-derived outputs and the metabolic dependencies induced in recipient cells. Finally, major methodological challenges are considered. Adipocyte-resolved profiling, lineage tracing, spatial multiomics, lipid flux analysis, and physiologically relevant models will be needed to distinguish transient remodeling from stable state transitions and to identify context-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218912.abstract: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a highly conserved serine/threonine kinase regarded as an indispensable energy sensor during metabolic stress, coordinating diverse biological processes, including glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, mitochondrial dynamics, and multiple stress-responsive signaling pathways. Growing evidence shows that dysregulated AMPK signaling plays closely linked roles in tumorigenesis. Depending on the context, AMPK signaling can suppress or promote tumor growth. Mechanistically, dysregulated AMPK kinase activity contributes to metabolic reprogramming, mitochondrial dysfunction, and epigenetic alterations, all recognized hallmarks of cancer. Consequently, targeting AMPK signaling has emerged as a promising strategy for cancer therapy. In this review, we summarize the molecular mechanisms regulating AMPK signaling, discuss its dual functions in tumor biology, highlight recent advances in AMPK-targeted therapeutic strategies, and address current challenges and future perspectives for the clinical translation of AMPK-targeted cancer therapy.
