doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106511.abstract: Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is an established biomarker for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, it remains unclear whether biomarkers reflecting amyloid-β metabolism (Aβ), tau (phosphorylated tau, pTau), and astrogliosis (glial fibrillary acidic protein, GFAP) can complement NfL in clinical applications. It is also unclear how Alzheimer's disease (AD) co-pathology affects disease progression in ALS. We studied 264 patients with ALS and 164 disease-control participants, analysing baseline cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) NfL, Aβ peptides, pTau181, pTau217, and GFAP. A two-step diagnostic strategy was examined in individuals with intermediate NfL values, using machine-learning models. Prognostic associations were evaluated using linear mixed-effects and Cox models adjusted for established predictors; survival was additionally examined in pooled analyses including an external ALS cohort (n = 153). Patients with ALS exhibited higher CSF NfL, Aβ38, Aβ40, Aβ42, pTau181, and pTau217 than controls, even within Aβ-negative subgroups. NfL discriminated ALS from controls with an AUC of 0.85 (0.82-0.88), which increased to 0.90 (0.88-0.92) in machine-learning models incorporating additional biomarkers. The machine-learning models maintained a high positive predictive value (0.90) for classifying cases with intermediate NfL values. Significant Aβ × NfL interactions were observed for longitudinal functional decline, and pooled survival analyses showed stronger associations between NfL and survival in the Aβ-positive ALS subgroup (14%) than in the Aβ-negative ALS subgroup (HR 4.02 [2.17-7.45] vs 1.62 [1.36-1.92]). Multiple biomarker assessments can reduce misclassification of individuals with intermediate NfL values. CSF Aβ positivity modified the association between baseline NfL and disease progression. Personalised diagnosis and prognosis based on fine-grained co-pathology evaluation may enhance clinical management of ALS. This study was primarily supported by JST SPRING (JPMJSP2125). doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106512.abstract: Disease features in resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTHβ), caused by THRB mutations, arise from insensitivity to thyroid hormone in tissues expressing thyroid hormone receptor (TR)β and from lifelong thyrotoxic effects in TRα1-expressing tissues, posing substantial cardiovascular morbidity/mortality. The T3-analogue triiodothyroacetic acid (Triac) holds potential as an effective treatment. Systematic data on Triac therapy in RTHβ are lacking, and the mechanisms through which Triac acts are unclear. This study aims to elucidate these knowledge gaps. Clinical and biochemical data were obtained through an, international retrospective cohort study in patients with RTHβ. Transcriptional activity of all TRβ mutants, on the background of the pituitary-expressed β2 receptor isoform and positively (DR+4-TRE) or negatively (TSHα-TRE) regulated reporter genes plus T3 or Triac, was studied. Thyroid function and TSH responses to T3 and Triac were tested in zebrafish expressing TRβ mutants. We collected data from 28 patients with RTHβ (range: 0.4-73.1 years) with 18 unique mutations treated with Triac in 6 centres. Triac reduced TSH (by 43%) and FT4 (by 37%) concentrations in all heterozygous patients, supported by consistent findings in zebrafish. Our functional studies showed that TRβ2 mutants exhibited reduced (all) or absent (G432del) T3-dependent transcriptional activity, with similar EC50 and IC50 values for T3 and Triac, except for R316H, which showed a 5-times lower EC50/IC50 value for Triac compared to T3. In this international, multicentre study we have documented that Triac lowers elevated FT4 concentrations in patients with RTHβ effectively. Integrating our clinical and molecular observations we suggest that Triac can act via different modes of action, with activation of the wild-type receptor being a relevant mechanism. Our study may inform clinical management and could shape future interventional studies in patients with RTHβ. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106515.abstract: rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccine is recommended for prevention of Ebola virus (EBOV) infection and disease (EVD). However, breakthrough EBOV infections have been observed in vaccinees. Currently available diagnostic and research assays cannot reliably distinguish individuals vaccinated against Ebola virus from those previously infected with the virus. This limitation complicates interpretation of vaccine-effectiveness studies, seroepidemiologic investigations, and estimates of infection or attack rates. The ability to differentiate vaccine-induced immune responses from those resulting from natural infection remains an important unmet public health and research need. We developed a multiplex sero-diagnostic assay simultaneously detecting IgA, IgG, and IgM antibodies against vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus nucleoprotein (VSV-N), a vaccine-specific marker absent in natural infection, and EBOV-GP, the vaccine's target antigen. We evaluated longitudinal samples from 30 individuals after vaccination and 30 placebo (saline) recipients, as well as 8 participants from a long-term vaccination follow-up study. We detected increase in all antibodies against both protein antigens in vaccinated individuals. Critically, the assay reveals that anti-VSV-N IgA responses emerge earlier and more robustly than anti-GP responses in vaccinees, establishing anti-N IgA as a definitive, early, and durable biomarker of rVSVΔG-ZEBOV-GP vaccination with high sensitivity and specificity. The assay enables rapid, accurate identification of vaccine recipients and supports real-time assessment of vaccine effectiveness during outbreaks. Furthermore, the assay's adaptability to the expanding pipeline of VSV-vectored vaccines positions it as a transformative diagnostic platform for accelerating preparedness for future infectious disease threats and outbreak response strategies. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106516.abstract: Adverse drug events (ADEs) are a critical indicator of patient safety but are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. The potential of recent advances in natural language processing (NLP), particularly generative large language models (LLMs), to identify ADEs remains understudied. This study aimed to compare the performance of multiple LLMs in identifying ADE-Drug relationships in inpatient and ambulatory clinical notes. We used clinical notes from the 2018 National NLP Clinical Challenge (n2c2) ADE dataset (inpatient; n = 505) and from outpatient encounters (n = 2555) between October 1, 2018, and December 31, 2019, at a large academic medical center based in New England. Notes were pre-processed into snippets for model input. Evaluated Models included: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.2-3B and their instruction fine-tuned variants (including low-rank adapters for Llama). Performance was assessed using both strict and relaxed evaluations (precision, recall, and F1) for all models, followed by manual evaluation (exact semantic match, partial match, missing ADE, drug mention only, not a drug, or wrong) of the two best-performing models. Of the 1048 notes in the local test split, 450 (42.9%) contained at least one ADE. The n2c2 test set included 202 notes, of which 155 (76.7%) contained at least one ADE. GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini were the top-performing models among those evaluated. GPT-4o consistently outperformed GPT-4o-mini in ADE extraction across both datasets, with higher F1-scores (0.524 vs. 0.381) and a more balanced precision-recall profile. Both models captured ADEs effectively in explicit and complex clinical contexts, although limitations included misclassification of pre-existing allergies and occasional conflation of therapeutic indications with adverse effects. GPT-4o achieved higher exact match coverage and fewer errors across clinical notes, indicating more reliable performance in both inpatient and ambulatory settings. This work establishes a foundation for integrating LLM methods into real-world drug safety surveillance, with direct implications for improving patient safety. None.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106517.abstract: Placental foetal vascular malperfusion (PFVM) is a chronic disorder characterised by impaired blood flow and abnormal vascular development, inducing adverse neonatal outcomes. Long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LC-PUFAs) play a crucial role in placenta health. We aimed to explore the role of genetic variation in LC-PUFA metabolism in PFVM risk as well as underlying mechanisms. Associations were examined between two functional polymorphisms (rs174538 and rs174556) of the fatty acid desaturase 1 (FADS1) gene encoding the rate-limiting enzyme for LC-PUFA metabolism and PFVM among pregnant women (n = 646). Placental transcriptomes were correlated with PFVM and FADS1 genotypes. Various assays were performed in human umbilical vein endothelial cells and trophoblasts with FADS1 inhibitor and LC-PUFA interventions to characterise their function changes. Low-function alleles of both polymorphisms were significantly associated with increased PFVM risk and decreased placental FADS1 transcription level. In placenta tissue, lower FADS1 expression is also associated with PFVM. PFVM-associated genes are enriched to pathways related to immune responses, apoptosis, and angiogenesis, which overlap with the genes and pathways associated with the risk alleles and demonstrate a cell-type enrichment to endothelial cells. In vitro, FADS1 inhibition impairs multiple functions of and interactions between endothelial and trophoblast cells. These impairments are reversed by LC-PUFA supplementation. These findings highlight the impact of maternal LC-PUFA homoeostasis in placenta health and suggest that maternal FADS1 variants can potentially be an early diagnostic marker for PFVM. Our data supports PUFA metabolism as a precision therapeutic or preventive target to reduce placental dysfunction risk. NIH, Wayne State University and Michigan State University.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106518.abstract: Adenomyosis has been shown to reduce live birth rates and increase the risk of pregnancy loss. The diagnosis is often established by ultrasonographic assessment using the revised Morphological Uterus Sonographic Assessment (MUSA) criteria. However, the reproductive impact of specific sonographic features remains unclear. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted to investigate whether individual ultrasonographic adenomyosis features influence pregnancy outcomes in women with infertility or pregnancy loss. We searched MEDLINE (PubMed), Embase, Cochrane Library (CENTRAL), Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar (most recent 200 records) from inception to May 11th, 2026. Observational and interventional studies reporting specific ultrasonographic features of adenomyosis in women with infertility and/or pregnancy loss were included. Primary outcomes were clinical pregnancy, live birth, and pregnancy loss. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed risk of bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools, as appropriate by study design. Meta-analyses were performed using random-effects models, with common-effects models applied where appropriate; remaining evidence was synthesised narratively. Certainty of evidence was assessed by GRADE. The protocol was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251077005). Of 2322 records screened, 29 studies comprising 19,510 patients (7569 with adenomyosis) were included. Diffuse adenomyosis was associated with lower odds of live birth compared with no adenomyosis (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.34-0.79; I2 = 63%), as well as internal adenomyosis compared with no adenomyosis (OR 0.49 95% CI 0.42-0.57 I2 = 0%). Narrative synthesis suggested poorer reproductive outcomes with adenomyosis features located near the endometrium and with larger uterine volume. The overall certainty was low or very low for 20 out of 21 outcomes, and moderate for one, primarily driven by imprecision and indirectness related to variation in diagnostic criteria across studies. Reproductive outcomes in adenomyosis vary according to specific ultrasonographic features, supporting feature-based reporting beyond a binary diagnosis. Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, including inconsistent ultrasonographic diagnostic criteria, variable application of MUSA definitions, and differences in fertility treatment protocols, warrants cautious interpretation of pooled estimates. Standardised definitions and reporting of adenomyosis features are needed to improve evidence synthesis and clinical translation. The Novo Nordisk Foundation and the Danish Research Council.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106526.abstract: Tecovirimat was developed as an antiviral countermeasure against orthopoxviruses and approved by the US Food and Drug Administration Animal Rule based on efficacy in preclinical studies and clinical pharmacokinetic and safety trials. However, recent randomised clinical trials in patients with mpox who initiated tecovirimat an average of 6-9 days after onset of symptoms did not show improvement in time to resolution of skin lesions. Here, we evaluated whether timing of tecovirimat initiation influenced antiviral efficacy following mpox infection in nonhuman primates and defined the therapeutic window for treatment initiation. In this randomised preclinical study, 32 cynomolgus macaques were challenged intravenously with 1 × 106 TCID50 mpox clade IIb virus. Oral tecovirimat (10 mg/kg, once daily for 14 days) treatment was initiated on Day 2 (post-exposure and pre-symptomatic), Day 5 (early symptomatic), or Day 9 (peak symptomatic) after mpox challenge, or no treatment was given as a control group. The primary study endpoint was area under the curve (AUC) and peak numbers of progressive skin lesions. The secondary endpoint was AUC and peak levels of plasma viral loads. Additional analyses included total skin lesions, adaptive immune responses, and transcriptomic signatures. Treatment adherence was 100%. All tecovirimat-treated animals survived to study completion on Day 28, whereas two untreated control animals required early euthanisation on Days 16 and 17. Tecovirimat efficacy was time-dependent. Progressive skin lesion AUC was significantly lower when treatment was initiated on Day 2 (P 0.99). In this randomised preclinical study, tecovirimat demonstrated antiviral therapeutic efficacy but only when initiated early prior to peak viraemia. These findings emphasise the importance of early initiation of treatment and define the therapeutic window for optimal tecovirimat treatment in nonhuman primates. This study was supported by SIGA Technologies.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106528.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) ranks among the deadliest malignancies, with limited survival benefits despite recent therapeutic advances. Few prognostic biomarkers are available for PDAC monitoring in clinical practice. We conducted a meta-analysis to evaluate and synthesise evidence on the prognostic significance of miRNA expression in PDAC. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023463542). We conducted a systematic search in PubMed, CENTRAL, and Embase on January 27, 2026, to identify studies assessing miRNA expression levels in patients with PDAC with reported overall survival (OS) or progression-free survival (PFS) outcomes. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using a random-effects model. Prediction intervals (PI) were reported if feasible. Separate analyses were performed by miRNA functional categories: oncogenic, tumour suppressor, chemoresistance-related, metastasis-related, and dual-role miRNAs. A total of 142 studies, including 13,824 patients, were included. High expression of oncogenic miRNAs was associated with worse univariate OS (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.38-2.10; 95% PI 0.63-4.57) and PFS (HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.63-3.10; 95% PI 1.11-4.55). High expression of chemoresistance-related miRNAs was associated with worse multivariate OS (HR 2.11, 95% CI 1.68-2.66; 95% PI 0.96-4.68) and PFS (HR 2.51, 95% CI 1.89-3.33; 95% PI 1.58-3.97). Between-study heterogeneity varied substantially across pooled analyses (I2 range 0-94%). miRNA-21 was the most frequently studied individual biomarker and showed a consistent association with worse multivariate OS (HR 2.24, 95% CI 1.95-2.57; 95% PI 1.92-2.61). Elevated expression of oncogenic and chemoresistance-related miRNAs is associated with worse survival outcomes in PDAC. However, substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction intervals observed in several pooled analyses indicate variability in effect sizes across studies. Among the investigated biomarkers, miRNA-21 has shown the most consistent prognostic association and may represent the strongest candidate for future clinical implementation. Further validation and standardisation are required before miRNA profiling can be integrated into routine clinical practice. None to declare.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106531.abstract: Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a highly pathogenic, tick-borne orthonairovirus responsible for severe human disease, yet no approved vaccines or therapeutics exist. The glycoprotein precursor (GPC), including its GP38, Gn, and Gc components, and the nucleoprotein (NP) have been explored as vaccine targets with varying success. A chimpanzee adenoviral vector (ChAdOx) vaccine encoding full-length GPC previously conferred complete protection in mice, supporting Phase I evaluation. However, the essential protective components and mechanisms of vaccine-induced immunity remain unclear. We evaluated ChAdOx2 vaccines encoding individual GPC subunits (GP38, Gn, or Gc), full-length GPC, or NP in a lethal interferon receptor-deficient mouse model. Protective efficacy and immune responses were assessed to define protective immunogens and mechanisms. Single-dose vaccination with ChAdOx2-GP38 or ChAdOx2-Gc conferred complete survival (6/6 per group; both p = 0.0005 vs PBS), with minimal histopathology and viral RNA burden at the 21-day study endpoint, comparable to full-length GPC (6/6; p = 0.0005 vs PBS). ChAdOx2-NP likewise conferred complete survival (6/6; p = 0.0008 vs PBS) and elicited robust NP-specific immune responses. In contrast, ChAdOx2-Gn conferred partial survival (2/6; p = 0.0101 vs PBS), while low-dose GPC vaccination provided limited protection (1/6; p = 0.0617 vs PBS) with impaired IgG responses while preserving T-cell responses. Immunological analyses showed that GP38, Gc, and full-length GPC constructs induced robust antibody responses with similar Fcγ receptor engagement and limited neutralising activity. These findings identify GP38 and Gc as individually protective immunogens while reinforcing GPC and NP as effective vaccine targets. Together, these data support roles for non-neutralising antibodies and T-cell responses in protection against CCHFV and continued development of ChAdOx-vectored vaccines for clinical use. This research was supported by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106533.abstract: Early life is a critical window for co-development of the brain and gut microbiome (GM). Evidence supports a role for the GM in brain development, but longitudinal human data remain limited, particularly regarding the influence of social disadvantage (SD), a powerful determinant of child mental health and neurodevelopment. Here, we examine longitudinal relationships between the GM and neurodevelopmental outcomes over the first three years of life, and the impact of SD on them. We sequenced and analysed stool samples of 187 children, collected at 5 timepoints over 4-36 months of life (MOL; 905 samples) using a whole-metagenome sequencing approach. Associations between GM-derived Gut-Brain Modules (GBM) and neuroactive potential were assessed using generalised linear mixed models, adjusting for covariates. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were evaluated by Bayley-III (cognitive, language, and motor), and neurobehavioural dysregulation and externalising/internalising-behaviour by the Infant-Toddler Social and Emotional Assessment (ITSEA) and Preschool Age Psychiatric Assessment (PAPA). Temporal changes were observed in GBMs, including glutamate/GABA synthesis and degradation pathways, as well as short-chain fatty acids. GM community structure and GBMs were significantly associated with concurrent and later Bayley-III outcomes, most consistently for cognition and language (FDR < 0.10). Several GBMs were associated with both neurobehavioural outcomes and SD, including S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) synthesis, butyrate synthesis, and glutamate and GABA synthesis II (FDR < 0.10). A partial mediating effect between SD and 36 MOL language outcomes was observed using SAM synthesis at 4 MOL (β = -0.042, P = 0.048). This longitudinal cohort study of GM neuroactive metabolic capacity across early transitional developmental windows reveals a dynamic pattern of GM-derived neuroactive metabolic pathways and identifies specific pathways associated with later neurodevelopmental (cognitive, language) and neurobehavioural outcomes, even after controlling for important covariates. These pathways are shaped by the socioeconomic status of mothers, starting with in-utero exposure, and GBMs partially mediated this effect. The study identifies microbial pathways associated with both SD and neurodevelopmental outcomes, highlighting potential biological processes that may contribute to neurodevelopmental risk and warrant further investigation. This work was supported by the National Institute of Mental Health, March of Dimes, Children's Discovery Institute, National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, and National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108365.abstract: The optimal salvage therapy for relapsed germ cell tumors (GCTs) remains undefined and the optimal timing for high-dose chemotherapy (HD-CT) is unclear. We analyzed data from the European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation registry to evaluate contemporary outcomes in patients treated with HD-CT across salvage lines. We extracted data of adult males with GCTs (excluding mediastinal primary) who received one or more courses of HD-CT with carboplatin and etoposide between 2000 and 2022. Patients treated within 3 months from diagnosis were excluded, as this was considered upfront therapy. Time from diagnosis to first HD-CT (TT) was categorized in 3-6, 6-12, and >12 months. A Cox model with restricted cubic splines was used to evaluate the nonlinear effect of TT on survival. Data from a total of 2204 patients were analyzed. Histology was available for 1074, of whom 69% had nonseminoma. Among 969 patients with primary site information, 69% had testicular GCT. International Prognostic Factors Study Group (IPFSG) categories were available for 500 patients: 17% very high, 38% high, 31% intermediate, 10% low, and 3.6% very low risk. TT was 3-6 months for 280 (13%), 6-12 months for 831 (38%), and >12 months for 1093 (50%). Of the patients, 1118 (51%) received three cycles of HD-CT. Median overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were 36.4 [95% confidence interval (CI) 30.3-58.7] and 9.9 months (95% CI 8.5-12.4), respectively. Spline analysis showed increasing hazard of progression and death with longer TT. No interaction was observed between TT and IPFSG risk for PFS (P = 0.62), whereas a significant interaction was found for OS (P = 0.04) in non-high-risk patients. In the largest contemporary series of salvage HD-carboplatin-etoposide in GCTs, HD-CT was effective regardless of TT as a surrogate of salvage line, with a significant interaction in non-high-risk patients, suggesting a nonlinear association between HD-CT timing and OS.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108533.abstract: The European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) Clinical Practice Guidelines for the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients with early and locally advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) were published in August 2025 and were adapted in November 2025 according to previously established standard methodology to produce the Pan-Asian adapted ESMO consensus guidelines for the management of Asian patients with early and locally advanced NSCLC. The adapted guidelines presented in this article represent the consensus opinions reached by a panel of Asian experts on the treatment of patients with early and locally advanced NSCLC representing the oncological societies of China (Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology), Indonesia (Indonesian Society of Hematology and Medical Oncology), India (Indian Society of Medical and Paediatric Oncology), Japan [Japanese Society of Medical Oncology (JSMO)], South Korea (Korean Society of Medical Oncology), Malaysia (Malaysian Oncological Society), the Philippines (Philippine Society of Medical Oncology), Singapore (Singapore Society of Oncology), Taiwan (Taiwan Oncology Society) and Thailand (Thai Society of Clinical Oncology), coordinated by ESMO and JSMO. The voting was based on scientific evidence and was independent of the current treatment practices, drug access restrictions and reimbursement decisions in the different regions of Asia. The latter are discussed separately in the article. The aim is to provide guidance for the optimisation and harmonisation of the management of patients with early and locally advanced NSCLC across the different countries of Asia, drawing on the evidence provided by both Western and Asian trials. Attention is drawn to the disparity in the drug approvals and reimbursement strategies among the different regions.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108550.abstract: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) is known to exhibit distinct metastatic patterns compared with carcinoma of no special type (NST); however, little is known about its specific propensity for central nervous system (CNS) and leptomeningeal (LM) involvement, particularly in estrogen receptor (ER)-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative subtype. We leveraged a multicenter study of 1710 patients with advanced breast cancer (BC). We recorded site of first metastatic recurrence and occurrence/type of the first CNS event. The study endpoints were CNS-free survival, LM-free survival, and post-LM survival. The risk of LM as the first CNS event across histological types was evaluated using a competing-risk framework. Among 1587 patients with known tumor histology, 15.5% had ILC. Within the ER-positive/HER2-negative BC cohort (n = 669), 31.5% of patients developed a CNS event. ILC and NST were associated with similar metastatic CNS-free survival [hazard ratio (HR) 1.30, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.95-1.77, P = 0.095]. In contrast, metastatic LM-free survival was significantly and independently shorter in ILC versus NST (multivariate analysis of LM events without concurrent brain metastases, adjusted HR 4.94, 95% CI 1.57-15.83, P = 0.006). Consistently, Fine-Gray competing-risk analysis confirmed a significantly higher risk of LM involvement as the first CNS event for ILC versus NST (adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio 5.07, 95% CI 1.57-16.41, P = 0.007). Among patients with ER-positive/HER2-negative BC and LM disease, ILC was associated with worse post-LM survival compared with NST (HR 2.79, 95% CI 1.03-4.17, P = 0.040). In patients with ILC presenting with extracranial metastatic disease, we observed similar LM-free survival between those treated with cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 inhibitors and those who were not (P = 0.286). In patients with ER-positive/HER2-negative advanced BC, ILC was independently associated with a higher cumulative incidence of LM as the first CNS event than NST. Patients with ILC who developed LM also experienced poorer post-LM survival. These findings highlight the need for heightened clinical awareness and support prospective studies evaluating earlier LM detection in this population.

The aim is to provide guidance for the optimisation and harmonisation of the management of patients with RCC across the different countries of Asia, drawing on the evidence provided by both Western and Asian trials. Attention is drawn to the disparity in drug approvals and reimbursement strategies between the different regions.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108584.abstract: We conducted a randomized phase II trial to evaluate whether adding erlotinib to platinum/docetaxel improves clinical outcomes in the first-line treatment of recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous-cell carcinomas, building on our previous single-arm phase II trial. This was a placebo-controlled, double-blind, single-center phase II study. Patients (N = 120) were randomly assigned (1 : 1) to receive platinum (carboplatin area under the curve 6 or cisplatin 75 mg/m2 every 21 days for six cycles) plus docetaxel (75 mg/m2 every 21 days for six cycles) with either erlotinib (150 mg/day orally until progression) or placebo. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included overall survival, response rates, duration of response, and correlations of erlotinib-induced rash/biomarkers with outcomes. Median PFS was 6.1 months with erlotinib versus 4.4 months with placebo [hazard ratio (HR) 0.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.42-0.95, P = 0.026]. Median overall survival was 17.0 months in the erlotinib arm compared with 13.7 months in the control arm (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.43-1.04, P = 0.0718), meeting the prespecified type I error threshold. Subgroup analyses demonstrated numerically favorable PFS HRs across most clinical subgroups, with a more pronounced benefit observed in patients with oropharyngeal and human papillomavirus-related tumors. Development of grade ≥2 rash during the first cycle of erlotinib was associated with significantly improved overall survival (HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.19-0.87, P = 0.021). The addition of erlotinib increased the incidence of grade 2-4 adverse events, particularly gastrointestinal toxicity, rash, fatigue, and dehydration but no unexpected safety signals were observed. The study met its primary endpoint, supporting the continued relevance of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibition in this disease. Although contemporary immunotherapy-based standards limit direct adoption of this regimen, these results provide clinically meaningful insight into EGFR biology and support further development of modernized, tyrosine kinase inhibitor-based EGFR strategies, including rational combinations and biomarker-driven approaches, to improve outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108596.abstract: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) are associated with poor outcomes, with many patients never receiving any cancer-directed treatment. Population-based registries from England, France, Italy and Spain share a similar picture: emergency presentation, rather than planned referral, accounts for roughly half of diagnoses, and >50% of patients with cholangiocarcinoma in England received neither surgery, systemic therapy nor stenting. This attrition is not exclusive to real-world settings: in PROOF-301 and FIGHT-302, a considerable proportion of eligible or randomly assigned patients never started their allocated treatment. BTC is also no longer a disease confined to older adults, with ∼7% of cases diagnosed in individuals <50 years of age. On top of this, access to reimbursed therapies, molecular profiling and expert multidisciplinary discussion remains markedly uneven across Europe. "Our patients deserve better" and closing these gaps in diagnosis, access to treatment and care delivery is as urgent as developing new drugs for this disease.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108602.abstract: Whether intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) offers measurable clinical benefits over intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) for oropharyngeal cancer remains debated. We pooled data from two phase III randomized trials and one matched cohort study comparing IMPT with IMRT and analyzed disease-control, survival, acute toxicity, and nutritional outcomes. The hazard ratio for locoregional recurrence was 1.37 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.56-3.36, I2 = 0%]; for progression-free survival, 0.90 (95% CI 0.61-1.33, I2 = 0%); and for overall survival, 0.79 (95% CI 0.32-1.98, I2 = 47%). Acute grade 3 dysphagia occurred in 24% of patients receiving IMPT, compared with 40.9% receiving IMRT [risk ratio (RR) 0.65, 95% CI 0.51-0.84, I2 = 0%]. Grade 3 xerostomia or oral/pharyngeal dryness occurred in 19.9% and 32.5%, respectively (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.54-0.95, I2 = 0%). Exploratory nutritional outcomes showed no definitive benefit, including 12-month gastrostomy dependence (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.08-1.28, I2 = 0%), weight loss ≥20% (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.12-9.38, I2 = 85.7%), and composite nutritional endpoints (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.12-7.07, I2 = 87.7%). IMPT's primary advantage is reducing acute toxicity, not improving efficacy.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108604.abstract: Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are established biomarkers of breast cancer immunogenicity and prognosis. Reproductive events induce durable immunological remodelling of the breast, but whether TIL levels at diagnosis reflect the immunological imprint of these events remains unclear. We included women diagnosed with invasive breast cancer between 1978 and 2012 in the Energy Balance and Breast Cancer Aspects throughout Life study, a substudy of the population-based Tromsø Study (Norway). Prediagnostic host factors were obtained. TILs were scored on an ordinal scale (1-4). Associations between host factors and the TIL score were analysed using ordinal logistic regression with interaction terms for hormone receptor (HR) status. Breast cancer-specific mortality was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox regression. A total of 425 women were included [median age at diagnosis 56.0 years, 360 (87.6%) parous], of whom 84 (19.8%) had HR-negative tumours. Among HR-negative cases, parity [odds ratio (OR) 10.14, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.97-52.22], longer breastfeeding duration [OR 1.87 per standard deviation (SD), 95% CI 1.10-3.17], and higher age at first birth (OR 1.79 per SD, 95% CI 1.06-3.01) were associated with higher TIL scores, whereas higher mean arterial pressure (OR 0.59 per SD, 95% CI 0.41-0.86) was inversely associated. Significant interactions with HR status were observed for parity and breastfeeding duration. No associations were observed in HR-positive tumours. High-TIL levels (scores 3-4 versus 1-2) were associated with lower breast cancer-specific mortality in HR-negative tumours (adjusted hazard ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.14-0.72) but not in HR-positive disease (hazard ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.58-1.68; Pinteraction = 0.023). These findings suggest that reproductive history and timing may shape the tumour immune microenvironment over the life course. If confirmed in larger studies, TILs may represent an intermediate phenotype linking upstream host characteristics to downstream clinical outcomes in breast cancer.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108607.abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has demonstrated substantial clinical benefit in patients with advanced human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive and HER2-low breast cancer. However, treatment-related adverse events-particularly interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pneumonitis-represent a clinically relevant limitation. While UGT1A1 polymorphisms influence toxicity with other topoisomerase I inhibitor-based therapies, their role in T-DXd-related toxicity appears limited. The PROCURE project aimed to investigate germline pharmacogenetic variants beyond UGT1A1 associated with T-DXd-induced ILD. The PROCURE project is a multicenter translational study conducted across 26 Spanish institutions. Germline DNA from patients with advanced HER2-positive or HER2-low breast cancer treated with T-DXd was genotyped using the Infinium Global Diversity Array enriched for pharmacogenomic variants. A candidate gene approach was applied to 14 genes involved in drug metabolism, transport, pharmacodynamics, and immune-mediated drug hypersensitivity. Logistic regression models were used to evaluate associations with ILD/pneumonitis. A total of 290 patients with clinical and genotyping data were included in the analysis. The median age was 58 years (range, 34-94 years). After a median follow-up of 18.3 months [95% confidence interval (CI): 15.4-20.5], the cohort registered 33 ILD cases (incidence of 11.4%). The strongest association signals mapped to variants within the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region, with the top single nucleotide polymorphism near HLA-F (rs9258213; OR 6.8, 95% CI 2.6-17.9, P = 9.5 × 10-5). Additional associations were observed in SLCO1B1 and CYP3A4, genes involved in T-DXd transport and metabolism. This study identifies host genetic variation within the HLA locus and drug pharmacokinetic pathways as potential contributors to T-DXd-induced ILD in patients with advanced breast cancer. Although no definitive pharmacogenomic predictor was identified, these findings provide insights into the biological mechanisms underlying this toxicity and support further investigation of pharmacogenomic biomarkers to improve risk stratification and guide personalized T-DXd therapy.

doi:10.1016/j.euo.2026.08.013.abstract: Screening for kidney cancer and other serious abdominal conditions in conjunction with lung cancer screening (LCS) is potentially feasible and cost-effective. Targeted Abdominal CT in Conjunction with Lung Cancer Screening (TACTICAL1) aims to pilot this integrated screening model in a real-world setting to inform a future large-scale randomised controlled trial (RCT). TACTICAL1 is a pilot study, with embedded process evaluation, of adding abdominal noncontrast computed tomography (CT; ANCCT) to low-dose CT (LDCT) thorax amongst ever smokers aged 55-70 yr at high risk of lung cancer who were attending the first round of LCS in Yorkshire, UK. There are two points of randomisation. First, participants are randomised 1:1 at the individual level to receive either an LCS invitation letter (invitation control) or an invitation letter for LCS with potential for an additional ANCCT (invitation intervention). Participants in the latter group are then cluster randomised 1:1 to be offered either LDCT thorax alone (scan control) or both LDCT thorax and ANCCT (scan intervention). TACTICAL1 has four primary endpoints and will assess the following: (1) whether the invitation intervention affects LCS uptake, (2) feasibility of cluster randomisation, (3) impact of adding ANCCT to LCS on scanning throughput, and (4) acceptability to participants and screening staff. Strengths include the real-world setting and robust randomisation. TACTICAL1 is a pilot study; therefore, it does not aim to evaluate the prevalence or stage of screen-detected findings nor survival. TACTICAL1 will inform the development of a future large-scale RCT assessing outcomes such as stage shift, earlier detection, and potential survival benefits. A previous study showed that it is possible to offer an additional computed tomography scan of the abdomen at the same time as lung cancer screening. This extra scan may help detect kidney cancer and other serious abdominal conditions early. TACTICAL1 is a pilot research study in which people are randomly assigned to different groups. Its aim is to test how this combined screening approach could work in practice. The results will help design a much larger future study to find out whether combining these scans can save lives.

doi:10.1016/j.euo.2026.09.015.abstract: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) remains incurable despite recent therapeutic advances. [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT (lutetium-177 labelled prostate-specific membrane antigen radioligand therapy) provides meaningful clinical benefit in selected patients. However, ∼30% of the patients do not respond to [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. Although several baseline prognostic factors are well known, reliable pretherapeutic predictive biomarkers are still lacking. We developed and compared several predictive machine learning (ML) models integrating clinical, biochemical, and imaging data, including [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET (gallium-68 labelled prostate-specific membrane antigen ligand positron emission tomography) radiomic features, to estimate overall survival (OS) in patients with mCRPC treated with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. This retrospective monocentric study included 102 patients with mCRPC treated with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA between January 2022 and March 2024. Five lesions per patient were segmented on their pretherapeutic [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/computed tomography (CT) scans. Radiomic features were extracted following Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative guidelines. Multimodal ML models integrating clinical, genomic, biochemical, and imaging features (including radiomics) were developed to predict OS. Median OS of the total cohort was 11.2 mo. Intralesional homogeneity, characterized by the second-order radiomic feature normalized inverse difference moment, was associated with shorter OS (p = 0.025). The best-performing ML model achieved a 12-mo area under the curve (AUC) of 0.778 by combining 22 clinical, biochemical, genomic, and radiomic features. The model leveraging PET data alone achieved strong performance, with an AUC comparable to the clinical model (0.715 vs 0.766). ML models based on [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT, including radiomic features, offer a noninvasive, standardized, and widely accessible approach to predict OS in patients with mCRPC treated with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT. This study highlights the strong predictive potential of PSMA PET imaging for patient stratification in a real-world setting.

doi:10.1016/j.euo.2026.10.001.abstract: Clinical T1 micropapillary urothelial carcinoma of the bladder is an aggressive variant histology for which early radical cystectomy (RC) is commonly recommended. However, there remain conflicting data on whether conditions in carefully selected patients may be managed with initial bladder-sparing approaches without compromising oncologic outcomes. The objective is to systematically review and synthesize the available literature comparing bladder-sparing approaches, such as Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) therapy, and early RC outcomes in clinical stage 1 primary tumor (cT1) micropapillary carcinoma of the bladder. A systematic search was performed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses statement and Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. The primary end points were overall survival (OS) and cancer-specific survival (CSS). The included articles were descriptively assessed and time-to-event analysis was performed for select endpoints. Among 461 identified reports, nine retrospective studies met the criteria for quantitative analysis, encompassing 9402 patients of whom 9287 (99%) had non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) and 1033 (11%) had a micropapillary subtype. A total of 625 patients (62%) underwent bladder-sparing approaches, whereas 392 (39%) underwent early RC. Of the bladder-sparing approaches, 88% of patients received intravesical BCG therapy. For a bladder-sparing approach for cT1 disease with a micropapillary component, pooled unadjusted hazard ratios were not statistically significant for CSS (hazard ratio [HR] 1.32, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.60-2.88, p = 0.5) and OS (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.68-1.07, p = 0.16) compared with early RC. Data evaluating bladder-sparing strategies beyond BCG were limited. NMIBC with micropapillary features is an aggressive disease conventionally managed with early RC. In retrospective cohorts of selected patients with micropapillary cT1, available unadjusted data did not provide clear evidence of statistically significant differences in CSS or OS between initial bladder-sparing approaches and early RC.

doi:10.1016/j.euo.2026.10.002.abstract: Transgender women (TGW) retain lifelong prostate cancer (PCa) risk despite gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT), yet its association with PCa incidence and severity is poorly synthesised. This study aimed to quantify pooled PCa incidence in TGW on GAHT relative to cisgender men and characterise disease severity. This is a systematic review with meta-analysis per Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews: CRD420261369142). Five databases were searched from inception to April 2026. Eligible studies reported PCa incidence or outcomes in ≥5 TGW or gender-diverse individuals with intact prostates receiving GAHT. Screening, extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment (Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies - of Interventions; JBI) were performed in duplicate. Random-effects meta-analyses pooled standardised incidence ratios (SIR), incidence rates, and proportions with recorded PCa. Nine studies drawn from six independent data sources (54 342 TGW on GAHT; 160 PCa cases) were included. Pooled SIR versus age-adjusted cisgender men was 0.224 (95% confidence interval = 0.146-0.344; κ = 2), a 77.6% relative reduction; pooled incidence rate was 22.9 versus 98.1 per 100 000 person-years. Among 36 cases with reported grade, 33.3% were International Society of Urological Pathology grade group 4-5; prostate-specific antigen (PSA) ranged from 6.5-18.0 ng/ml and was not pooled. Grade and stage data were derived from fewer than 40 patients with no matched cisgender comparison. Detected PCa incidence is substantially lower in TGW receiving GAHT, on very low certainty evidence. Case-level data include a non-negligible proportion of high-grade disease, but whether severity differs from matched cisgender populations remains uncertain. Clinicians should not equate population-level reduction with individual-level protection. Validated PSA thresholds and screening pathways are needed.

doi:10.1016/j.euo.2026.10.003.abstract: Active surveillance (AS) is a recommended option for favorable-risk Gleason grade group 2 (GG2) prostate cancer (PCa), but uptake varies. To describe the nature of progression of confirmed GG2 disease in a well-annotated AS cohort. Participants at the University of California, San Francisco, were diagnosed with cT1-2N0/xM0/x, prostate-specific antigen (PSA) <20 ng/ml, core positivity ≤50%, and GG2 PCa without expansile cribriform or intraductal carcinoma (EC/IDC) at diagnosis, with two or more biopsies on AS from 2000 to 2025. Active surveillance. Outcomes were upgrade (GG3 or higher), volume increase to >50%, EC/IDC, disease progression (upgrade, volume increase, or EC/IDC), active treatment, recurrence (biochemical recurrence or salvage treatment) after radical prostatectomy (RP), metastasis, and PCa-specific mortality (PCSM). Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to identify risk factors for AS outcomes. A total of 329 men were included. At 5 and 10 yr of follow-up, respectively, the upgrade rate was 31% and 58%, volume increase rate was 22% and 31%, EC/IDC development rate was 10% and 41%, disease progression rate was 44% and 79%, active treatment rate was 46% and 65%, and metastasis rate was 0.80% and 3.3%. The 5-yr post-RP recurrence rate was 32%. No PCSM events were recorded within 10 yr. PSA density (PSAD) and positive baseline multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI; Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System 4-5) were associated with disease progression and active treatment. Limitations include the single-institution cohort, a largely Caucasian population, and incomplete mpMRI and genomic testing. Men with confirmed favorable-risk GG2 PCa on AS have moderate rates of disease progression requiring treatment at 10 yr. Metastasis and PCSM rates were low, but confidence intervals are wide and require external validation. Positive mpMRI and increased PSAD were associated with disease progression and can help tailor AS intensity.

doi:10.1016/j.eururo.2026.08.013.abstract: Inguinal lymph node dissection (ILND) remains a cornerstone of nodal management in penile cancer, providing definitive treatment for clinically node-positive disease and surgical staging for high-risk clinically node-negative patients when dynamic sentinel node biopsy (DSNB) is unavailable. Despite its oncological importance, ILND is associated with substantial morbidity. Over the past decade, minimally invasive (MI) approaches have emerged as alternatives to open ILND, with the potential to reduce wound-related complications while maintaining oncological efficacy. This Surgery in Motion article provides a practical overview of contemporary open, video-endoscopic (VEIL), and robot-assisted (RAVEIL) ILND techniques, integrating anatomical principles, technical variations, and current clinical evidence. Open ILND remains the reference approach, particularly in patients with advanced nodal disease, while MI techniques may be considered in selected patients with limited nodal disease at experienced centres. Across all approaches, meticulous adherence to anatomical templates, appropriate patient selection, and preservation of lymphatic and vascular structures where oncologically feasible are key principles for minimising morbidity. Emerging robotic and image-guided technologies may further refine ILND, although their clinical benefits and long-term oncological outcomes require further evaluation. This stepwise educational review and accompanying surgical video aim to support surgical training, standardisation, and safe implementation of contemporary ILND techniques.

doi:10.1016/j.eururo.2026.09.005.abstract: The phase 2 randomized LUNAR trial previously demonstrated that neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 before stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with oligorecurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (orHSPC). We report updated efficacy and safety outcomes with extended follow-up. Patients with prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-detected orHSPC and one to five metastatic lesions amenable to SBRT were randomized 1:1 to SBRT alone or two cycles of neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT. The primary end point was PFS, defined as new lesions on PSMA PET/CT, initiation of salvage hormonal therapy, or death. Secondary end points included hormonal therapy-free survival (HT-FS) and 24-mo progression-free status. Exploratory end points included polymetastatic PFS (poly-PFS), castration-resistant disease-free survival (CRFS), and conventional imaging progression-free survival (CT-PFS). Between September 2022 and November 2023, 92 patients were randomized to SBRT alone (n = 47) or 177Lu-PNT2002 plus SBRT (n = 45). At a median follow-up of 31.9 mo, 177Lu-PNT2002 significantly improved PFS (median 17.6 vs 7.4 mo; hazard ratio [HR] 0.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.23-0.61; p < 0.001) and HT-FS (HR 0.57, 95% CI = 0.34-0.95; p = 0.03). Exploratory analyses demonstrated improved poly-PFS (HR 0.28, 95% CI = 0.08-1.03; p = 0.04), CRFS (HR 0.13, 95% CI = 0.02-1.10; p = 0.03), and CT-PFS (HR 0.46, 95% CI = 0.19-1.09; p = 0.07). No new safety signals were observed. With extended follow-up, neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 before SBRT produced durable improvements in PFS and HT-FS. While poly-PFS, CRFS, and CT-PFS were exploratory end points, their improvement provides hypothesis-generating evidence that the addition of radioligand therapy to SBRT may alter disease trajectory beyond delaying PSMA PET/CT-detected recurrence.

doi:10.1016/j.eururo.2026.10.007.abstract: There are substantial regional differences in prostate cancer (PCa) epidemiology reflecting differences in risk factors, screening, management, and access to care. To assess geographical differences and temporal trends in PCa incidence and mortality and PCa risk factors. Estimated incidence and mortality data for the year 2024 and projections to 2050 based on the assumption that 2024 age-specific incidence and mortality rates remain unchanged (not accounting for changes in risk factors and/or treatments) in 185 countries were derived from the International Agency for Research on Cancer's GLOBOCAN 2024 database. A narrative review of the literature summarized risk factors and preventive measures. Worldwide, 1.55 million new PCa cases were estimated in 2024, with an age-standardized rate (ASR) for incidence of 29 per 100 000. Northern America had the highest all-age incidence ASR (81), and South-Central Asia the lowest (7.2). PCa caused an estimated 420 000 deaths (7.5 per 100 000), with the highest mortality ASRs in the Caribbean (29) and the lowest in South-Central Asia (3.4). By 2050, new cases are projected to be 2.88 million (+86%) and deaths 924 000 (+120%), with the largest relative increases in Africa (+156%). Prostate-specific antigen-based screening influences both incidence and geographic variation. Family history, germ line pathogenic variants, polygenic risk scores, and ancestry are risk factors. Disparities in men of African versus European ancestry reflect both tumor biology and unequal access to care, with mortality gaps narrowing in equal-access health systems. No single nutrient or supplement has been shown to reduce PCa incidence. Cigarette smoking and obesity are associated with PCa-specific mortality, whereas physical activity and plant-based or Mediterranean dietary patterns are associated with a lower risk of disease progression. The global burden of PCa because of population increase and aging is projected to rise substantially by 2050, particularly in low- and middle-income regions. Family history, germ line pathogenic variants, and ancestry are risk factors for PCa. Evidence remains insufficient to support any specific preventive intervention, although smoking, diet, and physical activity may modify risk of progression or mortality.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.08.046.abstract: Clinical proton dose prescription uses a fixed relative biological effectiveness (RBE) factor of 1.1 despite preclinical and clinical evidence that RBE varies with dose, radiation quality, and tissue radiosensitivity, particularly near the distal edge of treatments. We present a proton clinical dose-prescription system which: (1) is consistent with the clinical RBE of 1.1 for target dose definition, (2) uses full microdosimetric spectral distributions including primary and secondary ions, and (3) accounts for RBE variations in a framework analogous to that clinically used in carbon ion radiotherapy. Monte Carlo simulations were performed using OpenTOPAS. The clinical dose was defined as the product of the absorbed dose, the biological RBE calculated with the Mayo Clinic Florida microdosimetric kinetic model (MCF MKM) relative to the mid of a reference 2 Gy (RBE) spread-out Bragg peak, and a clinical scaling factor. The clinical dose system was evaluated across various dose levels, target depths, and spread-out Bragg peak widths. The results were compared with calculations using the fixed RBE factor and two approaches based on dose-averaged linear energy transfer of protons only (Beltran and McNamara models). Across the investigated scenarios, the target-averaged MCF MKM-based RBE ranged from 1.08 to 1.18. The corresponding target-averaged RBE values obtained with the McNamara and the Beltran model were typically 1% lower (range, 86%-105%) and 9% higher (range, 103%-122%), respectively. For all models, substantially higher RBE values were observed at the distal edge and out-of-field. This work establishes a clinical dose system for proton radiotherapy inspired by corresponding Japanese system for carbon ions. The proposed approach maintains consistency with historical proton practice based on a fixed RBE of 1.1 and accounts for the spatial variations of the radiation quality using microdosimetric distributions that include all primary and secondary ions.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.018.abstract: To compare proton dynamic arc therapy (DynamicArc) with conventional intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) for breast/chest wall irradiation across diverse clinical anatomies. Forty patients were analyzed (10/cohort): tissue expanders, permanent implants, no reconstruction, and bilateral disease. DynamicArc plans used coplanar partial arcs (150-160°) with arc retracing; paired IMPT plans used 2-4 static fields. RayStation 2023BDTK-generated plans shared contours and prescriptions (50.4 Gy[RBE]/28; subset bilateral 42.56 Gy[RBE]/16) and were robustly optimized/evaluated (±5 mm setup,±3.5% range) with Monte Carlo dose calculation (0.5%uncertainty,40000ions/spot) and a 7.5cm range shifter. Target coverage and OAR endpoints were compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with FDR correction. Additionally, robustness pass rates, LETd metrics, and estimated treatment times were compared. DynamicArc achieved target coverage comparable to IMPT and improved robustness pass rates for selected targets. In the expander cohort, DynamicArc improved coverage posterior to the expander port and increased coverage of the chest wall evaluation volume and nodal targets. Improved D95% was accompanied by increased target V105% in several targets. DynamicArc increased thyroid mean dose and skin V95% in multiple cohorts, although skin D2cc and skin V100% remained low. Focal hotspot metrics for the esophagus, heart, and LAD were largely unchanged, with LAD D0.03cc numerically lower though not statistically significant in the expander cohort. Ipsilateral lung V20 was generally similar, with a reduction in implant cases. Several unadjusted significant findings did not remain significant after FDR correction. High-dose CTV LETd was broadly comparable between techniques with changes in the tails of the distribution. DynamicArc increased spots, energy layers, and beam-on time, but estimated total treatment time was comparable after accounting for IMPT room entry and imaging. DynamicArc achieved comparable target coverage with improved robustness in challenging anatomies, at the cost of increased V105%, thyroid mean dose, and skin V95% while maintaining comparable treatment times.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.019.abstract: While accelerated hypofractionated radiotherapy has increasingly been adopted in the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy, there is a paucity of randomized prospective evidence guiding utilization. Given the marked heterogeneity in the presentations of locally-advanced NSCLC, the American Radium Society (ARS) Thoracic Appropriate Use Criteria (AUC) Panel evaluated the appropriateness of accelerated hypofractionation in the context of multidisciplinary management. Five clinical variants representing manifestations of locally-advanced NSCLC were developed by the 15-member multidisciplinary ARS Thoracic AUC panel. The English-language medical literature was formally reviewed from 2010-2025 and scrutinized for prospective clinical trials utilizing accelerated hypofractionation for concurrent chemotherapy ineligible patients. All case variants were evaluated with respect to use of radiation technique, radiation fractionation, and utilization of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy with Modified Delphi methodology. Consensus recommendations were reviewed and approved by the ARS Executive Committee and subject to public comment. The literature review identified 228 articles, of which there were 14 prospective trials/registries including nine Phase I-II trials, four prospective registries, and one randomized Phase III trial. There was consensus that it is appropriate to utilize intensity modulated radiation therapy and proton therapy across presentations of locally-advanced NSCLC, with the aim of constraining the lung V20Gy<30% and heart V40Gy<20% with accelerated hypofractionation. When utilizing 15-fraction accelerated hypofractionation for disease abutting the esophagus or brachial plexus, there was consensus that it is inappropriate to exceed doses of 45-55 Gy. With respect to PD-L1 immunotherapy, there was consensus that consolidative immunotherapy after definitive radiation therapy is appropriate, but that concurrent immunotherapy is inappropriate. There was panel consensus that it may be appropriate to utilize induction PD-L1 immunotherapy prior to radiation therapy in cases of bulky or N3 disease to test disease biology. Across variants, there was consensus that conventionally fractionated radiotherapy to 60 Gy in 30 fractions remains appropriate. The ARS Thoracic AUC Panel has provided consensus case-based guidelines on the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced NSCLC ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy reflecting the heterogeneity of disease presentation in this population. In absence of randomized prospective data demonstrating superiority of accelerated hypofractionation, conventionally fractionated radiotherapy remains an appropriate option.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.020.abstract: Ultra-hypofractionated whole-breast radiotherapy has become an accepted option for early breast cancer, but evidence on the incorporation of a simultaneous integrated boost within a five-fraction schedule remains limited. The present study evaluated five-year late side effects after whole-breast irradiation with a simultaneous integrated boost delivered in five fractions in a prospective multicentre cohort. This prospective, non-randomized, multicentre cohort included 242 patients with early breast cancer treated between April and December 2020. All patients underwent breast-conserving surgery with clear margins. Whole-breast irradiation was delivered at 26 Gy in five daily fractions, and 157 patients received a simultaneous integrated boost to 29 Gy in five fractions. The primary endpoint was late normal-tissue side effects in the simultaneous integrated boost subgroup, assessed prospectively with clinical examination, photographic documentation, and LENT-SOMA scoring. Comparisons with patients treated without a boost were exploratory. Median follow-up was 64.7 months in both the overall cohort and the simultaneous integrated boost subgroup, and 221 of 242 patients completed the scheduled five-year visit. In the simultaneous integrated boost subgroup, cumulative any-grade pain was reported in 14.6% of patients at five years, and cumulative any-grade fibrosis in 8.9%. Other late side effects were uncommon, including breast oedema in 5.1%, arm oedema in 0.6%, atrophy in 1.9%, and telangiectasia in 0.6%; no ulceration was observed. In exploratory unadjusted analyses, pain was more frequent in the simultaneous integrated boost group than in the no-boost group, whereas no significant differences were observed for other late side effects. Chemotherapy receipt was also associated with persistent pain in exploratory analyses. Whole-breast irradiation with a 29 Gy simultaneous integrated boost in five fractions achieved low rates of objective late side effects and reassuring oncological outcomes after more than five years, while shortening treatment to a single one-week course compared with sequential or moderately hypofractionated schedules. Persistent low-grade breast pain was more frequent with the boost, but non-randomized allocation and its association with chemotherapy preclude causal attribution, supporting continued, careful use in selected patients alongside further prospective, randomized studies with baseline symptom assessment.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.021.abstract: High-dose hyper-fractionated radiotherapy has been recently included in NCCN guidelines for limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC), which clinical outcomes are dependent on actually delivered biologically effective dose (BED). However, most tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models rely on planed physical dose without considering inter-fractional deviations and BED of fractionization. This study aims to develop TCP and NTCP models for LS-SCLC incorporating CBCT-based inter-fractional anatomies and hyper-fractional radiobiological dose. Inter-fractional dose was accumulated based on deformable image registration between CBCT and planning CT (pCT). Both TCP and NTCP were formulated within a BED-based framework, using dose-volume parameters calculated from planned dose and CBCT-based accumulated dose for comparison. The LQ model with "4R" effects and Gompertzian tumor growth (LQRG) and Lyman-Kutcher-Burman (LKB) models were used for TCP and NTCP modeling. Based on the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), negative log-likelihood (NLL), and Akaike information criterion (AIC), model performances were assessed for local progression-free survival (LPFS), radiation pneumonitis and radiation esophagitis. Compared with pCT dose, CBCT dose showed superior discrimination of normal tissue toxicity. For grade ≥2 radiation pneumonitis, the CBCT-based NTCP model achieved significantly higher AUC (0.67 vs. 0.59) and lower NLL (62.39 vs. 66.13) than that of the pCT-based mode. Superiority of CBCT-based NTCP model was also observed for grade ≥3 radiation esophagitis, i.e., AUC (0.62 vs. 0.58) and NLL (55.55 vs. 56.64). Using the observed LPFS as reference, marginally improved TCP modeling was observed using CBCT dose than that of pCT, where the AUC values were 0.80 vs. 0.79 (GTV 45 Gy) and 0.77 vs. 0.75 (GTV 54 Gy). By incorporating inter-fractional deviation and biological effectiveness, the improved accuracy of TCP and NTCP models provides preliminary evidence supporting the treatment planning and toxicity management for LS-SCLC patients treated with the hyper-fractionated radiotherapy, which needs further clinical validation.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.022.abstract: There is a paucity of high-level evidence for adjuvant radiation therapy (ART) in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) creating practice variations. This study provides expert consensus recommendations on patient and tumor selection, timing, duration, dosage, and additional considerations for ART in node-negative CSCC. The Delphi panel included 35 experts in radiation oncology (15), dermatology/Mohs micrographic surgery (9), medical oncology (7), head and neck surgery (3), and surgical oncology (1). Consensus was defined as ≥80% concordance; near-consensus 70-79% concordance. Consensus was reached to recommend ART when further surgery is not possible, but the tumor has positive gross or histologic/microscopic margins (35/35, 100%). Key consensus or near-consensus recommendations for recommending ART to the tumor bed following negative-margin surgery include: 5-year cumulative incidence of local recurrence (29/35, 83%) or nodal metastasis (27/35, 77%) ≥ 20%; gross cortical bone/marrow invasion (32/35, 91%); skull base invasion (32/35, 91%); 4 risk factors (RF) (35/35, 100%); 3 RF (30-33/35, 86-94%); PNI ≥ 0.1 mm and one other RF (30/35, 86%); and clinical nerve invasion (31/35, 89%). Immune status influenced ART decision-making (30/35, 86%) with 77% (27/35) more likely to recommend ART for immunosuppressed patients. Consensus was reached to omit ART for pathologic complete response following neoadjuvant immunotherapy (34/35, 97%). Among radiation oncologists, 100% (15/15) agreed the optimal window for ART to the tumor bed is 4-8 weeks and that hypofractionated regimens can be appropriate (12/15, 80%). Consensus was reached for prescription doses of 60-66 Gy in 2 Gy/fx (15/15, 100%) or 50-55 Gy in 2.5 Gy/fx (13/15, 87%), and that superficial radiation and brachytherapy are inappropriate ART modalities for node-negative high-stage CSCC (14/15, 93%). There was no consensus on elective nodal basin irradiation. This Delphi study provides an expert consensus-based framework to standardize ART for node-negative high-stage CSCC following surgery, informing future guidelines and utilization.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.023.abstract: Radiotherapy confers a later risk of secondary malignancies, including radiation-associated breast cancer. Distinctive molecular profiles emerge in tumors from pre-irradiated tumor beds, but effects on therapeutic options remain understudied. We developed a murine model of radiation-associated breast cancer by transplanting p53-mutant mammary HC11 epithelial cells that had been previously exposed to radiation (HC11RT) into mammary fat pads (MFP) that had been previously irradiated. Tumor incidence from HC11RT cells increased two-fold when grown in irradiated MFP. Compared to tumors grown in sham-irradiated MFP, tumors from irradiated MFP had elevated TGFβ in both tumor and CD8+ T cells and elevated PD-L1 on CD4+ T cells, resulting in improved response to immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI). This study provides evidence that prior irradiation potentiates tumorigenesis and immune evasion through both tumor cell autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms. As a result, radiation-associated cancers may exhibit greater response to ICI than tumors of the same histology that are not associated with prior radiotherapy.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.10.012.abstract: Tumor hypoxia has been recognized as a barrier to effective radiotherapy. Preclinical work identified the FDA approved smooth muscle relaxant papaverine (PPV) as having an "off target" activity as a mitochondrial inhibitor that reduces hypoxia and radiosensitizes model tumors. We conducted an IRB-approved phase 1 clinical trial to evaluate safety and feasibility of adding PPV to stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) for tumors of the lung. Eligible patients with early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) or limited lung metastases who were candidates for SBRT (50 Gy in 4 or 5 fractions) were enrolled. Based on a Bayesian Optimal Interval (BOIN) design, patients were allocated to receive PPV 30-90 minutes prior to each SBRT fraction at 3 dose levels (DL): 0.5 mg/kg (DL-1), 1 mg/kg (DL1), or 2mg/kg (DL2). Nineteen patients enrolled and 18 completed study treatment and were evaluable, with a median follow up of 33.4 months. Among 18 evaluable patients, 7 had early-stage NSCLC, 2 had metastatic NSCLC, and 8 had lung metastases from other histologies. The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was determined to be DL2, which had a dose limiting toxicity (DLT) rate posterior estimate of 0.17 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.53). The 2-year controls rates for local, regional and distant control were 100%, 94% and 82%, respectively. We demonstrate the feasibility and safety of PPV as a hypoxic radiosensitizer for SBRT. The MTD for this patient population is at least 2 mg/kg of PPV. Encouraging clinical results indicate that further investigation of PPV's utility as a tumor-selective radiosensitizer is warranted.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.10.014.abstract: Total mesorectal excision (TME) is standard for low rectal cancer (≤5cm from anal verge) but causes permanent stomas, functional impairments and surgical risks. Local excision (LE) suits early tumors (cTis-T1N0) but has higher recurrence in cT2+; watch-and-wait (WW) after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy risks residual disease. Total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) improves outcomes, but prior LE trials had limitations. To evaluate TNT combined with planned LE for organ preservation in selected low rectal adenocarcinoma patients. Prospective single-arm phase 2 trial (June 2022-March 2024, tertiary center) enrolled 57/60 patients (cT1-3N0M0 nonmucinous adenocarcinoma, etc.). TNT: 50 Gy + 2 cycles of CapoX (standard capecitabine + oxaliplatin) + 4 consolidation CapoX. Clinical complete response (cCR)/near-complete clinical response (ncCR) patients had LE; others got TME. Patients with high-risk residual disease after LE also had additional TME. Median age was 61 years (28-79); 66.7% were male. cT3 tumors were present in 78.9%, and 78.9% had tumors ≤3 cm from the anal verge. After TNT, 47.4% achieved cCR and 38.6% achieved ncCR. Among surgically treated patients, the pathological complete response (pCR) rate was 68.6%; in the overall population, with WW counted as non-pCR, it was 61.4%. The total complete response rate, including pCR and cCR managed with WW, was 68.4%. Sphincter preservation was 94.7%. LE was associated with lower median blood loss (7 vs 50 mL; P<0.001) and shorter median hospitalization (7 vs 14 days; P=0.001) than TME. Grade 3 adverse events occurred in 22.8%, most commonly lymphocytopenia; no grade 4 or 5 events occurred. Low anterior resection syndrome (LARS) scores were assessed after TNT and at 1, 3, and 6 months postoperatively. At 6 months, LARS outcomes favored LE (80.0% vs 53.8% reporting no LARS; P=0.027). Wexner incontinence scores did not differ significantly between groups at any time point. TNT with planned LE is feasible in cT1-3N0M0 low rectal cancer, yielding a pCR rate of 61.4% in the overall population, 94.7% sphincter preservation, and acceptable toxicity. However, the non-randomized design and immature 3-year organ-preservation endpoint limit this study to a feasibility assessment and do not permit conclusions regarding comparative effectiveness versus WW. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05563922.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.10.015.abstract: Our purpose was to compare the safety and toxicity profiles of concurrent versus sequential administration of cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) and postoperative radiotherapy (RT) in patients with Positive regional nodes, operable, hormone receptor-positive (HR+), HER2-negative breast cancer (HER2-). We conducted a real-world, multicenter retrospective cohort study enrolling 364 patients with node-positive, operable HR+/HER2- breast cancer who received postoperative radiotherapy combined with CDK4/6 inhibitors between January 2019 and December 2024. Propensity score matching (PSM) was performed to balance baseline covariates between the two arms, yielding 87 patients in each matched group. The primary endpoint was permanent CDK4/6i discontinuation, and secondary endpoints included dose reduction, drug substitution, grade ≥3 toxicities, and symptomatic radiation-induced lung injury (sRILI). No significant intergroup differences were observed in CDK4/6i discontinuation rates before or after PSM (unmatched: 10.4% vs. 8.4%, P=0.536; PSM-matched: 10.3% vs. 9.2%, P=0.798). Similar non-significant findings were identified for dose reduction and drug substitution across unmatched and matched cohorts. For severe toxicities, univariate analysis of the unmatched cohort revealed a significantly higher rate of grade ≥3 drug eruption in the concurrent arm (4.3% vs. 0.4%, unadjusted P=0.013), while this association attenuated to borderline statistical significance after covariate balancing via PSM (4.6% vs. 0.0%, unadjusted P=0.059). No significant between-group differences were detected in sRILI, interstitial pneumonia, grade ≥3 radiation dermatitis, grade ≥3 diarrhea, or hematologic toxicities pre- and post-matching. All grade ≥3 drug eruptions occurred outside radiation fields and presented as diffuse maculopapular rashes involving the trunk and extremities, consistent with CDK4/6i-related hypersensitivity. Concurrent CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy and postoperative RT demonstrate a manageable safety and tolerance profile. Given that treatment discontinuation due to ≥G 3 toxicities was observed in both groups, close toxicity monitoring and comprehensive management throughout the treatment course should be implemented when combining RT with CDK4/6i.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.10.017.abstract: Uniform radiation dose escalation has not improved outcomes in locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), and locoregional failure remains common despite multimodal therapy. We evaluated whether fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET)-guided dose escalation to metabolically active tumor subvolumes reduces locoregional failure compared with standard chemoradiation. PET-BOOST was a multi-institutional, open-label, phase 2 randomized trial conducted at 7 Canadian centers (January 2017-May 2022). Eligible patients had inoperable, FDG-avid stage IIIA/IIIB NSCLC and an achievable boost dose of at least 65 Gy. Patients were randomized 1:1 to standard chemoradiation with 60 Gy in 30 fractions or metabolically adaptive radiotherapy with an integrated boost to FDG-avid subvolumes to a maximum of 85 Gy in 30 fractions. Concurrent platinum-based chemotherapy was planned, and consolidation durvalumab was permitted after 2018. The primary endpoint was 2-year locoregional failure; secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), grade ≥3 treatment-related toxicity, and quality of life (QOL). Seventy-eight patients were randomized: 40 to standard radiotherapy and 38 to dose escalation, with a median follow-up of 5.0 years. Median age was 64.4 years; 53% were male, 62% had stage IIIA disease, and 76% received consolidation durvalumab. Median prescription boost dose was 75 Gy. Two-year locoregional failure was 27.5% with standard radiotherapy versus 18.4% with dose escalation (P=.13). Two-year OS (72.5% vs. 73.7%; P=.91) and PFS (52.5% vs. 57.9%; P=.74) did not differ between arms. Grade ≥3 treatment-related toxicities occurred in 25% versus 37% of patients (P=.26), with one grade 5 pulmonary hemorrhage in the dose-escalation arm. QOL did not differ between arms. Metabolically adaptive PET-guided radiotherapy dose escalation was feasible in the context of consolidation immunotherapy and resulted in a numerically lower rate of locoregional failure, but did not significantly improve locoregional control or survival. The lower-than-anticipated event rate may have limited statistical power, and larger studies would be required to determine whether selective dose escalation provides a clinically meaningful improvement in locoregional control.
