doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.10.018.abstract: This Special Report analyzes current radiotherapy data standards, determines which radiotherapy data elements should propagate between them, and identifies the barriers to that propagation to improve interoperability and data utilization in clinical care and research. We compared five data standards-OMOP, CDISC SDTM, FHIR, NAACCR, and the Operational Ontology for Oncology (O3)-and one ontology framework, the OBO Foundry, for radiotherapy data representation, strengths, limitations, and implementation maturity, and examined harmonization initiatives including NRG's O3-based conversion frameworks, CodeX mCODE, and ESTRO and IAEA efforts. We then scored a 90-item benchmark drawn from radiotherapy operational and trial-reporting requirements, partitioned the radiotherapy items by whether and where they should propagate, and matched each barrier to a remediation route and owning body. Counting only unqualified matches, O3 covered 46 of 62 radiotherapy-specific items (74%) versus 15 (24%) for OMOP, 12 (19%) for NAACCR, 11 (18%) for FHIR, and none for OBO Foundry; on the 28 general clinical items the ordering reversed (OMOP 79%, FHIR 71%, NAACCR 46%, O3 25%, OBO Foundry 4%). Each standard is strongest on the items its target function was built to serve. Wholesale propagation is therefore unwarranted: 20 course-summary elements should converge across standards, 26 planning and adaptive elements warrant selective adoption, and 16 voxel- and machine-level artifacts should be referenced by DICOM unique identifier rather than replicated. Harmonization requires ontology-driven approaches using O3 as the semantic backbone with mappings to FHIR, OMOP and CDISC, applied to a defined tier of elements rather than the full element set. The principal barriers are process barriers-structural, terminological, burden-related and tooling-related-each with a named owner and an existing route. Standardized formats alone are insufficient; they require robust information systems, validation, and governance. Harmonization improves real-world data utility but cannot resolve biases inherent to nonrandomized data. Coordinated international collaboration remains critical for advancing precision radiation oncology.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.10.019.abstract: Radiation injury to growth plates commonly leads to skeletal late complications including short stature, limb length-discrepancy, and scoliosis/kyphosis in pediatric oncology patients. We aimed to understand the acute responses of direct growth plate irradiation that result in skeletal late complications. We first established an in vivo murine model of focal growth plate irradiation that recapitulates the clinical development of skeletal late complications and used it to explore the responses of growth plate chondrocytes within the first 72 hours of radiation exposure. To monitor acute effects of radiation exposure on human chondrocytes, rare human growth plate biopsies were exposed to ionizing radiation ex vivo. Using these approaches, we applied clonal genetic tracing and immunofluorescence to monitor changes at the cellular and molecular levels. Functional in vivo perturbations were conducted with clinically-relevant autophagy inhibitor, hydroxychloroquine. Growth plate irradiation disrupted the continuous production of chondrocytes required for bone elongation and was associated with DNA damage throughout the growth plate. Indicators of growth plate activity, SOX9 and the phosphorylated form of ribosomal protein S6, decreased during a 6- and 24-hour post-irradiation window but returned to normal levels 72 hours after irradiation. We identified a surge in autophagic flux throughout the growth plate during this window, based on temporal SQSTM1 and LAMP1 protein levels. The earliest stages of these response mechanisms are conserved between species and relevant to humans. Hydroxychloroquine treatment immediately after radiation injury in mice impaired growth plate regeneration, resulting in more severe late complications. Our findings demonstrate that autophagy is an important acute response to irradiation in growth plate chondrocytes, revealing a novel potential therapeutic target for preventing radiation-induced skeletal late complications.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.10.020.abstract: Cardiac toxicity is a well-recognized, but poorly understood complication of radiotherapy (RT). In non-oncological settings, there is an established relationship between resting heart rate and cardiovascular health. To study the incidence and pattern of resting heart rate (rHR) as an early sign of cardiotoxicity among patients with non-metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with RT. We retrospectively analyzed serial rHR measurements of consecutive patients with locally advanced NSCLC treated with definitive chemoradiation (CRT) over 6-7 weeks of daily radiation treatments followed by immunotherapy (durvalumab) between 2017-2022. Radiation dose to the heart and 17 cardiac substructures were extracted. Associations between heart rate elevation, tachycardia, cardiac substructure dose and outcomes were evaluated using generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) and regression analysis. We identified 110 patients, 56.4% with pre-existing heart disease. Median follow-up was 33.6 months. Median age was 70.4 years. Median rHR increased significantly during RT, rising from 81.5 bpm to 93 bpm at end of RT (p < 0.0001), remaining elevated in 30.6% of patients 12 months post-RT. Tachycardia incidence rose from 11.2% at baseline to 36.5% at 1-month post-RT (p < 0.0001). After adjusting for comorbidities, higher mean sinoatrial node (SAN) dose was associated with higher rHR elevation, delayed HR recovery and persistent tachycardia (all p < 0.05). Higher rHR during and after RT (β = 0.23, p = 0.005, and β = 13.49, p = 0.049, respectively), as well as the incidence of tachycardia episodes during RT were associated with increased odds of developing an arrhythmia (OR, 2.97, 95% CI, 1.17-7.52, p = 0.022). Elevated rHR and tachycardia are observed during and after RT for NSCLC and are associated with higher mean SAN dose. HR elevation was associated with increased risk of de novo arrhythmias, suggesting that heart rate may represent a non-invasive biomarker of subclinical cardiac injury. Prospective studies might be warranted to test the potential of routine HR monitoring and proactive dose reductions to the SAN to enable early detection and help mitigate the risk of post-treatment arrhythmia.

doi:10.1016/j.immuni.2026.09.010.abstract: CD4+ tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells are crucial for relapse in allergic skin conditions. However, the mechanisms underlying their maintenance and pathogenic potential remain poorly defined. Here, across multiple models of allergic dermatitis, we identified a C-X-C chemokine receptor 6 (CXCR6+) subpopulation within CD4+ TRM cells as a distinct pathogenic subset that rapidly induces relapse. This subset is supported by C-X-C chemokine ligand 16 (CXCL16)-dependent interactions with CD301b+ conventional type 2 dendritic cells (cDC2s) for in situ maintenance. Functional blockade of the CXCL16-CXCR6 signaling pathway impaired proliferation and maintenance of CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM cells. In human atopic dermatitis (AD), CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM cells co-localized with CD301+ cDC2s in perivascular clusters even after successful anti-IL-13 therapy. These findings point to CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM cells as a pathogenic reservoir sustaining chronic and recurrent inflammation and suggest the CXCL16-CXCR6 axis as a therapeutic target to prevent relapse in allergic skin diseases.

doi:10.1016/j.immuni.2026.09.015.abstract: Macrophages are among the most versatile differentiated cell types in the body, serving as key regulators of tissue development, homeostasis, inflammation, repair, and immunity. Their functional diversity cannot be captured by fixed subsets, binary activation states, or single-marker definitions. Macrophage identity emerges instead from the integration of developmental origin, tissue niche, epigenetic history, local environmental cues, and disease-associated signals. Advances in single-cell genomics, spatial profiling, epigenomics, in vivo perturbation, and computational modeling now show that this behavior is organized through modular gene programs, so that any given macrophage state is best described as a weighted combination of program activities rather than a discrete label. We argue that embracing this modular architecture matters not only for annotation but for therapy: macrophage-directed interventions will require defining disease-associated states, identifying surface-accessible entry points into them, and rewiring the underlying programs with spatial and temporal precision.

doi:10.1016/j.immuni.2026.09.022.abstract: Monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation is a central process that shapes immune responses across diverse contexts, yet how inflammatory cues engage metabolism to instruct monocyte fate commitment remains unclear. Here, using a CRISPR-based metabolic screen combined with monocyte-specific perturbations in bacterial lung infection, we identified lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) as a key metabolic regulator of monocyte commitment to the nitric oxide synthase 2 (NOS2)+ macrophage fate in vivo. LDHA-dependent cytosolic nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) regeneration enabled selective hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF1α) translation through its 5' untranslated region (UTR) and is associated with structural remodeling of this region. HIF1α then functioned as a downstream effector that promoted the NOS2+ macrophage fate. Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) further acted as an upstream metabolic priming signal that enhanced LDHA-dependent HIF1α regulation and supported this differentiation process. Together, these findings suggest that metabolic redox state regulates monocyte fate commitment through selective mRNA translation coupled to RNA structural remodeling.

doi:10.1016/j.immuni.2026.09.025.abstract: Inflammatory transcriptional responses mediated by NF-κB are diverse despite similar upstream activation signals. Because phosphorylation of the NF-κB subunit RelA/p65 promotes interaction with co-activators CREB-binding protein/E1A binding protein p300 (CBP/p300) and selectively affects gene expression, we asked whether this modification distinguishes regulatory architectures underlying distinct immune functions. In macrophages carrying a Rela Ser276Ala mutation, p65 phosphorylation at serine 276 (S276) was dispensable for NF-κB binding to primed enhancers but essential for recruitment to nucleosome-occluded regions lacking pre-bound transcription factors (TFs) and activating histone marks. Such latent enhancers required phosphorylated NF-κB to recruit CBP/p300, promote histone acetylation, and open chromatin. Genes linked to these enhancers, including inflammatory mediators, were selectively impaired in S276A macrophages. Although antiviral responses remained intact, Rela Ser276Ala mice resisted endotoxin shock but were susceptible to bacterial infection. Thus, NF-κB responses are functionally partitioned by enhancer architecture: phosphorylation-sensitive sites define a latent enhancer compartment with NF-κB-dominated regulatory architecture, whereas primed sites are embedded in broader networks of lineage-determining and inducible TFs, yielding distinct biological outputs.

doi:10.1016/j.jclinane.2026.112329.abstract: To evaluate the first-hour arterial-to-end-tidal carbon dioxide gradient as a marker of recorded 90-day mortality, distinguishing association, component interpretation and incremental prediction. Retrospective cohort study. INSPIRE v1.4.2, covering surgery from 2011 to 2020. Adults undergoing their first eligible intracranial operation with arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO₂) recorded within 60 min of anesthesia start. End-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO₂) was paired within ±5 min. The outcome was database-recorded all-cause death within 90 days. Firth regression evaluated the gradient without conditioning on either component. The revised principal association model included clinical covariates and contemporaneous mean arterial pressure, heart rate and minute ventilation. Component and internally validated prediction models were secondary. Among 1907 patients, 95 deaths were recorded. The clinical gradient odds ratio (OR) per 5 mmHg was 1.38 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.09-1.73). The revised principal association model included 1830 patients and 92 events (OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.06-1.69). Conditional component estimates did not establish predominance of either component. Adding the gradient to clinical variables, contemporaneous physiology and ETCO₂ changed optimism-corrected area under the curve from 0.832 to 0.833, without improving the Brier score. A larger first-hour gradient was associated with recorded mortality in patients selected for early paired monitoring. Within the evaluated models and metrics, incremental prediction was limited. These findings do not establish a causal mechanism, treatment target or externally validated prediction tool.

doi:10.1016/j.jclinane.2026.112337.abstract: The external oblique intercostal (EOI) plane block is a fascial plane block that targets the unilateral cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves, and spares the sympathetic trunk. We hypothesized that the ultrasound-guided EOI plane block might provide superior analgesia compared to systemic analgesia alone for patients after open liver surgery. In this double-blind, randomized controlled trial, 74 patients scheduled for open liver surgery were assigned to receive either EOI plane block with 30 mL of 0.375% ropivacaine (n = 37) or no EOI plane block (n = 37). All patients received postoperative standard patient-controlled intravenous analgesia. Primary outcome was the resting numerical rating scale (NRS) pain score at 3 h postoperatively. The key secondary outcomes included opioid consumption, and the total number of analgesia interventions at 3 h, 6 h, 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h postoperatively; opioid-related side effects and block-related complications; postoperative functional recovery outcomes; total ropivacaine plasma concentrations at 5, 10, 30, 60, 120, and 180 min post-block. The primary outcome, the resting NRS pain score at 3 h postoperatively, was significantly lower in the block group than in the control group. The block group showed a shorter length of hospital stay. There were no significant differences in cumulative opioid consumption, frequency of analgesia, or opioid-related side effects. No block-related complications were observed, and total ropivacaine plasma concentrations remained below the toxicity threshold. Ultrasound-guided EOI plane block reduces early postoperative pain. This technique should be regarded as a safe and effective component within a comprehensive postoperative multimodal analgesia regimen.

doi:10.1016/j.jclinane.2026.112353.abstract: Intraoperative hypotension (IOH) is associated with myocardial injury, acute kidney injury, perioperative stroke, and 30-day mortality. Deep learning (DL) refers to a family of machine-learning methods that learn multiple levels of data representation through nonlinear transformations. In perioperative monitoring, DL models can learn patterns from time-varying physiological signals and combine them with clinical variables to estimate impending IOH risk. DL algorithms applied to continuous physiological waveforms therefore represent a rapidly expanding paradigm for early IOH prediction, but their pooled diagnostic accuracy has not been synthesised within a unified diagnostic-accuracy framework. To quantify the pooled diagnostic accuracy of DL-based IOH prediction models and to identify factors that modify their performance. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched through March 2026. Methodological quality was appraised with PROBAST+AI and certainty of evidence with GRADE. A bivariate random-effects model generated pooled sensitivity, specificity, and SROC-AUC; heterogeneity was quantified by τ2(Se), τ2(Sp), and ρ. Subgroup analyses (prediction window, DL architecture, modality, IOH reference, analysis unit) and random-effects meta-regression were performed. Twelve studies were included; nine contributed 22 validation datasets. Pooled sensitivity was 0.78 (95% CI 0.73-0.81), specificity 0.88 (0.82-0.92), and SROC-AUC 0.87 (0.83-0.90); diagnostic odds ratio 24.7 (16.1-37.9), positive likelihood ratio 6.31, negative likelihood ratio 0.26. Heterogeneity was τ2(Se) = 0.25, τ2(Sp) = 1.04, ρ = -0.28. The 5-min window achieved the highest performance (sensitivity 0.81; specificity 0.91). Meta-regression identified DL architecture as the only significant moderator of specificity (P = 0.02), with hybrid CNN-RNN exceeding pure CNN (β = 1.77, 95% CI 0.45-3.09). Deeks' test was non-significant (P = 0.06). GRADE certainty was Low. DL models for IOH prediction achieve moderate diagnostic accuracy, with hybrid CNN-RNN architectures and 5-min prediction windows showing the most favourable performance. Universal absence of formal calibration assessment, scarce external validation, and geographic concentration constrain immediate clinical translation. PROSPERO CRD420261377604 Reporting guideline: PRISMA-DTA.

doi:10.1016/j.jhep.2026.09.024.abstract: Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy (CCM), a clinically consequential comorbidity of cirrhosis, remains undefined and underappreciated in children. This study aimed to characterize myocardial structural, functional, morphometric, and histopathologic features in pediatric cirrhosis and objectively derive a reliable echocardiographic (2DE) metric to predict perioperative adverse events, including mortality. 2DE, morphometry, histopathology, and vasoactive-inotropic score (VIS) were compared between children with (n=226) and without (n=160) cirrhosis listed for liver transplantation (LT) over 2011-2021. Discriminatory performance of left ventricular mass index (height)2.7(LVMI g/m2.7) for predicting waitlist decompensation, composite serious adverse events post liver transplant and mortality was assessed using ROC analysis, with AUCs and optimal thresholds compared against PELD-Cr/MELD scores. LV mass was significantly higher in children with cirrhosis on 2DE and necropsy specimens compared to non-cirrhotic controls, with ∼25% demonstrating LV hypertrophy, with OR of 6.9 [CI 3,16], p< 0.0001. In the cirrhotic cohort, LVMI correlated with vasoactive needs under stress of LT (p <0.001) and was significantly higher in patients with WLD, CSAE, and non-survivors. In cirrhosis, LVMI values ≥ 88 g/m2.7, ≥ 91 g/m2.7, and ≥ 95 g/m2.7 were independently associated with WLD, CSAE, and mortality, when adjusting for PELD-Cr/MELD, bilirubin, and INR (p <0.01). Combining LVMI + PELD-Cr/MELD significantly outperformed PELD-Cr/MELD in discriminating both WLD and CSAE, whereas LVMI alone significantly outperformed PELD-Cr/MELD for CSAE and was comparable for WLD. All three models performed comparably in discriminating death. LVMI is a strong predictor of morbidity and mortality, serving as a prognostic marker in children with cirrhosis. Incorporating LVMI into PELD-Cr/MELD may enhance risk stratification and organ allocation.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103063.abstract: Cisplatin resistance remains a major obstacle in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet the contribution of the vascular microenvironment and its variation across HPV statuses remains unclear. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and bioinformatics analyses to characterize cisplatin resistance-associated cellular states in HNSCC. Cisplatin resistance scoring, pseudotime analysis, transcriptional regulatory network analysis, and cell-cell communication analysis were used to identify resistant subpopulations. Spatial localization, survival analysis, immune infiltration assessment, and drug sensitivity prediction were further performed to evaluate key candidate genes. Cisplatin resistance signals were preferentially enriched in tumor endothelial cells and were stronger in HPV-negative HNSCC. Endothelial cells with high resistance scores exhibited enhanced angiogenesis, extracellular matrix remodeling, hypoxia, and inflammatory programs. Multidimensional screening identified SERPINE1 as a key resistance-associated endothelial gene, showing significant upregulation and positive correlation with resistance scores. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses consistently demonstrated vascular-associated enrichment of SERPINE1, particularly in HPV-negative tumors. High SERPINE1 expression was associated with poor survival and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Drug sensitivity prediction suggested increased sensitivity of SERPINE1-high tumors to EGFR/SRC- and MAPK-pathway inhibitors, whereas no significant differences were observed for conventional cytotoxic agents. SERPINE1 defines a tumor endothelial state associated with cisplatin resistance in HNSCC and may contribute to HPV-related differences in the vascular microenvironment, providing a potential basis for therapeutic stratification.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103064.abstract: Renal cystic conditions are heterogeneous. We used a broad renal cyst-associated disease-gene framework to identify molecular programs shared with clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), without modeling a specific cystic disorder or direct cyst-to-cancer progression. We identified 237 shared genes between renal cyst disease and ccRCC (TCGA-KIRC), performed functional enrichment, Mendelian randomization, and built a random survival forest (RSF) risk score benchmarked against published signatures and immunotherapy cohorts. Single-cell (Scissor, SCENIC, scTenifoldKnk virtual FOXM1 knockout) and spatial transcriptomics (RCTD, CellChat) were integrated with fibroblast subclustering and oncoPredict drug screening. Candidate FOXM1 inhibitors were prioritized by docking and 100-ns molecular dynamics, with isovitexin validated functionally. The shared program was enriched for epithelial development and ECM remodeling. Two direction-specific Mendelian randomization analyses supported associations between genetic liability to kidney cancer and related renal cystic phenotypes. The RSF score showed robust prognostic discrimination across cohorts and separated immunotherapy outcomes. High-risk tumors were enriched for Tregs, B cells, and fibroblasts. FOXM1+ malignant epithelium represented the high-risk state, with elevated CNV burden and regulon activity; virtual FOXM1 knockout identified COL6A1 and CD44 among 129 significant non-target perturbation hits. Convergent single-cell and spatial analyses nominated a COL6A1-CD44 communication axis associated with fibroblast remodeling, with F5_SFRP2+ fibroblasts as the most plausible receiving state. These fibroblasts showed ECM-remodeling, adverse prognosis, and pathway activation. Isovitexin emerged as a lead FOXM1-targeting compound, significantly suppressing ccRCC proliferation, migration, and invasion. These findings support a testable communication model involving FOXM1+ epithelium, COL6A1-CD44 and F5_SFRP2+ fibroblasts. The in vitro results also support further evaluation of isovitexin in ccRCC.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103065.abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) poses a distinct modeling challenge. The disease varies by region, histology, metastatic site, and treatment history. It also develops within a gastric niche shaped by acid, mucus, polarity, microbes, and stroma. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) can preserve tumor-linked epithelial states and support living biobanks. They also enable genotype-phenotype studies and functional testing of therapeutic vulnerabilities. Their clinical value depends on representation, not model complexity alone. The assay must also return clear results within a useful clinical window. This review evaluates GC PDOs as functional companion models for precision oncology rather than stand-alone treatment decision tools. We discuss four barriers that limit clinical readiness. Establishment bias reduces representation of diffuse-type, scirrhous, and signet-ring cell carcinomas. Standard organoid lumens do not reproduce gastric acidity, stratified mucus, or Helicobacter pylori-driven polarity loss. Long-term expansion can select culture-adapted clones and weaken clinical representativeness. PDO drug screening also remains difficult to align with urgent treatment timelines. Fresh-sample assays may shorten turnaround time but reduce scale and depth. We further highlight biological insights gained from GC organoids. These include niche independence, epigenetic dependencies, ARID1A-linked vulnerabilities, and chemotherapy resistance. We propose a readiness framework based on six criteria: tumor authenticity, subtype coverage, niche fidelity, turnaround time, assay standards, and outcome validation. This framework may help define where GC PDOs can support clinical reasoning.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103066.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is characterized by marked epithelial heterogeneity and dynamic tumor-microenvironment interactions. However, epithelial states associated with progression across the normal-adenoma-carcinoma sequence remain incompletely defined. Single-cell RNA sequencing data from normal colorectal mucosa, adenoma, and tumor tissues were analyzed using inferCNV, Monocle, Slingshot, CytoTRACE, CellChat, and SCENIC. An OLFM4⁺ tumor cell risk score (OTRS) was constructed using Cox and LASSO regression, and TIMP1 function was evaluated in vitro. Eight major cell types and nine tumor epithelial subtypes were identified. C3 OLFM4⁺ cells showed elevated transcriptional activity, stemness, metabolic activity, and greater representation in carcinoma than adenoma tissues. Trajectory analyses positioned these cells in an early-to-intermediate transitional state. CellChat predicted prominent fibroblast-C3 OLFM4⁺ interactions, including a putative WNT2B-FZD/LRP axis, while SCENIC identified XBP1, NFIA, PPARG, HDAC2, and UBE2K as subtype-associated regulators. The C3 OLFM4⁺-derived OTRS stratified prognosis; high OTRS was associated with poorer survival, macrophage-enriched infiltration, higher stromal, immune, and TIDE scores, and differential predicted drug sensitivity. TIMP1 knockdown suppressed malignant behaviors in CRC cells. C3 OLFM4⁺ cells represent a stem-like, metabolically active tumor epithelial state associated with CRC progression, fibroblast-derived WNT signaling, immune-evasion-related features, and unfavorable prognosis. The OTRS model may support prognostic and therapeutic assessment, while TIMP1 contributes to malignant CRC cell behavior.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103067.abstract: Chemotherapy non-response remains a major challenge in bladder cancer, yet the endothelial states and intercellular communication programs associated with treatment failure remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, bulk transcriptomic data, computational analyses, and in vitro experiments to characterize endothelial programs associated with chemotherapy response. A non-response-related transcriptional program was preferentially enriched in endothelial cells and was most prominent in the TipEC_2 tip-like endothelial subset. Integrative analyses identified DLL4 as a key feature of this endothelial state. Spatial and ligand-receptor analyses further supported a DLL4-associated tip-like endothelial niche and inferred DLL4-NOTCH3-related communication between endothelial and malignant compartments, together with RBPJ-associated transcriptional activity in DLL4-positive TipEC_2 cells. Consistently, cisplatin-resistant bladder cancer cells showed increased expression of NOTCH3 and downstream transcriptional targets, whereas pharmacological Notch inhibition suppressed downstream HES1 and HEY1 expression and partially restored cisplatin sensitivity. Elevated DLL4 expression was associated with chemotherapy non-response and unfavorable survival. In a separate prognostic analysis, a DLL4-positive TipEC_2-associated risk model stratified patients by overall survival in TCGA-BLCA and GSE13507. Collectively, these findings identify a DLL4-associated tip-like endothelial niche linked to chemotherapy non-response and suggest DLL4-NOTCH3 signaling as a potential molecular link between vascular remodeling and treatment resistance in bladder cancer.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103068.abstract: Antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) activity and target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity depends in part on which cells express the target antigen, a feature that bulk assays cannot resolve. We analyzed a publicly available whole-transcriptome CosMx breast tumor dataset including 154,816 cells and 18,934 genes. Eleven clinically relevant ADC targets were profiled across seven annotated lineages. Findings were contextualized using TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues) and assessed in two public Xenium breast cancer specimens. HER2 (ERBB2), TROP2 (TACSTD2), HER3 (ERBB3), NECTIN4 and MUC1 were enriched in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 (CD276) was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, with similar mean expression in stromal and tumor cells. PSMA (FOLH1) was enriched in endothelium. TCGA-BRCA tumor-normal differences did not identify these cellular sources. No overall-survival association remained after multiple-testing correction or covariate adjustment. HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurred in both Xenium specimens, whereas EGFR was not tumor restricted. Cell-resolved spatial profiling separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from those expressed in vascular and stromal compartments. B7-H3 and PSMA localization was consistent with prior immunohistochemical reports and is confirmatory. These RNA-level results do not establish surface-protein abundance, ADC response, or clinical toxicity. Low-abundance microenvironmental findings remain based on a single discovery specimen and require protein-level validation. Protein-level confirmation, and correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity, are required before these maps can inform clinical decisions.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103069.abstract: Hypoxia-driven epigenetic remodeling is a critical determinant of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) progression and therapeutic resistance, yet the epigenetic mechanisms coordinating hypoxia signaling with tumor microenvironment remodeling remain incompletely understood. Here, by integrating LUAD cell models, murine tumor models, and spatial transcriptomics with reference-based cell-type deconvolution, we identify SATB2 as a previously unrecognized hypoxia-inducible epigenetic regulator in LUAD. HIF-1α, unlike HIF-2α, directly interacts with the promoter of SATB2, promoting its expression in hypoxic environments. Increased levels of SATB2 have been linked to more severe clinical and pathological characteristics as well as poorer outcomes for patients. Mechanistically, SATB2 physically interacts with HIF-1α and p300, while SATB2 loss reduces H3K27 acetylation and elongating RNA polymerase II occupancy at HIF-1 target loci, supporting a model in which SATB2 facilitates HIF-1α-dependent transcriptional elongation and establishes a positive feedback circuit that amplifies hypoxia-responsive transcriptional programs. Spatial transcriptomic analyses further show that SATB2-associated hypoxic programs are preferentially enriched within malignant tumor niches and are associated with remodeling of the local tumor microenvironment. Functionally, SATB2 promotes LUAD growth, metastasis, angiogenesis, and bevacizumab resistance in a HIF-1α-dependent manner, whereas genetic disruption of SATB2 or pharmacological inhibition of p300 enhances sensitivity to anti-angiogenic therapy. Collectively, these findings identify the SATB2-p300-HIF-1α axis as a hypoxia-responsive epigenetic regulatory mechanism linking transcriptional adaptation to malignant progression and resistance to anti-angiogenic therapy, and provide a preclinical rationale for further investigation of this pathway as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in LUAD.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103071.abstract: Acquired resistance to programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitors presents a major clinical challenge in the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This study aims to elucidate the epigenetic mechanisms underlying PD-1 inhibitor resistance, with a specific focus on the expression profiles of PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) and their associated signaling networks. High-throughput RNA sequencing was performed on matched pre- and post-resistance plasma samples from three NSCLC patients to identify differentially expressed piRNAs. The top five candidate piRNAs were selected for subsequent verification. Plasma piRNA levels and comprehensive clinical data from an independent cohort of 50 NSCLC patients (evaluated at both pre- and post-resistance stages) were analyzed. Downstream target genes of the candidate piRNAs were predicted using TargetScan and miRanda algorithms, followed by Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) functional enrichment analyses. Target gene expression was experimentally validated via quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). Spearman's rank correlation was utilized to assess the relationship between piRNA expression and systemic inflammatory indices. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Five candidate piRNAs (Hsap_2765751, Hsap_249, Hsap_1847317, Hsap_681799, and Hsap_857420) exhibited significant differential expression. Notably, Hsap_1847317 was robustly upregulated following the development of resistance (P < 0.001). Bioinformatic and experimental analyses implicated Hsap_1847317 is implicated in the Wnt signaling pathway, while qRT-PCR demonstrated significantly higher AXIN2 mRNA expression after resistance (P < 0.001). these associative data do not establish direct regulation. Furthermore, the systemic neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) significantly increased during the resistance phase (P < 0.001) and exhibited a positive correlation with Hsap_1847317 expression (r = 0.395, P = 0.005). ROC curve analysis demonstrated excellent predictive efficacy, yielding an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.944 for Hsap_1847317 and 0.720 for NLR in this cohort. Our findings indicate that plasma Hsap_1847317 and NLR are candidate non-invasive biomarkers for monitoring acquired resistance to PD-1 inhibitors in NSCLC. This study association between Hsap_1847317, Wnt-related enrichment, and AXIN2 mRNA provides a hypothesis for further mechanistic testing rather than evidence of a causal Hsap_1847317/Wnt/AXIN2 axis.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103072.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype of breast cancer characterized by high molecular heterogeneity and a lack of effective targeted therapies. Increasing evidence indicates that metabolic reprogramming and redox homeostasis are critical determinants of TNBC progression; however, the transcriptional mechanisms linking these processes to mitochondrial function remain incompletely understood. In this study, integrative bioinformatics analyses identified nuclear receptor subfamily 3 group C member 2 (NR3C2) as a potential regulatory factor in TNBC. NR3C2 expression was significantly decreased in TNBC and was associated with patient prognosis. Functional assays demonstrated that NR3C2 overexpression markedly inhibited cell proliferation and migration in vitro and suppressed tumor growth and dissemination in zebrafish xenograft models. Mechanistically, RNA sequencing identified NDUFB3, an accessory subunit of mitochondrial complex I, as a downstream target of NR3C2. Dual-luciferase reporter assays further confirmed that NR3C2 directly regulates NDUFB3 transcription. Functional analyses revealed that NR3C2 modulates mitochondrial activity, as evidenced by increased mitochondrial membrane potential and complex I activity, accompanied by reduced ATP production and elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. Notably, NR3C2-induced ROS accumulation promoted apoptosis, whereas these effects were partially reversed by NDUFB3 knockdown or treatment with the ROS scavenger N-acetylcysteine (NAC). Consistently, in vivo experiments demonstrated that NR3C2 suppresses tumor growth and metastasis in a ROS-dependent manner. Collectively, these findings indicate that NR3C2 inhibits TNBC progression by regulating mitochondrial function and ROS homeostasis, at least in part through NDUFB3. This study provides new insights into the interplay between transcriptional regulation and mitochondrial redox balance and highlights NR3C2 as a potential therapeutic target for TNBC.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103073.abstract: To investigate the roles of CARM1 and its regulatory effect on YIPF2 in breast cancer progression. Breast cancer cells were transfected with CARM1 siRNA to knock down CARM1 expression. Cell proliferation, apoptosis, migration, and invasion were assessed using EdU, CCK-8, Annexin V/PI flow cytometry, wound-healing, and transwell assays, respectively. Co-expression of CARM1 and YIPF2 was evaluated using the GEPIA database and validated by qRT-PCR. Co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) was performed to assess the association between CARM1 and YIPF2, and asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) signals in YIPF2 immunoprecipitates were assessed. Rescue experiments were performed following YIPF2 overexpression. In vivo studies were conducted to examine the anti-tumor effects of CARM1 inhibition. We found that CARM1 was upregulated in breast cancer patients and cell lines. Higher CARM1 expression was associated with poorer survival. CARM1 knockdown inhibited proliferation, colony formation, migration, and invasion of breast cancer cells, and induced apoptosis. The correlation analysis indicated that CARM1 and YIPF2 were positively co-expressed. Co-IP experiments supported an association between CARM1 and YIPF2. CARM1 knockdown reduced the ADMA signal in YIPF2 immunoprecipitates, consistent with CARM1-dependent YIPF2 methylation. In addition, elevated YIPF2 predicted worse survival outcomes in breast cancer patients. Overexpression of YIPF2 partially rescued the suppression of tumor progression induced by CARM1 knockdown. Finally, tumors derived from sh-CARM1 cells were markedly smaller than those from control cells. Collectively, our findings support a role for CARM1 in breast cancer progression and provide evidence of its association with YIPF2 and CARM1-dependent YIPF2 methylation, offering insights into the CARM1-YIPF2 regulatory axis and potential therapeutic strategies.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103074.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) lacks reliable biomarkers for early detection and remains a highly aggressive disease. Ephrin type-A receptor 2 (EphA2), a receptor tyrosine kinase frequently overexpressed in advanced cancers, undergoes MMP14-mediated cleavage that releases soluble N-terminal fragments. Here, we investigated the diagnostic and functional significance of this fragment in TNBC. Immunohistochemical analysis of clinical specimens revealed elevated EphA2 expression in TNBC tissues, with a trend toward higher levels in tumors of advanced stage and grade. To enable non-invasive detection, we established a dual-epitope sandwich ELISA targeting spatially distinct regions of the EphA2 extracellular domain. The assay showed concentration-dependent detection of recombinant EphA2 (EC₅₀, 48 ng/mL) and detected soluble EphA2 in TNBC cell-conditioned media. Serum analysis showed significantly higher EphA2 levels in TNBC patients compared with healthy controls (median 93.3 vs 25.6 ng/mL). In this exploratory cohort, ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.912 (95% CI, 0.862-0.962), with a sensitivity of 95.0% (95% CI, 86.3-98.6%) and a specificity of 78.3% (95% CI, 66.4-86.9%), and higher levels were associated with lymph node metastasis and higher histological grade. Functionally, recombinant EphA2-P328 promoted TNBC-cell migration and induced cell context-dependent changes in EMT-associated markers in vitro. Collectively, these findings support the soluble N-terminal EphA2 fragment as a candidate serum biomarker and an in vitro modulator of TNBC cell migration, warranting validation in larger independent cohorts and further mechanistic investigation.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103075.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the clinical, pathological, and immune characteristics of macrotrabecular hepatocellular carcinoma (MT-HCC) to identify distinct features, evaluate prognostic significance, and explore potential therapeutic targets for MT-HCC. A total of 83 MT-HCC and 111 CV-HCC patients who underwent liver resection were included. Clinicopathological data were analyzed using statistical methods. Among these cases, immunohistochemical (IHC) staining was performed on 48 cases of massive trabecular hepatocellular carcinoma to evaluate the distribution of immune cells across different tumor regions. The Friedman test, Spearman's correlation analysis, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, and Cox regression analysis were used to examine the relationships between immune infiltration characteristics and prognosis. MT-HCC exhibited more aggressive features, such as higher serum AFP levels (68% vs. 21%, p < 0.001), larger tumor size (7.65 cm vs. 4.47 cm, p < 0.001), and a higher frequency of vascular invasion (22% vs. 4%, p < 0.001), satellite nodules (41%vs. 16%, p < 0.001), and tumor necrosis (84% vs. 47%, p < 0.001). Survival analysis showed worse overall survival and higher recurrence rates in MT-HCC. The immune microenvironment displayed a typical "immune desert" phenotype, characterized by the spatial distribution of adaptive immune cells: sparse distribution within the tumor, enrichment at tumor margins, and enrichment adjacent to the tumor. In MT‑HCC, PD‑L1 expression was extremely low across all three tumor regions, whereas CTLA‑4 showed specific high expression at the tumor margins. Intratumoral CD8⁺ T cells exhibited a significant positive correlation with PD‑1 and CTLA‑4 (r = 0.701, P < 0.001), suggesting the dual exhaustion state of intratumoral T cells. Multivariate analysis identified cross‑regional FOXP3⁺ Treg infiltration, maximum tumor diameter, and macrovascular invasion as independent risk factors for overall survival. Conversely, peritumoral CD4⁺ T cells served as protective immune markers and were associated with reduced mortality risk in patients. The findings suggest that MT-HCC possesses invasive clinical characteristics and exhibits distinctive spatial immune heterogeneity, where immune cell distribution plays a critical role in prognosis. Targeting specific immune cell populations may offer new therapeutic strategies for MT-HCC and improve patient outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103076.abstract: Gastrodin is a natural compound with anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antitumor activities; however, its therapeutic role and molecular mechanisms in colorectal cancer (CRC) remain unclear. In this study, we explored the anti-CRC mechanisms of gastrodin through integrated bioinformatics and experimental validation. The potential targets of gastrodin were obtained from public databases. Transcriptomic data of CRC were retrieved from TCGA and GEO datasets, and the differentially expressed genes were screened. The CRC-related genes were subjected to gene-set variation analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and the core genes were identified by the LASSO regression, support vector machine, and random forest algorithms, followed by SHAP analysis. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), immune infiltration analysis, consensus clustering, molecular docking, and in vitro experiments were further performed. A total of 628 potential gastrodin targets and 15 overlapping CRC-related genes were identified. Five core hub genes, including NFE2L3, UBE2S, CA9, CCNB1, and CFD, were screened, among which NFE2L3 showed the highest SHAP importance score. The scRNA-seq data indicated cell-type-specific expression patterns of these genes in CRC tissues. Immune infiltration analysis further suggested that gastrodin may regulate the CRC immune microenvironment by regulating the activated B cells, activated CD4⁺ T cells, and other immune cells. Molecular docking revealed favorable binding affinity between gastrodin and the five core proteins. Moreover, NFE2L3 was highly expressed in CRC tissues and cell lines, and its knockdown significantly inhibited the proliferation, migration, and invasion of the tumor cells. Gastrodin may suppress CRC progression by targeting key genes, particularly NFE2L3, and modulating the tumor immune microenvironment. Furthermore, our study has identified the potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets for CRC.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103078.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is molecularly, cellularly and spatially heterogeneous, and current staging systems and biomarkers incompletely explain prognosis and treatment response. This study integrated transcriptomics, machine learning, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics and in vitro experiments to prioritize candidate CRC-associated markers and characterize their potential biological and clinical relevance. GSE44861 and GSE44076 from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and The Cancer Genome Atlas Colon Adenocarcinoma (TCGA-COAD) were used for differential expression, consensus differentially expressed gene (DEG) identification and functional enrichment analyses. Four machine-learning algorithms were applied for feature selection. Candidate genes were prioritized by differential expression, model importance and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) performance. GSE231559 single-cell data and spatial transcriptomics characterized the cellular source, pseudotime dynamics and spatial distribution of the core gene. TCGA-COAD assessed prognosis, pathways and computationally predicted drug sensitivity. Western blotting, Transwell and MTT assays were used for experimental validation, and public immunohistochemistry images from the Human Protein Atlas were used as supplementary protein-expression evidence. We identified 544 consensus DEGs enriched in leukocyte migration, chemotaxis, extracellular matrix organization, cytokine activity and metabolic pathways. Six genes were jointly selected: CLDN1, CDH3, KRT24, MMP7, NEBL and SCGN. CLDN1 was markedly upregulated and showed the highest tumour-versus-normal discrimination among the six candidates in the TCGA-COAD cohort. Single-cell and spatial analyses showed that CLDN1 was mainly expressed in CRC epithelial cells, displayed increasing expression across the inferred pseudotime ordering, and was enriched in malignant and mixed regions. In the TCGA-COAD cohort, high CLDN1 expression was associated with poorer overall survival and pathways involving the cell cycle, proteasome, autophagy, Hippo, ErbB and CRC. CLDN1 manipulation altered CRC-cell invasion and in vitro response to Nutlin-3a (-). These findings support CLDN1 as a candidate CRC-associated marker linked to malignant epithelial-cell states, tumour-associated spatial heterogeneity, invasive phenotype and Nutlin-3a (-) response. Further independent and prospective validation is required to determine its clinical diagnostic, prognostic and treatment-response relevance.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103080.abstract: Mutation-based liquid biopsy supports diagnosis and disease monitoring in hematologic malignancies, but interpretation of plasma variants may be complicated by clonal hematopoiesis, treatment-related changes, and nonmalignant blood-cell turnover. This structured narrative review evaluates whether cell-free DNA (cfDNA) fragmentomics, DNA methylation, and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) provide complementary information beyond mutation detection. Direct plasma evidence is most developed for selected fragmentomic and 5hmC applications, although most studies remain retrospective, internally validated, or proof of concept. Fragmentomic studies have reported associations with lymphoma classification, outcome assessment, and longitudinal tumor-effector profiling during chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, but routine clinical utility and decision thresholds are not established. Plasma 5hmC studies have reported associations with lymphoma classification, treatment response, prognosis, and measurable residual disease in acute myeloid leukemia, whereas pharmacodynamic monitoring during Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibition remains hypothesis-generating. DNA methylation may support source-cell or lineage inference, but lineage assignment does not establish malignant fraction, and key disease-assessment studies remain largely tissue-based, cellular-DNA-based, cross-cancer, or methodological. The novelty of this review is a structured evidence map that distinguishes direct plasma evidence from indirect support and compares the three modalities by biological information, assay compatibility, and validation maturity. We also propose a hypothesis-generating framework for sample-level integration using separate assay-specific aliquots and computational combination of outputs. No universal analytical order or clinically validated integrated workflow has been established. Fragmentomic and epigenomic profiling should therefore be regarded as investigational complements to mutation-based testing, requiring independent prospective validation against established genomic, cellular, imaging, and tissue-based methods.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103103.abstract: Intestinal fibrosis is a major complication of Crohn's disease, for which targeted therapies remain unavailable. Fibrosis is defined by excess matrix deposition, which may result from inadequate phagocytic clearance, yet how phagocytosis shifts here is unclear. Using single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, we identify fibrosis-associated CD47hi fibroblasts coupled to SIRPAhi macrophages in fibrotic regions. Cell-cell communication analyses and neutralizing-antibody experiments identify interleukin-1β as a mediator of their crosstalk, forming a profibrotic niche characterized by phagocytic evasion. Genetic disruption of fibroblast Cd47 or macrophage Sirpa enhances fibroblast clearance and attenuates fibrosis. Mechanistically, checkpoint disruption reprograms macrophages toward an NRF2-associated pro-phagocytic state, linking enhanced clearance to the antifibrotic response. Furthermore, therapeutic antibody blockade of this checkpoint attenuates intestinal fibrosis in mouse models with schedule-dependent efficacy. Collectively, these findings support CD47-mediated phagocytic evasion as a key pathogenic mechanism in intestinal fibrosis and identify CD47-SIRPα blockade as a promising therapeutic target.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103111.abstract: Immunotherapy for colorectal cancer (CRC) remains limited due to the inherently low tumor immunogenicity and the profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Herein, capitalizing on the metabolic traits and anatomical accessibility of CRC, we propose a broadly applicable oral strategy based on metabolically engineered bacteria (EcN-HlpA-CGL [EHC]) for CRC immunotherapy. Mechanistically, cystathionine γ-lyase expressed by EHC disrupts redox homeostasis, triggering ferroptosis in CRC cells and thereby enhancing tumor immunogenicity. Concurrently, the intrinsic adjuvant activity of the bacteria amplifies the cancer-immunity cycle driven by immunogenic cell death and remodels the immunosuppressive TME. In vivo studies demonstrate that this orally delivered engineered bacterial platform not only suppresses the growth of orthotopic CRC tumors but also inhibits metastatic progression, indicating the induction of a potent systemic immune response. Immune profiling confirms robust systemic and gut mucosal immune activation following oral administration. Collectively, this oral metabolically engineered bacterial platform is precisely tailored to the features of CRC and offers a safe and effective immunotherapeutic strategy for this malignancy.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103112.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability, and non-invasive stimulation of deep brain circuits such as the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) remains challenging. This randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial recruits 96 adults with moderate-to-severe MDD who received 10 sessions of 2 mA low-current, 15 mA high-current, or sham transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) targeting the left sgACC. The high-current group shows significantly greater reductions in depressive symptoms (17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale [HDRS-17] score) post-treatment and at 1-month follow-up compared with sham and outperforms the low-current group post-treatment. Exploratory Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) analyses suggest improved sleep quality in both active groups, whereas anxiety outcomes show no intergroup differences. High-current tTIS is safe and well tolerated, with only transient tingling. These findings provide preliminary evidence that sgACC-targeted tTIS relieves depressive symptoms safely, with more robust short-to medium-term effects observed under the 15 mA protocol. This trial registers on Chictr.org.cn (ChiCTR2400094971).

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103113.abstract: PD-L1-mediated immunosuppression is a key mechanism underlying tumor immune evasion, whereas PD-1/PD-L1 blockade therapies remain limited by low response rates and acquired resistance. Through small-molecule screening, we identify isobavachalcone (IBC), a naturally derived compound that modulates PD-L1 homeostasis by targeting the deubiquitinase OTUB1. Mechanistically, IBC targets OTUB1 at the His217 residue and suppresses its deubiquitinase activity, thereby promoting K48-linked polyubiquitination of PD-L1 and its proteasome-dependent degradation. Functionally, IBC reduces tumor cell PD-L1 expression and enhances CD8+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity. In PD-L1-deficient tumor models, IBC fails to further enhance antitumor activity, indicating that PD-L1 is required for IBC-mediated immune regulation. Moreover, IBC combined with anti-CTLA-4 therapy further enhanced antitumor efficacy. Together, these findings highlight IBC as a potential drug candidate that promotes PD-L1 degradation and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of targeting the OTUB1-PD-L1 axis to improve immune checkpoint therapy.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103115.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2) are produced in enteroendocrine L cells and control energy homeostasis. GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) activation improves glucose homeostasis and induces satiety and weight loss, whereas GLP-2 receptor (GLP-2R) signaling promotes intestinal growth and nutrient absorption. GLP-1R and GLP-2R agonism also reduce intestinal damage in preclinical studies. Here, we demonstrate that endogenous GLP-1R and GLP-2R signaling are essential for protecting the intestine from T cell-mediated enteropathy. Gut injury induced by T cell activation is increased in Glp1r-/- and Glp2r-/- mice, as well as in mice with selective loss of intestinal proglucagon gene expression (GcgGut-/-). Conversely, the GLP-2R agonist teduglutide and the GLP-1R agonist semaglutide, administered separately or together, attenuate αCD3-induced intestinal damage in GcgGut-/- mice. Collectively, these findings demonstrate distinct biological roles for endogenous GLP-1R/GLP-2R activity in immune-mediated intestinal injury and highlight the therapeutic potential of glucagon-like peptides, alone or together, for ameliorating T cell-mediated mucosal injury.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103116.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has achieved remarkable success in hematologic malignancies, but durable efficacy remains limited by insufficient CAR-T cell persistence. Here, we show that activated CAR-T cells upregulate multiple NKG2D ligands (NKG2DLs), increasing their susceptibility to natural killer (NK) cell-mediated CAR-T cell cytotoxicity. To address this vulnerability, we engineer CAR-T cells to overexpress full-length NKG2D (CAR-NG). NKG2D overexpression reduces the surface accessibility of endogenous NKG2DLs without decreasing their total protein abundance. In parallel, engagement of tumor-expressed NKG2DLs in trans provides additional costimulatory signals, enhancing CAR-T cell activation and proliferation while attenuating exhaustion-associated phenotypes. In hematologic and solid tumor models, CAR-NG cells exhibit reduced susceptibility to NK-cell-mediated cytotoxicity, improved tumor control, increased in vivo expansion, deeper tumor infiltration, and no evident additional toxicity compared with conventional CAR-T cells. These findings identify NKG2D overexpression as an engineering strategy that enhances CAR-T antitumor activity primarily through tumor NKG2DL-dependent trans costimulation.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103117.abstract: Squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) comprise a group of lethal malignancies, yet developing SCC-specific therapies remains challenging, largely due to a lack of druggable targets. We identify SOX2 condensation as a shared cancer hallmark across esophageal, head and neck, and lung SCCs. Within SOX2, the activation domain 1 (AD1) acts as the condensate-promoting region via its aromatic and hydrophobic residues. Site-specific mutagenesis, orthotopic mouse models, and multi-omics sequencing demonstrate that SOX2 condensates upregulate oncogene expression by enhancing SOX2 chromatin occupancy, H3K27ac enrichment, and chromatin interactions at oncogenic loci such as FGFR2, thereby promoting SCC progression. An FDA-approved drug screen reveals that the proteasome inhibitor ixazomib disrupts SOX2 condensates in an HSP70-dependent manner. Upon ixazomib treatment, the substrate-binding domain of HSP70 blocks SOX2 AD1, selectively dissolving SOX2 condensates, downregulating oncogene expression, and suppressing condensate-positive SCC patient-derived xenografts. These findings highlight targeting SOX2 condensates with proteasome inhibitors as an SCC-specific, biomarker-guided therapeutic strategy.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103120.abstract: The role of senescent tumor cells in modulating the immune microenvironment and influencing immunotherapy efficacy remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the function of the senescence-associated gene membrane magnesium transporter 1 (MMGT1) in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) immunotherapy. MMGT1 is upregulated in TNBC and correlates with poor prognosis. Mammary gland-specific knockout of Mmgt1 significantly impedes tumor growth. Mechanistically, MMGT1 promotes lipid metabolism by facilitating translocation of the SCAP-SREBP1 complex to the Golgi apparatus, thereby suppressing cellular senescence. Notably, senescent TNBC cells enhance CD8+ T cell proliferation and cytotoxicity through CCL20 secretion. Furthermore, a positive feedback loop exists between MMGT1 and SREBP1. In vivo, AZ191 downregulates MMGT1 expression, which suppresses tumor growth and enhances the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy. Collectively, these findings reveal a critical role for MMGT1 in shaping the TNBC immune microenvironment and suggest that targeting MMGT1 represents a promising strategy to improve anti-PD-1 immunotherapy outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103121.abstract: Acute graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD), following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and organ rejection are serious immune-mediated complications driven by alloreactive T cells. CTPS1, a crucial enzyme for de novo CTP synthesis, is essential for the proliferation of activated T cells, representing an attractive therapeutic target for controlling T cell-mediated pathologies. In this study, using Ctps1-deficient T cells in fully MHC-mismatched and haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplantation models, a complete blockage in the induction of aGVHD is observed in association with significantly reduced alloreactive effector T cell expansion. In skin graft rejection models, expansion of alloreactive Ctps1-deficient T cells is reduced, and graft destruction is delayed but not prevented. Notably, the healing process allows T cells to mediate skin graft rejection independently of CTPS1. Finally, treatment with a specific CTPS1 inhibitor rescues mice from lethal aGVHD. Our results underscore the pivotal role of CTPS1 in driving alloreactive T cell responses, highlighting its potential for aGVHD treatment.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103123.abstract: Radiotherapy is often limited by tumor-intrinsic DNA repair and an immunosuppressive microenvironment, both of which are reinforced by lactate accumulation. Here, we develop a CXCR4-engineered enucleated hepatocyte cytoplast platform decorated with Au-Pt Janus nanorobots (AP/LCCXCR4) to deplete intratumoral lactate and amplify radiation-induced oxidative stress. The hepatocyte cytoplasts home to tumors and consume lactate through gluconeogenesis, reducing repair-associated protein lactylation and impairing MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 (MRN) co-fractionation and chromatin recruitment, thereby impairing double-strand break repair. In parallel, the Au-Pt nanorobots enhance reactive oxygen species generation under acidic tumor conditions, increasing radiation damage. In radioresistant colorectal cancer models and a metastatic cervical cancer model, AP/LCCXCR4 combined with radiotherapy sustains DNA damage, promotes immunogenic cell death, reduces immunosuppressive myeloid and regulatory T (Treg) cell populations, enhances dendritic cell maturation and CD8+ T cell activation, and improves tumor control and survival.

doi:10.1016/j.xgen.2026.101358.abstract: Somatic mosaicism is widespread in human biology and disease, yet robust benchmarks are scarce. The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Consortium mixed six HapMap cell lines to create artificial somatic variants spanning 0.25%-16.5% variant allele fractions. We developed a technology-agnostic method that builds pangenome graphs from individual assemblies to create unified benchmarking sets: >6 million single-nucleotide variants, >1.8 million small insertions/deletions, >49,000 structural variations, and 10,000 mobile element insertions across autosomes and mitochondrial chromosomes. We validated the variants using ultra-deep simulated reads and developed a binomial-based model to estimate coverage requirements for variant detection. Evaluating multiple callers showed that telomere-to-telomere CHM13 alignment improves structural variant detection and offers advantages in difficult-to-map regions compared to GRCh38. Low-allele-fraction variant detection remained particularly challenging in repeat-rich genomic regions and falsely duplicated genes. This accurate, versatile resource enables systematic evaluation of somatic variant detection technologies.

doi:10.1016/j.xgen.2026.101386.abstract: Midbody remnants (MBRs), once considered inert cytokinetic debris, are now recognized as architecturally specialized, translationally active organelles whose functions reflect the mode of cell division. This review compares MBR biology in symmetric somatic mitosis and asymmetric oocyte meiosis. In somatic cells, MBRs can be retained or secreted as large extracellular vesicles that carry midbody proteins, RNAs, and translation machinery; their enrichment in stem and cancer cells implicates them in cell-state regulation and identifies them as promising, though unvalidated, substrates for liquid-biopsy biomarkers and therapeutic targeting. In oocytes, meiotic midbodies form a distinctive ring-cap architecture that concentrates local translation and restricts maternal products to the egg, thereby supporting developmental competence. Together, these studies establish division mode as a key determinant of midbody architecture, cargo, fate, and translational potential, linking cytokinesis to cancer biology and reproductive medicine.

doi:10.1016/j.xgen.2026.101390.abstract: Mosaic mutations in normal tissues occur at low variant allele fractions (VAFs), complicating detection. To benchmark variant-calling strategies, the SMaHT Network created a cell-line mixture (1:49) and produced ultra-deep short- and long-read whole-genome sequencing data across five centers (170×-470× per center). We assembled a reference set of mosaic SNVs and indels, cross-validated with long-read data to expose short-read limitations. We also partitioned the genome by mappability to examine the impact of genomic context, added a negative reference set, and accounted for culture-derived mutations. When seven institutions applied twelve pipelines, callsets were largely discordant across tools and replicates, partly reflecting stochastic sampling of low-VAF mutations in biological replicates. For SNVs with VAFs above 2%, sensitivity and precision approached 80% at ≥300×, with little gain from additional sequencing. This work establishes a framework and best practices for reliably detecting low-VAF mutations in non-cancer tissues and provides a valuable resource for the community.

doi:10.1016/j.xgen.2026.101391.abstract: The importance of gene-environment interactions (G × E) for complex human traits is heavily debated. Recently, biobank-based genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have revealed many statistically significant G × E signals, though most lack clear evidence of biological significance. Here, we partly explain this discrepancy by showing that many G × E signals simplify to additive effects on a different phenotype scale, a classical concern that is currently underappreciated. Our results clearly distinguish G × sex effects on height, which vanish on the log scale, from G × sex effects on testosterone, where the log scale uncovers biologically meaningful female-specific effects. Across 32 phenotypes in UK Biobank, we find that scaling by a power transformation can explain 45% of polygenic score (PGS) × sex interactions and that simple log transformation can explain 23%, with similar results for other environments. We also show that the phenotype scale can substantially impact GWAS discovery and the construction and evaluation of polygenic scores. Finally, we provide a set of guidelines to consider and choose phenotype scales in modern genetic studies.

doi:10.1016/j.xgen.2026.101397.abstract: Accurate identification of immunogenic neoantigens remains a bottleneck in personalized cancer vaccine development, particularly in low-mutation-burden tumors such as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). We developed NeoBridge, a hybrid ensemble integrating gradient boosting and a deep neural network across four biologically grounded feature dimensions: HLA binding and processing, differential agretopicity, tumor neoantigen abundance, and TCR recognition potential. Trained on 11,188 experimentally validated neoantigens, NeoBridge achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.904 on held-out data, with cross-cancer generalization (AUC: 0.73-0.82), including 0.82 in pancreatic cancer, and outperformed established tools. Differential agretopicity emerged as the dominant predictive feature. In 118 PDAC patients with resolved phylogenies and complete follow up, subclonal neoantigen load was associated with worse progression-free survival (p < 0.001) and overall survival (p = 0.038). These findings are hypothesis generating and require prospective immunopeptidomic and functional validation.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.09.018.abstract: To determine whether plasma and serum extracellular vesicles (EV) are interchangeable for immunoaffinity-enriched proteomic profiling in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), and whether an EV protein signature improves diagnostic performance beyond CA-125 for detecting ovarian cancer. We performed immunoaffinity-enriched proteomic profiling of EV subpopulations from 243 paired EDTA plasma and serum samples in a nested case-control cohort from the UK Ovarian Cancer Population Study (controls, benign, borderline, and HGSOC). Analyses assessed proteomic depth, plasma-serum concordance, and diagnostic performance using machine learning. Plasma-derived EV subpopulations showed greater proteomic depth than serum, with 6439 versus 5451 protein groups identified and 2838 versus 840 proteins detected at 50% prevalence. Protein intensities were highly concordant between matrices (r = 0.86, p < 0.001), maintained across disease groups and cancer stages. For distinguishing HGSOC from non-cancers, an EV-augmented CA-125 model achieved an AUROC of 0.97 in plasma and 0.96 in serum, improving plasma sensitivity to 99% (95% CI 89-100) and specificity to 85% (95% CI 68-91) versus 96% (95% CI 82-100) sensitivity and 65% (95% CI 15-73) specificity for CA-125 alone, with similarly high discrimination in serum. Surface epitope-targeted EV subpopulation enrichment yields specific proteomic profiling of HGSOC with highly concordant biomarker signatures across plasma and serum, supporting their interchangeable use in clinical and biobank settings. The EV-augmented CA-125 model outperformed CA-125 alone, with recurrent EV proteins reflecting mucin-mediated immune evasion, and metabolic reprogramming, underscoring the translational potential of this approach for blood-based ovarian cancer detection.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.001.abstract: Surgical randomized trials have transformed gynecologic oncology by redefining the extent and route of surgery, nodal assessment, and multimodality care. However, the effect of a surgical trial does not end at publication. Unlike medical therapies, surgical interventions depend on operator expertise, team coordination, pathology support and perioperative infrastructure. Beyond controlled trial settings, these conditions may change, creating technical drift, indication drift, and inequitable adoption. Implementation should therefore be considered a distinct, structured phase of surgical research. The period is particularly vulnerable because landmark trials often evaluate de-escalation or technically complex innovations. Expanding de-escalation beyond trial-tested eligibility can cause undertreatment, whereas diffusion of complex procedures without sufficient expertise or infrastructure can increase morbidity. Disparities in access to specialist surgeons, imaging, pathology, molecular testing, perioperative support, and long-term follow-up amplify these risks. Responsible translation requires trial reports to define the technical, institutional, and patient-selection conditions under which outcomes were achieved. Strategies may include credentialing expectations, operative standards, and risk-appropriate guidelines. Once findings sufficiently resolve equipoise, post-implementation surveillance should determine whether effective procedures are adopted-or ineffective ones abandoned-and whether appropriate use, technical fidelity, safety, equity, and outcomes are maintained as practice spreads. Secondary databases can evaluate utilization, perioperative safety, equity, practice-change attribution, and selected real-world outcomes at scale, but incompletely capture appropriateness, technical fidelity, granular complications, recurrence, and patient-reported quality of life. Surveillance should therefore use a multilevel approach that matches each objective to where information is generated and supplements broad databases with targeted clinical, procedural, and patient-reported data. Treated as an active research phase, surveillance can ensure that surgical innovation reaches the right patients and settings, with outcomes consistent with the supporting evidence.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.003.abstract: To describe the current landscape of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) to treat surgical menopause following bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) in individuals with hereditary ovarian cancer risk in British Columbia, Canada. We aimed to describe current use of HRT, identify factors associated with HRT use and identify potential barriers for uptake and access. Individuals with germline pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in an ovarian cancer susceptibility gene were identified through the BC Cancer Hereditary Cancer Program (HCP) Progeny database. A cross-sectional survey was administered to collect participant demographics, personal and family cancer history, and participant experiences with HRT. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize the sample and logistic regression used to explore associations between sociodemographic variables and reported HRT use. Open text fields were analyzed using inductive quantitative content analysis. In total, 374 responses were received from 1284 potential participants (29.1% response rate). Of participants who have had a BSO, 41% (101/245) report HRT use. In open-text responses, 22% of participants reported lack of support by healthcare professionals and 26% described gaps in counselling about HRT and surgical menopause. In the regression analysis, HRT use was less likely in individuals who: were of increasing age, reported a history of any cancer type and who reported receiving no counselling about HRT (all p < 0.0011 after Bonferroni correction). Barriers to HRT access and uptake exist for individuals at increased risk of ovarian cancer. Together this data indicates that patients require additional support in this area particularly as it relates to education and resources.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.004.abstract: Metformin is a potential anticancer agent; however, evidence of benefit in endometrial neoplasia is limited. We evaluated whether adding metformin improved the outcomes of progestin-based fertility-sparing treatment. In this multicenter, open-label, randomized, phase IIb trial using blinded central adjudication, women aged 18-42years with an institutional diagnosis of atypical endometrial hyperplasia (AEH) or presumed stage IA grade 1 endometrioid carcinoma were assigned (1:1:1) to medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) alone, MPA plus metformin 750mg/day, or MPA plus metformin 1500mg/day. Central pathological review reclassified baseline specimens according to the 2020 World Health Organization criteria and adjudicated remission and recurrence. The primary endpoint was the 3-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) rate from treatment initiation. Secondary endpoints included remission, pregnancy outcomes, and safety. Analysis included 154 patients. Median body mass index was 24.3 (range, 15.6-57.1) kg/m2. The Kaplan-Meier estimates of the 3-year RFS rate were 44.7% with MPA alone and 44.5% with the pooled metformin groups. The prespecified log-rank test showed no significant difference (P=0.825). Remission rates were 54.0%, 58.8%, and 50.9% in the MPA-alone, metformin 750mg, and metformin 1500mg groups, respectively. Among the 57 women who attempted to conceive, pregnancy occurred in 36.8%, 57.9%, and 42.1%, and live birth in 31.6%, 52.6%, and 31.6%, respectively. Metformin increased gastrointestinal adverse events and was associated with less MPA-associated weight gain; no new safety signals emerged. Adding metformin to MPA did not improve RFS or remission rates, suggesting limited benefit in fertility-sparing treatment of endometrial neoplasia.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.005.abstract: As immunotherapy (IO) is increasingly utilized for treatment of endometrial cancer (EC) and cervical cancer (CC), optimal treatment strategies after IO remains poorly defined. We evaluated clinical outcomes, treatment patterns, toxicity, and survival among patients with recurrent EC and CC who received IO after prior IO. An Institutional Review Board approved, single-institution retrospective cohort study was conducted among patients with recurrent EC or CC treated with subsequent IO between January 1, 2017, and January 1, 2025. Patients were included if they received at least one dose of IO after prior IO. Clinical characteristics, immune-related adverse events, response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) were abstracted from the electronic medical record. Of fifty eligible patients, 36 had EC and 14 had CC. Pembrolizumab was the most common first IO agent in both cohorts. Second IO regimens differed by disease site, with pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib most common in EC and pembrolizumab alone most common in CC. Following second IO exposure, objective response rate was 27.8% for EC and 14.3% for CC, while disease control rate was 55.6% and 64.3%, respectively. Median PFS with second IO exposure was 8.1 months in EC and 9.7 months in CC. Grade 3/4 immune-related adverse events occurred in 20.0% during second IO. IO retreatment demonstrated clinical activity in selected patients with recurrent EC and CC after prior IO, with disease control achieved in more than half of patients. Prospective studies are needed to define optimal patient selection and post-IO treatments.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.006.abstract: The PERSONA-Ovary study evaluated germline pathogenic/likely-pathogenic variant prevalence, feasibility of unselected multigene testing integration in routine clinical care, and germline-somatic BRCA concordance in ovarian cancer patients. We conducted a prospective observational study of consecutive ovarian carcinoma patients treated at a tertiary-cancer care center, between July 2018 and September 2021. Germline multigene panel testing was performed using next-generation sequencing. Feasibility was assessed by informative rate and turnaround time. Germline-somatic concordance was assessed in patients with paired tumor BRCA results. Among 320 patients, pathogenic/likely-pathogenic variants were identified in 95 (29.7%, 95% CI 24.7-35.0); 81 (85.3%, 95% CI 76.5-91.7) carried mutations in ovarian cancer susceptibility genes, including 60 with BRCA alterations (63.2%, BRCA1 n=43, BRCA2 n=17). Germline testing was informative in all patients (100%). Median turnaround time was 221days (IQR 173-284), improving significantly across study periods (p<0.001). Tumor BRCA testing was available in 298 patients (93.1%), with germline-somatic concordance of 94.0% (κ=0.82, 95% CI 0.72-0.90). A germline-first strategy with reflex tumor testing achieved complete detection with fewer assays than parallel testing; a tumor-first strategy required the fewest assays (366 vs 596) but missed two germline BRCA carriers (detection rate of 96.3%). Unselected germline multigene panel testing was technically feasible and clinically informative in routine ovarian cancer care. Pathogenic/likely-pathogenic variants were identified in 29.7% of patients, supporting germline testing integration into contemporary ovarian cancer management. Although germline-first strategies maximize hereditary cancer detection, dedicated molecular workflows remain necessary to ensure clinically actionable turnaround times.
