doi:10.1053/j.jvca.2026.09.054.abstract: To evaluate the effect of autologous platelet-rich plasma (aPRP) on perioperative allogeneic blood product transfusion requirement in patients undergoing cyanotic congenital heart disease (CCHD) surgery and patients' prognosis. A retrospective cohort study. A tertiary university hospital. A total of 95 patients with CCHD who underwent cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) between January 2020 and August 2025 were included, of whom 81 (85.3%) underwent redo operation. Patients were divided into the aPRP group and the control group according to whether aPRP apheresis was employed. In the aPRP group, aPRP was harvested after anesthesia and transfused back to the patient after protamine neutralization, whereas the concurrently collected concentrated red blood cells (cRBCs) were reinfused during CPB or chest closure (from weaning from CPB to skin closure). In the original cohort, the aPRP group had significantly lower packed red blood cell (PRBC) transfusion rates, as well as PRBC and fresh-frozen plasma (FFP) transfusion volume, than the control group. After propensity score matching, the intraoperative PRBC transfusion rate no longer differed significantly between groups (aPRP v control: 17.4% v 43.5%, p = 0.180). However, the PRBC transfusion volume remained significantly lower in the aPRP group, both as total volume (0 [0, 0] v 0 [0, 400] mL; p = 0.037) and as weight-adjusted volume (0 [0, 0] v 0 [0, 15.7] mL/kg; p = 0.045). The matched intraoperative FFP transfusion requirements were also significantly reduced in the aPRP group (200 [0, 600] v 600 [400, 1,000] mL, p < 0.05). Viscoelastic testing indicated significantly improved coagulation and platelet function following aPRP administration in the treatment group. No difference in intraoperative blood loss, postoperative allogeneic blood products, 24-hour chest tube drainage, use of coagulation agents, postoperative ventilation time, or intensive care unit stay was observed. In a predominantly redo cohort of patients with CCHD undergoing cardiac surgery, the use of aPRP was associated with reduced intraoperative allogeneic blood and plasma transfusion requirements, and it also effectively preserved hemostatic function in these patients. However, the reduction in allogeneic product use may not be primarily due to the preserved hemostatic function conferred by aPRP but rather to autologous substitution of allogeneic products.

doi:10.1053/j.jvca.2026.09.055.abstract: To evaluate the association between the addition of enteral chloral hydrate to a postoperative sedation protocol and benzodiazepine exposure, sedation quality, withdrawal, delirium, and short-term clinical outcomes in children undergoing congenital heart surgery. Single-center retrospective before-and-after cohort study. Pediatric cardiac intensive care unit of a tertiary referral center. Eighty-six children who underwent congenital heart surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, required postoperative mechanical ventilation for more than 24 hours, and received sedation for at least 24 hours. Patients were treated according to the institutional postoperative sedation protocol before (July 2021-June 2023) and after (August 2023-July 2025) implementation of enteral chloral hydrate as an adjunctive sedative. The primary endpoint was cumulative midazolam exposure during the pediatric cardiac intensive care unit stay. Secondary endpoints included sedative and analgesic requirements, sedation and pain scores, withdrawal, delirium, and clinical outcomes. Compared with the preprotocol group, the chloral hydrate group had significantly lower cumulative midazolam exposure (10.2 v 13.2 mg/kg, p = 0.010) and peak midazolam infusion rates (0.15 v 0.20 mg/kg/h, p < 0.001), and a lower observed frequency of delirium (14.6% v 37.8%, p = 0.015). No significant between-group differences were observed in sedation quality, pain scores, withdrawal, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of stay in the pediatric cardiac intensive care unit or hospital, or mortality. Addition of enteral chloral hydrate to a postoperative sedation protocol was associated with reduced benzodiazepine exposure and a lower observed frequency of delirium without statistically significant differences in sedation quality or short-term clinical outcomes. Prospective multicenter studies are warranted to confirm these findings.

doi:10.1056/nejmcp2516040.abstract: Attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a medical condition that is present in approximately 2.5% of adults worldwide and manifests in a variety of different ways across the lifespan. Adults with ADHD often have coexisting psychiatric disorders such as anxiety, mood, sleep, substance use, and personality disorders and are at increased risk for coexisting somatic conditions such as obesity, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and immune and inflammatory conditions. Hence, such adults may be seen by clinicians providing care for a wide range of psychiatric and somatic conditions. Nevertheless, ADHD remains unrecognized and undiagnosed in many persons. Assessment requires interviewing of the patient for core ADHD symptoms, coexisting conditions, and their functional effects, which can be facilitated by using standardized rating scales. Key components of treatment are psychoeducation and psychostimulant or nonstimulant medication, mostly in combination with psychosocial interventions and lifestyle guidance.

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2518753.abstract: In eastern and southern Africa, approximately 1 million people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and receiving oral therapy do not have viral suppression because of adherence challenges. We conducted a phase 3b, open-label, randomized trial to compare long-acting injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine with oral dolutegravir-based therapy among adults with virally suppressed HIV type 1 (viral load, <200 copies per milliliter) and suboptimal adherence or care engagement. The participants were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive intramuscular injections of cabotegravir (600 mg) plus rilpivirine (900 mg) every 8 weeks, with the first two injection visits occurring 4 weeks apart, or to continue daily oral dolutegravir-based therapy; baseline drug-resistance testing was not performed. The primary end point was a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter at week 48; noninferiority was assessed with a margin of -10 percentage points. Confirmed virologic failure (two consecutive viral loads of ≥200 copies per milliliter) was a key secondary end point. A total of 540 participants were enrolled across seven sites in Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda; 537 were included in the primary analysis. At 48 weeks, 244 of 268 participants (91.0%) in the long-acting-therapy group had a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter, as compared with 240 of 269 participants (89.2%) in the oral-therapy group (risk difference, 1.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -3.1 to 6.9), which met the criterion for noninferiority. The results of a per-protocol analysis were consistent with those of the primary analysis. Confirmed virologic failure occurred in 5 participants (1.9%) in the long-acting-therapy group and in no participants in the oral-therapy group (risk difference, 1.9 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.3 to 3.5). Serious adverse events were reported in 11 of 271 participants (4.1%) who received long-acting therapy and in 8 of 269 participants (3.0%) who received oral therapy (risk difference, 1.1 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.1 to 4.2). Among persons with HIV in Africa who have adherence challenges, long-acting cabotegravir plus rilpivirine was noninferior to oral dolutegravir-based therapy for maintaining a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter. (Funded by Johnson & Johnson; IMPALA ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05546242; Pan African Clinical Trials Registry number, PACT202301600757432TMC278LAHTX3005.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2601088.abstract: Sjögren's disease is a complex, systemic autoimmune disease with no approved targeted therapies. Ianalumab is an IgG1 monoclonal antibody with a dual mechanism of action, depleting B cells through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and inhibiting B-cell activation and survival through blockade of B-cell activating factor receptor. We conducted two 52-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving patients with active Sjögren's disease. Patients in the NEPTUNUS-1 trial were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive subcutaneous ianalumab (300 mg monthly) or placebo; patients in the NEPTUNUS-2 trial were assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive 300 mg of ianalumab monthly or every 3 months or placebo. The primary end point was the change from baseline in the score on the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) Sjögren's Syndrome Disease Activity Index (ESSDAI) at week 48 (scores range from 0 to 123, with higher scores indicating greater disease activity). The first key secondary end point in the hierarchical plan for the NEPTUNUS-1 trial was an ESSDAI response (≥5-point reduction) at week 48; for the NEPTUNUS-2 trial, it was the change from baseline in the score on the Sjögren's Syndrome Symptom Diary (SSSD) or EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Patient Reported Index (ESSPRI) at week 48. Overall, 275 patients underwent randomization in the NEPTUNUS-1 trial (ianalumab monthly, 137 patients; placebo, 138 patients) and 504 in the NEPTUNUS-2 trial (ianalumab monthly, 168 patients; ianalumab every 3 months, 167 patients; and placebo, 169 patients). In both trials, ianalumab monthly led to a significantly greater decrease in the ESSDAI score at week 48 than placebo, with a between-group difference of -1.3 points (95% confidence interval [CI], -2.6 to 0.0; P = 0.0496) in NEPTUNUS-1 and -1.0 points (95% CI, -2.0 to 0.0; P = 0.04) in NEPTUNUS-2. No significant differences in the incidence of an ESSDAI response or in the change from baseline in SSSD or ESSPRI scores were observed at week 48. The incidence of serious adverse events was similar with ianalumab and placebo. Nonserious local injection-site and systemic injection-related reactions were more common in the ianalumab groups. In these two trials involving patients with active Sjögren's disease, ianalumab at a dose of 300 mg monthly resulted in a significantly greater decrease in disease activity at week 48 than placebo, although there were no significant differences in the incidence of an ESSDAI response or in the change from baseline in SSSD or ESSPRI symptom scores. (Funded by Novartis Pharma; NEPTUNUS-1 and NEPTUNUS-2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05350072 and NCT05349214, respectively.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2604435.abstract: Monoclonal antibodies targeting the interleukin-23 pathway are effective in treating inflammatory bowel disease. However, these therapies must be administered intravenously or by subcutaneous injection. We conducted a phase 2b, double-blind, randomized trial of oral icotrokinra, a peptide that blocks the interleukin-23 receptor, in adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis. Participants were assigned to receive icotrokinra at a once-daily dose of 400 mg, 200 mg, or 100 mg or placebo. The primary end point was clinical response at week 12. Secondary end points included clinical remission, remission of symptoms, and endoscopic improvement at week 12. A total of 252 participants underwent randomization: 63 were assigned to the 400-mg group, 62 to the 200-mg group, 64 to the 100-mg group, and 63 to the placebo group. All the doses of icotrokinra were superior to placebo with respect to a clinical response at week 12, which occurred in 63% of the participants in the 400-mg group, 58% in the 200-mg group, and 55% in the 100-mg group, as compared with 27% in the placebo group (P<0.001 for all comparisons with placebo). The percentage of participants with clinical remission at week 12 was also significantly higher in the 400-mg group than in the placebo group (30% vs. 11%, P = 0.006), as were the percentage of participants with symptomatic remission (46% vs. 19%, P<0.001) and the percentage of participants with endoscopic improvement (37% vs. 14%, P = 0.002). Clinical remission at week 12 occurred in 24% of the participants in the 200-mg group (P = 0.054 for the comparison with placebo); in accordance with the fixed-sequence testing procedure to account for multiple comparisons, no further formal testing of secondary end points was conducted. Through week 28, the percentage of participants with adverse events was 60% in the 400-mg group, 66% in the 200-mg group, 66% in the 100-mg group, and 62% in the placebo group. For serious adverse events, the percentages were 2%, 5%, 0%, and 10%, respectively. Among participants with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, a clinical response at week 12 was significantly more common with once-daily oral icotrokinra at each of three tested doses than with placebo. (Funded by Johnson & Johnson; ANTHEM-UC ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06049017.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2606208.abstract: The outcome of Philadelphia-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph-positive ALL) has greatly improved with the use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy. In this trial, we randomly assigned adult patients with Ph-positive ALL in a 2:1 ratio to receive ponatinib plus blinatumomab (intervention group) or imatinib plus chemotherapy (control group) as frontline treatment. A crossover to the intervention group was allowed for patients with persistence or reappearance of measurable residual disease in the control group. The primary end point was event-free survival. A total of 236 patients underwent randomization: 158 to the intervention group and 78 to the control group. The median age of the patients was 55 years (range, 24 to 82). At a median follow-up of 23.7 months, the estimated 24-month event-free survival was 86% in the intervention group and 67% in the control group (P<0.001). Survival with no measurable residual disease was 68% and 42%, respectively. At the end of induction, a complete hematologic response was observed in 94% of the patients in the intervention group and in 79% of those in the control group. After blinatumomab consolidation, a molecular response was observed in 71% and 49% of the patients, respectively. After crossover to the intervention group, 20 of 31 patients (64%) had a molecular response. Overall survival was 90% in the intervention group and 85% in the control group. The cumulative incidence of relapse was 5% and 13%, respectively. As of this report, only 19% of the patients in the intervention group had undergone hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation after having had a first complete hematologic response. In this phase 3 trial, a frontline chemotherapy-free targeted and immunotherapeutic approach was superior to the use of imatinib and chemotherapy. (Funded by Associazione Italiana per la Ricerca sul Cancro and others; GIMEMA ALL2820 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04722848.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2607544.abstract: In patients with IgA nephropathy, complement activation drives glomerular inflammation, which leads to hematuria, proteinuria, and nephron loss. Ravulizumab is a terminal complement inhibitor that prevents formation of C5a and C5b-9. In this phase 3 trial, we enrolled adults with IgA nephropathy who had an estimated glomerular filtration rate of at least 30 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and proteinuria (24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio [with protein and creatinine both measured in grams] of ≥0.75 or total urinary protein excretion of ≥1.0 g per day), despite standard therapy. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive an intravenous infusion of either ravulizumab or placebo every 8 weeks. In the prespecified interim analysis, the primary efficacy end point was the change from baseline in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 34. Safety was also assessed. In all, 485 patients underwent randomization, with 240 patients assigned to the ravulizumab group and 245 to the placebo group; 352 patients (176 in each group) were included in the interim analysis. In the ravulizumab group, the geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at baseline and at week 34 was 1.56 and 0.83, respectively; in the placebo group, it was 1.60 and 1.48, respectively. At week 34, a significant reduction in the geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was observed with ravulizumab (-46.6%) as compared with the reduction observed with placebo (-5.6%), corresponding to an adjusted geometric mean 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio that was 43.4% (99% confidence interval, 30.1 to 54.2) lower with ravulizumab than with placebo (P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 69.5% of the patients receiving ravulizumab and in 75.8% of those receiving placebo; serious adverse events occurred in 4.6% and 9.0%, respectively. No meningococcal infections or deaths occurred. In adults with IgA nephropathy, ravulizumab resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo at week 34. (Funded by Alexion, AstraZeneca Rare Disease Unit; I CAN ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06291376; EU Clinical Trials number, 2023-507851-31-00.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2608397.abstract: The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain. In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90. The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group. Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2608571.abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has been shown to be beneficial in persons with type 1 diabetes and others with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, but its role in the treatment of persons with type 2 diabetes not being treated with insulin has needed further study. In a 26-week trial conducted at 22 primary care practices in the United States, we randomly assigned adults with type 2 diabetes who were not using insulin to either CGM or routine care (control). The primary outcome was the glycated hemoglobin level at 26 weeks. Key CGM-measured secondary outcomes were tested hierarchically to control the type I error rate. A total of 145 participants were assigned to the CGM group, and 138 to the routine-care group. Participants ranged in age from 21 to 84 years. The mean (±SD) glycated hemoglobin level decreased from 8.8±1.3% at baseline to 7.2±1.1% at 26 weeks in the CGM group and from 8.7±1.2% to 8.0±1.4% in the routine-care group (adjusted mean difference, -0.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.1 to -0.6; P<0.001). The mean percentage of time that the CGM-measured glucose level was in the glucose-level range of 70 to 180 mg per deciliter was 21 percentage points higher (95% CI, 16 to 26) with CGM than with routine care (P<0.001). The between-group difference in the percentage of time that the glucose level was below 54 mg per deciliter was -0.17 percentage points (95% CI, -0.27 to -0.11; P<0.001 for noninferiority); the difference in the percentage of time that the glucose level was below 70 mg per deciliter was -0.20 percentage points (95% CI, -0.43 to -0.09; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P = 0.004 for superiority). No severe hypoglycemia events were reported. Among adults with type 2 diabetes that was not being treated with insulin and was being managed in a primary care setting, the use of CGM led to a greater reduction in the glycated hemoglobin level and to a lower risk of hyperglycemia than routine care. (Funded by Dexcom; CONNECT ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06601166.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2608682.abstract: B-cell activating factor (BAFF) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) have distinct roles in IgA-producing B-cell populations and appear to be central to the pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy. Povetacicept, an enhanced, variant transmembrane activator and calcium-modulator and cyclophilin-ligand interactor (TACI)-Fc fragment fusion therapeutic, is engineered for dual inhibition of BAFF and APRIL. In this ongoing, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, participants with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy receiving stable background therapy were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive povetacicept at a dose of 80 mg or placebo subcutaneously every 4 weeks. The primary end point of this prespecified interim analysis was the change in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 36. Secondary end points were the change at week 36 in galactose-deficient IgA1 levels and hematuria resolution at week 36 among participants with baseline hematuria. A total of 557 participants received povetacicept (372 participants) or placebo (185 participants). Efficacy analyses included the first 199 participants who had undergone randomization (131 in the povetacicept group and 68 in the placebo group). The 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio decreased by 52.0% with povetacicept and by 4.3% with placebo by week 36 (adjusted difference, -49.8 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -58.6 to -39.2; P<0.001). Galactose-deficient IgA1 levels decreased by 77.4% with povetacicept and increased by 9.1% with placebo (adjusted difference, -79.3 percentage points; 95% CI, -82.2 to -75.9; P<0.001). Among the participants with baseline hematuria, resolution occurred in 85% with povetacicept and in 23% with placebo (adjusted difference, 62 percentage points; 95% CI, 45 to 78; P<0.001). The incidence of adverse events (75% with povetacicept and 78% with placebo) and serious adverse events (3% and 4%, respectively) were similar in the trial groups. Povetacicept led to a significantly greater reduction in the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo by week 36 in participants with IgA nephropathy. (Funded by Vertex Pharmaceuticals; RAINIER AIS-D08 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06564142.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2609127.abstract: Sibeprenlimab, a humanized monoclonal antibody, selectively inhibits the cytokine A proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL), a key driver of IgA nephropathy. Preliminary trial results with regard to the primary end point of the 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at 9 months after treatment as compared with baseline have been reported, but secondary end points, including outcomes regarding estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), have not. We randomly assigned adults with IgA nephropathy to receive subcutaneous sibeprenlimab (at a dose of 400 mg) or placebo every 4 weeks. The key secondary end point was the annualized slope of the eGFR over 24 months. Other secondary end points included the change in eGFR from baseline to 24 months, a composite kidney end point of kidney-function decline or kidney failure, and pharmacodynamic and safety end points. A total of 510 patients underwent randomization - 259 to receive sibeprenlimab and 251 to receive placebo. The annualized eGFR slope over 24 months was 0.3 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area per year (95% confidence interval [CI], -0.4 to 0.9) with sibeprenlimab and -4.2 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year (95% CI, -4.9 to -3.6) with placebo (between-group difference, 4.5 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year; 95% CI, 3.6 to 5.4; P<0.001). The least-squares mean treatment difference for the change in eGFR from baseline to 24 months was 9.2 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, 7.1 to 11.4; P<0.001). A composite kidney end-point event occurred in 1 patient (0.4%) in the sibeprenlimab group and in 28 patients (11.2%) in the placebo group (adjusted difference, -10.8 percentage points; hazard ratio, 0.029; 95% CI, 0.004 to 0.214; P<0.001). Adverse events occurred in 235 patients (90.7%) in the sibeprenlimab group and 226 patients (90.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 21 patients (8.1%) and 32 patients (12.7%), respectively; and serious infections in 5 patients (1.9%) and 10 patients (4.0%). No deaths were reported. Among patients with IgA nephropathy, treatment with sibeprenlimab stabilized the eGFR slope over 24 months, a finding consistent with a reduced risk of kidney-function decline. (Funded by Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development and Commercialization; VISIONARY ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05248646.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2610103.abstract: Atacicept resulted in a significantly greater reduction in the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio than placebo in a previously published analysis of this trial, ORIGIN 3. Final prespecified efficacy results are reported here. We randomly assigned adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy to receive weekly subcutaneous atacicept at a dose of 150 mg or placebo. We carried out final analyses of two secondary end points: the change in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) at week 52 and the annualized eGFR slope through week 104; additional hierarchically tested end points and safety were assessed. Of 431 patients who underwent randomization, 428 received atacicept or placebo (214 per group). At week 52, the mean change in the eGFR was -0.11 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area (95% confidence interval [CI], -1.44 to 1.22) with atacicept and -5.69 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -7.04 to -4.35) with placebo (mean difference, 5.58 ml per minute per 1.73 m2; 95% CI, 3.68 to 7.48; P<0.001). Through week 104, the mean annualized eGFR slope was -0.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -1.62 to 0.41) with atacicept and -5.60 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 (95% CI, -6.64 to -4.57) with placebo (difference, 5.00 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 per year; 95% CI, 3.55 to 6.45; P<0.001). Composite kidney-disease progression occurred in 11 patients (5.1%) in the atacicept group and in 38 patients (17.8%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.24; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.48; P<0.001); no patients in the atacicept group had progression to dialysis, transplantation, or death, as compared with 7 patients in the placebo group. Adverse events occurred in 160 of 214 patients (74.8%) in the atacicept group and in 167 of 214 patients (78.0%) in the placebo group; serious adverse events occurred in 7.0% and 15.4%, respectively. One patient (in the placebo group) died. Atacicept slowed and stabilized the decline in the eGFR as compared with placebo. (Funded by Vera Therapeutics; ORIGIN 3 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04716231.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2611477.abstract: Retatrutide, an investigational triple agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide 1, and glucagon receptors, may be useful for treating obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). In two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials nested within larger basket trials of once-weekly subcutaneous retatrutide, we assigned adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and a body-mass index (the weight in kilograms divided by the square of the height in meters) of at least 27, without (TRIUMPH-1-OSA) or with (TRIUMPH-2-OSA) type 2 diabetes, to receive retatrutide (4, 9, or 12 mg) or placebo. The primary end point was the change in the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep) at 80 weeks with 9 mg and 12 mg of retatrutide. For OSA-related end points, a hybrid-treatment estimand was applied, with a hypothetical strategy used for participants who had intercurrent events suggesting treatment failure and a treatment-policy strategy used elsewhere. We also report intention-to-treat (ITT) results. A total of 243 participants underwent randomization in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and 448 in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The baseline mean AHI was 58.6 and 55.9 events per hour, respectively, and the mean body weight was 119.6 and 115.9 kg. At 80 weeks, the mean changes in the AHI (hybrid-treatment estimand) with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-1-OSA were -22.9 (4 mg), -34.3 (9 mg), and -31.7 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -9.9 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -13.0 [95% confidence interval {CI}, -23.0 to -3.0], -24.4 [95% CI, -34.1 to -14.7], and -21.9 [95% CI, -32.2 to -11.5], respectively). The changes with retatrutide in TRIUMPH-2-OSA were -19.2 (4 mg), -24.7 (9 mg), and -25.4 (12 mg) events per hour, versus -10.3 with placebo (difference vs. placebo, -8.9 [95% CI, -15.9 to -2.0], -14.4 [95% CI, -21.6 to -7.2], and -15.1 [95% CI, -22.5 to -7.7]). For the ITT estimand, the corresponding differences from placebo were -13.2 (95% CI, -22.6 to -3.9), -24.7 (95% CI, -34.1 to -15.3), and -22.5 (95% CI, -31.9 to -13.1) in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -8.8 (95% CI, -15.8 to -1.7), -13.9 (95% CI, -21.3 to -6.6), and -15.0 (95% CI, -22.5 to -7.4) in TRIUMPH-2-OSA. The mean percent change in body weight with retatrutide (key secondary end point) was -12.5 to -22.2% in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and -12.1 to -18.5% in TRIUMPH-2-OSA, versus -4.8% and -5.6% with placebo (treatment-regimen estimand). The most common adverse events were gastrointestinal. In adults with OSA and obesity or overweight with or without type 2 diabetes, retatrutide resulted in significantly greater decreases in the AHI than placebo. (Funded by Eli Lilly; TRIUMPH-1 and -2 ClinicalTrials.gov numbers, NCT05929066 and NCT05929079.).

doi:10.1056/nejmra2414530.abstract: The discovery of Helicobacter pylori has revolutionized the prevention and treatment of gastritis, peptic ulcers, and, most important, gastric cancer. In the past 40 years, enormous progress has been achieved in the clinical and basic research on H. pylori infection. However, challenges in preventing and treating H. pylori infection exist owing to the lack of an H. pylori vaccine and the ever-increasing resistance to antibiotics worldwide. This review summarizes the history of and key milestones in H. pylori research, provides an update on the understanding of the pathogenesis and global burden of H. pylori infection and the screening strategy for the primary prevention of gastric cancer, and focuses on the emerging trends in the management of H. pylori infection.

doi:10.1080/2162402x.2026.2740432.abstract: Membrane-associated proliferating cell nuclear antigen (mPCNA) is an attractive tumor-selective antigen for antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) development. We generated a chimeric IgG1 ADC, RC14-MMAE, to exploit three key properties of mPCNA that support its use as an efficient delivery platform. First, flow-cytometric and imaging analyses show abundant mPCNA surface expression on multiple tumor cell lines and in JIMT1 xenografts, providing accessible epitopes for binding. Second, comparative profiling against non-malignant counterparts and normal mouse tissues reveals minimal or undetectable mPCNA at the plasma membrane of healthy cells, indicating a sharp tumor-normal differential expected to limit off-tumor targeting and improve the therapeutic window. Third, live-cell internalization assays demonstrate that RC14 rapidly accumulates in LAMP1-positive lysosomes after engaging mPCNA, confirming efficient trafficking along the endolysosomal pathway required for protease-mediated cleavage of the valine-citrulline linker and release of monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE). Consistent with this target profile, RC14-MMAE exhibits potent antigen-dependent cytotoxicity in mPCNA-positive tumor models in NSG mice, favorable pharmacokinetics, sustained payload retention in serum, robust in vivo antitumor activity with limited overt toxicity, and a significantly increased fraction of F4/80⁺ tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells within dissociated tumors. These findings establish mPCNA as a functionally validated, tumor-selective internalizing target and support RC14-MMAE as a first-in-class mPCNA-directed ADC with broad translational potential.

doi:10.1080/2162402x.2026.2746847.abstract: Sex steroid exposure is a major risk factor for breast cancer initiation and progression through incompletely understood mechanisms. Novel therapeutics for prevention and treatment of estrogen-dependent breast cancer are needed. Cell-cell interactions within the microenvironment contribute to breast cancer progression through extracellular signaling. Here, extracellular proteins were sampled directly from live normal human breast tissue and breast cancers using microdialysis, and 1,101 proteins were quantified. Mechanistic studies were performed in cultured intact normal human breast tissue and mast cells. Findings were validated in vivo using ER+ breast cancer models in immunocompetent and immunocompromised mice and in a zebrafish xenograft model. We identified a breast tissue-specific extracellular protein signature comprising 150 proteins associated with local estradiol (E2) levels, of which several were linked to mast cell biology, including stem cell factor (SCF). Human ER+ breast tumors exhibited increased extracellular SCF levels and higher mast cell density, which was associated with poorer overall survival. In normal human breast tissue, E2 increased mast cell abundance and activity. In vitro, E2 rapidly activated mast cells, an effect blocked by desloratadine. In mouse breast cancer models, E2 increased and fulvestrant reduced mast cell density. In the zebrafish, mast cells promoted ER+ breast cancer growth, which was further enhanced by E2 and abrogated by desloratadine. Overall, our findings identify mast cells as estrogen-responsive stromal mediators and support targeting mast cell-dependent pathways as a potential strategy for the prevention and treatment of estrogen-dependent breast cancer.

doi:10.1080/2162402x.2026.2751848.abstract: Although first-line immune-based combinations have reshaped the management of metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC), relevant unmet clinical needs remain. Sarcomatoid feature is a negative prognostic factor that confers sensitivity to immunotherapy, yet the optimal ICI combination in this subgroup is still unclear. The Meet-URO 33 is an Italian multicenter retrospective/prospective observational study enrolling patients with mRCC receiving first-line systemic therapy in routine clinical practice. In the present sub-analysis, objective response and survival outcomes were compared between ICI-ICI and ICI-TKI regimens in patients with documented sarcomatoid differentiation and IMDC intermediate-/poor-risk disease. Among 1695 patients enrolled from 58 centers, 180 (10.6%) had sRCC and among them, 107 (58.2%) were intermediate-risk and 56 (30.4%) were poor-risk. With a median follow-up of 21.8 months, in the I/P-sRCC population with available data (n = 155), univariable analysis showed longer overall survival (OS) with ICI-ICI compared to ICI-TKI (HR 0.58, p = 0.04). However, in propensity score-weighted analyses, point estimates slightly favored ICI-ICI, but no statistically significant differences were observed for OS, PFS, or ORR. In this real-world analysis comparing ICI-ICI and ICI-TKI in sarcomatoid mRCC, propensity score-weighted models showed no statistically significant differences between treatment combinations on clinical outcomes. These findings highlight the relevance of baseline disease and patients characteristics in shaping treatment outcomes and confirm the effectiveness of ICI-containing combinations in the treatment of sarcomatoid mRCC.

doi:10.1080/2162402x.2026.2752644.abstract: Mast cells (MCs) display phenotypic heterogeneity across tissues and disease contexts, yet their relevance in melanoma remains unclear. Here, we investigated MC phenotypic programs associated with melanoma progression using high-dimensional phenotyping of MCs co-cultured with melanoma spheroids, trajectory inference, and transcriptomic analyzes. Human melanoma tissues showed differences in MC phenotypic composition despite comparable abundance between outcome groups, with metastatic melanomas enriched for Tryptase⁺ Chymase- MCs. Melanoma exposure induced MC phenotypic remodeling, characterized by loss of lineage- and effector-associated features and increased PD-1 expression, with more pronounced changes following metastatic melanoma co-culture. Trajectory analysis was consistent with a continuum toward a PD-1⁺ Chymase- phenotype, which was detected in melanoma tissues and enriched within intratumoral regions of metastatic melanomas. Experimentally defined protein changes were used to derive two MC-associated transcriptomic signatures with opposing clinical associations, reflecting lineage- and effector-enriched versus melanoma-remodeled programs. The MC-LE signature was associated with favorable survival and interferon-responsive pathways, whereas the MC-MR signature was associated with poorer survival and tumor-associated pathways. These transcriptomic associations extended beyond melanoma across multiple TCGA cancer cohorts, and independent analysis of MCs from healthy skin, basal cell carcinoma, and melanoma showed corresponding differences in MC-LE-related features. Together, these findings support distinct mast cell phenotypic programs associated with melanoma progression and identify a PD-1⁺ Chymase- MC phenotype enriched in metastatic disease and linked to transcriptomic features of poor survival.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkad027.abstract: Abstract Static biomarkers like programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) are insufficient to accurately predict response to immune checkpoint inhibition. Therefore, on-treatment biomarkers, which measure immediate therapy-associated changes, are currently shifting into the focus of immuno-oncology. A prime example of a simple predictive on-treatment biomarker is the early C-reactive protein (CRP) kinetics with its predictive CRP flare-response phenomenon. Here, we were able to confirm the predictive value of CRP flare-response kinetics in the pivotal phase III OAK trial (NCT02008227), which compared atezolizumab with docetaxel in patients with non-small cell lung cancer. Of note, CRP flare-response predicted favorable outcomes only in the immune checkpoint inhibition–treated subgroup, which suggests that it is an immunotherapy-specific phenomenon. In conclusion, we have for the first time validated the high predictive value of early CRP kinetics in a pivotal phase III trial, justifying the broad use of this cost-effective and easy-to-implement on-treatment biomarker to optimize therapy monitoring for patients with non-small cell lung cancer.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag106.abstract: Abstract This cross-sectional study examined patient-provider communication about colorectal cancer screening options using the 2024 Health Information National Trends Survey. The outcome measure was respondents’ report of being informed by a health care professional about multiple colorectal cancer screening tests. Covariates included race/ethnicity, income, education, number of health care visits, insurance, age, and sex. Uninsured participants had lower odds (adjusted OR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.46–0.93) of reporting colorectal cancer screening discussions than insured participants. Those who earned <$20,000 had lower odds (adjusted OR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.41–0.81) of reporting colorectal cancer screening discussions than those earning ≥$100,000. The predicted probability of a health care provider visit was lowest among respondents with no health care visits (adjusted probability, 33.3%; 95% CI, 25.3–41.2), compared with those in the other health care visit categories. Differences in colorectal cancer screening discussions were observed across groups. Further research should identify contributing factors.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag108.abstract: Breastfeeding reduces ovarian cancer risk, but the underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. We examined the association between a previously reported metabolite-based breastfeeding score with incident epithelial ovarian cancer risk in case-control studies nested within the Nurses' Health Studies (NHS/NHSII, n = 436) and Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial (PLCO, n = 300) using conditional logistic regression to calculate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for each study and conducted a meta-analysis. We investigated 606 individual breastfeeding-metabolite associations among 9,904 mid-life parous women in NHS/NHSII and 663 one-year postpartum women in the Vitamin D Antenatal Asthma Reduction Trial (VDAART). Metabolites associated with breastfeeding at p ≤ 0.05 after multiple testing correction for number of effective tests (NEF) were then assessed for their associations with ovarian cancer. Metabolite set enrichment analysis using Normalized Enrichment Score (NES) identified metabolite classes associated with breastfeeding using false discovery rate (FDR) were used for multiple testing correction. The highest quartile of metabolite-based breastfeeding score was inversely associated with ovarian cancer risk (meta-analyzed odds ratio [OR]=0.62, 95%CI=0.39-0.99). Of the 14 individual metabolites associated with breastfeeding in NHS/NHSII and also measured in VDAART, similar direction of associations was observed for 11 metabolites. Phosphatidylcholines (PCs; NES=1.94; FDR=0.004) and phosphatidylethanolamines (PEs; NES=1.82; FDR=0.01) were positively enriched with increased breastfeeding duration. Ten metabolites including PCs and PEs were positively associated with breastfeeding and inversely associated with ovarian cancer. Our results suggest alterations of systemic metabolism, particularly among PC and PE pathways, provide insight into biological pathways underlying the inverse breastfeeding-ovarian cancer association.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag109.abstract: Redlining, introduced in 1933 by the Homeowners' Loan Corporation, created enduring structural inequities in housing, health care access, and neighborhood investment. These historical patterns may contribute to persistent disparities in breast cancer screening. This study examines how historical redlining, alongside contemporary socioeconomic factors, shapes screening disparities across the University of Kansas Cancer Center (KUCC) catchment area. We conducted a census tract-level spatial analysis across 123 counties (Kansas and western Missouri) by linking CDC PLACES breast cancer screening data with historical redlining maps. Explanatory variables included rurality, mammography facility availability, income inequality, gender pay gap, and uninsured rates. Logistic regression assessed overall associations, while geographically weighted binomial logistic regression evaluated spatial heterogeneity. Screening rates ranged from 56.9% to 84.5% across census tracts. Redlining was associated with lower screening odds in unadjusted models but was attenuated after accounting for socioeconomic and geographic factors. Rurality and income inequality were consistently associated with lower screening, whereas greater mammography facility availability was associated with higher screening rates. Spatial analyses revealed meaningful geographic variation, with localized negative associations of redlining and persistent, spatially varying effects of socioeconomic factors. Breast cancer screening disparities in this region reflect the combined influence of historical structural inequities and current socioeconomic conditions. Expanding access to mammography and implementing spatially targeted, equity-focused interventions may improve screening uptake and reduce disparities in underserved communities.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag110.abstract: COVID-19 has been associated with an increased thrombotic risk, potentially exacerbated in patients with active cancer. We conducted a retrospective cohort study including 119 cancer patients with COVID-19 and 214 matched pre-pandemic controls. Patients with COVID-19 had poorer performance status and were more frequently treated with palliative intent. After a median follow-up of 32.7 months, overall thrombotic event rates did not differ between groups. However, after adjustment for clinically relevant covariates and accounting for death as a competing event, COVID-19 status and palliative treatment intent remained independently associated with a higher cumulative incidence of thrombotic events. In conclusion, COVID-19 may increase thrombotic risk in patients with cancer and occurs more frequently in patients with poorer clinical status. These findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger prospective studies.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag111.abstract: Abstract Background The incidence of gastro-entero-pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (GEP-NENs) has increased, alongside novel therapies and care models. Whether these advances translated into improved survival is unclear. Methods Population-based retrospective cohort study of GEP-NENs between 2000–2019. Overall survival (OS) was analyzed using time-to-event methods. Restricted cubic splines assessed non-linear associations between diagnosis year and hazards of death; multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, primary site, and metastatic status. Results Among 9,420 patients, 5-year OS was 75.8% overall, 88.8% for non-metastatic disease, and 57.0% for metastatic disease. Mortality risk declined in more recent years, with diagnoses in 2013–2019 associated with lower hazards of death (adjusted HR 0.91, 95%CI 0.83–0.99). Improvements were confined to non-metastatic disease and to pancreas, stomach, and rectal primaries. Conclusion OS has modestly improved over two decades, largely reflecting stage migration rather than clear therapeutic gains. Advances that meaningfully improve survival in advanced GEP-NENs are needed.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag112.abstract: Abstract Introduction We sought to evaluate the associations of post-diagnostic consumption of flavonoids and flavonoid-rich foods with survival among patients with stage III colon cancer enrolled in a clinical trial. Methods We conducted a prospective observational study of 1625 patients with stage III colon cancer enrolled in the CALGB/SWOG 80702 (Alliance) randomized adjuvant chemotherapy trial who completed a self-reported food frequency questionnaire within 6 weeks of and again 14-16 months post-randomization. Intakes of flavonoids overall and by subclasses (anthocyanidins, flavanones, flavan-3-ols, flavones, flavonols, isoflavones) were computed by multiplying the consumption frequency of each dietary item by the nutrient content of its respective specified portions. Multivariable analyses for the primary (disease-free survival [DFS]) and secondary (overall survival [OS]) endpoints were adjusted for sociodemographic, clinical, dietary, and lifestyle factors. Bonferroni corrections were applied for analyses of flavonoid subclasses and flavonoid-rich foods. Results Over median follow-up of 5.9 years, flavonoid consumption either overall or by subclasses was not significantly associated with survival outcomes, with a hazard ratio (HR) (95% confidence interval [CI]) of 1.01 (0.75-1.37) for DFS among those in the highest relative to lowest consumption quintiles of total flavonoids. Exploratory analyses of flavonoid-rich foods intake did not demonstrate significant associations with DFS or OS after Bonferroni correction. Conclusion Among resected stage III colon cancer patients who received standardized treatment and follow-up within a nationwide randomized clinical trial, consumption of flavonoids was not associated with survival outcomes. doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag113.abstract: Abstract PURPOSE To examine whether Medicare’s 2018 National Coverage Determination (NCD) for next-generation sequencing (NGS) was associated with changes in the use of targeted oral anticancer therapies among older adults with lung cancer. METHODS Retrospective cohort study. Multivariable logistic regression was used to estimate the probability of initiating an oral targeted therapy within 12 months of diagnosis. Key exposures were (1) diagnosis before versus after the NCD and (2) residence in a region with versus without pre-NCD NGS. Data were drawn from the SEER–Medicare linked data with Part D claims, including diagnosis years 2016–2019 with follow-up through 2020. The analytic sample included Medicare fee-for-service Part D beneficiaries aged 65 years or older with newly diagnosed lung cancer. RESULTS Among 30,855 Medicare fee-for-service Part D beneficiaries with lung cancer, 7.1% used targeted oral anticancer therapies. The NCD was not associated with a significant overall change in targeted therapy use (0.4 Percentage Point; 95% CI, −1.6 to 2.4; p = 0.71). Before NCD implementation, targeted therapy use was 1.0 PP higher in regions with pre-NCD NGS coverage than in regions without such coverage (95% CI, 0.2–1.9; p = 0.015). In stage-stratified analyses, the additional post-NCD change was significant among patients with distant-stage disease (3.2 PPs; 95% CI, 2.6–4.0; p < 0.001) but not among those with regional-stage disease (p = 0.29). CONCLUSIONS Medicare's NCD for NGS was not associated with a significant overall increase in targeted oral anticancer therapy use but was associated with increased use among patients with distant-stage disease. Targeted therapy use remained higher in regions with preexisting NGS coverage.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag115.abstract: Comprehensive genomic profiling has expanded the ability to identify potentially actionable molecular alterations across cancers, but identification of an actionable finding does not ensure that a patient will receive a genomically matched therapy. Studies of precision-oncology programs and molecular tumor boards consistently demonstrate substantial attrition between treatment recommendation and treatment initiation. The reasons extend beyond molecular interpretation and include the timing of genomic profiling, clinical deterioration, geographic availability of biomarker-selected trials, insurance and financial barriers, and disparities in access to specialty cancer care. Importantly, these barriers arise after a potentially useful molecular finding has already been identified, creating a distinction between molecular actionability and practical treatment access. This commentary argues that the next implementation challenge for precision oncology is to make clinically meaningful genomic findings realistically actionable. Comprehensive genomic profiling should occur early enough to inform treatment planning; molecular tumor board recommendations should be linked to realistic treatment and trial opportunities; financial and insurance barriers should be anticipated when recommendations are made; and equity should be evaluated beyond access to testing to include receipt of genomically informed treatment. As genomic profiling becomes increasingly integrated into routine cancer care, precision oncology should be judged not only by its ability to identify therapeutic opportunities but also by whether patients can reach those opportunities while they remain clinically relevant.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag077.abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) tumors pose a major global health challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where outcomes remain disproportionately poor. The global CONCORD-3 study (Lancet Oncology) highlighted stark disparities in five-year survival (2010-2014): from ∼15% in Thailand to 46% in Japan among adults, and from ∼ 80% in Denmark to < 40% in Brazil among children. Limited access to specialized pathology and molecular diagnostics in LMICs results in diagnostic uncertainty and restricted treatment options. DNA methylation-based tumor classification, has revolutionized CNS tumor diagnosis and got incorporated into the 2021 world health organization (WHO) CNS5 classification. However, its accessibility, feasibility, and performance in LMICs remain insufficiently explored. Importantly, several ethnic groups common in LMICs are underrepresented in current reference datasets. To address this, the Molecular Neuro-Pathology (MNP) Outreach Consortium was launched in Heidelberg, partnering with 11 countries-including nine LMICs from Asia, Africa, and South America. Early insights from Brazil, Jordan and Argentina, show methylation profiling changing diagnosis in up to 25% cases. Gains are greatest in pediatric and adolescents and young adults (AYA) populations. In addition, it reduced the designation of not otherwise specified (NOS) from 51.3% to 8.8% across 476 CNS tumours in Brazil.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag168.abstract: Pediatric brain tumors (PBTs) remain a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in children, underscoring the need for more effective therapeutic strategies. These tumors arise from disrupted neurodevelopmental programs and evolve within a developmentally constrained immune landscape that is tolerogenic, epigenetically plastic, and susceptible to tumor-mediated co-option. Increasing evidence indicates that, besides molecular heterogeneity, the tumor immune microenvironment critically influences clinical outcomes. Despite its therapeutic promise, immunotherapy has yet to demonstrate consistent clinical benefit in most PBTs, highlighting the need for rational multimodal strategies guided by deeper understanding of tumor-immune interactions in the developing brain. To provide a comprehensive perspective on fetal immune ontogeny and its tumor-driven dysregulation we used medulloblastoma, pediatric gliomas, atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors, and ependymoma as representative entities. Drawing on insights from developmental neurobiology, tumor immunology, and emerging multi-omic studies, we outline how PBTs exploit physiological immune maturation programs to establish immune evasion, sustain chronic inflammation, and promote therapy resistance. We further discuss emerging multimodal immunotherapeutic strategies and next-generation CAR T-cell approaches currently under clinical investigation. In addition, we highlight therapeutic avenues such as targeting tumor-associated myeloid populations and key inflammatory regulators that may offer promising opportunities for future clinical translation. We believe this Review will help address current limitations in preclinical models, improve patient stratification and guide rational design of therapeutic strategies.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag169.abstract: Sequential chemoradiotherapy remains a standard treatment option for patients with isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant gliomas. The results of the phase III INDIGO trial have led to the recent regulatory approval of vorasidenib, a brain-penetrant IDH1 and IDH2 inhibitor, indicated for patients with IDH1- or IDH2-mutant WHO grade 2 astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma after biopsy or resection. While IDH inhibitors represent a significant advancement for patients with IDH-mutant glioma, there is substantial controversy regarding which patients are most likely to derive benefit from IDH inhibition and how this strategy can be optimally integrated into clinical practice. Specifically, whether IDH inhibitors should be used prior to, in conjunction with or potentially in lieu of radiation-based treatment strategies are fundamental questions for the neuro-oncology community. Additionally, whether IDH inhibitors can be extrapolated to higher-grade disease settings or utilized in higher-risk patient populations remains unknown. These open questions provide an opportunity for the field of radiation oncology to develop pragmatic biomarker-based approaches to guide patient selection, to monitor treatment response and to identify optimal treatment strategy and timing/sequencing of treatment. Several candidate biomarkers have emerged for IDH-mutant glioma with unique potential to be rationally integrated into radiation oncology workflows to personalize care.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag229.abstract: Abstract Background The FET-PET in Glioblastoma (FIG) study (TROG 18.06) assessed the impact of adding FET-PET to MRI on radiotherapy gross tumor volume delineation in newly diagnosed glioblastoma. Methods This multicenter prospective phase 2 study evaluated participants with newly diagnosed glioblastoma IDH-wildtype undergoing postoperative MRI and FET-PET imaging before adjuvant radiotherapy, delivered according to standard MRI-based planning. The FET-PET-positive biological tumor volume (BTV) was used to derive the Hybrid (FET-PET+MRI) gross tumor volume (Hybrid-GTV). Primary outcomes were: (1) BTV excluded from the GTV defined on MRI alone (MR-GTV); (2) Hybrid-GTV excluded from the MR-GTV with both comparisons analyzed by non-overlap volume (cm3 and %), dosimetry (D98 and V95), and spatial similarity metrics; (3) clinically meaningful change in GTV non-overlap percentage volume with the addition of FET-PET. Results There were 172 participants recruited, n = 140 evaluable. Median BTV was 23.1 cm3, median MR-GTV was 32.1 cm3, and median Hybrid-GTV was 46.0 cm3. Hybrid-GTV was significantly larger than the MR-GTV (P < .001), with a larger Hybrid-GTV observed in 83% of cases. Comparing BTV to MR-GTV, median non-overlap volume was 10.1 cm3 and non-overlap percentage volume 53.5%. Comparing Hybrid-GTV to MR-GTV, median non-overlap volume was 14.9 cm3 and non-overlap percentage volume 33.9%. D98 and V95 were lower for the Hybrid-GTV than for the MR-GTV, suggesting lower dose coverage. Applying a > 20% non-overlap percentage volume threshold, 76% of participants had a meaningful change in GTV with the addition of FET-PET. Conclusion FET-PET differed significantly from MRI-based GTV delineation, with its incorporation leading to a clinically meaningful change in GTV in the majority of participants.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag231.abstract: Abstract Background It is unclear whether glioma subtypes differ in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) over time. Methods We analyzed data from the CODAGLIO 2.0 database, comprising 16 randomized controlled trials with HRQoL assessed using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-BN20 questionnaires. Differences in mean HRQoL at baseline (before postoperative treatments) and 3 months were compared across glioma subtypes. Linear mixed models (LMMs) were used to identify factors independently associated with HRQoL, and anchor-based minimally important differences determined clinical relevance. Results A total of 4,301 patients had baseline HRQoL data; 75% completed follow-up. In stratified analyses, at 3 months, physical, social, role, and cognitive functioning were statistically and clinically significantly worse in glioblastoma than in astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma. In adjusted LMMs, compared with glioblastoma, patients with astrocytoma had worse physical (−2.78, 95% CI, −4.68 to −1.01) and cognitive functioning (−3.63, −6.18 to −1.05), more pain (2.74, 0.41-4.95), communication deficits (5.03, 2.44-7.66), and seizures (4.49, 2.55-6.72). Patients with oligodendroglioma had worse social functioning (−5.39, −10.57 to −0.11), communication deficits (7.40, 1.63-12.81), and seizures (8.61, 4.17-14.26). None of these differences exceeded clinical relevance thresholds. Performance status was the only variable associated with clinically meaningful HRQoL changes across most scales. Conclusions At 3 months, patients with glioblastoma show clinically worse HRQoL than IDH-mutant glioma patients in unadjusted analyses. However, after adjusting for clinical variables, glioblastoma patients exhibit statistically but not clinically better HRQoL in several domains. Performance status emerges as the key factor independently associated with HRQoL and should play a central role in clinical decision-making.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag232.abstract: Abstract Background H3 K27-altered diffuse midline gliomas (H3-DMGs) are driven by stem-like and proliferative tumor cells resulting from global H3K27me3 loss. Here, we aimed to identify key molecular mechanisms involved in the interplay between epigenetic and epitranscriptomic regulation underlying this process. Methods Patient-derived spinal cord H3-DMG stem-like spheres and serum-induced differentiated cells were used to model tumor plasticity. Multi-omics approaches, including single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, RNA m6A profiling, CUT&Tag, ATAC-seq, and in vitro and in vivo assays were performed to dissect epigenetic and epitranscriptomic regulation of stemness. Results Differentiation reduced stemness markers, proliferation, H3K27M expression, and global m6A levels, while increasing H3K27me3. METTL3 was significantly downregulated during differentiation and positively correlated with stemness and proliferation in patient tumors. METTL3 promoted tumor stemness and growth by stabilizing SOX11 mRNA through YTHDC2-dependent m6A recognition. In parallel, H3K27me3 loss relieved transcriptional repression at both METTL3 and SOX11 loci, leading to SOX11 overexpression. Functionally, SOX11 interacted with SMARCA4, the core ATPase of the SWI/SNF complex, to enhance chromatin accessibility and activate stemness-associated transcriptional programs marked by H3K27ac and H3K4me3 enrichment. Clinically, METTL3 and SOX11 were upregulated in H3K27M-mutant tumors, and high SOX11 expression correlated with increased proliferation, poor prognosis, and enhanced sensitivity to the SMARCA4 inhibitor BRM014. Conclusions H3K27M-driven epigenetic dysregulation promotes SOX11 overexpression through combined H3K27me3 loss and METTL3-mediated m6A modification. SOX11 sustains tumor stemness and proliferation by recruiting SMARCA4 to remodel chromatin and serves as both a prognostic biomarker and a predictor of response to SMARCA4-targeted therapy in spinal cord H3-DMG.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag238.abstract: Targeted therapy has made important contributions to improving outcomes for patients with many solid tumors, but has had only limited activity so far in patients with gliomas, notably glioblastoma. Failure of targeted therapy in glioblastoma is likely due to redundance of oncogenic pathway activation and so far the inability to identify suitable targets and apply biomarker-based enrichment strategies in clinical trial designs. In contrast, in non-glioblastoma tumors, there are promising developments which have already changed clinical practice: inhibition of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) exemplified by vorasidenib, the first approved drug specifically for IDH-mutant gliomas, has changed the landscape for targeted therapy of WHO grade 2 gliomas. Furthermore, dordaviprone, an antagonist of dopamine receptor D2/3 (DRD2/3) and an allosteric agonist of the mitochondrial protease caseinolytic mitochondrial matrix peptidase proteolytic subunit (ClpP), emerges as a potentially active agent in patients with recurrent K27M-mutant diffuse midline gliomas. Finally, BRAF mutations, neurotrophic tyrosine receptor kinase ( r fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) gene fusions continue to raise interest as therapeutic targets at least for subsets of patients with gliomas. Almost no targeted therapy approaches for ependymomas have emerged. Improved clinical trial designs including shared control arms early on and using pharmacodynamic endpoints ideally in enriched patient populations are the path forward towards the identification of further active treatments for patients with gliomas.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag255.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) invasion is clinically decisive but difficult to model systematically. Existing patient-derived xenograft (PDX) resources rarely couple reproducible in vivo invasion phenotypes with matched multi-omic profiles at scale, limiting mechanistic insight and phenotype-informed therapeutic hypotheses. We established the HGCC Phenobank, comprising 65 patient-derived GBM stem-like cultures with matched multi-omic profiling and orthotopic engraftment in 449 mice. Blinded histopathology quantified ten invasion traits per case. These phenotypes were integrated with RNA sequencing, DNA methylation, and mass-spectrometry-based proteomics. Multi-Omic Factor Analysis (MOFA) identified latent molecular programs. Phenotype-specific RNA signatures were matched to LINCS drug-perturbation profiles and validated in 3D gliomasphere and ex vivo brain-slice assays. Two dominant, reproducible invasion modes emerged across models: diffuse parenchymal infiltration and perivascular/condensed growth. Proneural cultures formed more aggressive tumors in immunodeficient mice, and mouse survival showed a modest correlation with patient survival in matched cases (Pearson r=0.1832, p=0.045). MOFA identified 15 latent factors; Factor 1, marked by ASCL1/OLIG1/OLIG2 programs across multiple molecular layers, was associated with increased tumor formation and diffuse invasion in mice. Higher Factor 1 scores were associated with significantly longer postoperative survival in both the matched patient cohort (p = 0.00018) and TCGA (p = 0.017), although Factor 1 was not associated with survival of the xenografted mice. Drug-signature matching separated mechanisms targeting diffuse versus perivascular invasion. Experimental validation confirmed phenotype-selective sensitivities, and inhibitors PIK-75 and buparlisib suppressed invasion dynamics across representative models in 3D and brain-slice assays. The HGCC Phenobank provides the first openly available PDX resource that systematically links GBM invasion phenotypes to multi-omic programs and therapeutic predictions. This framework enables reproducible model selection, mechanistic dissection of invasion modes, and phenotype-guided therapeutic discovery.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag257.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across neuro-oncology domains to analyze complex, high-dimensional, multimodal data. Despite major advances in the biological understanding and classification of CNS tumors, clinical outcomes for many of them remain poor, reflecting intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity and limitations of conventional reductionist approaches. AI offers a paradigm shift to capture this heterogeneity and provide quantitative, reproducible diagnostic, predictive, and prognostic insights. This article describes a joint effort across the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) working groups to provide an overarching review of the AI use across six key domains of neuro-oncology: neuroimaging, neuropathology, laboratory medicine, neurosurgery, drug discovery, and clinical trials. Applications closest to clinical use include imaging segmentation and quantification, AI-assisted image reconstruction, DNA methylation-based classification, and workflow optimization. Radiogenomics, WSI-based molecular prediction, AI-guided surgical targeting, liquid biopsy interpretation, AI-guided drug discovery, digital twins, and in silico trials remain promising but require stronger prospective validation. Key challenges include limited availability of large diverse datasets, variability in data acquisition and reference standards, and limited external validation. This review provides a unifying framework for understanding the role of AI across neuro-oncology and highlights key considerations for its responsible implementation, emphasizing standardization, reproducibility, multi-institutional validation, and human oversight.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag258.abstract: Diffuse gliomas are frequently associated with epilepsy, particularly in low-grade variants. Seizures are key events to be considered in glioma management, including during surgery. Optimizing resection of epileptic areas may affect not only postoperative epilepsy but also glioma prognosis in the context of interactions between glioma growth and neuronal activities. As for glioma tissue resection, surgery of epileptic networks requires a deeper understanding of their organization and reliable biomarkers. We investigated the spatiotemporal dynamics of the transition from interictal to ictal-like events (ILEs) using ex vivo human peritumoral tissue from glioma patients. Slices were recorded with multi-electrode arrays during the transition from the spontaneous interictal state to pharmacologically induced seizures considering the dynamics of slow versus fast oscillatory neuronal activities. Transition to seizure was characterized by the emergence of preictal discharges (PIDs), allowing subdivision of the preictal phase into build-up, steady-state, and trigger periods. PIDs progressively increased in amplitude, duration, and slope with significant changes during the trigger phase. Concurrently, high-frequency activity (180-550 Hz) and high-frequency oscillations (HFOs) increased across the transition period, particularly during the trigger phase. In addition to such preictal recruitment, the reinforcement of HFOs was accompanied by a spatial organization in additive microdomains, peaking at seizure onset and encompassing slow field potential dynamics. In the periglioma human cortex, seizures arise from progressively recruited neuronal assemblies sculpted together with HFOs, providing new insights into the microphysiological processes of glioma-related ictogenesis and requiring consideration of the preictal fast and focal neuronal activity.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag259.abstract: Differentiating true progression (TP) from pseudoprogression (PsP) after chemoradiation for glioblastoma remains clinically difficult. We evaluated externally validated diagnostic performance of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based machine learning models and appraised study quality and transparency. PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE, and Cochrane Library were searched through October 1, 2025 (PROSPERO registration CRD420251144894). Eligible adult glioblastoma studies used MRI-based machine learning to distinguish TP from PsP against histopathology and/or clinicoradiologic follow-up. The primary meta-analysis included external test cohorts with extractable 2 × 2 data; internal and combined internal and external test analyses were secondary. Diagnostic accuracy was synthesized with bivariate random-effects models. Thirty-one studies including 2,344 patients undergoing imaging assessment were included. Seven external test cohorts, including 219 patient observations, entered the primary meta-analysis. Pooled sensitivity was 0.78 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.63-0.88), specificity was 0.75 (95% CI, 0.63-0.84), and summary area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was 0.81 (bootstrap 95% CI, 0.69-0.91). Internal test cohorts showed higher apparent performance than external cohorts (AUC, 0.91 vs 0.81), but the difference was not statistically significant (difference, -0.09; 95% CI, -0.22 to 0.02; P = 0.12). Risk of bias was frequently high or unclear, and reporting transparency was heterogeneous. MRI-based machine learning showed moderate-to-good external validation performance for TP-versus-PsP discrimination, but evidence remains limited by small external test cohorts, bias, and incomplete reporting. Larger transparent multicenter validations are needed before routine clinical implementation.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag260.abstract: Brain metastases (BM) are frequent in EGFR-mutated (EGFRm) non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and remain challenging after prior EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy. This exploratory study evaluated high-dose fimmonertinib and explored subtype-specific spatial biology. iFORCE was a prospective, single-center, single-arm study. Eligible patients had advanced NSCLC harboring EGFR mutations with previously treated BM following EGFR-TKI therapy, or intracranial disease progression. Patients received 160 mg firmonertinib once daily. The primary endpoint was intracranial progression-free survival (iPFS). Archival paired primary tumors and BM specimens from an independent retrospective cohort underwent exploratory digital spatial profiling (DSP). Twenty-three patients were enrolled. At a median follow-up of 19.7 months (95% CI, 14.5-25.3), median iPFS was 14.6 months (95% CI, 4.2-not estimable [NE]), with 12- and 18-month iPFS rates of 53.8% and 46.1%, respectively. Based on the best intracranial overall response, intracranial objective response and disease control rates were 34.8% (95% CI, 16.4-57.3) and 91.3% (95% CI, 72.0-98.9). Median systemic PFS was 10.7 months (95% CI, 3.9-NE). Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 13 (56.5%) patients, mostly grade 1; one patient (4.3%) developed grade 3 stomatitis. No treatment discontinuations or treatment-related deaths were observed. DSP revealed distinct EGFR subtype-specific BM ecosystems: exon 19 deletion tumors retained immune-enriched inflammatory programs, whereas L858R-mutated tumors showed tumor-intrinsic cell-cycle, DNA-repair, RNA-splicing, apoptosis-resistance, and immune-evasion features. Fimonertinib 160 mg showed promising intracranial activity with a manageable safety profile in EGFR-TKI-treated EGFRm NSCLC with BM. L858R BM displayed tumor-intrinsic, microenvironment-independent biology, suggesting preferential sensitivity to high-dose firmonertinib.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag261.abstract: Hippocampal avoidance whole-brain radiotherapy (HA-WBRT) with memantine reduces, but does not eliminate, cognitive decline. Left hippocampal dose may be more closely associated with cognitive outcomes. We investigated whether unilateral (left) HA-WBRT is equivalent to bilateral HA-WBRT for neurocognitive function. In this randomized, single-blind, phase 2 equivalence trial, patients with brain metastases were assigned 1:1 to unilateral (left) or bilateral HA-WBRT (30 Gy in 10 fractions) with concurrent memantine. The primary endpoint was relative decline in Hopkins Verbal Learning Test-Revised (HVLT-R) memory score from baseline to 6 months; equivalence required the 90% CI for the between-arm difference to fall within ±15 percentage points. Among 73 patients (unilateral, n = 36; bilateral, n = 37; median follow-up, 13.2 months), mean 6-month relative HVLT-R decline was 4.75% versus 5.05% (difference, -0.31%; 90% CI, -12.02% to 11.40%; TOST P = .02), meeting the equivalence criterion. Brain progression-free survival (10.3 vs 10.8 months; P = .96), overall survival (17.8 vs 12.8 months; P = .94), acute toxicity (≥ grade 2, 44.4% vs 35.1%; P = .43), and 6-month neurocognitive failure (61.1% vs 56.8%; Gray test P = .78) were similar. Global health status appeared more stable with unilateral HA-WBRT (interaction, P < .001). Exploratory plasma BDNF trajectories varied by neurocognitive failure status (FDR q = .09). Unilateral (left) HA-WBRT with memantine met the prespecified equivalence criterion for verbal memory, with comparable oncologic outcomes and safety; non-verbal memory was not assessed. These findings warrant validation, particularly when bilateral avoidance is challenging.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag262.abstract: Contrast enhancement is generally considered an adverse prognostic feature in adult glioma. However, its significance in newly diagnosed grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma remains uncertain, with important implications for use of the mutant IDH inhibitor vorasidenib. We evaluated survival outcomes associated with preoperative enhancement in this population. We retrospectively evaluated consecutive patients with grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma treated at two institutions between 2010 and 2021. Preoperative MRIs were assessed for intratumoral enhancement by two independent readers with third-reader adjudication. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were evaluated by Kaplan-Meier analysis, univariate and multivariable Cox regression. Among 325 evaluable patients, median age was 37 years, 47% had 1p/19q-codeletion, and 35% had gross-total resection. Median follow-up was 10.5 years. Preoperative enhancement was observed in 53 (16%) patients, most commonly nonmeasurable (72%) or ill-defined (62%); most (87%) had no residual postoperative enhancement. Preoperative enhancement was not associated with OS or PFS in either univariate analyses (OS HR 1.16 [0.67-2.01], p = 0.591; PFS HR 1.25 [0.88-1.80], p = 0.216) or multivariable analyses adjusting for established prognostic factors (OS HR 0.86 [0.46-1.61], p = 0.633; PFS HR 1.29 [0.86-1.92], p = 0.219). Enhancement characteristics (measurable size, well-defined morphology) were not associated with OS. In grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma, preoperative enhancement was not associated with OS or PFS. These findings suggest that preoperative enhancement does not identify a higher-risk subgroup in this population, and that its presence alone should not preclude consideration of vorasidenib in eligible patients.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag266.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) harboring EGFRvIII represents a biologically distinct and highly aggressive tumor subset characterized by aberrant receptor signaling, marked intratumoral heterogeneity, and profound immune remodeling. Rather than acting as a constitutively active truncated receptor, EGFRvIII represents a structurally rewired EGFR variant whose altered extracellular architecture, receptor assembly, and trafficking promote ligand-independent signaling and signaling plasticity, thereby supporting tumor proliferation, stemness, invasion, and angiogenesis. Beyond tumor-intrinsic effects, EGFRvIII also contributes to the formation of a spatially heterogeneous, myeloid-dominant and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, characterized by myeloid-cell expansion, impaired T cell effector function, and mesenchymal-like tumor-immune plasticity. Despite extensive therapeutic efforts including tyrosine kinase inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, immune checkpoint blockade, and EGFRvIII-targeted CAR-T cell strategies, durable clinical efficacy remains limited by the interplay of antigen heterogeneity, adaptive signaling, clonal evolution, and microenvironmental immunosuppression. Taken together, EGFRvIII can be viewed as a structural and evolutionary regulator that links receptor rewiring and signaling plasticity with immune ecosystem remodeling and therapeutic resistance, underscoring the need for integrated strategies that target both tumor cell-intrinsic signaling and the suppressive microenvironment.
