doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0104.abstract: Abstract Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) have emerged as critical immune niches within the tumor microenvironment across various cancers. However, their structural organization and functional roles in non–muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) remain poorly characterized. In this study, we comprehensively characterized TLS in NMIBC using en bloc resected primary diagnostic specimens, which enabled high-resolution spatial mapping and quantitative histologic assessment across a large cohort of primary tumors (97 patients). Compared with TLS in inflammation-driven cystitis, tumor-associated TLS showed heterogeneous spatial organization, altered immune composition, and disrupted follicular dendritic cell (FDC) networks with reduced high endothelial venule density. TLS density increased with NMIBC grade and stage and correlated with higher recurrence risk and shorter progression-free survival in multivariable analysis. Paired analysis of primary and recurrent tumors showed a reduction in FDC density and a shift from M1 to M2 differentiation in tumor recurrences, suggesting the development of an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Single-nuclei RNA sequencing of TLS from NMIBC and cystitis samples revealed impaired germinal center activity in tumor-associated TLS, with asynchronous B-cell maturation and reduced B-cell interactions with both T follicular helper cells and FDC. Tumor-associated TLS also showed increased myeloid infiltration and altered dendritic cell function, including reduced MHC class II antigen presentation and downregulation of costimulatory (CD86–CD28) and migration-related (CD99) pathways compared with TLS from cystitis samples. Overall, we found that NMIBC-associated TLS are structurally and functionally impaired, which may limit effective local immune responses and suggests they may be relevant as biomarkers and targets for immunomodulatory therapy in bladder cancer.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0104.title: A High Density of Impaired Tertiary Lymphoid Structures Is Associated with Higher Tumor Stage and Recurrence in Non–Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0181.abstract: T-cell exhaustion limits durable antitumor responses and remains a barrier to adoptive cell therapies (ACT) in solid tumors. To identify regulators of T-cell persistence, we performed genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens in primary human CD8⁺ T cells expressing an NY-ESO-1-specific T-cell receptor and subjected them to repeated tumor cell rechallenge. These screens revealed enrichment of single-guide RNAs targeting components of Cullin-RING E3 ligases, particularly Cullin-5 (CRL5) assemblies comprising CUL5, RNF7, and ARIH2. Disruption of CRL5 genes in T cells preserved cytotoxic activity and enhanced cytokine production while sustaining effector-associated transcriptional programs and suppressing exhaustion-related signatures. Pharmacologic inhibition of cullin neddylation with the NEDD8-activating enzyme inhibitor MLN4924 recapitulated CRL5 loss and enhanced T-cell effector function in vitro. In a human melanoma xenograft model, ACT with CRL5-deficient T cells improved tumor control. Together, these findings identify CRL5 as a negative regulator of T-cell fitness and a potential therapeutic target to enhance ACT durability in solid tumors.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0305.abstract: Malignant ascites provides a window into cancer-immune interactions in the peritoneal cavity. Using Cytometry by Time of Flight (CyTOF), we analyzed ascitic immune cells collected from patients with advanced gastrointestinal cancers, nonmalignant forms of hepatitis (NMH), and healthy control peripheral blood mononuclear cells (HC PBMCs). Compositionally, ascitic immune cells shared a myeloid-rich, B and naïve T cell-low signature relative to HC PBMCs. Underneath the shared ascitic compositional signature, three major functional immunophenotypes emerged in response to exogenous stimulation along a suppressive to cytotoxic axis, aligning with Luminex measurements of ascitic cytokine levels: IL-10 enriched, Nonpolarized, and Granzyme B (GZMB) enriched. In our cohort, the IL-10 enriched functional immunophenotype was exclusive to samples from patients with cancer while the GZMB enriched response was dominated by NMH samples. Ascites from patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) contained a persistent anti-cancer humoral response characterized by IgG that bound to autologous ascitic PDAC cells and multiple allogeneic PDAC cell lines.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0367.abstract: Despite advances in adoptive T cell therapy, therapeutic efficacy in solid tumors remains inconsistent, and the mechanistic determinants of treatment failure are incompletely understood. Increasing evidence suggests that effective antitumor responses depend not only on direct recognition of malignant cells but also on interactions with the tumor microenvironment, including non-malignant host cells that cross-present tumor antigens. Using an HLA-A2-transgenic syngeneic mouse cancer model that enables near-physiological presentation of human tumor antigens by both malignant and host cells, we investigated how TCR antigen sensitivity relates to therapeutic outcome. We compared T cell receptor-engineered (TCR-)T cells with different antigen sensitivities directed against the same HLA-A2-restricted melanoma antigen. Although high- and low-sensitivity TCR-T cells recognized tumor cells comparably in vitro, only high-sensitivity TCR-T cells mediated durable tumor regression in vivo. Improved tumor control correlated with enhanced recognition of cross-presented tumor antigen on tumor-associated CD11b+ myeloid cells and increased intratumoral effector activity. IFN-γ levels in tumor tissue and peripheral blood reflected intratumoral T cell activity and correlated with therapeutic response. Together, these findings identify host cell antigen recognition as a sensitivity-dependent functional correlate of TCR-T cell efficacy and provide a mechanistic explanation for the superior activity of higher-sensitivity TCRs in solid tumors.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0433.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the treatment of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet a large proportion of patients do not respond. The lung microbiome is a key modulator of antitumor immunity, however, the functional contribution of active microbial communities and their interaction with host transcriptional programs in shaping ICI outcomes remain poorly defined. Here, we prospectively analyzed bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) samples from 71 NSCLC patients prior to ICI initiation. We profiled the microbiome and host transcriptome in the BAL to look for microbial and host signatures in the lower airways associated with treatment response. We found that enrichment of the lower airway microbiome with oral commensals was associated with disease progression and worse prognosis of patients treated with ICI. Metatranscriptomics-derived microbial clustering revealed distinct functional profiles. The microbial cluster enriched with oral commensals, which was only present among patients with poor response to ICI, had differential regulation of pathways involved in the metabolism of short-chain fatty acids, methane, and pyruvate. This cluster also correlated with host immune pathways including upregulation of interferon signaling, neutrophil degranulation, and mitophagy, all of which could contribute to the poor response to immunotherapy. In a preclinical murine model of lung cancer with dysbiosis, inoculating lung tumor-bearing mice with oral commensals increased intratumoral neutrophils and Th17 responses and impaired ICI efficacy. Our findings support the concept that microbial communities in the lower airways influence tumor-immune interactions via defined metabolic-immune axes.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0433.title: Lower airway microbiome transcriptional and metabolic activities influence responsiveness to immunotherapy in NSCLC.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0497.abstract: Metabolic dysregulation in obesity reshapes immune function, but how lipid signals drive immune suppression remains unclear. Herein, we identify a FABP4-PD-L1 axis that links lipid metabolism to immune checkpoint regulation in myeloid cells. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed a distinct FABP4high immunosuppressive splenic macrophage subset enriched under high-fat diet (HFD) conditions, characterized by impaired antigen presentation and elevated PD-L1 expression. Mechanistically, palmitic acid (PA) was shown to induce FABP4 and promote PD-L1 palmitoylation, leading to its stabilization on the cell surface independent of transcriptional regulation. FABP4 was essential for this process, which enabled PD-L1 surface stabilization, immunosuppression and mammary tumor progression. In humans, a conserved CD14intCD16⁺ monocyte population exhibited elevated FABP4-PD-L1 signaling and correlated with obesity and invasive breast cancer. These findings establish PD-L1 as a metabolically regulated protein and reveal a mechanism by which lipid excess drives immune evasion, suggesting FABP4 as a potential therapeutic target in cancer immunotherapy.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0608.abstract: Engineered T-cell therapies are limited by progressive dysfunction under chronic tumor antigen exposure, and genetic perturbation of negative regulators has emerged as a promising strategy to sustain effector activity. We reanalyzed a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen in primary human T cells under repetitive tumor stimulation; protein-protein interaction mapping revealed seven members of the Cullin-RING Ligase 5 (CRL5) complex as an enriched hit cluster. Knockout of any of these members (CUL5, ARIH2, RNF7, UBE2F, UBE2L3, CISH, DCUN1D3) enhanced tumor serial killing, and CUL5, the complex scaffold, emerged as the strongest target. CUL5 knockout T cells exhibited sustained cytotoxicity, elevated effector cytokine production, and fewer exhaustion marker-positive cells while retaining antigen specificity and cytokine dependence. Quantitative ubiquitylation proteomics in resting, and acutely and chronically stimulated T cells mapped CRL5-dependent candidate substrates beyond the canonical JAK/STAT axis, including nutrient transporters, receptor trafficking proteins, and TCR signaling components. The benefit of CUL5 knockout extended across CARs targeting CD19, BCMA, and HER2 with different costimulatory domains, and to 1XX-modified CAR and HLA-independent TCR architectures. Combining CUL5 ablation with a tumor-induced IL-2 circuit produced tumor control across nine rounds of repetitive stimulation, whereas either modification alone eventually failed. In vivo, CUL5 knockout BCMA CAR T cells were enriched in the bone marrow following repeated tumor rechallenge and exhibited enhanced ex vivo cytotoxicity after nearly 90 days in tumor-bearing mice. These findings position CUL5 perturbation as a strategy to improve T-cell persistence and the efficacy of adoptive cell therapies, potentially with engineered cytokine support.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0706.abstract: Concomitant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) is a standard-of-care treatment for unresectable locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA-SCCHN), but its immune effects, particularly relative to radiotherapy (RT) alone, remain incompletely understood. Using syngeneic murine models, we integrated Nr4a3-Tocky reporter analysis with single-cell transcriptomics and T cell receptor clonotyping to comprehensively profile intratumoural CD8⁺ T-cell responses following RT and CRT. We show that CRT uniquely drives robust clonal expansion of antigen-engaged CD8⁺ T-cells and biases differentiation toward progenitor-exhausted (TPEX) states, whereas RT favours terminal exhaustion (TEX). Single-cell analyses further reveal preferential clonal dominance within TPEX populations following CRT. In peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients treated with CRT, TEX populations predominated early after treatment, followed by delayed expansion of circulating TPEX-like populations at 3 months, suggesting phased recovery of progenitor-like T-cell states. Together, these findings demonstrate that CRT and RT induce distinct CD8⁺ T-cell differentiation trajectories and clonal architectures, providing insight into treatment-induced immune remodelling in LA-SCCHN.

doi:10.1158/2326-6066.cir-26-0770.abstract: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a major dose-limiting toxicity of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, yet the upstream mechanisms driving macrophage activation remain incompletely understood. Here, we established a xenograft model of human CAR T-cell therapy that recapitulates key features of CRS and combined single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with pharmacological intervention to define the inflammatory programs underlying CRS. CAR T-cell treatment induced dose-dependent systemic inflammation and remodeled the host myeloid compartment, leading to the accumulation of a distinct population of CRS-associated macrophages. Analysis of clinical scRNA-seq datasets from CAR T cell-treated glioblastoma patients confirmed enrichment of the CRS-associated macrophage gene signature following therapy in patients, supporting the clinical relevance of our findings. Transcriptomic analyses identified marked upregulation of the chemokine receptors CCR1 and CCR2 together with activation of CCL3- and CCL2-associated signaling pathways. Pharmacological inhibition of CCR1 and CCR2 significantly reduced clinical CRS, inflammatory cytokine production, and macrophage activation while preserving CAR T-cell expansion, effector cytokine production, and in vivo antitumor efficacy. These findings identify CCR1/CCR2-dependent chemokine signaling as a critical regulator of macrophage-driven CRS and support chemokine receptor blockade as a promising strategy to improve the safety of CAR T-cell therapy without compromising therapeutic efficacy.

doi:10.1159/000546697.abstract: Background and Aims: We conducted an updated network meta-analysis to evaluate and identify the optimal first-line treatment for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) among all relevant interventional and targeted therapies. Methods: We analyzed 16 phase 2 or 3 randomized controlled trials involving 9,482 patients with metastatic or unresectable HCC published between 2018 and 2024. The trials evaluated 11 systemic agents and 5 interventional treatments in combination with systemic therapy, using either sorafenib or lenvatinib as the control. The primary outcome was overall survival (OS), and secondary outcomes included progression-free survival (PFS) and grade 3–4 adverse events. Subgroup analyses were conducted to assess individual treatment efficacies in specific clinical settings. Results: Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) combined with lenvatinib provided the greatest improvement in OS over sorafenib, with a hazard ratio of 0.41 (95% confidence interval, 0.30–0.58), followed by sintilimab + IBI305 (0.57; 0.43–0.75), camrelizumab + rivoceranib (0.62; 0.48–0.80), atezolizumab + bevacizumab (0.66; 0.51–0.85), lenvatinib + pembrolizumab (0.77; 0.62–0.97), and tremelimumab + durvalumab (0.78; 0.64–0.95). These combinations, except for tremelimumab + durvalumab, also showed significantly superior PFS to sorafenib. TACE + lenvatinib was ranked first in OS analyses with the other current standard-of-care regimens (lenvatinib, atezolizumab + bevacizumab, and tremelimumab + durvalumab) as controls. TACE + lenvatinib, sintilimab + IBI305, and atezolizumab + bevacizumab demonstrated consistently significant extension of OS over sorafenib in subsets with portal invasion, extrahepatic metastasis, and hepatitis B. All immunotherapy-based combinations were significantly associated with a higher risk of adverse events than sorafenib. Conclusions: For advanced HCC, our first-line analysis consistently scored TACE + lenvatinib the best for survival outcomes, followed by various immunotherapy-based combinations. However, the superior efficacy of TACE + lenvatinib should be interpreted with consideration of its derivation from a region with high hepatitis B virus prevalence.

doi:10.1159/000546697.title: Updated Network Meta-Analysis of First-Line Systemic Treatments for Advanced HCC: Consistent Role of TACE

doi:10.1159/lic/admag006.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) represents an increasing global health challenge, associated with poor prognosis and an epidemiological shift towards an aging and comorbid population. Frailty is a multidimensional syndrome of reduced physiological reserve. It is recognized as a robust predictor of clinical outcomes in chronic liver disease and some cancers but remains underexplored in HCC. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the clinical significance of frailty in HCC, focusing on its impact on outcomes, evidence for targeted interventions, and potential role in clinical decision-making. Frailty is associated with adverse outcomes in HCC, including increased healthcare utilization, reduced treatment tolerance, and decreased survival. However, heterogeneity in frailty assessment methods and limited prospective data preclude its clinical application. Early evidence suggests that structured exercise programs are safe, feasible, and may improve frailty measures, although larger prospective studies are required to determine whether these translate into meaningful clinical benefits. Frailty is an emerging prognostic marker and may inform supportive care in HCC. Standardized assessment and interventional trials are needed to support routine integration of frailty for more personalized HCC management.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag011.abstract: Portal vein tumor thrombus (PVTT) is the most common form of macrovascular invasion in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and is associated with poor prognosis, rapid intrahepatic dissemination, and limited responsiveness to systemic therapy. Increasing evidence indicates that PVTT is not merely an intravascular extension of the primary tumor, but rather a biologically distinct and highly adaptive immunosuppressive niche that contributes to immune escape and therapeutic resistance. This review summarizes current genomic, transcriptomic, single-cell, and spatially resolved evidence regarding the immune landscape of PVTT in HCC. We discuss how early clonal divergence, hypoxia-associated metabolic rewiring, and stromal-vascular remodeling cooperatively shape the PVTT microenvironment. PVTT is characterized by enrichment of suppressive myeloid populations, activation of cancer-associated fibroblast programs, extracellular matrix accumulation, endothelial barriers to immune-cell trafficking, and progressive dysfunction or exclusion of effector lymphocytes. Together, these features establish a strongly immune-excluded and immunosuppressive ecosystem, providing a mechanistic basis for the limited efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade in patients with HCC-PVTT. We further highlight the translational implications of this framework for biomarker development, patient stratification, and rational combination strategies targeting suppressive myeloid and stromal programs, vascular barriers, and metabolic-immune crosstalk. PVTT should be regarded as a distinct immunosuppressive niche rather than a passive vascular extension of the primary tumor. Its immune landscape is shaped by coordinated interactions among tumor evolution, metabolic adaptation, stromal remodeling, and immune dysfunction. A better mechanistic understanding of PVTT may support biomarker-guided stratification and the development of more effective precision therapies for HCC with macrovascular invasion.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag012.abstract: Hepatobiliary oncology is at an inflection point. Parallel advances in surgical technique, locoregional therapy, systemic treatment, and understanding of tumour biology have expanded the boundaries of curative-intent care yet have also exposed a critical reality that technical resectability is not synonymous with oncologic resectability. Technically successful resection or liver transplantation may be futile when tumour biology is aggressive, leading to early recurrence and limited survival benefit. Modern hepatobiliary surgical and transplant oncology must therefore move beyond anatomy-driven decision-making towards biologically informed strategies that incorporate tumour behaviour, treatment response, and temporal disease stability. The Asia-Pacific Transplant Oncology Symposium (APTOS) 2024 examined how Eastern and Western paradigms intersect across hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, and colorectal liver metastases, identifying pathways towards integration. Eastern and Western programmes have historically approached hepatobiliary oncology through distinct and longstanding philosophies. Eastern centres, frequently operating within living donor liver transplantation-dominant systems characterized by organ scarcity and the ethical principle of double equipoise, have traditionally leveraged high operative volume and technical expertise in complex resections. These environments have favoured surgery-first approaches when resection appears technically feasible, alongside response-driven conversion strategies aimed at expanding operability. Western centres, shaped by deceased-donor allocation frameworks and trial-oriented oncology models, have more consistently prioritized biological selection and longitudinal validation of disease control before proceeding to curative-intent intervention, particularly in borderline-resectable disease. These differences are driven by infrastructural and ethical factors, including donor availability, transplant systems, and biomarker integration, rather than surgical capability. This article is an expert statement reflecting the opinion of an international multidisciplinary faculty of hepatobiliary surgeons, transplant surgeons, hepatologists, and medical and clinical oncologists from Eastern and Western centres. It is a narrative expert perspective and not a formal consensus or guideline. This expert statement proposes that the next phase of hepatobiliary oncology requires harmonized, biology-driven definitions of resectability, transplantability, and futility. Comparative evaluation of regional strategies is essential to clarify how treatment sequencing affects recurrence and survival, an effort that is time-sensitive as advances in systemic therapy may soon obscure strategy-specific effects. Rather than competing models, Eastern procedural expertise and Western biology-centred frameworks should be viewed as complementary, supporting context-dependent or sequential approaches that integrate surgery with biology-guided systemic or locoregional therapy. Aligning these paradigms within ethical stewardship of donor organs can establish globally coherent, biology-driven standards that maximize durable survival while minimizing futile surgery and transplantation.

doi:10.1159/lic/admag013.abstract: Abstract Introduction Despite the availability of several approved therapies, continued investigation of novel treatment options is needed to further improve outcomes in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The phase 2 KEYSTEP-004 study evaluated the safety and efficacy of quavonlimab coformulated with pembrolizumab (quavonlimab/pembrolizumab) plus lenvatinib as first-line therapy for advanced HCC. Methods Adults with confirmed advanced HCC and no prior systemic therapy were enrolled. In the safety lead-in phase, participants received intravenous quavonlimab 25 mg coformulated with pembrolizumab 400 mg every 6 weeks plus oral lenvatinib 12 mg (body weight ≥60 kg) or 8 mg (body weight <60 kg) once daily (dose level 0 [DL0]). Allocation to the efficacy expansion phase was permitted if lenvatinib DL0 plus quavonlimab 25 mg coformulated with pembrolizumab 400 mg every 6 weeks was determined to be tolerable. Primary endpoints were objective response rate (ORR) per RECIST v1.1 by blinded independent central review (BICR) and safety. Secondary endpoints included duration of response (DOR) and progression-free survival (PFS) per RECIST v1.1 by BICR, and overall survival (OS). Results As of June 22, 2023, 116 participants were enrolled, and 115 were treated. No dose-limiting toxicities were observed in the safety lead-in phase. Lenvatinib DL0 in combination with quavonlimab 25 mg coformulated with pembrolizumab 400 mg every 6 weeks was determined to be tolerable. Median study follow-up was 18.0 months (range, 12.0–26.6). Confirmed ORR was 37.4% (95% CI: 28.5–46.9). Median DOR was 10.6 months (range, 1.2+ to 23.1+), median PFS was 8.2 months (95% CI: 6.2–10.2), and median OS was 22.1 months (95% CI: 15.5-not reached). Grade 3–5 treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 66 participants (57.4%); 14 (12.8%) required high-dose steroids for management of a treatment-related AE. Conclusion Quavonlimab coformulated with pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib is an active combination and has a manageable safety profile in advanced HCC.

doi:10.1182/blood.2025030377.abstract: Phosphatase Mg2+/Mn2+ dependent 1D protein (PPM1D) is a serine threonine phosphatase known to regulate oncogenic pathways. PPM1D mutations are enriched in therapy-related MDS and AML, but the role of PPM1D in myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) remains largely unexplored. By sequencing 519 MPN patients, we detected activating PPM1D mutations in 3.1% of them. Importantly, PPM1D was overexpressed in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in most PPM1D wild-type (WT) MPN cases. To elucidate the impact of PPM1D mutations on MPN HSPCs, we generated isogenic JAK2V617F+/PPM1D-WT and JAK2V617F+/PPM1D mutant (MUT) induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines from a MPN patient. Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) of iPSC derived HSPCs revealed altered TP53, DNA damage response and cell cycle regulation. scRNA-seq analysis of primary PPM1D-MUT MPN patient mononuclear cells (MNCs) further confirmed upregulation of MYC, mTORC1, OXPHOS, JAK/STAT, and NF-κB pathways and corresponding genes in HSCs. The allosteric PPM1D inhibitor (PPM1Di) GSK2830371 preferentially inhibited colony formation in myelofibrosis (MF) samples. Combination treatment of GSK2830371 with low dose inhibition of HDM2, a negative regulator of p53, significantly improved targeting of JAK2V617F+ HSPCs, while sparing normal HSPCs. Single-cell mutational and protein analysis of a clonally complex MF patient sample treated with this combination strategy revealed reduced mutated clones and increased WT clones by >4-fold. Dual PPM1D and HDM2 targeting also significantly decreased leukemic burden in a xenograft MPN model. These findings support PPM1D as a critical MPN HSPCs regulator and support dual PPM1D/HDM2 inhibition as a treatment strategy for MF patients.

doi:10.1182/blood.2025031114.abstract: Interactions of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) with the bone marrow microenvironment are critical to regulate stem cell function in homeostasis, emergency hematopoiesis and ageing. The dynamic behavior of endogenous HSCs in their niches has been challenging to study due to the complexity of markers required to define pure HSCs. Multiple recently developed reporter strategies advanced our capacity to identify HSCs in situ. Yet, they provide different levels of HSC enrichment and are frequently not stable in situations of perturbed hematopoiesis, leading to contradictory observations of HSC localization and migratory behavior. Here we employed a new double reporter strategy by combining the Hoxb5-mKO2 and Vwf-GFP reporters, that are stably expressed in homeostasis, stress and ageing. Hoxb5+Vwf+ cells represent a subset of highly pure and potent long-term HSCs with a platelet-biased pattern of differentiation, that are included in the populations identified by other reporter strategies. Intravital microscopy revealed Hoxb5+Vwf+ cells to be non-migratory in homeostasis, ageing, or following acute thrombocytopenia when these cells are actively proliferating, indicating that this non-migratory behavior is independent of cell cycle status. We found Hoxb5+Vwf+ HSCs in perivascular niches with a higher coverage by LepR+ mesenchymal cells but not preferentially located closer to megakaryocytes, when compared to Hoxb5+Vwf- cells. Nevertheless, stress-induced megakaryopoiesis following acute thrombocytopenia bring megakaryocytes into closer proximity of Hoxb5+Vwf+ HSCs, revealing previously unrecognized niche dynamics in HSC regulation during regeneration.

doi:10.1182/blood.2026033409.abstract: RAS mutations are recurrent in acute myeloid leukemia (AML); yet, their genomic and clinical landscape remain poorly characterized. We analyzed centralized molecular profiling data in 8,553 patients with newly diagnosed AML. Of these, 1,775 (21%) harbored RAS mutations: NRAS in 1,103 (13%), KRAS in 445 (5%), and both in 227 (3%). RAS mutations primarily clustered in P-loop hotspots (G12/G13, 70%), with NRAS showing higher Q61 mutation prevalence (24% vs. 9%) and KRAS showing additional K117/A146 hotspots. Multiple RAS mutations occurred in 23% of patients. Convergent evolution of RAS signaling mutations emerged as a key feature of RASmut AML. RTK/RAS pathway mutations were non-uniformly enriched: PTPN11, KIT and FLT3-TKD mutations were positively associated, CBL mutations showed no association, and FLT3-ITD mutations were negatively associated. The prognostic impact of RAS mutations was dependent on the genomic background and treatment. In multivariate analyses in intensively treated patients, NRAS mutations showed opposing associations with overall survival (OS): adverse in patients with AML, myelodysplasia-related (HR=1.32, p=0.036) and favorable in those with NPM1 (HR=0.61, p=0.036) or FLT3-ITD (HR=0.63, p=0.048) mutations, among others. KRAS mutations predicted inferior OS (HR=1.41; p=0.003). In patients treated with non-intensive, venetoclax-based regimens, RAS mutations were associated with markedly inferior OS in patients with NPM1 (HR=2.98, p=0.007) or IDH1/2 mutations (HR=4.06, p<0.001). These data inform risk stratification and development of RAS-targeting strategies in AML.

doi:10.1182/blood.2026033478.abstract: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is characterized by chronic hemolytic anemia and a propensity to acute exacerbations such as post-transfusion hyperhemolysis syndrome (HHS). While erythrocyte injury is secondary to hemoglobin S polymerization, the underlying pathophysiologic driver, the mechanism by which sickle erythrocytes are then removed from circulation is largely regulated by the immune system. Multiple pathways potentially play a role, driven by pathological changes within both the cellular and humoral immune system. The review examines what is known regarding changes to the outer membrane of the sickle erythrocyte (including the expression of phosphatidylserine (PS), mannose, CD47 and CD95/Fas), the role of plasma-derived opsonins (including Gas6, MFG-E8, Protein S, MBL, TSP1, IgG and C3b) and the macrophage receptors that recognize and bind these molecules (including TREM2, TIM4, MerTK, integrins αvβ3/5, CD206, CD209/DC-SIGN, SIRPα, FasL, FcR, and CR). Drawing upon the results of investigations by our group and others, we conclude with a proposed model for clearance of erythrocytes in SCD, in which chronic hemolysis predominantly occurs through extravascular erythrophagocytosis, whereas acute hemolytic events involve a shift towards intravascular hemolysis via complement assembly into the membrane attack complex, Fas-mediated erythronecroptosis, and heme-mediated ferroptosis. The process by which transfusion may accelerate these pathways and induce HHS is also considered.

doi:10.1182/blood.2026033885.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CART19) therapy represents a breakthrough for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma (rrLBCL). However, suboptimal CART19 activity can lead to therapeutic failure and dismal outcomes. Through single cell RNA-sequencing of tumors at the time of progression from CART19, we show that a subset of tumor contain clonally expanded and proliferating populations of CART19 cells that acquire transcriptional features of dysfunction, suggestive of ongoing tumor cell engagement and chronic stimulation. Using an in vitro system to model this process, we show that iterative rechallenge of CART19 cells with target cells drives failure of tumor control associated with acquired transcriptomic features of T-cell dysfunction and reduced IL2 signaling. Pegenzileukin, a non-alpha IL2-receptor agonist, prevented CART19 dysfunction, improving T-cell expansion and tumor control in vitro. To test this concept in vivo, we developed a cell line model from a post-CART19 progression tumor that reproduces the response and failure kinetics observed in the originating patient. In vivo CART19 alone led to transient response followed by progression and secondary central nervous system relapse in this model, while the addition of pegenzileukin to CART19 led to the complete eradication of tumors. This provides mechanism-informed pre-clinical rationale for the use of non-alpha IL2 receptor agonists in combating T-cell exhaustion, a critical mechanism of CART19 failure.

doi:10.1182/blood.2026034288.abstract: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is limited not only by donor cell number and recipient conditioning, but also by loss of stem-cell fitness during collection and processing. Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells normally reside in a physiologically hypoxic marrow environment, yet routine ex vivo handling exposes them to ambient oxygen outside this niche. Although ambient oxygen exposure during ex vivo handling impairs hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) function, the metabolic basis for this effect remains incompletely defined. Using hypoxic handling as a physiologic reference, we examined whether functionally relevant consequences of ambient oxygen exposure remain modifiable in human CD34+ cells during ex vivo handling. Quantitative LC-MS profiling revealed that ambient oxygen exposure rapidly increased intracellular amino acids, including branched-chain amino acids, together with activation of nutrient-sensing pathways. This metabolic shift was associated with increased mTORC1 signaling, attenuation of lysosomal programs, and impaired primary and secondary engraftment. Complementary single-cell analyses supported a coordinated transition toward nutrient-activated states under ambient oxygen, whereas hypoxia preserved relative metabolic restraint. Transient restriction of essential amino acids or branched-chain amino acids during ex vivo handling restored lysosomal programs and improved engraftment of normoxia-handled human CD34+ cells. Pharmacologic LAT1 inhibition similarly improved engraftment. Together, these findings identify disruption of amino acid homeostasis as a previously underappreciated consequence of ambient oxygen exposure during routine ex vivo handling and demonstrate that a functionally relevant component of this injury remains modifiable after exposure to improve human HSPC engraftment.

doi:10.1182/blood.2026034428.abstract: Emicizumab has transformed hemophilia A (HA) management by enabling effective subcutaneous prophylaxis independent of inhibitor status. However, its constitutive activity and lack of sensitivity to anticoagulant feedback contribute to excessive thrombin generation under certain conditions, particularly when combined with bypassing agents, a liability increasingly recognized as a class effect of FVIII-mimetic antibodies. We engineered an "AutoRegulated" (AR) FVIII-mimetic antibody by integrating a short thrombin cleavable peptide sensitive to the proteolytic activity of thrombin in the hinge region of both emicizumab arms. Insertion of the peptide did not impair structural integrity and biological function with AR-emicizumab demonstrating EC50 values of FVIII-mimetic activity and correction of blood loss in HA mice comparable to the parental emicizumab. However, the presence of thrombin-mediated AR enabled thrombin-responsive proteolytic inactivation upon exposure to supra-physiological thrombin levels, whereas the parental emicizumab remained unaffected. The dynamic control provided by AR efficiently reduced the procoagulant effects induced by co-administration of activated Prothrombin Complex Concentrates (aPCC). In thrombin generation assays, AR-emicizumab significantly attenuated the excessive thrombin peak observed with emicizumab. Similarly, in vivo, the presence of thrombin-mediated AR prevented platelet consumptive coagulopathy and reduced the microvascular pulmonary thrombosis induced by the parental molecule without affecting the systemic levels of the therapeutic antibody. This on-demand self-limiting mechanism aligns therapeutic activity with local hemostatic needs, may offer a promising therapeutic approach for HA patients, while establishing a generalizable strategy to improve the safety profile of next-generation hemostatic biologics.

doi:10.1182/blood.2026034923.abstract: Germline DDX41 variants are a recognized cause of adult myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS), characterized by distinct biological features and favorable prognosis. The independent effect of DDX41 status on outcomes after allogeneic transplantation, the role of conditioning intensity, and treatment-related toxicity risk remain unresolved. To address this gap, we analyzed 1,514 patients with MDS undergoing transplantation prior to routine DDX41 testing alongside a wild-type comparator, providing an unbiased benchmark for this molecular subgroup. Forty-nine patients (3.2%) carried pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) germline DDX41 variants; 19 (39%) had an additional somatic DDX41 mutation, most commonly p.R525H. P/LP DDX41 cases were older (median 63 vs 59 years) and showed lower IPSS-M risk with absent TP53 mutations (0% vs 21%). In terms of outcome, 2-year relapse incidence was significantly lower in P/LP DDX41 (17% vs 34%, p=0.01). In multivariable analysis, the presence of a DDX41 P/LP variant independently associated with lower risk of relapse (hazard ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.21-0.88; p=0.02), concentrated in the reduced-intensity/nonmyeloablative stratum. Adjusted models showed significantly improved disease-free survival (DFS) for P/LP DDX41 (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.95; p=0.03) and no significant association with non-relapse mortality (NRM) or graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). In summary, these findings identify DDX41-associated MDS as a transplant subgroup with superior DFS regardless of conditioning intensity driven by reduced relapse risk and lack of excess NRM and GVHD supporting incorporation of germline DDX41 status into transplant planning.

doi:10.1182/blood.2026035372.abstract: Gene therapy for hemophilia A (HA) aims to provide durable hemostatic control and reduce treatment burden, but AAV-based products to date have limitations: inconsistent peak expression, declining factor levels, and immunogenicity causing transaminitis and expression loss. ASC618 (ASC Therapeutics, Milpitas, CA, USA) was developed as a second-generation gene therapy product to overcome some of these limitations, using ET3, a bioengineered chimeric human/porcine B-domain-deleted FVIII transgene, paired with a minimal liver promoter and liver codon optimization. In a phase 1/2 trial (NCT04676048), two patients received ASC618. Despite initial factor expression, both developed high-titer FVIII inhibitors and are now maintained on emicizumab prophylaxis. Although inhibitor titers have declined, both remain high-titer nearly two years after a single infusion. The best explanation for inhibitor formation is that the novel FVIII with the human-porcine hybrid construct (ET3) contained epitopes for which these patients had not developed tolerance despite both having more than 1000 exposure days to exogenous FVIII in the past. Although this trial has been halted, these cases provide important lessons for the development of future hemophilia gene therapies. They highlight the need for careful immunogenicity assessment when using bioengineered transgenes, even in previously treated patients with extensive factor VIII exposure.

doi:10.1182/blood.2026035389.abstract: In randomized studies, addition of FLT3 inhibitors failed to improve survival in older patients with FLT3-ITD AML unfit for intensive chemotherapy. Although hypomethylating agents or low-dose cytarabine combined with venetoclax is standard, FLT3-ITD is an important mechanism of resistance and a barrier to improved survival. Recent studies show promise for the addition of gilteritinib or quizartinib to less intensive venetoclax-based therapy, however resulting marrow toxicity requires substantial reductions to administered treatment. The INTERVENE study (Investigating Novel Triplets to Extend Remission with VENetoclax in Elderly AML) (ACTRN12619001655134) examined the role of midostaurin (M) administered sequentially after low-dose cytarabine (L) combined with venetoclax (V) in patients with newly diagnosed AML ≥60 years with non-adverse karyotype. After a run-in phase (n=18) established that LDAC combined with venetoclax from days 1-28 and midostaurin from days 11-28 was tolerable, 120 patients were randomized 2:1 to receive either LVM or LV. For the primary endpoint, LVM did not improve composite complete remission (CRc), compared to LV (72% vs 68%). Combining midostaurin with LV enhanced CRc among the sub-group of patients (n=29) with FLT3-ITD (82% vs 57%, difference = 25%, 0.85 posterior probability true difference > 5%, 95% CrI: -10 to 59%) and improved FLT3-ITD clearance as measured by ultrasensitive NGS (65% vs 0%), resulting in longer OS (median 24.2 vs 8.8 months, HR=0.34, 95% CrI: 0.071 to 0.960), compared to LV. In conclusion, midostaurin combined with low-dose cytarabine and venetoclax is well-tolerated and may have a role in newly diagnosed FLT3-ITD AML unfit for intensive chemotherapy.

doi:10.1186/gb-2008-9-3-r54.abstract: Abstract Background Gene duplication is the primary source of new genes with novel or altered functions. It is known that duplicates may obtain these new functional roles by evolving divergent expression patterns and/or protein functions after the duplication event. Here, using yeast ( Saccharomyces cerevisiae ) as a model organism, we investigate a previously little considered mode for the functional diversification of duplicate genes: subcellular adaptation of encoded proteins. Results We show that for 24-37% of duplicate gene pairs derived from the S. cerevisiae whole-genome duplication event, the two members of the pair encode proteins that localize to distinct subcellular compartments. The propensity of yeast duplicate genes to evolve new localization patterns depends to a large extent on the biological function of their progenitor genes. Proteins involved in processes with a wider subcellular distribution (for example, catabolism) frequently evolved new protein localization patterns after duplication, whereas duplicate proteins limited to a smaller number of organelles (for example, highly expressed biosynthesis/housekeeping proteins with a slow rate of evolution) rarely relocate within the cell. Paralogous proteins evolved divergent localization patterns by partitioning of ancestral localizations ('sublocalization'), but probably more frequently by relocalization to new compartments ('neolocalization'). We show that such subcellular reprogramming may occur through selectively driven substitutions in protein targeting sequences. Notably, our data also reveal that relocated proteins functionally adapted to their new subcellular environments and evolved new functional roles through changes of their physico-chemical properties, expression levels, and interaction partners. Conclusion We conclude that protein subcellular adaptation represents a common mechanism for the functional diversification of duplicate genes.

doi:10.1186/gb-2012-13-10-r84.abstract: Abstract Background Aberrant CpG island promoter DNA hypermethylation is frequently observed in cancer and is believed to contribute to tumor progression by silencing the expression of tumor suppressor genes. Previously, we observed that promoter hypermethylation in breast cancer reflects cell lineage rather than tumor progression and occurs at genes that are already repressed in a lineage-specific manner. To investigate the generality of our observation we analyzed the methylation profiles of 1,154 cancers from 7 different tissue types. Results We find that 1,009 genes are prone to hypermethylation in these 7 types of cancer. Nearly half of these genes varied in their susceptibility to hypermethylation between different cancer types. We show that the expression status of hypermethylation prone genes in the originator tissue determines their propensity to become hypermethylated in cancer; specifically, genes that are normally repressed in a tissue are prone to hypermethylation in cancers derived from that tissue. We also show that the promoter regions of hypermethylation-prone genes are depleted of repetitive elements and that DNA sequence around the same promoters is evolutionarily conserved. We propose that these two characteristics reflect tissue-specific gene promoter architecture regulating the expression of these hypermethylation prone genes in normal tissues. Conclusions As aberrantly hypermethylated genes are already repressed in pre-cancerous tissue, we suggest that their hypermethylation does not directly contribute to cancer development via silencing. Instead aberrant hypermethylation reflects developmental history and the perturbation of epigenetic mechanisms maintaining these repressed promoters in a hypomethylated state in normal cells.

doi:10.1186/s12943-026-02740-4.abstract: The tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) is a spatially organized ecosystem in which the distribution and interaction of cellular and molecular components have a significant impact on disease progression and therapeutic response. Traditionally, bulk analyses have failed to capture the critical spatial context governing these dynamics. The latest breakthroughs in spatial multi-omics technologies, including spatial transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics, have completely transformed our ability to characterize the TIME at unprecedented resolution. These advanced platforms enable precise mapping of immune cell distribution, reconstruction of intercellular communication networks, and identification of pattern structures such as tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS). We reviewed the current experimental methods of spatial omics and highlights how their applications provide novel insights into tumor biology. We further discussed how insights from spatial profiling could inform the development of novel therapeutic strategies aimed at actively remodeling the TIME, provide information for prognosis prediction, and shape responses to treatments such as immunotherapy. Despite the challenges in standardization and clinical translation, spatial multi-omics provides an indispensable dimension for understanding tumor immunobiology, paving the way for more precise tumor diagnosis, prognosis and treatment methods.

doi:10.1186/s12943-026-02741-3.abstract: Tumors are embedded within complex microenvironments composed of malignant, immune and stromal cells, yet how coordinated cellular organization shapes tumor biology across cancers remains incompletely understood. Here we integrate single-cell transcriptomic profiles from over two million cells spanning 19 human epithelial cancers to construct a comprehensive pan-cancer atlas of tumor microenvironment (TME) organization. We identify cell subsets selectively enriched in tumors compared with normal tissues and show that their relative abundance is associated with clinical outcomes. By clustering tumors according to their cellular composition, we define eight recurrent cellular ecosystem subtypes that capture coordinated variation in immune and stromal architectures across cancer types. Comparative analyses reveal that these ecosystem states are associated with distinct tumor-intrinsic molecular programs, including differences in signaling pathway activity, transcriptional regulation and copy number alterations. We further uncover subtype-specific patterns of ligand-receptor interactions linking malignant cells with immune and stromal compartments and provide independent spatial support for these interactions using spatial transcriptomic data. Together, this work provides a unified framework for tumor ecosystem stratification and highlights cellular organization as a key dimension of tumor heterogeneity with potential implications for precision cancer therapy.

doi:10.1186/s12943-026-02746-y.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive malignancy characterized by late diagnosis, rapid progression, and resistance to conventional therapies. Mutations in the tumor suppressor gene TP53 are prevalent in this cancer and have been associated with gain-of-function activities that promote tumor survival. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability. However, the influence of mutant p53 on ferroptosis susceptibility remains poorly understood. We employed isogenic pancreatic cancer cell models, including CRISPR-Cas9-mediated TP53 Knockout (TP53-KO) and transient overexpression of common mutant TP53 variants, to examine ferroptosis sensitivity. Cell viability, reactive oxygen species accumulation, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial integrity, and metabolic profiling were assessed following treatment with ferroptosis inducers. Transcriptional changes were analysed by RNA sequencing, and functional contributions of glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration were evaluated using metabolic flux assays. Pharmacological reactivation of wild-type p53 was tested in combination with ferroptosis inducers in vitro and in orthotopic murine models. Deletion of mutant TP53 sensitized pancreatic cancer cells to ferroptosis, accompanied by increased oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction. Mutant TP53 expression preserved mitochondrial integrity and sustained bioenergetic flexibility under ferroptotic stress. Transcriptomic analyses revealed a multi-layered adaptive program, including upregulation of antioxidant and metabolic genes, and activation of PI3K-AKT signaling, which is associated to a selective glycolytic shift to maintain ATP levels. Functional modulation confirmed that glucose supplementation enhanced, whereas glycolytic inhibition impaired, survival under ferroptotic conditions in mutant TP53-expressing cells, but not in TP53-KO cells. Pharmacological reactivation of wild-type p53 disrupted this adaptive network, abrogating glycolytic reprogramming and significantly increasing ferroptotic cell death both in vitro and in vivo. Mutant p53 orchestrates transcriptional and metabolic plasticity that confers ferroptosis resistance in pancreatic cancer. Reactivating wild-type p53 in combination with ferroptosis induction overcomes this resistance, highlighting a therapeutically actionable vulnerability and supporting the development of combinatorial strategies for this aggressive malignancy.

doi:10.1186/s12943-026-02747-x.abstract: Precision oncology in colorectal cancer (CRC) has been profoundly informed by genomic and transcriptomic profiling, yet molecular stratification remains only partially predictive of therapeutic benefit. This reflects a broader challenge: moving from static molecular information to dynamic, adaptive, and time-resolved predictions of drug response for individual patients along their clinical history. In CRC, this challenge is compounded by extensive inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity, clonal evolution, chromosomal instability, phenotypic plasticity and tumor-microenvironment (TME) interactions, all of which reshape therapeutic vulnerabilities over time.Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) have emerged as a functional platform to address this gap, with CRC providing one of the most fertile contexts for their development and application. By preserving key histopathological, molecular, and phenotypic features of parental tumors while remaining experimentally tractable, expandable, and amenable to pharmacological and genetic perturbation, PDOs add a functional layer to precision oncology in CRC. Living organoid biobanks and ex vivo screening studies have shown that PDOs can capture interpatient heterogeneity, uncover mechanisms of sensitivity and resistance, and, in selected contexts, mirror clinical responses to chemotherapy and targeted agents. The same experimental tractability has made these systems powerful tools for investigating tumor initiation and clonal evolution, while enabling exploration of cellular plasticity through the lens of dynamic cellular hierarchies. In parallel, next-generation CRC organoid systems incorporating stromal and immune components may extend functional testing to TME-dependent processes, including response to immunotherapy.In this review, we discuss the conceptual foundations of organoid technology and its emergence as a functional precision oncology platform in CRC. We examine how CRC organoids have advanced understanding of tumor initiation, evolution, chromosomal instability, and phenotypic plasticity; summarize their applications in drug discovery, therapy-response prediction, and resistance modeling; and highlight the development of next-generation multicellular organoid systems incorporating immune and stromal components. Finally, we address the major technical, biological, and clinical challenges that must be overcome to translate PDO-based approaches into robust and clinically actionable tools for precision medicine.

doi:10.1186/s12943-026-02749-9.abstract: The translation of the transcriptome into a functional proteome is not a passive readout of mRNA abundance but a primary regulatory layer that actively shapes the oncogenic landscape. In hematologic malignancies, convergent oncogenic signaling pathways, including MYC, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and tyrosine kinase fusions, directly reprogram the translational apparatus, driving a qualitative shift toward the selective synthesis of pro-survival, proliferative, and stemness-associated proteins. This deregulated program is orchestrated through multiple interconnected axes: the accelerated biogenesis of ribosomes within the nucleolus, the assembly of the eIF4F initiation complex, the activation of stress-adaptive programs like the integrated stress response (ISR), and a sophisticated layer of epitranscriptomic, tRNA, and RNA-binding protein-mediated regulation. Hematologic cancers provide a uniquely informative framework for deconstructing these processes, illustrated by inherited ribosomopathies, such as Diamond-Blackfan anemia syndrome and Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, which resolve the paradox of how ribosomal insufficiency can evolutionarily transition into malignant transformation. Beyond pathogenesis, the translational machinery represents a rich landscape of actionable vulnerabilities. Pharmacological targeting of RNA Polymerase I, eIF4A, and the ISR has demonstrated selective antitumor activity and synergistic potential with established therapies, including BCL-2 inhibition. This review synthesizes mechanistic and clinical evidence to position the ribosome as an active regulatory node rather than a passive decoding machine. We further examine the challenges facing the field, including translational plasticity under therapeutic pressure, the lack of validated companion biomarkers, and the emerging role of translational control in modulating anti-tumor immunity. Ultimately, we argue that defining the disease-specific translational states of leukemia and lymphoma is essential for the next generation of precision oncology, moving beyond genomic landscapes toward a proteomic-centered understanding of malignancy.

doi:10.1186/s12943-026-02797-1.abstract: Abstract CD58, the primary ligand of the co-stimulatory receptor CD2, plays a crucial role in the formation of the immunological synapse (IS) and the initiation of antitumor immunity involving T cells and natural killer (NK) cells. Aberrant CD58 expression, resulting from genomic inactivation, epigenetic silencing, transcriptional repression, and post-translational modifications, disrupts the architecture of the IS, impairs T and NK cell activation and effector functions, and promotes an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Consequently, restoring CD58 expression or function has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy, with approaches such as epigenetic drugs to reverse CD58 silencing, engineered T cells to restore CD2 co-stimulation, and neutralizing agents targeting soluble CD58. In this review, we summarize the current understanding of how CD58 expression is regulated across multiple dimensions and how its dysfunction drives immune evasion and therapy resistance. We also explore the therapeutic potential of targeting the CD58-CD2 axis in cancer treatment, aiming to provide novel theoretical insights and innovative strategies to advance cancer immunotherapy.

doi:10.1186/s12943-026-02808-1.abstract: The dynamic and reversible N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modification has emerged as a pivotal layer of epitranscriptomic regulation in cancer, governing RNA metabolism and function. Concurrently, deubiquitylating enzymes (DUBs), key components of the post-translational modifications (PTMs) system, orchestrate protein stability and signaling pathways crucial for tumorigenesis. Recent evidence reveals extensive and intricate crosstalk between these two regulatory systems, forming a complex network that can influence cancer progression. This review systematically explores the bidirectional interplay between DUBs and m6A modification. On one hand, specific DUBs can deubiquitinate and stabilize core m6A "writers" (methyltransferases), "erasers" (demethylases), or "readers" (recognition proteins), thereby influencing RNA metabolism and downstream gene expression. On the other hand, m6A modification can regulate the expression of certain DUBs, either by influencing the stability and translation of their mRNAs or by controlling associated regulatory factors. This reciprocal regulation profoundly impacts key oncogenic processes, including cell proliferation, metastasis, metabolic reprogramming, and therapy resistance. By integrating current findings, this review highlights the significance of the DUB-m6A axis as a critical regulatory hub in cancer biology. Deciphering this crosstalk not only provides novel insights into tumor mechanisms but also unveils promising therapeutic targets for overcoming drug resistance and developing innovative anti-cancer strategies.

doi:10.1186/s12943-026-02821-4.abstract: Abstract Objectives Copper is an essential redox cofactor required for mitochondrial respiration and antioxidant defense, yet its dysregulation creates a therapeutic vulnerability that can be exploited by copper active agents. Elesclomol and neocuproine are two potent copper active compounds, but whether they induce the same form of cuproptosis , a copper-dependent cell death mechanism, has remained unclear. We aimed to elucidate the cytotoxic programs triggered by these two agents and to determine whether distinct mechanistic forms of cuproptosis exist. Methods Our study integrates limited-proteolysis proteomics to identify compound-responsive changes in protein structural accessibility, whole-genome CRISPRa (activation) screening, transcriptomic analysis of 436 CCLE cancer cell lines, mass spectrometry-based analysis of cellular and tumor copper abundance, genetic perturbation studies, mitochondrial functional assays, and mitophagy analyses. Pathway enrichment and functional validation were used to identify adaptive survival programs and compound-specific copper-handling mechanisms. Results Building on the previously established FDX1-dependent cuproptosis mechanism induced by elesclomol, we designate this pathway as canonical cuproptosis (c-CPX) and identify neocuproine as inducing a mechanistically distinct, FDX1-independent form of cuproptosis, which we term non-canonical cuproptosis (nc-CPX). In c-CPX, FDX1 mediates elesclomol delivered Cu(II) to Cu(I) reduction, leading to rapid oligomerization of lipoylated mitochondrial proteins and subsequent proteotoxic stress. In contrast, neocuproine induces n-CPX, a FDX1-independent copper-dependent death program that preferentially engages neocuproine stabilized Cu(I)-handling and stress-adaptation networks. Despite its FDX1 independence, neocuproine rapidly induces oligomerization of lipoylated DLAT, identifying an early point of convergence with canonical cuproptosis. Large-scale analysis of CCLE cancer cell lines further revealed that sensitivity to both neocuproine and elesclomol is associated with enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) transcriptional programs. Notably, neocuproine-sensitive cancer cells additionally displayed significantly higher mesenchymal/EMT scores across multiple independent gene-expression signatures, linking an OXPHOS-enriched, mesenchymal cell state to increased susceptibility to neocuproine-induced copper-dependent cell death. Limited-proteolysis profiling identified ATOX1 among the prominent neocuproine-responsive proteins. Functional validation demonstrated that ATOX1 depletion partially attenuates neocuproine-induced cytotoxicity, but not elesclomol toxicity, while ATOX1 loss itself promotes DLAT oligomerization, supporting a specific contribution of ATOX1-dependent Cu(I) handling to nc-CPX. CRISPRa screening further revealed that adaptive programs enriched during neocuproine exposure predominantly involve proteasomal and lysosomal pathways; whereas elesclomol is associated with distinct signaling and bioenergetic programs, including PI3K, JAK–STAT, and MAPK pathways, as well as oxidative phosphorylation and glutathione metabolism. The functional relevance of the neocuproine-associated pathways was supported by enhanced cytotoxicity upon pharmacological inhibition of proteasomal or lysosomal function. Despite their divergent initiation mechanisms, both canonical and non-canonical cuproptosis converge on early oligomerization of lipoylated mitochondrial proteins followed by Fe–S-protein loss, respiratory-chain dysfunction, mitochondrial remodeling, impaired mitochondrial quality control, and respiratory failure. Both compounds also induce cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ROS and late apoptotic features. Continuous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) exposure reduced the labile intracellular Cu(I) signal and rescued cytotoxicity; whereas NAC pretreatment followed by washout did not protect against subsequent neocuproine or elesclomol exposure. Together with the lack of rescue by caspase inhibition and the delayed appearance of apoptotic features, these findings support ROS accumulation and apoptosis as predominantly downstream consequences rather than defining initiating mechanisms. Conclusion Our findings establish a mechanistic framework distinguishing canonical FDX1 dependent cuproptosis from non-canonical FDX1 independent cuproptosis. Rather than representing separate downstream death programs, c-CPX and nc-CPX constitute distinct upstream copper-handling routes that converge on a shared mitochondria-centered proteotoxic program. These results provide insight into copper-driven cytotoxicity and suggest FDX1 dependency, ATOX1-dependent copper-handling, EMT/OXPHOS state, and proteostasis pathways as candidate biomarkers and therapeutic vulnerabilities for further investigation.

doi:10.1186/s13045-026-01851-1.abstract: AXL is a membrane-accessible receptor tyrosine kinase and a potential antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) target, but its therapeutic relevance in soft-tissue sarcoma remains incompletely defined. We evaluated the AXL-directed pyrrolobenzodiazepine ADC ADCT-601/mipasetamab uzoptirine using a sarcoma tissue microarray, patient-derived cell lines, and patient-derived xenografts. AXL expression was broad but heterogeneous, with the highest histotype-level expression in myxofibrosarcoma and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma. In the patient-linked tissue-microarray cohort, AXL H-score was not associated with metastasis-free or overall survival after clinicopathologic adjustment. ADCT-601 was substantially more potent than a non-targeting anti-gp120 control ADC carrying the same SG3199-containing payload. Free-payload sensitivity varied between cell lines, indicating that intrinsic payload susceptibility contributes to activity, while the payload-matched comparison supports an additional effect of AXL-mediated delivery. ADCT-601 induced cell-cycle perturbation, apoptosis, and γ-H2AX accumulation. Combination experiments identified enhanced activity with DNA damage-response inhibition, particularly ATR inhibition, and in vivo studies supported antitumor activity in two sarcoma xenograft models. These data support biomarker-enriched development of next-generation AXL-directed ADC strategies while emphasizing antigen heterogeneity and therapeutic-index optimization.

doi:10.1186/s13045-026-01854-y.abstract: Large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) encompasses a biologically and clinically heterogeneous group of aggressive B-cell lymphomas, and outcomes remain poor in high-risk and relapsed/refractory settings. Beyond conventional anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies, the Fc-modified anti-CD19 antibody tafasitamab, the CD79b-directed antibody-drug conjugate polatuzumab vedotin, and CD20×CD3 bispecific antibodies are expanding treatment options across disease stages and patient populations. At the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting, the phase 3 frontMIND trial provided randomized evidence for tafasitamab plus lenalidomide and R-CHOP in newly diagnosed high-risk disease, while OLYMPIA-3 further explored CD20×CD3 bispecific antibody intensification in the same setting. In older or treatment-unfit patients, early-phase nonrandomized studies of epcoritamab plus R-mini-CVP and mosunetuzumab monotherapy suggested the feasibility of chemotherapy-attenuated and chemotherapy-free approaches. In relapsed/refractory LBCL, SUNMO established a progression-free survival advantage for mosunetuzumab plus polatuzumab vedotin in autologous stem-cell transplantation (ASCT)-ineligible disease, whereas EPCORE NHL-2 supported epcoritamab-based salvage therapy in transplant-eligible patients. Collectively, these findings broaden the role of antibody-based regimens from frontline intensification and reduced-intensity treatment to nontransplant and transplant-directed salvage. Longer follow-up and randomized comparisons are needed to establish response durability, refine patient selection, and define optimal treatment sequencing.

doi:10.1186/s13045-026-01855-x.abstract: Over recent years, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has markedly improved outcomes for patients with relapsed or refractory hematological malignancies. Nevertheless, a substantial proportion of patients still experience relapse or progression after treatment, driven by factors including antigen escape, suboptimal CAR-T cell expansion and persistence, functional exhaustion, and remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. In the context of managing patients who fail initial CAR-T therapy, CAR-T-centered sequential therapy has been increasingly investigated as a potential therapeutic approach. The selection of therapeutic targets and treatment approaches may be informed by resistance mechanisms, changes in target antigen expression, and disease progression patterns following prior treatment, with the aim of prolonging disease control and improving long-term outcomes. This review summarizes recent progress in CAR-T-centered sequential therapy, with particular emphasis on same-target retreatment, switching to different antigens, multi-target stepwise CAR-T regimens, and the sequential integration of CAR-T with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, radiotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and other immunomodulatory approaches. We further discuss the biological rationale and clinical settings of these CAR-T-centered sequential approaches in the context of antigen escape, CAR-T cell functional decline, tumor clonal evolution, and immune microenvironment remodeling. Additionally, we discuss factors that may inform the selection of subsequent regimens, including the initial treatment response, antigen status at relapse, CAR-T cell persistence, and the patient's therapeutic window, as well as the clinical settings in which these sequential approaches have been explored.

doi:10.1186/s13045-026-01855-x.title: CAR-T-centered sequential therapy: current status, challenges, and future clinical perspectives.

doi:10.1186/s13045-026-01856-w.abstract: Metastatic cancer remains a major clinical challenge, which is driven by the continuous adaptation of disseminated tumor cells to diverse tissue environments and therapeutic pressures. Although current treatments, including conventional therapies, small-molecule drugs, antibody-drug conjugates, and immunotherapies, have improved clinical outcomes in selected patients, they rarely achieve durable disease control, largely because each stage of the metastatic cascade presents distinct therapeutic bottlenecks. This review examines these bottlenecks and identifies therapeutic vulnerabilities that can be targeted at each metastatic stage. Cross-stage adaptive programs, encompassing genetic, epigenetic, metabolic, immune, and microenvironmental alterations, are linked to the specific modes of therapeutic failure they drive, thereby connecting underlying mechanisms with their corresponding clinical consequences. Emerging therapeutic strategies are discussed in the context of the metastatic stage, and general design principles for combination regimens are proposed. We also highlight the potential of liquid biopsy-guided dynamic treatment adjustment and advanced preclinical models to inform patient selection, treatment timing, and the design of therapies aimed at overcoming resistance. By integrating metastatic biology, mechanisms of therapeutic failure, and emerging interventions, this review provides a framework for understanding and targeting the bottlenecks that limit durable disease control in metastatic cancer.

doi:10.1186/s13045-026-01857-9.abstract: The rapidly global deployment of COVID-19 mRNA-LNP vaccines established the clinical feasibility of combining RNA medicine with LNP delivery systems, transforming a long-standing experimental concept into a scalable therapeutic modality, previously considered impossible. Currently, the value of mRNA-LNPs has been expanding from infectious disease vaccines to cancer immunotherapy, personalized neoantigen vaccination, in vivo immune-cell engineering, protein replacement therapy, mRNA-encoded biologics and genome editing, with particular relevance to hematology and oncology. However, in hematologic and oncologic settings, therapeutic success is constrained by biological barriers that less prominent in prophylactic vaccination. Systemically administered LNPs are strongly influenced by hepatic sequestration, protein corona formation and mononuclear-phagocyte clearance; solid tumors additionally present heterogeneous vasculature, variable enhanced permeability and retention, dense extracellular matrix, elevated interstitial pressure and limited intratumoral diffusion. Hematologic applications face a different set of constraints, including access to spleen and bone marrow, selective delivery to T cells, NK cells and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), and preservation of the normal marrow niche. In this Review, we therefore discuss the molecular and principles of formulation that underpin mRNA-LNP performance in hematology and oncology, including mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle architecture, intracellular trafficking and selective organ targeting(SORT) delivery strategies, oncology applications spanning neoantigen vaccines, tumor-microenvironment reprogramming, mRNA-encoded biologics, gene editing and combination therapy; and hematology applications including in vivo CAR-T, CAR-NK and HSPC engineering. We further consider how inefficient extrahepatic delivery, limited endosomal escape, context-dependent reactogenicity, repeat-dosing constraints and the manufacturing complexity of individualized products continue to limit broader clinical translation. Emerging strategies, including artificial-intelligence-guided RNA and lipid design, self-amplifying RNA, circular RNA and next-generation thermostable formulations, may help address these application limitations in the fields of hematology and oncology.

doi:10.1186/s13045-026-01858-8.abstract: Cancer progression does not occur in isolation: malignant-cell states and fates are shaped by specialized microenvironments, or cancer niches. Within primary tumors, vascular, stromal, immune and neural interactions create local hypoxic, metabolic and mechanical conditions that together influence malignant-cell behavior. These local environments sustain stem-like states, regulate immune surveillance and vascular remodeling, and influence dissemination and treatment response. Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles and other systemic signals connect primary tumors to distant organs, conditioning tissues before tumor-cell arrival and subsequently modulating disseminated tumor-cell seeding, dormancy, reactivation and outgrowth. Cancer niches therefore operate across spatial scales and disease stages, shaping tumor behavior in ways that cannot be explained by tumor-cell-intrinsic properties alone. Advances in single-cell and spatial profiling, organoid systems and intravital imaging are revealing their cellular composition, local architecture and evolution. In this review, we integrate primary, pre-metastatic and metastatic niche biology, examine how local environments evolve and influence one another during cancer progression, compare organ-specific metastatic niches and assess emerging therapeutic strategies. Effective niche-directed therapy will require identifying the interactions that sustain disease, showing that treatment disrupts them and determining which patients are most likely to benefit. Greater spatial, temporal and functional resolution may reveal new therapeutic vulnerabilities and create opportunities to prevent relapse and achieve more durable disease control.

doi:10.1186/s13045-026-01858-8.title: Niches in cancer: from primary tumors to metastatic disease.

doi:10.1186/s13045-026-01860-0.abstract: Activation of the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway is a mechanistically compelling strategy for cancer immunotherapy, but first-generation STING agonists have shown limited clinical activity despite clear pharmacodynamic induction of interferon-related signals. This translational gap suggests that therapeutic benefit depends not only on pathway engagement but also on where, in which cells, at what amplitude, and for how long STING is activated. In this review, we summarize the cellular context of cGAS-STING signaling, the pharmacological evolution and clinical experience of STING agonists, and the major barriers imposed by route, species differences, biological heterogeneity, and systemic inflammatory toxicity. We then examine how nanoengineering may improve agonist protection, cytosolic access, tissue and cell-type selectivity, and temporal exposure. Importantly, we distinguish improved delivery or tumor accumulation from direct evidence of altered signaling kinetics or a wider therapeutic window. Representative lipid, polymeric, inorganic, biogenic, biomimetic, antibody-directed, and prodrug-based platforms are evaluated together with mechanism-based combination sequencing, hematologic malignancy-specific considerations, biomarker-guided patient selection, repeated-dose safety, and manufacturability. Overall, nano-STING therapy should be developed toward immunodynamic control rather than simple delivery enhancement, with benefit judged by the relationship among delivery, cell-resolved pharmacodynamics, antitumor efficacy, and toxicity.

doi:10.1186/s13045-026-01861-z.abstract: Breast cancer develops within spatially organized, multicellular microenvironments in which particular tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) states can influence immune access and stromal remodeling. Conventional M1/M2 classification and total macrophage density fail to capture the developmental, transcriptional, metabolic, and spatial heterogeneity that determines TAM function. This macrophage-focused review examines breast cancer within its multicellular microenvironment, integrating lineage-tracing, single-cell, spatial, mechanistic, and clinical evidence while distinguishing breast-specific findings from hypotheses extrapolated from other tumors. We examine how tissue-resident and monocyte-derived macrophages are recruited, retained, expanded, and reprogrammed across primary and metastatic sites, emphasizing interactions with malignant cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, vasculature, adipose tissue, and lymphoid populations. In defined breast-tumor contexts, TAM programs have been implicated in immune exclusion, invasion, metastatic dissemination, and adaptation to systemic treatment, although evidence strength varies across mechanisms and therapeutic modalities. Small and heterogeneous clinical studies have not established a benefit from broad CSF1/CSF1R-axis targeting in breast cancer, despite encouraging preclinical findings. Accordingly, we highlight a shift toward state-selective, spatially resolved, and temporally coordinated targeting. Emerging approaches include restoring phagocytosis, disrupting chemokine and fibrotic circuits, metabolic reprogramming, and converting suppressive TAMs into inflammatory, antigen-presenting effectors. A major focus is chimeric antigen receptor macrophage (CAR-M) therapy, which combines antigen-directed phagocytosis with tumor infiltration, matrix remodeling, antigen presentation, and recruitment of endogenous immunity. Although early clinical data support manufacturing feasibility, tumor trafficking, and acceptable initial safety, limited antitumor activity underscores challenges involving antigen heterogeneity, persistence, metabolic fitness, biodistribution, and scalable production. We propose a translational roadmap integrating spatial biomarkers, quantitative target selection, macrophage-adapted CAR design, checkpoint-resistant phagocytosis, metabolic engineering, safety switches, and biomarker-guided combination therapy. This framework positions macrophage reprogramming as a context-dependent strategy for modifying selected breast-tumor niches, with therapeutic targets chosen according to the macrophage program and its surrounding cellular architecture.
